A PROCLAMATION.

GEORGE R.

WHEREAS Our Parliament stands prorogued to Thwrfday the Tenth Day of this Ini tan t October: We, with the Advice of Our Privy Council, do hereby publifl) and declare, That the said Parliament shall be further prorogued, on the said Tenth Day of this Instant October, to the Twenty-

sixth Day of November next: And We have given Order to Our Chancellor of Great Britain to prepare a Commission for proroguing the same accordingly. And We do hereby further declare Our Royal Will

and Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall, on the said Twenty-sixth Day of November next, be held for the Dispatch of divers weighty and important Affairs: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens,* and Burgesses, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of tire House of Commons, are hereby required to give Attendance accordingly, „at JVefimlnJiei', on the said Twenty-sixth Day of November next

THE House being met, pursuant to the Proclamation hereunto annexed;

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty s Commission, desire the immediate Attendance of this honourable House, in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers: Where the Commission was read, for proroguing the Parliament, until the Fifth Day

of December next: And the Parliament was accordingly prorogued until Thursday the Fifth Day of December next.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

Since the Close of the last Session, I have employed My whole Time in that Care and Attention which the important and critical Conjuncture of public Affairs required of Me.

Ilolt

4 5° Decembris. 1782.

The King’s Speech.

I loft no Time in giving the necessary Orders to prohibit the farther Prosecution of offensive War upon the Continent of North America. Adopting, as My Inclination will always lead Me to do, with Decision and Effect, whatever I collect to be the Sense of My Parliament and My People; I have pointed all My Views and Measures, as well In Europe as in North America, to an entire and cordial Reconciliation with those Colonies.

finding it indispensable to the Attainment of this Object, I did not hesitate to go the full Length of the Powers veiled in Me, and offered to declare them Free and Independent States, by an Article to be inserted in the Treaty of Peace. ProVifional Articles are agreed upon, to take Effect whenever Terms of Peace shall be finally settled with the Court of France.

In thus admitting their Separation from the Crown of these Kingdoms, I have sacrificed every Consideration of My own, to the Wilhes and Opinion of My People. I make it My humble and earnest Prayer to Almighty God, that Great Britain may not feel the Evils which might result from so great a Dismemberment of the Empire; and, that America may he free from those Calamities, which have formerly proved in the Mother Country how essential Monarchy is to the Enjoyment of Constitutional Liberty. — Religion — Language — Interest — Affections may, and 1 hope will yet prove a Bond of permanent Union between the Two Countries: To this find, neither Attention nor Disposition, on My Part, shall be wanting.

While I have carefully abftaiped from all offensive Operations in America, I have directed My whole Force by Land and Sea against the other Powers at War, with as much Vigour, as the Situation of that Force, at the Commencement of the Campaign, would permit I trull that you feel the Advantages resulting from the Safety of the great Branches of Our Trade. You mull have seen with Pride and Satisfaction the

Silant Defence of the Governor and Garrison of ibraltar; and My Fleet, after having effected the Object of their Destination, offering Battle to the combined Force of France and Spain on their own Coasts; those of My Kingdoms have remained at the same Time perfectly secure, and your domestic Tranquillity uninterrupted. This respectable State, under the Blessing of God,-1 attribute to the entire Confidence which subsists between Me and My People, and to the Readinels which has been shewn by My Subjects in My City of London, and in other Parts of My Kingdoms, to (land forth in the general Defence. Some Proofs have lately been given of public Spirit in private Men, which would do Honour to any Age, and any Country.

Having manifested to the whole World, by the most lasting Examples, the signal Spirit and Bravery of My People, I conceived it a Moment not unbecoming My Dignity, and thought it a Regard due to the Lives and Fortunes of such brave and gallant Subjects, to shew Myself ready on My Part, to embrace fair and honourable Terms of Accommodation with all the Powers at War.

I have the Satisfaction to acquaint you, that Negotiations to this Effect are considerably advanced; the Result of which, as soon as they are brought to a Con-elusion, shall be immediately communicated to you.

I have every Reason to hope and believe, that I shall have it in My Power, in a very short time, to acquaint you, that they have ended in Terms of Pacification, which, I trust, you will fee just Cause to approve. — I rely, however, with perfect Confidence, in the Wisdom of My Parliament, and the Spirit of My People, that, if any unforeseen Change in the Dispositions of the Belligerent Powers should frustrate My confident Expectations, they will approve of the Preparations I have thought it adviseable to make, and be ready to second

the most vigorous Efforts in the farther Prosecution of the War.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have endeavoured, by every Meafore in My Power, to dimioi(h the Burthens of My People. — I lpft no Time in taking the most decided Measures for introducing a better Oeconomy into the Expenditure of the Army.

I have carried into drift Execution the several Reductions in My Civil List Expences, directed by an Act of the last Session. — I have introduced a further Reform into other Departments, and suppressed several Sinecure Places in them. I have by this Means so regulated My Edablishments, that My Expence shall not in future exceed My Income.

I have ordered the Edimate of the Civil Lid Debt, laid before you last Session, to be completed. The Debt proving somewhat greater than could be then correctly dated, and the proposed Reduction not immediately taking place, I trud you will provide for the Deficiency; securing, as before, the Re-payment out of My annual Income.

I have ordered Enquiry to be made into the Application of the Sum voted in Support of the American Sufferers; and I trud that you will agree with Me, that a due and generous Attention ought to be shewn towards those, who have relinquished their Properties or Professions from Motives of Loyalty to Me, or Attachment to the Mother Country.

As it may be necessary to give Stability to some Regulations by Act of Parliament, I have ordered Accounts of the several Establishments, incidental Expences, Fees, and other Emoluments of Office, to be laid before you. Regulations have already taken place in feme, which it is my Intention to extend to all; and which, besides expediting all Business, mud produce a very considerable Saving, without taking from that ample Encouragement, which ought to be held forth to Talents, Diligence, and Integrity, wherever they are to be found.

I have directed an Enquiry to be made into w hat-ever regards the landed Revenue of My Crown, as well as the Management of My Woods and Forests, that both may be made as beneficial as possible, and that the latter may furnish a certain Refeurce for supplying the Navy, Our great National Bulwark, with its first Material.

I have directed an Investigation into the Department of the Mint, that the Purity of the Coin, of so much Importance to Commerce, may be always adhered to; that by rendering the Difficulty of counterfeiting greater, the Lives of Numbers may be saved, and every needless Expence in it suppressed.

1 must recommend to you an immediate Attention to the great Objects of the public Receipts and Expenditure; and above all, to the State of the Public Debt. — notwithstanding the great Increase of it during the War, it is to be hoped, that such Regulations may (till be established — such Savings made — and future Loans so conducted, as to promote the Means of its gradual Redemption, by a fixed Course of Payment — I must, with particular Earnestness, distinguish, for your serious Consideration, that Part of the Debt which conlifts of Navy, Ordnance, and Victualling Bills: The enormous Discount upon some of these Bills (hews this Mode of Payment to be a most ruinous Expedient

I have ordered the several Estimates, made up as correctly as the present Practice would admit, to be laid before you. I hope that such further Corrections, as may be necessary, will be made before the next Year. It is My Desire, that you should be appriled of every Expence before it is incurred, as far as the Nature of each Service can possibly admit — Matters of Account can never be made too public*

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Scarcity and consequent high Price of Corn requires your instant Interposition.

The great Excess, to which the Crimes of Theft and Robbery have arisen, in many Infiances accompanied with personal Violence, particularly in the Neighbourhood of this Metropolis, has called of late for a strict and severe Execution of the Laws. It were much to be wished that these Crimes could be prevented in their Infancy, by correcting the Vices become prevalent in a most alarming Degree.

The liberal Principles adopted by you concerning the Rights and the Commerce of Ireland, have done you the highefi Honour, and will, I trufi, increase that Harmony, which ought always to subsist between the Two Kingdoms. I am persuaded that a general Increase of Commerce throughout the Empire, will prove the Wisdom of your Measures with regard to that Object. I would recommend to you a Revision of Our whole Trading System, upon the feme comprehensive Principles, with a View to its utmost possible Extension.

The Regulation of a vast Territory in , opens a

large Field for your Wisdom, Prudence, and Forefight.

I trufi that you will be able to frame some fundamental Laws, which may make their Connection with Great Britain a Blefiing to Indiaand that you will take therein proper Measures to give all Foreign Nations, in Matters of Foreign Commerce, an entire and perfect Confidence in the Probity, Punctuality, and good Order of Our Government You may be allured, that whatever depends upon Me shall be executed with a Steadinels, which can alone preserve that Part of My Dominions, or the Commerce which arises from it.

It is the fixed Object of My Heart to make the general Good, and the true Spirit of the Confiitution, the invariable Rule of My Conduct, and on all Occasions to advance and reward Merit in every Pro- . session.

To ensure the full Advantage of a Government conducted on such Principles, depends on your Temper, your Wisdom, your Difinterestedness, collectively and individually.

My People expect these Qualifications of you; and I call for them.

Address on A Motion was made, and the Question being pros'* ^D8’s posed. That an humble Address be presented to His p*ec Majesty, to return His Majesty our sincere and hearty Thanks for His Royal Care and Attention to the important and critical State of Public Affairs since the last Session, and particularly for having been graciously pleased to direct His Meaiares to promote a cordial Reconciliation between Great Britain and America: To express our Satisfaction, that His Majesty, in the Exercise of the Powers which are vested in him, has laid the Foundation of a Peace with that Country, and has actually agreed upon Articles to be concluded whenever Terms are finally settled with the Court of France: That we most ardently wish, that Religion, Language, Interests, and Affection, may yet prove the Bond of permanent Union between the Two Countries.

To allure His Majesty, how sensible we are of the Advantages resulting from the Safety of the great Branches of our Trade, ana of the happy Success which we owe to the Spirit of His Majesty’s Governor and Garrison of Gibraltar, and to the Skill and Bravery of His Fleet: And that we reflect with peculiar Pleasure on the uninterrupted Continuance of our Domestic Tranquillity, and the signal Instances of Public Spirit which the Situation of the Country has called forth.

That we rejoice to learn, that Advances have been made towards a general Pacification, at a Moment lo suitable to His Majesty’s Dignity, and to His Gracious Vol. 39.

and Parental Regard to the Lives of His brave and gallant Subjects.

To thank His Majesty, for having promised to acquaint us as soon as the Terms are concluded; and to allure Him of our Resolution to take every Measure to second the most vigorous Efforts in the farther Prosecution of the War, if any unforeseen Change in the Dispositions of the Belligerent Powers should frustrate His Majesty’s confident Expectations of Peace.

To offer to His Majesty the warmest Return of Gratitude, for His Gracious Disposition to diminish the Burthens of His People; and to assure Him, that His faithful Commons will, as they ought, moll zealously co-operate in such Measures as may be necessary to give Stability to Regulations for that Purpose: That we will chearfully provide for the Deficiency of the Sum granted the last Year, for the Discharge of the Debt on His Majesty’s Civil List.

That we will apply ourselves, with the moll serious Attention, to the many important Points which His Majesty is pleased to recommend to our Consideration: That w-e will do every thing in our Power to remedy the Evils which may be apprehended from the great Scarcity of Corn; to put a Stop to the alarming Excels of Theft and Robbery, and the Causes from which those Crimes originate; and to lay the Foundation of a gradual Redemption of the Public Debt, by a fixed Course of Payment.

That we recollect with great Satisfaction those liberal Measures adopted with regard to the Rights and Commerce of Ireland, which will, we trust, insure the Harmony which ought always to subsist between the Two Kingdoms; and shall be ready to consider of such a general Revision of our Trading System, as may, in the present Circumstances, be wife and expedient.

That we are sensible of the Necessity of framing such Regulations as are adapted to the Situation of Affairs in The East Indies; and to assure His Majesty, that it will be our great Object, in all our Deliberations, to manifest that Temper, and those Principles, which His Majesty inculcates, and which are required of us by the Duty we owe to His Majesty, to our Constituents, and to Ourselves.

Prayers.

MR. Speaker acquainted the House, That he had Lord

received from the Right honourable Lord Rodney Rodney’s the following Letter, in return to the Thanks of this *°

House, signified to him by Mr. Speaker, in Obedience to their Commands of the 22d Day of May, in the last Session of Parliament.

Montagu, Port Royal

J21ft, 1782.

Sir,

I am now to solicit your kind Acceptance of my belt and warmest Acknowledgments, for your polite Communication of the signal Distinction which the honourable House of Commons have been graciously pleased to confer upon me, by their Vote of Thanks, for the Share I had in the Action of the 12th of April, against the French Fleet. To fulfill the Willies, and execute the Command, of my Sovereign, was my Duty; to command a Fleet so well appointed, both in Officers and Men, was my good Fortune, as, by their undaunted Spirit and Valour, under Divine Providence, the Glory of that Day was acquired. Unequal to the Talk of expressing, in Language adequate to my Feelings, the high Sense I entertain of this repeated Testimonial of their honourable Attention, I rely wholly, Sir, upon your kind Aid, to convey to the House of Commons my heartfelt Gratitude for their condescending Approbation of my Services; as also my Alfiirances that, whill't I have Health enough to act, I shall ever consider the remaining Portion of my Life devoted to the Commands of my Sovereign and of my Country.

I have the Honour to remain,

With the highest Respect,

Sir,

Your most obedient,

and most humble Servant,

Rodney.

The Right honourable C. IV. Cornwall,

Setting forth, That the Lands and Grounds situate within the said Level, and Parts adjacent, having been subject to be overflowed, several Powers and Provisions were from Time to Time made for draining and preserving the said Lands and Grounds, under the Controul, Management, and Direction of the Commissioners of Sewers for the said Level and Parts adjacent, and great Progress hath been made in draining and preserving the fame, and the said Lands and Grounds have thereby been very considerably improved; but the Powers and Provisions made as aforesaid, are not sufficient for effectually draining and preserving the said Lands and Grounds; and that the said Level and Parts adjacent might be much better drained and preserved, if the said Commissioners of Sewers were iin-powered to make a new Outfall Drain, from a certain Drain or River within the said Level, called The North River, to the River Trent, in the County of Lincoln, and also to make a Sluice or Clough in the Bank of the said River Trent;and that certain Lands and Grounds, belonging to, or held in Trust for, the Benefit of the Petitioners, within the said Level and Parts adjacent, are chargeable with the Expences of draining and preserving the Whole of the Lands and Grounds so subject to be overflowed; and the Petitioners are desirous that the said Outfall Drain and Sluice, or Clough, should be made, and the Expence thereof charged and raised upon the Lands and Grounds belonging to, or held in Trust for the Benefit of the Petitioners as aforesaid, in like Manner as the other Expences of draining and preserving the said Level and Parts adjacent, are charged and raised; and that the making of the said new Outfall Drain and Sluice, or Clough, will be of great Benefit and Advantage to the Owners and Proprietors of the Lands and Grounds liable to be overflowed as aforesaid: And therefore praying,

That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill fur making such new Outtall Drain and Sluice, or Clough, as aforesaid, with proper Banks on each Side of the said new Drain, in such Manner, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as the House shall think proper.

Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Resolved, That, in all Cases of controverted Elections for Counties in England and Wales, the Petitioners do, by themselves or by their Agents, within a convenient Time, to be appointed by the House, deliver to the Sitting Members, or their Agents, Lists of the Persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the Sitting Members; giving, in the said Lifts, the several Heads of Objection, and distinguishing the same against the Names of the Voters excepted to; and that the Sitting Members do, by themselves or by their Agents, within the same Time, deliver the like Lists, on their Part, to the Petitioners, or their Agents.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from Time to Time, take into his Custody any Stranger, or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody without the special Order of the House.

6° Decembm.

Ordered, That all Persons who will question any Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, do quel-tion the same within Fourteen Days next, and so within Fourteen Days next after any new Return shall be brought in; and that all Members who are returned for Tw o or more Places, do make their Election by this Day Three Weeks, for which of the Places they will lerve, provided there be no Question upon the Return for that Place; and if any Thing shall come in Question touching the Return or Election of any Member, he is to withdraw during the Time the Matter is in Debate; and that all Members returned upon Double Returns do withdraw till their Returns are determined.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in parliament.

hefolved. That, where this House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the ‘House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery or any other corrupt Practices, this House wil{ proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

'Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a High Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence, in any Case, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Vo i. 39.

Ordered, That the Back Door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger, or Strangers, into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take Care, that, from Eleven of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple Bar and Westminster Hall shall be kept free and open; and that no Obstructions be made, by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting to take Care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster Hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance, by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westminster; and that he do fee the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, do take Care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in the Room appointed for the Footmen attending the Members of this House to w ait in.

Committee, appointed Yesterday, to draw up an Act- King's dress to be presented to his Majesty, That the Com- Speech, mittee had drawn up art Address accordingly; which they bad directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament aft’etnbled, return Your Majesty the Thanks of this House, for Your most Gracious Sjieech from the Throne.

We beg Leave to acknowledge, with (incere and hearty Thanks, Your Majesty’s Royal Care and Attention to the important and critical State of Public

Affairs

23 Geo. III. 6° Decembris. 11

Affairs face the last Session, and particularly for having been graciously pleased to direct Your Measures to promote a cordial Reconciliation between Great Britain and America.

Permit us to express to Your Majesty our Satisfaction that Your Majesty, in the Exercise of the Powers which were veiled in Your Majesty, has laid the Foundation of a Peace with that Country, and has actually agreed upon Articles to be concluded whenever Terms are finally settled with the Court of France. We most ardently wish, that Religion, Language, Interests, and Affection, may yet prove the Bond ot permanent Union between the Two Countries.

We are impressed with a due Sense of the Advantages resulting from the Safety of the great Branches of our Trade, and of the happy Succefe which we owe to the Spirit of Your Majesty’s Governor and Garrison of Gibraltar, and to the Skill and Bravery of Your Majesty’s Fleet: And we reflect with peculiar Pleasure on the uninterrupted Continuance of our Do-meftic Tranquillity, and the signal Instances of Public Spirit which the Situation of the Country has called forth.

We rejoice to learn that Advances have been made towards a general Pacification, at a Moment so suitable to Your Majesty’s Dignity, and to Your Gracious and Parental Regard to the Lives of Your Majesty’s brave and gallant Subjects.

We desire to thank Your Majesty for having promised to acquaint us, as soon as the Terms are concluded; and to allure Your Majesty of our Resolution to take every Measure to second the most vigorous Efforts in the further Prosecution of the War, if any unforeseen Change in the Dispositions of the Belligerent Powers should frustrate Your Majesty’s confident Expectations of Peace.

We are anxious to offer the warmest Return of Gratitude to Your Majesty, for Your Gracious Disposition to diminish the Burthens of Your People; and to assure Your Majesty, that Your faithful Commons will, as they ought, most zealously co-operate in such Measures as may be necessary to give Stability to Regulations for that Purpose. We will chearfully provide for the Deficiency of the Sum granted last Year for the Discharge of the Debt on Your Majesty’s Civil List.

We will apply ourselves, with the most lerious Attention, to the many important Points which Your Majesty is pleased to recommend to our Consideration: We will do every Thing in our Power to remedy the Evils which may be apprehended from the general Scarcity of Corn; to put a Stop to the alarming Excess of Tnest and Robbery, and the Causes from which those Crimes originate; and to lay the Foundation of a gradual Redemption of the Public Debt, by a fixed Course of Payment.

We recoiled, with great Satisfaction, those liberal Measures adopted with regard to the Rights and Commerce of Ireland, which will, we trust, insure the Harmony which ought always to subsist between the Two Kingdoms. And we shall be ready to consider of such a general Revision of our Trading System, as may, in the present Circumstances, be wife and expedient

We are truly sensible of the Necessity of framing such Regulations as are adapted to the Situation of Affairs in The East Indies. And we beg Leave to assure Your Majesty,. that it will be our great Object, in all our Deliberations, to manifest that Temper, and those Principles, which Your Majesty is pleased to inculcate, and which are required of us by the Duty we owe to Your Majesty, to our Conftltuents, and to Ourselves.

apprehend it to be an unjustifiable Attempt to injure a Company who have, with much Hazard to their Property, obtained great Advantages to the Neighbourhood of Birmingham: And therefore praying, that the Bill for extending the Old Canal may pals into a Law, and that the Bill for making the fad New Canal may be rejected.

Answer to Mr. Speaker reported to the House, That the House Addrefc. attended His Majesty on Saturday last with their Address;

to which His Majesty was pleased to give this most Gracious Answer:

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you Thanks for this loyal and dutiful Address.

1 am happy to receive your Assurances of Satisfaction, on being acquainted that Articles have been agreed upon with America, to take Effect whenever Terms of Peace shall be finally settled with the Court of France; and that, while you rejoice to learn that Advances have been made towards a general Pacification, you are, at the same Time, resolved to second the most vigorous Efforts in the farther Prosecution of the War, if any unforeseen Change in the Disposition of the Belligerent Powers should frustrate My confident Expectations of Peace.

Bilston Navi- Sir Robert Lawtey reported from the Committee, to gation. whom the Petition of the several Gentlemen, Land-owners, Tradesmen, Manufacturers, and others, of the Town of Birmingham, and the Counties of Warwick and Stafford, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Navigation Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; ris.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Robert Whitworth, an Engineer, was called in; and being shewn the Plan of the intended Navigation, said. That he had surveyed the Lands through which the Canal and Collateral Cuts are intended to be made; and that he made the Plan now before the Committee, by which it appears, that a Canal, with proper Collateral Cuts, for the Navigation of Boats, Barges and other Vessels, may be conveniently made from certain Mines of Coal and Ironstone, in the Liberty of Bilston, in the Parish of Wolverhampton, and in the several; Parishes of Sedgley, Tipton, otherwise

nesbury, and Westbromxvich, in the County of Stafford, through the said Liberty and Parishes, and allb through the Parish of Handsworth, in the same County, to or near a Piece of Land called The Barn Close, in the Parish of Aston Juxta Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, belonging to Heneage Legg, Esquire, and now or late in the Occupation of the Widow Lloyd, and from thence through or near the several Parishes of Sutton Coldfield, Curdworth, Lea Marston, Kingsbury, and Middleton, in the County of Warwick, and Drayton Bajjett, in the County of Stafford, to join and communicate with the Covertly Canal (intended to be compleated from Atherstone, in the said County of Warwick, to join the Canal from the River Trent to the River JMerfey) at or near Fazeleyin the Parish of Tamworth,

in the said County of Stafford, and from or near the said Piece of Land called The Bam Close, to or near to the said Town of Birmingham.

And being further examined, he said, That the making such Canal and Collateral Cuts may be a Means of opening a Communication between the said Mines and the Oxford and Cooentry Canals, and the River Trent, and will also be the Means of opening a considerable Intercourse between Birmingham and other manufacturing Towns in the Neighbourhood thereof, and the Ports of Liverpool and Hull, which will be of great Benefit and Advantage to Trade. — The Witness being asked. Whether he can speak decidedly as to a constant Supply, of Water? he said, Yes. — And being further asked, Whether the Water taken for the Supply of the new Canal will not be the Means of depriving several Mills of their Water ? he said, the principal Supply of Water for this Canal will be from Fire Engines, which are now erected, and will be erected, if the Canal takes place. — And being then asked, Where the Water runs into, that is now raised by the present Fire Engines? he said, It runs down the Common Watercourse at the Foot of Wednesbury, into the River Tame.

Mr. Isaiah Danksbeing examined, said, That the making the said intended Canal and Collateral Cuts will be the Means of opening a considerable Intercourse between Birmingham and other manufacturing Towns in the Neighbourhood thereof, and the Ports of Liverpool and Hull, which will be of great Benefit and Advantage to Trade.

And being further examined, he said, It will reduce the Price of Coals — That they can be delivered at Braunslon, in Northamptonshire, at 15 w \d. per Ton, at Banbury at 2 os. 1 \ d. per Ton, and at Ox-' ford at 24 s.d. per Ton, including Lock Dues and Carriage.

Mr. William Kendrick being examined, laid, That he knows the Situation of the Coal Mines, and thinks they will be sufficient for the Supply of the Counties of Northampton, Warwick, Oxford, and Bucks, at a cheap and easy Rate. — And being asked, Whether Wednesbury Coal and Cooentry Coal are of equal Quality and Price? he laid, They are not; that he was told at Banbury, that the Wednesbury Coal was Two Pence per Hundred Weight more than the Coventry Coal — That he cannot tell what Difference there is in the Price between Canal and Land Carriage of the above Coal — That the Price of Wednesbury Coal at Banbury is now Eighteen Pence per Hundred Weight; and if the Canal is made, it will be Five Pence Halfpenny per Hundred Weight cheaper.

Mr. William Careless being examined, said, That the present Price of Wednesbury Coals, at Oxford, is 20 d. per Hundred Weight, or 1 /. 135. 4 per Ton; and at Braunston Wednesbury Coal is 1 Ad. per Hundred Weight,

11. 3s. Ad- per Ton — That the Price of Coventry Coal, at Braunston, is gd. per Hundred Weight, or 15 s.per Ton — That if the Canal is made, the Price at Braunston will be 15 s. 11 per Ton, which will be a Reduction of 7 s.Aid. per Ton — And the Witness added, That as the County of Bucks is supplied from the Banbury Wharf, they will of course be supplied proportionably cheaper.

Sir. r. Cur- 'll TR. Speaker acquainted the House, That he had , IS *-An[wer 1Y1 received, from Sir Roger Curtis, the following to ’ Letter, in Return to the Thanks of this House, signified to him by Mr. Speaker, in Obedience to their Commands of Thursday last:

December 14th, 1782.

Sir,

I have this Morning been favoured with your Letter of the 12th Iostant, accompanying a Resolution of the House of Commons, passed the same Day, whereby their Thanks were given to certain Officers (amongst whom I have the Honour to be named) and to the other Officers, the Soldiers, and Sailors, lately employed in the Defence of Gibraltar.

I am not capable. Sir, to express how very sensibly I am affected by the high Honour that has been thus conferred on me. I hope, therefore, the House will believe I feel as much as any Man can, how honourable it is to obtain the Approbation of the House of Commons. The Officers and Men who served in my Department at Gibraltar will, I am sure, join with me in thel'e Sentiments, as theydid most heartily in their best Endeavours towards the Defence of that Fortress.

I have the Honour to be,

With the greatest RespeCfc,

Sir,

Your most obedient,

and most humble Servant,

Roger Curtis.

The Right honourable the Speaker, <Sfc. <Spc. Sf

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Bilston Navi-Coventry Canal Navigation, was presented to the House, gation. and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, Application hath been made to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill for making a Navigable Canal from certain Coal Mines, in the Liberty of Bilston, in the Parish of Wolverhampton, and in the Parishes of Sedgley, Tipton otherwise Tibbington, Wednesbury, and Westbromwich, in the County of Stafford, to or near the Town of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, and from thence to join the Coventry Canal at or near Fazeley, in the Parish of Tamworth, in the said Counties of Warwick and Stafford; and that the Petitioners conceive the making such Navigable Canal will be a Means of enabling the Petitioners and the Proprietors of the Oxford Canal to finish and complete their Canals, and thereby open a certain Communication by Water between the said Mines and the Oxford and Coventry Canals, to the great Advantage of the Public in general, and of the Petitioners in particular: And therefore praying,

That the said Bill may pass into a Law, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as the House shall think proper.

A Petition of the several Gentlemen, Merchants, Ditto. Tradesmen, Manufacturers, and principal Inhabitants, of the Liberty of Bilston, in the Parish of and the several Parishes of Wednesbury, Wt Darlaston, and Tipton otherwise Tibbington, in the County of Stafford, was also presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Application mentioned in the preceding Petition; and setting forth,

That the Petitioners conceive the Completion of the said intended Canal will enable the Proprietors of the Oxford and Coventry Canals to ftnish their Undertakings, by Means whereof the Owners of the Mines will be induced to open the fame, and enabled to supply several remote Parts of the Counties of Warwick, Northampton, and Oxford with Coals at an easy Rate; and that, by Means of the said Canal, a navigable Communication may be effected between the Ports of London and Hull, and the said Liberty and Parishes; and heavy manufactured Goods, as well as Iron, and various Raw Materials, will have a safe, cheap, and expeditious Conveyance between the said Ports, and the said Liberty and Parishes; and that the opening the said Coal Mines, and the establishing the said navigable Communication, is of the utmost Consequence to the Commercial Interests of the said Liberty and Parishes, and will tend to furnish full Employment to great Numbers of industrious Poor: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may pals into a Law, in

A Petition of Peter Perring, late of Fort Saint George, Madras, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner went to

Madras, as a Writer in the Service of the East India Company, in 1758, and from that Time continued in India, in the Service of the Company, in different Stations, for Twenty-two Years, viz. until 1780, without ever having been in England, and without having had his Conduct cenlured or complained of, either by his Superiors or Inferiors: and that the Petitioner, on the 8th of October 1777, took his Seat as one of the Council of Fort Saint George, and so continued till April 1780, when the Petitioner, with the Permission of the Governor and Council, left Madras, and came to England for the Benefit of his Health; and that, in October 1777, when the Petitioner took his Seat as one of the Council of Fort George, John

Whitehill, Esquire, was Governor, and so continued till February 1778, when Sir Thomas Rumbold arrived, and Vo I. 39.

wftio held the Government during the Remainder of the Petitioners Stay at Fort Saint George; and that during the Time the Petitioner held the Office of One of the Council of Fort Saint George, the Government confided of a Governor and Council, and a Select Committee; and that the Governor and Council consisted of Sir Thomas Rumbold, John Whitehill, Esquire, Sir Hector Munro, Charles Smith, Esquire, Samuel Johnson, Esquire, and the Petitioner, and they managed Matters of Revenue and Trade only; and that the Select Committee consisted of Sir Thomas Rumbold, Mr. Whitehill, Sir Hector Monro, and- Mr. Smith; and to this Committee alone all Matters, Military and Political, were committed, and the Petitioner never was a Member of the Select Committee; and that the Conduct and Measures of the Select Committee, particularly those which are charged to have brought on the Invasion of the Carnatic by Hyder Ally, and the consequent public Calamities, led to and produced the present Complaints and Invef-tigation by Parliament; and accordingly, the Charges in the Bill for inffifting Pains and Penalties on Sir Thomas Rumbold and the Petitioner are formed to censure those Measures; and it seems obvious to the Petitioner, that if the Select Committee never furniftved Matter for those Charges, or if those Charges were expunged, there would not remain any Subject for a Bill of Pains and Penalties; the Measures of the Select Committee were of a public and political Nature, and are supposed to have led to great public Calamities; the other Matters in the Bill are few in Number, and of a civil and private Nature, and are such as, when taken unconnected with the other Charges, by no Means call for the Interposition of Parliament; and that, although the Petitioner never was a Member of the Select Committee, yet he has great Reason to apprehend, that a Want- of Attention to this Fast has been the principal, if not the foie, Cause of his being introduced into the Bill of Pains and Penalties; for that the Secret Committee of the House, in their Resolutions, which were afterwards adopted by the House, named and considered the Petitioner as one of that Board; and the Petitioner is still treated and called in the said Bill, and also in the Restraining Bill, a Member of the Select Committee; and that this well-known Fast so distinguishes the same of the Petitioner from that of Sir Thomas Rumbold, that, upon its now being pointed out, the Petitioner still hopes the House will be of Opinion that his Name ought to be expunged from the Bill of Pains and Penalties, as none of the Charges which affect him, in his Capacity of a Member of the Council, are of a Nature to call for such a Proceeding, at least not against him; and that the Petitioner conceives, the only Charges in the Bill of Pains and Penalties, which by Implication may be extended to affect the Petitioner, are, that he concurred with the Governor and the other Members of the Council, in Resolutions for effecting the following Measures; viz.

lft. Letting the Chicacole Demesne Lands to Sitteram Rauze, for Ten Years.

2d. Staying the Committee of Circuit, and, in its stead, convening the Zemindars at Madras.

3d. Enforcing a Reconciliation between the Brothers Viziaram and Sitteram Rauze, and appointing Sitteram as Duan, or Manager, of the Affairs of Viziaram, and other Regulations in the Affairs of that Family.

4th. Lastly, Leafing the Jaghire Lands to the Nabob of Arcot for Three Years.

That these Resolutions are charged to be in Breach of the Spirit of the Company's Orders; but it is not even suggested that they, in the most distant Degree, led to the War in the Carnatic; and that, in thele Measures, the Petitioner is not charged with any active Part, nor is it insinuated by the Prosecutors, that he had any corrupt Motive for assenting to the

Resolutions

Rumbold and Perring not to quit the Kingdom.

Bilston Navi- A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the taboo. Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the Petitioners were impowered to make a Navigable Canal from the River Severn, between Bewdley and Titton Brook, in the County of Worcester, to communicate with a Canal -then intended to be, and Vol. 39.

since made, between the River Trent and the River Mersey, at or near Haywood Mill, in the County of Stafford', and that, in the Tenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, another Act was passed, to explain and amend the said first-mentioned Act, and particularly to authorize the Petitioners to raise such further Sums of Money, for compleating the said Navigation, as are therein mentioned, the Money which the Petitioners were authorized to raile for making and compleating the said Canal, by virtue of the mid first-mentioned AQ, being found insufficient for that Purpose; and that the said Navigation hath been since compleated, at the Expence of 150,000l. and upwards; and that the principal Inducement to the Petitioners to undertake the making of the said Navigation, was the Advantage expected to arise from Coals to be raised at the Mines in the Neighbourhood of Bils Wednesbury, and Tipton, in the said County of , and navigated on the said Canal in general, and more particu- . larly along the same down to the River Severn, for the Supply of the Counties of Worcester, Gloucester, Hereford, and Part of the Counties of Wanoick and Somerset', and that there are Yearly navigated upon the said Canal to the River Severn, for the Supply of the Parts above-mentioned, very large Quantities of Coals raised at the Mines afore-mentioned, which yield to the said Company the greater Part of the Tonnage received by them; and that the Petitioners apprehend the Venders of Coals at the Severn Market, raised at the said Mines in the Neighbourhood of Bilston, Wednesbury, Sedgley, and Tipton, do now render the same at that Market at as cheap a Rate as is possible for them to do, and consequently that any Scheme tending to advance the Price of the said Coals must be destructive of the Severn Trade therein; and that the Petitioners observe by the Votes, that a Petition hath been presented for Leave to bring in a Bill, for making and maintaining a Navigable Cut or Canal from the Coal Mines in the Liberty of Bilston, in the Parish of Wolverhampton, and in the Parishes of Sedgley, Tipton otherwise ton, Wednesbury, and Westbromwich, in the said County of Stafford, to or near Birmingham, and- from the Neighbourhood of Birmingham, to communicate with the Coventry Canal Navigation (intended to be compleated between Atherstone and the Canal from the Trent to the Mersey) at or near Fazeley, in the Parish of Drayton Basset, in the said County of Stafford', and that the Petitioners are under the greatest Apprehensions, that, if the said intended Canal shall take place, large Quantities of Coals, to be raised at the Mines aforementioned, w'ill be carried along such intended Canal into remote Parts of the County of Warwick, and also into the County of Oxford, and other distant Parts, by Means whereof the Demand for Coals will be lo much increased, that the Price thereof at the Mines will be advanced, lo that those Persons who are now employed in, and supported by, the Trade in Coals from the Mines before-mentioned to the River Severn, will be obliged to decline the fame; and the Petitioners will also be thereby deprived of the principal Benefit arising upon the Space of Twenty-five Miles and upwards of their said Canal, which is more than One Half of the Extent thereof, and the Public will likewise be greatly injured thereby; and that the Petitioners are also under Apprehensions, that, in case the said intended Canal shall take place, and the said Coventry Canal shall be compleated between Atherstone and the Canal from the Trent to the Mersey, the Petitioners will be thereby entirely deprived of the Tonnage on Merchandize passing between the Navigable River Trenf and the Town of Birmingham, and which is now carried along Twenty Miles or upwards, other Phrt of their said Canal, (to wit) from the Junction thereof with the said Canal from the Trent to the Mersey, at Hey-wood Mill, to Autherley, in the Parish of Tettenhall, in the

A Petition of the Proprietors of the Brine Pits and Salt Works, and other the Inhabitants of the Borough of Droitwich, in the County, of Worcester,

was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners perceive, by the Votes, that Application hath been made, for Leave to brino in a Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Cut, or Canal, from that Part of one of the Collateral Cuts now belonging to the Birmingham Canal Navigation, leading to Wednesbury Holloway, which leads

from Riders Green, in the Parish of , in

the County of Stafford, by or near Great Bridge, and from thence through the Lands of Elizabeth Dudley, Widow, George Birch, Esquire, the Reverend Mr. Best, Thomas Hoo, Esquire, the Right honourable Lord Viscount Dudley and Ward, and terminating near Broadwater Fire Enginein the Parish of Wednesbury, in the said County of Stafford, together with Five fuiall Collateral Branches leading to different Coal Mines, in the Parishes of Tipton,

Sedgeley, Wolverhampton, and Wednesbury, in the said County of Stafford; and that the Petitioners conceive, if such Extension were made, it would increase the Quantity of Coals on the present Birmingham Canal Navigation, without opening any new Markets for the lame, by which the Petitioners, and the adjacent Country, may derive great Advantages, as it may tend to prevent any further Advance on the Price of Coals from those as well as all other Mines that now supply them, which, from the present great Consumption, there is every reason to fear would be attended with many very injurious Consequences to the Salt Works in the said Borough, which are productive of so large a Revenue to this Kingdom: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may pass into a Law, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie. upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Birmingham Canal Navigation is referred.

Ordered, That the Chaplain to this House do preach before this House, at Saint Margaret's, Westminster, upon Tomorrow Sevennight, the 30th Day of this Instant January.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed, to enquire what Laws are expired, or near expiring, and to report their Opinion, from Time to Time, to the House, which of them are fit to be revived, or continued.

And a Committee was appointed of Mr. Ord, Mr. Elwes, &c. :And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber.

A Petition of the Nobility, Gentry, Clergy, Freeholders, and others, the Inhabitants of the County of Sussex, was presented to the House, and read; Vol. 39.

Setting forth, That the Petitioners, thdrotighly fenfi-ble of the Excellence of the Constitution, and of that elsential Branch of it, the Representation of the Commons in Parliament, cannot but lament the present State of the same so partially elected, and having frequently a separate Interest from the People, are unequal to express the general Sense of the said Commons; and that the Petitioners consider the same as a Grievance materially affecting the Petitioners, and the whole Kingdom: And therefore praying the House, to take the same into their speedy Consideration, and to afford such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Samuel Petrie, was presented to the Cricklad# House, and read; Setting forth, That, on the 18th Eleaion; Day of December last, the Petitioner presented a Petition to the House, complaining of the undue Election and Return of the Honourable George Richard St. John, at the last Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Qricklade, in the County of Wilts, alleging, that the Petitioner conceives himself duly elected at the said Election to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, and ought to have been returned, as also, that the Petitioner was informed, that at the Time of the said Election the said George Richard St. John was a Minor, being under the Age of Twenty-one Years; which Petition the House has ordered to be taken into Consideration on Tuesday, the 4th of next Month; and that the Petitioner, in January 1781, commenced Actions against Paul Benfeld, Esquire, a Member of the House, and John M'Pherson, Esquire, who at that Time had likewise a Seat in the House by an undue Return, for Bribery and Corruption practised by them at the Election, in September 1780, of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Cricklade, but which Actions the Petitioner has been prevented from bringing to Issue by the Abuse of the Privilege of Parliament, exercised by the said Paul Benfeld _and John M'Pherson;and that afterwards the said Paul Benfeld and John M commenced Actions against the Petitioner upon an unjust Charge of Bribery and Corruption, and, by the perjured Evidence of the Witnesses who were examined upon the Trials of the said Actions, obtained Verdicts against the Petitioner; and that against Two of those Witnesses, without whose Evidence no Verdict would have been given against the Petitioner, Bills of In-didment for wilful and corrupt Perjury in their Evidence in the said Causes were found by the Grand Jury at Marlborough, so long ago as tine Michaelmas Quarter Sessions 1781, but, by the Management of the Solicitors of the said Paul Benfeld and John , M(Pherson, the Petitioner has been hitherto prevented from bringing them to Trial; and that on Thursday, the 9th of this present Month of January, by virtue of Writs from Robert Taylor and Benjamin,

Esquires, Sheriffs of the County of Middlesex, dated the 28th of November last, directed to Richard Hayes,

John Doe, and Richard Roe, and sued out by Melfrs.

Wallis and Troward, Solicitors to the said Paul Bcn-feld and John McPherson, the Petitioner was taken in Execution upon the Judgments obtained on the said Verdicts, by the said Richard Hawes, and carried by him to the House of David Simpson, a Sheriff’s Officer, in Brook Street, Holborn, where he has ever since been, and where he uow is; and that the Petitioner, conceiving the Privileges of the House to be violated in the Person of the Petitioner, therefore prays the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant to the Petitioner such Relief as to them shall seem meet.

and that, at the time of passing the Act, the Petitioner was not in this Kingdom, having left it in November 1781, when no Proceedings had been commenced against him, either in the Courts of Law or Equity, nor had he any Intimation of any Charge preferred, or any Refelution passed or agitated in either House of Parliament, affecting his Conduct in India; and that the Petitioner foleninly declares, that the Cause of his leaving the Kingdom was not from any Apprc-hensions of the Consequences of an Enquiry into his Conduct, nor with the remotest Design of withdrawing himself, or his Property, from the Justice of Parliament; and that the Petitioner begs Leave to Iblicit the Attention of the House to his present Situation, in respect to the Charges that have been exhibited against him of Misconduct in India; that he is in the State of one accused only, but not convicted, and that he has not hitherto been heard in his Defence; and that the Petitioner admits, that, by the before-mentioned Act, a limited Period was allowed him to return into this Kingdom, and to controvert those Charges, under the Conditions in the Act mentioned, and the Petitioner is folly sensible of the Weaknels and Impropriety of his Conduct in not having so done; but the Petitioner, throwing himself upon the Mercy and Compassion of the House, hopes he shall be deemed not altogether unworthy of their Forgive-ness for this Default, when they shall be pleased to consider, in Addition to the infirm Condition of his Health, the utter Inability the Petitioner was under, from the State of his Affairs, of complying with the Requisitions of the Act, in respect to the Sureties thereby required, and the Apprehensions he was under from his private Creditors, to whom he was largely indebted, and whom, from the Bulk of his Property being the n, as it still is, in India, he was utterly unable to fetisfy, or even to procure Bail to any Actions that might be brought against him; and that the Petitioner, notwithstanding the Weight of these Difficulties still pressing u|>on him, has returned into this Kingdom, for the Purpose of submitting himself to the Justice of Parliament, and of laying open his Fortune and his Conduct to the fullest Inveitigation which the House may think proper to institute; and the Petitioner doubts not that, if by the Indulgence of the House he shall be permitted to be let into his Defence against the Charges of Misconduct in India, he shall be able fully to vindicate himself; and that the Petitioner begs Leave to represent, that very little Delay has been hitherto occasioned by his Absence, in the Prosecution against him; and the Petitioner solemnly declares, that he has not, in the mean Time,

The said Report is as followeth; viz.

Vo 1.. 39.

To the Honourable the Knights, Citizens, and BurgefleS#-in Parliament assembled.

The Eighth Report of the Commissioners appointed to examine, take, and state, the Public Accounts of the Kingdom.

In all the Acts by which we have been constituted, one of the express Purposes of our Appointment, and# in the last Act, the only one particularly mentioned, is " to examine, and state, in what Manner, and at what " Times, the Receipts, Blues, and Expenditures of the Public Monies are now accounted for; and to con-1 " fider and report, by what Means and Methods the " Public Accounts may in future be passed, and the Accountants compelled to pay the Balances due from " them, in a more expeditious, more effectual, and less " expensive Manner."

In our Examination into the Pay Offices of the Navy And Army, we found the Accounts very far in Arrear; Seventy-five Millions, the Blues of upwards of Twenty-four Years, to October 1780, for the Navy Services#

Forty-(even Millions, the I flues of Sixteen Years, to the same Period (exclusive of the unsettled Account of Lord Holland) for the Army Services, were unaccounted for.

So striking a Circumstance would have led us, of Course, to that Office, where the Public Accounts of the Kingdom are audited, that we might endeavour to discover the Causes of this Delay; whether it arises from any Want of Power to compel Persons to come to Account, or from any Neglect in the Exercise of that Power; whether from any Defect in the Constitution, or in the Execution of the Office that audits the Accounts; or whether it is occasioned by any Obstructions thrown in the Way by the accountable Persons themselves.

We inquired, in the first Place, whether there exists any compulsive Power to bring in Public Accountants, and what Steps are taken previous to their accounting. ^0Deix*4 Upon these Points, Mr. John Hughfon, Clerk of the N. Debentures, in the Office of the Auditor of the Exche- N, quer; Adam Martin, Esquire, First Clerk in the Office of the King’s Remembrancer in the Exchequer; and n* 3.

Mr. Alexander Bennet, one of the sworn Clerks in the same Office, gave us the following Information.

The Power of compelling Public Accountants to come to Account, is lodged in the Court of Exchequer:

It is exercised by either an Ordinary or an Extraordinary Process. The Ordinary Process, is a Writ of Distringas ad Computandum, issued by the King’s Remembrancer, periodically, and of Course, after every ifiuable Term.

The Extraordinary Process, is a Writ of Capias ad Computandum, which issues by special Order of the Court of Exchequer, where the Sum to be accounted for is in Danger, and upon particular Application made to them for that Purpose.

The Proceedings upon the Ordinary Process are in the following Manner:

All Money issued from the Exchequer by the Auditor of the Receipt, is issued either upon Account, or without Account: It does not depend upon his Discretion, which of these Forms he shall make use of; he is governed by the Authority that directs the Blue; that is, either by an Act of Parliament, or by the King’s Warrant under the Great or Privy Seal; and by no other Authority than these can Money be issued out of the Exchequer.

Twice in every Year, after each of the issuable Terms, the Auditor of the Receipt makes out a Roll, called. The General Imprest Roll, which contains all the Sums issued from the Exchequer upon Account, during the preceding Half Year, with the Names of the Persons to whom, and for what Services, issued.

4 $ 33° Janmrii. . A. 1783.

Eighth Report on Public Accounts.

8th and 9th William I lid. hap. 28th.

V4.

N* 5.

This Roll is recorded by the Clerk of the Pells, and transmitted to the Office of the King’s Remembrancer; a Mode of Proceeding directed by the Act for the better Observation of the Course anciently used in the Receipt of the Exchequer.

About the same Time that this Imprest Roll comes to the King’s Remembrancer, the Auditors of the Imprest make out and send to him a Certificate of the Accounts depending in their Office: By these Means the King's Remembrancer has every Half Year full Information to regulate his Proceedings; the General Imprest Roll tells him what Persons are become accountable, and for what Sums; and the Imprest Certificate (hews him which of those Persons are proceeding to pass their Accounts, and how far any of them have proceeded in passing the m. This Officer exercises a discretionary Power, both as to the Persons against whom, and the Time w hen, he shall issue the Distringas: He pays little Attention to the General Imprest Roll, for Two Rea-fons; First, because many of the Sums mentioned therein to have been issued on Account, are nevertheless in their Nature not subject, nor intended to be accounted for; as Salaries, and Payments for small Services performed. And, Secondly, because those Sums which are intended to be accounted for, having been issued so recently as within the last Half Year only, may not have been applied to the Purposes for which they were intended, or, if they have, the Accountants can hardly be supposed to be ready with, and to have prepared their Accounts for Examination so loon after the Application.

The Imprest Certificate is the Instrument by which the King’s Remembrancer, in Conlultation with the Deputy Auditor of the Imprest, is governed as to the Persons against whom he shall issue this Process. "Where the Accounts therein stated appear to be of very ancient Date* or depending and in a Train of Prosecution, such Accountants are not put in Process; if the Accounts are of late Date, and the Accountants, having had a reasonable Time for Preparation, have taken no Steps for the Prosecution, against these the Distringas ifl’ues.

All Accountants, unless the Place of their Abode is specified, are supposed to relide, and most of the great Accountants do in Fast reside, within the Jurisdiction of the Sheriffs of London and Middlesex: To them, therefore, the Distringas against these Accountants issues. We required from the King’s Remembrancer ‘.ie Wri of Distringas that issued to those Sheriffs after the last Hilary Term, with the Return and Schedules annexed, for our Inspection; a Copy of the Writ and Return is inserted in the Appendix.

The Schedules annexed to this Writ are very numerous; many of them contain large Sums. They are of various Dates; and some very ancient, as far back as the Year 1698. Each contains the Name of the Accountant, and, frequently, the Sum for which he is to account, and the Service for which it was illiied. The Return of the Sheriffs to the Writ before 11s is, as to all the Accountants in the several Schedules thereto annexed, indiscriminately, that none of them had any Lands or Chattels in his Bailiwick by which he could distrain them; nor were they found in the same; that is, in the Language of Office, a Return, or Nulla bona, and Non inventus.

From the Information of Mr. John , the

principal Clerk in the Office of the Sheriff of Middlesex, we learn the Practice of the Office relative to this Writ. It is ufued not to execute it; it is a Process of Courier; and the Return indorsed upon the Writ l>e-fore us, is the constant regular Return upon every one of these periodical Writs of Distringas ad Compu-tandum.

The King’s Remembrancer, after it is returned to his Office, takes olf from the Bundle of Schedules the

4

returned Writ, together with those Schedules in which the Purpose of the Distringas has been satisfied, and files them with the Writ: The Remainder of the Schedules, with the Addition of the Names and Schedules taken from the last Imprest Certificate, are annexed to the renewed Writ, and are issued again to the Sheriff. Upon his Apposal in the Court of Exchequer, the new Schedules are read to him, and he is questioned upon his Oath relative to the Execution of this Writ: His Answer is usually agreeable to his Return. Sometimes the Baron of the Exchequer before whom he is apposed, where the particular same strikes him, directs the Sheriff to return Issues to a certain Amount: In that Cafe, the Sheriff alters his Return, and indorlbs upon the Writ the Issue3 di-rested, which are transmitted to the Pipe Office, to be levied by Process from thence; but of this Proceeding the Instances are rare, and the Officer of the Sheriff of Middlesex recollects but one Instance in Thirty-three Years, where Issues were drawn down to the Pipe, and levied.

Having thus examined into the Means of compelling Public Accountants to come to an Account, we proceeded, in the next Place, to the Office where these Accounts are audited; that is, to the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest. Of the Constitution, Authority, and Execution of this Office, we received Information from John Bray, Esquire, late Deputy jjo 6 Auditor, and from Charles Harris, Esquire, one of the N. _ present Deputy Auditors in the Office of Lord Mount-stuart.

This Office is instituted for the sole Purpose of auditing and examining the Public Accounts: It is executed by Two Auditors, independent of each other; each having a separate and distinct Office, his own Deputies, Officers, and Clerks. He is appointed by Letters Patent Upon Inspefition of those by which Lord Sondes and Lord Mountstuart now enjoy this Office, it appears that he is appointed Auditor of the Preft or Imprest, and foreign Accounts, to execute the Office by himself, dr his Deputy or Deputies, during his good Behaviour. The Power therein delegated to him is, to audit and determine, with the Advice, Authority, and Consent of the Commissioners of the Treasury and Chancellor of the Exchequer, the Accounts and Views of Accounts of several Officers and Duties therein particularly specified, and, in general, of all Persons being accountable for any Sums of Money received by the Name of Imprest from the King, or any other Person in his Name, and to be applied about the Affairs of the King: It is confined to the Examination of the Accounts; he has no Power to bring the Accountants before him; if not compelled by the Exchequer Process, they come at their own Pleasure only. By the General Imprest Roll from the Exchequer every Half Year, he learns who are become accountable, and for what Sums issued from thence. The Yearly Accounts of some, and the Final Accounts of other of the great Accountants, inform him of the Insupers or Sub-accountants; but in the Imprest Certificate, which he transmits every Half Year to the King’s Remembrancer, he inserts those Accountants only whose Accounts are then depending; and, when once inserted, he has no Authority to leave them out; their Names mult remain upon all fubi’e-quest Certificates, until their Accounts are passed; and from thence it arises that Accounts of a Very ancient Date, Debts obsolete and del'perate, constantly appear upon these Certificates.

The Accounts audited in this Office' are of Two Kinds; Ordinary, and Extraordinary. The Ordinary Accounts are prepared, made up, and presented to the Lords of the Treasury for Declaration, by virtue of the Authority vested in the Auditor by the Letters

Patent.

Patent. The Extraordinary Accounts are prepared, made up, and presented for Declaration, in pursuance of a special Warrant obtained for that Purpose, either from the King or from the Treasury; previous to the Application for this Warrant, tire Auditor examines the Account and Vouchers, makes up a State of it, and presents it to the Treasury for their Approbation and Allowance. In consequence of such Allowance, a Warrant is procured; which directs the Auditor to prepare, make up, and present for Declaration, the Account, conformably to the State of it so approved of and allowed. Which of thel'e Extraordinary Accounts require the King’s, and which a Treasury Warrant, does not feein to be ascertained by any known Distinction; the Auditor is taught by the Usage of Office only, which he is to apply for. The Accounts of Governors and Quarter Mailers General are passed by the King’s Warrant; the Accounts of Contractors by a Treasury Warrant.

Some of the Accounts are Annual, and have a Continuance; as those of the Treal'urer of the Navy, and Paymaster General of the Forces; such Accounts are usually passed, a Year’s Account alternately in each Office; other Accounts are carried, at the Option of the Accountant, to which of the Two Offices he chuses; but it is in the Power of the Lords of the Treasury to direct an Account to be audited in either Office; and there are some Accounts, such as those of the Bank and South Sea Company, which are audited by both Officers jointly.

Having thus obtained a general Knowledge of the Mode of transacting the Business of this Office, we proceeded to inquire into the Application of these general Rules to the auditing and passing the particular Accounts.

The Two Abstracts are, the Navy, and the Victualling. The Navy-Abstract is an Index, in which all the Bills are entered under general Heads, ranged Alphabetically, expressing for the moll Part, either the Services, or the Species of Stores or Materials, which is the Subject Matter of the Payment. Each Entry contains the Sum, and the Person to whom paid; and the Payments under each Head are call up to a Total. To this is prefixed an alphabetical Index of all the Heads, with their several Totals, call up into One Sum; this is called the Abstract abstracted.

The other Abstract contains the Victualling Payments, digested and ranged in a Method similar to that of the Navy Abstract. Thele Materials, collected together, form a complete Ledger of a Year’s Account of a Treasurer of the Navy: From them is composed the formal Account, which palfes through various Offices, and to a State of which the Treasurer swears.

Sections of the Ledgers, and the other Papers, are lent, from Time to Time, from 'the Pay Office of the Navy to the Office of the Auditor of the Imprest; but none of the Vouchers for the Entries are sent with them (except the Receipts for the Extra Payments, which are very few); nor does the Auditor inspect any of these Vouchers; he allows the Payments upon a different Ground. The last Page of the Voluntary Charge, and every Page of the Ledgers, which contain the Entries of the Navy, Victualling, and Sick and Hurt Bills, or the last Page, where the Entry of a Bill takes up more Pages than One; every Page containing the Payments on the Ship, Yard, Hospital, and Sick Quarters Books, and on the Half Pay j^ilt, is signed at the Bottom by Three Commissioners of the Navy. After he has received all the Materials from the Pay Office, the Official Account is compiled, and redueed to the following Form: — The First Division is the Charge; which comprehends the Arrears due from the Treasurer on the Foot of his last Account, the Money imprested to him from the Exchequer, and his Voluntary Charge. The Imprelt Part is an English Translation of the Imprest Roll (which is in Latin) but retaining the Latin Names of the Terms in which the Sums were issued. The First Part of the Voluntary Charge consists of Imprefts in former Treasurerships, cleared in the Time of this Account. The Auditor ranges the Articles under this Head in the Account in a Manner different from that in the Ledger. In the latter, they are entered in the Order of Time in which the Imprefts are brought to the Office to be cleared; but the Auditor transposes them into the Order of Time in which the original Bills issued. By this Arrangement he can refer more easily o the Insuper Lift in the Final Account of that Treasurer who issued them, in order to mark them, off as cleared. The other Parts of the Voluntary Charge are copied from the Abstract, and consist of the Total Sums only, paid under the several Heads. This comprehends the whole Charge, unlefe Errors in the Account afford Matter of Surcharge.

The other Division of the Account is the Discharge. Of this the greatest Part is taken from the Abstrafit abstracted. The Heads are copied into the Account, with the Total Sum paid for each Head, not the particular Articles composing that Total, except in the following Instances. In the Navy Discharge — Bounties, D'dburfements, Extra Payments, Pensions, Salaries, Sick and Hurt Payments, Ships Books, Rent, and Rewards. In the Victualling Discharge — Extra Payments, Salaries, Rent, and Workmanship. Of these Heads it has been the Usage of Office to enter upon the Account each particular Article; and for this Reason; it enables the Auditor to refer with greater Facility to former Accounts, and guard against a second Credit of the same Payment. He does not range the Articles under each Head exactly in the Order they stand in the Abstract; he disposes them as belt suits his own Ideas and Convenience. The Fees for passing the Account, and the Balance due from the Treasurer, conclude the Account of the Year; unless it be his Final Account, and then the Voluntary Charge contains several other Articles of a similar Kind, copied into the Account in like Manner with the rest -, and there is also added at the End, a List of the Insupers, that is, of those Persons to whom Sums have been issued upon Account, but which have not been cleared during the Time of the Treasurership, with the Sums and Dates of the Imprest Bills. The Treasurer has no Credit in his Annual Account for the Sums imprested and not cleared by him in each Year; they are reserved for, and entered in, his Final Account, where he has Credit for them all, and the Responsibility is transferred to the Persons themselves who have received the Sums, and they are returned accountable. This Lift, in a long Treasurer-lliip, swells to a great Size; it is transmitted from the Pay-Office of the Navy, signed by Three Commissioners, and admitted upon the Authority of that Signatures

The Names on the transmitted Lift are entered in the Order of Time in which the Imprest Bills were paid; but they are transposed upon the Account into an alphabetical Order, for Two Reasons; that all the Sums imprested to the same Person may be brought together; and that each Article may be the more easily found hereafter, to be marked in the Margin, when it is cleared in a subsequent Account: But in the Final Accounts that are now making up in the Treasurer s Office, the Mode of ranging the Names of the Insupers alphabetically is adopted. The last Step, is, comparing the Balance ltated by the Auditor with the Baluuce of the Treasurer; and if it agrees, the Account is completed. A short State of this Account is drawn up in the Auditor’s Office; this State the Accountant swears to, or, if a Peer, attests, before the Barons of the Exchequer, or Commissioners appointed by them. The Total Charge upon Mr. Grenville in this Account, for the Year 1759, is Six millions Six hundred Seventy-four 6,674,11ft. thousand Two hundred Twenty-six Pounds; the Total Discharge, Four millions Five hundred Fifty-live thousand £.4.sis»*°s-One hundred and Five Pounds.

Of every Account Two Parts are made out in the Auditor’s Office; the one on Paper, called The Declared Account, or Declaration; the other on Parchment, called, emphatically, The Account; both of them are signed by the Deputy Auditors, prefeuted to the Lords of the Treasury for Declaration, signed by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, by Two other Lords of the Treasury, and by the Chief Baron of the Exchequer. The Declaration is preserved in the Auditor’s Office; and the Account is carried to the Offices of the King’s Remembrancer and of the Lord '1 rea-surer’s Remembrancer, and then to the Pipe; where it remains, and from whence the Treasurer receives his Quietus.

Such is the Progress of an Account of a Treasurer of the Navy through the Office of the Auditors of tire Imprest.

As none of the Vouchers, except those for the Extra Payments, are produced to the Auditor, but he relies for the Existence, as well as for the Truth of them, upon the Subscription of the Three Commissioners of the Navy, we thought it necessary to enquire what is the Examination given in the Navy Office to these Accounts, that warrants the Commissioners in stamping lb great a Credit upon these Entries. The Year’s Account of a Treasurer of the Navy is made out in the Three Branches of his Office, each Branch attending to that Part of the Account which
