Time to the House, which of them are fit to be revived or continued; That the Committee had enquired accordingly, and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, as relates to the regulating the Fees of the Officers of the Customs in America, and for extending the same to the Naval Officers there, which was to be in Force from the ill Day of August 1770, for the Term of Two Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which was by three Acts, made in the Twelfth, Fourteenth, and Nineteenth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, further continued until the ill Day of August 1782, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That lo much of an Act, made in the Sixteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for allowing the Exportation of certain Quantities of Wheat, and other Articles, to His Majesty’s " Sugar Colonies in America, and to the Island of Saint " Helena, and to the other Settlements belonging to the " United Company of Merchants of England, trading to " the East Indies, and of Biscuit and Pease to " foundland. in the Seventeenth, Eighteenth, Nineteenth, Twentieth, Twenty-first, and Twenty-second Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, was continued until the ill Day of May 1783, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the Seventeenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for repealing the Eleventh Rule in the Book of " Rates, lo far as the same relates to making any Allowance upon the Importation of damaged Currants " and Raisins, and for making the Importer of such " Goods an Abatement in the Duties, in lieu thereof, " and for explaining the said Rule with Respect to such " Allowance for Damage on other Goods, and to permit " the Exportation of Tobacco-pipe Clay from this " Kingdom to the British Sugar Colonies or Plantations " in the West Indies, for a limited Time," as permits the Exportation of Tobacco-pipe Clay from this Kingdom to thf British Sugar Colonies or Plantations in the West Indies, which was to continue in Force until the 24th Day of June 1779, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which, by an Act made in the Twentieth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, was continued until the 24th Day of June 1783, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Luna, 27° die Januarii;

Mr. Elites reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several of the Trustees for putting into Execution an Act of Parliament, made in the Third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing the Reeds from Maidenhead Bridge to Reading, and from the said Bridge to Henley Bridge, in the County of Berks, was referred; That the Committee had examined and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been Complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; vis

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read: And,

Mr. James Payne, Mr. Richard Simeon, and Mr. Thomas Cooper, Treasurers to the different Districts of the Roads comprised in the said Act, being examined, said, That there are considerable Sums of Money due and owing upon the Credit of the Tolls authorized to be collected in their respective Districts, which cannot be paid off, or the Roads kept in sufficient Repair, unless the Term of the said Act be enlarged, and feme further Powers granted.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the Term, and altering and enlarging the Powers, of an Act of the Third Year of His present Majesty, for repairing the Roads from Maidenhead Bridge to Reading, and from the said Bridge to Henley Bridge, in the County of Berks: And that Mr. Elwes, and Mr. Winchcombe Hartley do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day for the Second Reading of the Bill for continuing an Act, passed in the Twenty-second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for retraining Sir Thomas tf Rumbold, Baronet, and Peter Perruig, Esquire, from

" going out of this Kingdom for a limited Time, and u for discovering their Estates and Effects, and preventing the transporting or alienating the fame," be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

The said Bill was read a Second Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

The Order of the Day for the Call of the House being read;

Ordered, That this House be called over upon this Day Fortnight, the 7th Day of February next.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raisingthe Supply granted to His Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning next. Ten of the Clock.

Anno 23 Georgii IIP1* Regis, 1783.

Prayers.

MR. Duncombe presented to the House, according N0rthDeigh.

to Order, a Bill for dividing and inclosing several ton inclosure. Open Fields, and a Parcel of Meadow Ground, within the Township of North Deighton, in the County of York: And the same was received; and read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town of Birmingham Northampton, was presented to the House, and read; Canal.0 Setting forth, That the Petitioners have been informed there are, at this Time, two different Plans, both -of which will be laid before Parliament in the present Session, and both of which have for their Object a Navigable Canal, to communicate with the Coventry Canal at Fazeley, in the Parish of Tamworth, in the County of Warwick; and that the Petitioners conceive the making such Navigable Canal will be of great Public Utility, as thereby a Communication will be opened from the Coal Mines in Staffordshire, with the Counties of Warwick', Northampton, and Oxford, which will tend greatly to reduce the Price of Staffordshire Coal in the Town of Northampton, and its Neighbourhood: And therefore praying, That one of the before-mentioned Plans may he adopted for making such Navigable Canal as aforesaid, leaving it to the Wisdom of the House, which of them will belt answer the Purposes above mentioned.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

viz.

Translation of the Preliminary Articles of Peace, between His Britannic Majesty, and the Most Christian King, signed at the 20th January 1783.

In the Name of the Most Holy Trinity.

The King of Great Britain, and the Most Christian King, equally animated with a Desire of putting an End to the Calamities of a destructive War, and of re-establishing Union and good Understanding between them, as necessary for the Good of Mankind in general, as for that of their respefitive Kingdoms, States, and Subjects, have named for this Purpose, On the

Part of His Britannic Majesty, Mr. Alleyne Fitz-Herbert, Minister Plenipotentiary of His said Majesty the King of Great Britain; and on the Part of His Most Christian Majesty, Charles Grader Comte de Vergennes, Councillor in all his Councils, Commander of His Orders, Councillor of State, Minister and Secretary of State, and of the Commands and Finances of His said Majesty for the Department of Foreign Affairs; who, after having duly communicated to each other their full Powers in good Form, have agreed on the following Preliminary Articles:

Article 6.

With regard to the Right of Fithing in the Gulph of St. Laurence, the French shall continue to enjoy it conformably to the Fifth Article of the Treaty of Paris.

Article 7.

The King of Great Britain shall restore to France the Island of St. Lucia, and shall cede and guaranty to her that of Tobago.

Article 8.

The Most Christian King shall restore to Great Britain the Islands of Grenada, and the Grenadines, St. Vincent's, Dominica, St. Christophers, Nevis, and Montserrat: And the Fortrefies of those Islands conquered by the Arms of Great Britain, and by those of France, shall be restored in the same Condition in which they were when the Conquest of them was made; provided that the Term of Eighteen Months, to be computed from the Time of the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, shall be granted to the respective Subjects of the Crowns of Great Britain and France, who may have settled in the said Islands, and in other Places which shall be restored by the Definitive Treaty, to fell their Estates, recover their Debts, and to transport their Effects, and retire without being restrained on Account of their Religion, or any other whatever, except in Cafes of Debt, or of criminal Prosecutions.

Article 1.

As feon as the Preliminaries shall be signed and ratified, sincere Friendship shall be re-established between His Britannic Majesty and His Most Christian Majesty, their Kingdoms, States, and Subjects, by Sea and by Land, in all Parts of the World: Orders shall be sent to the Armies and Squadrons, as well as to the Subjects, of the Two Powers, to stop all Hostilities, and to live in the most perfect Union, forgetting what is passed, of which their Sovereigns give them the Order and Example; and for the Execution of this Article, Sea Pafies shall be given on each Side for the Ships which shall be dispatch to carry the News of it to the Possessions of the said Powers.

Article 2.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain shall preserve in full Right the Island of N, and the adjacent Islands, in the same Manner as the Whole was ceded to Him by the Thirteenth Article of the Treaty of Utrecht, save the Exceptions which shall be stipulated by the Fifth Article of the present Treaty.

Article 3.

His Most Christian Majesty, in order to prevent Quarrels which have hitherto arisen between the Two Nations of England and France, renounces the Right of Fishing, which belongs to Him by virtue of the said Article of the Treaty of Utrecht, from Cape Bonavisla to Cape St. John, situated on the Eastern Coast of Newfoundland, in about 50 Degrees of North Latitude: Whereby the French Fishery shall commence at the said Cape St. John, shall go round by the North, and, going down the Western Coast of the Island of Newfoundland, shall have for Boundary the Place called Cape Rape, situated in 47 Degrees 50 Minutes Latitude.

Article 4.

The French Fishermen shall enjoy the Fishery tffligned them by the foregoing Article, as they have a Right to enjoy it by virtue of the Treaty of Utrecht.

Article 5.

His Britannic Majesty will cede in full Right to His Most Chciftian Majesty the Islands of St. Pierre and Miguelon.

Article 9.

The King of Great Britain shall cede and guaranty in full Right to His Most Christian Majesty, the River of Senegal, and its Dependencies, with the Forts of St.

Podor, Galam, Arguin, and Portendie: His Britannic Majesty shall restore likewise the Island of which shall be given up in the Condition in which it was when the British Arms took Possession of it.

Article 10.

The Most Christian King shall, on His Side, guaranty to His Majesty the King of Great Britain, the Possession of Fort James, and of the River Gambia.

Article 11.

In order to prevent all Discussion in that Part of the World, the Two Courts shall agree, either, by the Definitive Treaty, or by a separate Afit, upon the Boundaries to be fixed to their respective Possessions. The Gum Trade shall be carried on in future, as the English and French Nations carried it on before the Year 1755.

Article 12.

In regard to the rest of the Coast of Africa, the Subjects of both Powers shall continue to frequent them, according to the Custom which has prevailed hitherto.

Article 13.

The King of Great Britain shall restore to His Most Christian Majesty all the Establishments which belonged to Him at the Commencement of the present War on the Coast of Orica, and in Bengal, with Liberty to surround Chandemagor with a Ditch for draining the Waters; and His Britannic Majesty engages to take such Measures as may be in His Power, for securing to the Subjects of France in that Part of India, as also on the Coalts of Orixa, Coromandel, and Malabar, a safe, free, and independent Trade, such as was carried on by the late French East India Company, whether it be carried on by them as Individuals, or as a Company.

Article 14.

Pondicherry, as well as Karical, shall likewise be restored and guarantied to France; and His Britannic Majesty shall procure to serve as a Dependency round Pondicherry, the Two Districts of Valanour and Bahour;

and

'll Geo. III. 270 Januariu 115

and as a Dependency round Karical, the Four contiguous Magans.

Article 15.

France shall again enter into Possession of Make, and of the Comptoir at Surat; and the French shall carry on Commerce in this Part of India, conformably to the Principles laid down in the Thirteenth Article of this Treaty.

Article 16.

In case France has Allies in India, they shall be invited, as well as those of Great Britain, to accede to the present Pacification; and for that Purpose, a Term of Four Months, to be computed from the Day on which the Proposal shall be made to them, shall be allowed them to make their Decision; and in case of Refusal on their Part, their Britannic and Most Christian Majesties agree not to give them any Alfillance, directly or indirectly, against the British or French Possessions, or against the ancient Possessions of their respective Allies; and their said Majesties shall offer them their good Offices towards a mutual Accommodation.

Artic.e 17.

The King of Great Britain, desirous of giving His Most Christian Majesty a sincere Proof of Reconciliation and Friendship, and of contributing to the Solidity of the Peace which is on the Point of being re-established, will consent to the Abrogation and Suppression of all the Articles relative to Dunkirk, from the Treaty of Peace concluded at Utrecht in 1713, inclusively, to this Time.

Article 18.

By the Definitive Treaty, all those which have existed till now between the Two high contracting Parties, and which shall not have been derogated from, either by the said Treaty, or by the present Preliminary Treaty, shall be renewed and confirmed; and the Two Courts shall name Commissioners to enquire into the State of Commerce between the Two Nations, in order to agree upon new Arrangements of Trade, on the Footing of Reciprocity and mutual Convenience. The said Two Courts shall together amicably fix a competent Term for the Duration of that Business.

Article 19.

All the Countries and Territories which may have been or which may be conquered, in any Part of the World whatsoever, by the Arms of His Britannic Majesty, or by those of His Most Christian Majesty, and which are not included in the present Articles, shall be restored without Difficulty, and without requiring Compenfetion.

Article 20.

As it is necessary to assign a fixed Epoch for the Restitutions and the Evacuations to be made by each of the high contracting Parties, it is agreed, That the King of Great Britain shall cause to be evacuated the lllands of St.Pierre and Miquelon, Three Months after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, or sooner if it can be done; St. Lucia, in the West Indies, and Goree in Africa, Three Months after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, or sooner, if it can be done. The King of Great Britain shall, in like Manner, at the End of Three Months after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, or sooner, if it can be done, enter again into Possession of the lllands of Grenada, the nadines, St. Vincent, Dominica, St. Christophers, , and Montserrat.

France shall be put into Possession of the Towns and Comptoirs which are restored to Her in the East Indies, and of the Territories which are procured for Her, to serve as Dependencies round Pondicherry, and round

Karical, Six Months after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, or sooner if it can be done.

Vol. 39.

France shall, at the End of the same Term of Six Articles of Months, restore the Towns and Territories which Her p*ace Arms may have taken from the English, or their Allies, rance* in the East Indies.

In conl'equence whereof, the necessary Orders shall be sent by each of the high contracting Parlies, with reciprocal Passports for the Ships which shall carry them, immediately after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty.

Article 2 i.

The Prisoners made respectively by' the Arms of His Britannic Majesty, and his Molt Christian Majesty, by Land and by Sea, shall be restored reciprocally and bond Jide, immediately after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, without Ransom, and on paying the Debts they may have contracted during their Captivity; and each Crown shall respectively reimburse the Sums which shall have been advanced for the Sub-(istence and Maintenance of their Prisoners, by the Sovereign of the Country where they shall have been detained, according to the Receipts and attested Accounts, and other authentic Titles, which shall be produced on each Side.

Article 22.

In order to prevent all Causes of Complaint and Dispute which may arile on Account of Prizes which may be made at Sea after the Signing of thele Preliminary Articles, it is reciprocally agreed, That the Vessels and Effects which may be taken in the Channel, and in the North Seas, after the Space of Twelve Days to be computed from the Ratification of the present Preliminary Articles, shall be restored on each Side.

That the Term shall be One Month, from the Channel, and the North Seas, as far as the Canary Islands, inclusively, whether in the Ocean or in the Mediterranean.

Two Months, from the said Canary Islands, as far as the Equinoctial Line, or Equator. And lastly, Five Months in all other Parts of the World, without any Exception, or any other more particular Description of Time and Place.

Article 23.

The Ratifications of the present Preliminary Articles shall be expedited in good and due Form, and exchanged in the Space of One Month, or sooner if it can be done, to be computed from the Day of the- Signature of the present Articles.

In Witness whereof, we the under-written Ministers Plenipotentiary of His Britannic Majesty, and of His Most Christian Majesty, by virtue of our respective full Powers, have signed the present Preliminary Articles, and have caused the Seal of our Arms to be put thereto.

Done at Versailles, the Twentieth Day of January 1783-

Alleyne Fitz-Herbert. Graoier de Vergennes.'

Rico-Hombre in Aragon by Birth, Grandee of Spain of the First Class, Knight of the Order of the Golden Fleece, and of that of the Holy Ghost, Gentleman of the King’s Bedchamber in Employment, Captain General of His Armies, and His Ambassador to His Most Christian Majesty; who, after having duly communicated to each other their full Powers in good Form, have agreed on the following Preliminary Articles:

Article 1.

As soon as the Preliminaries shall be signed and ratified, sincere Friendthip shall be re-established between His Britannic Majesty and His Catholic Majesty, their Kingdoms, States, and Subjects, by Sea and by Land, in all Parts of the World. Orders shall be sent to the Armies and Squadrons, as well as to the Subjects of the Two Powers, to (top all Hostilities, and to live in the most perfect Union, forgetting what has passed, of which their Sovereigns give them the Order and Example. And for the Execution of this Article, Sea PafiTes shall be given on each Side for the Ships which shall be dispatch to carry the News of it to the Possessions of the said Powers.

Article 2.

His Catholic Majesty shall keep the Island of

Minorca.

Article 3.

His Britannic Majesty shall cede to His Catholic Majesty East Florida, and His Catholic Majesty shall keep West Florida, provided that the Term of Eighteen Months, to be computed from the Time of the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, shall be granted to the Subjects of His Britannic Majesty, who are settled as well.in the Island of Minorcaas in the Two Floridas, to fell their Estates, recover their Debts, and to transport their Effects, ds well as their Persons, without being restrained on Account of their Religion, or under any other Pretence whatsoever, except that of Debts and criminal Prosecutions. And His Britannic Majesty shall have Power to cause all the Effects that may belong to him in East Florida, whether Artillery or others, to be carried away.

Article 4.

His Catholic Majesty shall not for the future suffer the Subjects of His Britannic Majesty, or their Workmen to be disturbed or molested, under any Pretence whatsoever, in their Occupation of cutting, loading, and carrying away Logwood, in a District of which the Boundaries shall be fixed; and for this Purpose they may build without Hindrance, and occupy without Interruption, the Houses and Magazines necessary for them, for their Families, and for their Effects, in a Place to be agreed upon either in the Definitive Treaty, or within Six Months after the Exchange of the Ratifications-; and His said Catholic Majesty allures to them by this Article, the entire Enjoyment of what is above stipulated, provided that these Stipulations shall not be considered as derogatory in any Respect from the Rights of his Sovereignty.

Article 5.

His Catholic Majesty shall restore to Great Britain

— s.- ..... '

the Islands of Providence and the Bahamas, without Exception, in the same Condition in which they were when they were conquered by the Arms of the King of Spain.

Article 6.

All the Countries and Territories which may have been or may be conquered, in any Part of the World whatsoever, by the Arms of His Britannic Majesty, or by those of His Catholic Majesty, and which are not included in the present Articles, shall be restored, without Difficulty, and without requiring Compensations.

Article 7.

By the Definitive Treaty, all those which have existed till now between the Two high contracting Parties, and which shall not be derogated from either by the said Treaty, or by the present Preliminary Treaty, shall be renewed and confirmed; and the Two Courts shall name Commissioners to enquire into the State of Commerce between the Two Nations, in order to agree upon new Arrangements of Trade on the Footing of Reciprocity and mutual Convenience; and the Two said Courts shall together amicably fix a competent Term for the Duration of that Business.

Article 8.

As it is necessary to assign a fixed Epoch for the Restitutions and Evacuations to be made by each of the high contracting Parties, it is agreed, that the King of Great Britain shall cause East Florida to be evacuated Three Months after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, or sooner if it can be done.

The King of Great Britain shall likewise enter again into Possession of the Bahama Islands without Exception, in the Space of Three Months after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty.

In consequence whereof, the necessary Orders shall be sent by each of the high contracting Parties, with reciprocal Passports for the Ships which shall carry them, immediately after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty.

Article 9.

The Prisoners made respectively by the Arms of His Britannic Majesty and His Catholic Majesty, by Sea and by Land, shall, immediately after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, be reciprocally and bond Jide restored without Ransom, and on paying the Debts they may have contracted during their Captivity; and each Crown shall respectively reimburse the Sums which shall have been advanced for the Subsistence and Maintenance of their Prisoners by the Sovereign of the Country where they shall have been detained, according to the Receipts and attested Accounts, and other authentic Titles, which shall be produced on each Side.

Article 10.

In order to prevent all Causes of Complaint and Deputes which may arise on Account of Prizes which may be made at Sea after the signing of these Preliminary Articles, it is reciprocally agreed, that the Ships and EffeCls which may be taken in the Channel, or in the North Seas, after the Space of Twelve Days, to be computed from the Ratification of the present Preliminaiy Articles, shall be restored on each Side.

That the Term shall be One Month from the Channel and the North Seas, as far as the Canary Islands, inclusively, whether in the Ocean or in the Mediterranean; Two Months from the said Canary Islands, as far as the Equinoctial Line, or Equator; and lastly,-Five Months in all other Parts of the World, without Exception, or other more particular Description of Time and Place.

Article 11.

The Ratifications of the present Preliminary Articles shall be expedited in good and due Form, and ex-

Copy of Provisional Articles, signed at Paris, November 30th 1782, by the Commissioner of His Britannic Majesty, and the Commissioners of the United States of America.

Articles agreed upon, by and between Richard Oswald, Eiquiie, the Commissioner of His Britannic Majesty, for treating of Peace with the Commissioners of the United States of America, in Behalf of His laid Majesty, on the one Part; and John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, John Jay, and Henry Laurens, Four of the Commissioners of the said States for treating of Peace with the Commissioner of His said Majesty, on their Behalf, on the other Part; to be inserted in, and to constitute, the Treaty of Peace, proposed to be concluded between the Crown of Great Britain and the said Uni d States; but which Treaty is not to be concluded until Terms of a Peace shall be agreed upon between Great Britain and France, and His Britannic Majesty shall be ready to conclude such Treaty accordingly.

Whereas reciprocal Advantages and mutual Convenience are found by Experience to form the only permanent Foundation of Peace and Friendship between States; it is agreed to form the Articles of the proposed Treaty on such Principles of liberal Equity and Reciprocity, as that partial Advantages (those Seeds of Dif-cord) being excluded, such a beneficial and satisfactory Intercourse between the Two Countries may be established, as to promise and secure to both perpetual Peace and Harmony.

Article lft.

His Britannic Majesty acknowledges the said United States, vits. New Hampshire, Massachusets Bay, Rhode Island and Providence Plantations, Connecticut, New Yorke, New Jersey, Pensylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia, to be Free, Sovereign, and Independent States; that he treats with them as such; and for himself, his Heirs, and Successors, relinquishes all Claim to the Government, Propriety, and Territorial Rights of the lame, and every Part thereof: And that all Disputes which might arise in future, on the Subject of the Boundaries of the said United States, may be prevented, it is hereby agreed and declared, that the following are and shall be their Boundaries; vis'.

Article 2d.

From the North West Angle of Nova Scotia, viz*. that Angle which is formed by a Line drawn due North from the Source of Saint Croix River to The Highlands, along the said Highlands which divide those Rivers that empty themselves into the River Saint Lawrence, from those which fall into the Atlantic Ocean, to the North-Westernmost Head of River; thence

down along the Middle of that River, to the Forty-fifth Vol. 39.

Degree of North Latitude; from thence, by a Line due Articles of West on said Latitude, until it strikes the River Iroquois or Cataraquy; thence along the Middle of said River, menca* into Lake Ontario, through the Middle of said Lake, until it strikes the Communication by Water between that Lake and Lake Erie; thence along the Middle of said Communication, into' Lake Erie, through the Middle of said Lake, until it arrives at the Water Communication between that Lake and Lake Huron; thence along the Middle of said Water Communication, into the Lake Huron;thence through the Middle of said

Lake, to the Water Communication between that Lake and Lake Superior-, thence through Lake Superior, Northward of the lfles Royal and Phelipeaux, to the Long Lake; thence through the Middle of said Long '

Lake, and the Water Communication between it and the Lake of the Woods, to the said Lake of the Woods; thence through the said Lake, to themost North-Western Point thereof and from thence, on a due West Course, to the River Mississippi; thence, by a Line to be drawn along the Middle of the said River Mississippi, until it shall intersect the Northernmost Part of the Thirty-first Degree of North Latitude; — South, by a Line to be drawn due East from the Determination of the Line last mentioned, in the Latitude of Thirty-one Degrees North of the Equator, to the Middle of the River Apalachicola, or Catahouche; thence along the Middle thereof, to its Junction with the River; thence straight to the Head of Saint Mary's River, and thence down along the Middle of Saint Marys River to the Atlantic Ocean; — East, by a Line to be drawn along the Middle of the River Saint Croix, from its Mouth in the Bay of Fundy to its Source, and from its Source directly North, to the aforesaid Highlands which divide the Rivers that fall into the Atlantic Ocean from those which fall into the River Saint Lawrence, comprehending all Islands within Twenty Leagues of any Part of the Shores of the United States, and lying between Lines to be drawn due East from the Points where the aforesaid Boundaries between Nova Scotia on the one Part, and East Florida on the other, shall respectively touch the Bay of Fundy, and the Atlantic Ocean; excepting such Islands as now are, or heretofore have been, within the Limits of the said Province of Nova Scotia.

Article 3d.

It is agreed, That the People of the United States shall continue to enjoy, unmolested, the Right to take-Fish, of every Kind, on the Grand Bank, and on all the other Banks of Newfoundland-, also in the Gulpb of Saint Lawrence, and at all other Places in the Sea, where the Inhabitants of both Countries used at any Time heretofore to fish; and also, that the Inhabitants of the United States shall have Liberty to take Fish, of every Kind, on such Part of the Coast of Newfoundland as British Fishermen shall use (but not to dry or . cure the same on that Island); and also on the Coasts,

Bays, and Creeks, of all other of His Britannic Majesty’s Dominions in America; and that the American Fishermen shall have Liberty to dry and cure Fish in any of the unsettled Bays, Harbours, and Creeks, of Nova Scotia, Magdalen Islands, and Labrador, so long as the same shall remain unsettled; but so soon as the fame, or either of them, shall be settled, it shall not be lawful for the said Fishermen to dry or cure Fish at such Settlement, without a previous Agreement for that Purpose with the Inhabitants, Proprietors, or Post'essors of the Ground.

Article 4th.

It is agreed, That Creditors on either Side shall meet with no lawful Impediment to the Recovery of the full Value, in Sterling Money, of all jide Debts heretofore contracted.

Articles of Peace with America.

Article 5th.

It is agreed, That the CoDgress shall earnestly recommend it to the Legislatures of the respective States, to provide for the Refutation of all Estates, Rights, and Properties, which have been confiscated, belonging to real British Subjects, and also of the Estates, Rights, and Properties, of Persons rCfident in Districts in the Possession of His Majesty’s Arms, and who have not borne Arms again!! the said United States; and that Persons of any other Description shall have free Liberty to go to any Part or Parts of any of the Thirteen United States, and therein to remain Twelve Months umnolefted in their Endeavours to obtain the Restitution of Such of their Estates, Rights, and Properties, as may have been confiscated; and that Congrels Shall also earnestly recommend to the Several States, a Reconsideration and Revision of all Acts or Laws regarding the Premises, So as to render the said Laws or Acts perfectly confident, not only with Justice and Equity, but with that Spirit of Conciliation, which on the Return of the BlefiTings of Peace should univerlally prevail; and that Congress shall also earnestly recommend to the several States, that the Estates, Rights, and Properties of Such last mentioned Persons Shall be restored to them, they refunding to any Persons who may be now in Possession the bond side Price (where any has been given) which such Persons may have paid on purchasing any of the said Lands or Properties Since the Confiscation.

And it is agreed. That all Persons who have any Interest in coufifcated Lands, either by Debts, Marriage Settlements, or otherwise, shall meet with no lawful Impediment in the Prosecution of their just Rights.

Article 6th.

That there shall be no future Confiscations made, nor any Prosecution commenced against any Person or Persons, for or by Reason of the Part which he or they may have taken in the present War; and that no Person shall on that Account suffer any future Loss or Damage, either in his Person, Liberty, or Property; and that those who may be in Confinement on Such Charges, at the Time of the Ratification of the Treaty in shall be immediately Set at Liberty, and the Prosecutions So commenced be discontinued.

Article 7th.

There shall be a firm and perpetual Peace between His Britannic Majesty and the said States, and between the Subjects of the one and the Citizens of the other; wherefore, all Hostilities, both by Sea and Land, shall then immediately cease: All Prisoners on both Sides shall be Set at Liberty, and His Britannic Majesty shall, with all convenient Speed, and without causing any Destruction, or carrying away any Negroes, or other Property of the American Inhabitants, withdraw all his Armies, Garrisons, and Fleets, from the said United States, and from every Port, Place, and Harbour within the same, leaving in all Fortifications the American Artillery that may be therein; and shall also order and caufo all Archives, Records, Deeds, and Papers, belonging to any of the said States, or their Citizens, which, in the Course of the War, may have fallen into the Hands of His Officers, to be forthwith restored and delivered to the proper States and Persons to whom they belong.

Article 8th.

The Navigation of the Mississippi, from its Source to the Ocean, shall for ever remain free and open to the Subjects of Great Britain, and the Citizens of the United States.

Article 9th.

In case it should so happen, that any Place or Territory belonging to Great Britain, or to the United States, should be conquered by the Arms of either, from the other, before the Arrival of these Articles in America, it is agreed, that the same shall be restored without Difficulty, and without requiring any Compensation.

Setting forth, That the Common Gaol b the Town and County of the Town of Kingston upon Hull is a very ancient Building of small Dimensions, and in great Decay, and, Handing in the Middle of the said Town, and in a dole and confined Situation, without the Advantage of any adjaceut Ground, is attended with many Inconveniencies to the Health and lafe Culiody of the Prisoners, and the Grand Jury, at the Allizes and General Gaol Delivery held for the said Town and County, have presented the said Gaol as bsufficient; and that the building a new Gaol, b a more airy and commodious Situation in some other Part of the said Town or County, will greatly contribute to the Health of the Prisoners, and render the Custody of them more safe, and will also be a general Convenience to the said Town and County, and an Advantage to the Public; and that the Population of the Parish of The Holy Trinity, in the said Town of Kingston upon Hull, hath for many Years greatly increased, and the Inhabitants of the said Parish are become^ so numerous, that the Church Yard and Burial Places belonging to the same are not sufficiently large to contain the Bodies of those who die in the said Parish, without much Inconvenience and Annoyance to the Inhabitants; and that it would contribute much to the Convenience of the said Town, and to the Health of the Inhabitants, as well as to the decent and orderly Interment of the Dead, if a convenient Piece of Ground should be purchased for an additional Burial Place for the Use of the said Parish, and it is expedient to raise Money for the several Purposes aforesaid; and that, in the said Town of Kingston upon Hull, and the Liberties and Precincts thereof, many Hackney Coaches and Vo l. 39.

and several other very considerable Annoyances and Irregularities are committed and prevail b the said Town, and the Liberties and Precincts thereof, which might be prevented and restrained if certain Regulations were established, and the Police of the said Town, Liberties, and Precincts, was placed under more proper and certain Rules and Restrictions; and that the Haven of the Town and Port of Kingston upon Hull, in which Goods and Merchandize have been accustomed to be laden and shipped, landed and discharged, lies within the Town and County of the Town of Kingston upon Hull, and, by an Act, passed in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, a Dock or Bason, for the Reception and Accommodation of Ships and Vessels, hath been made and is now in Use, the South Side and East End whereof are in, or contiguous to, the said Town or County of the Town of Kingston upon Hull, and the North Side and West End thereof are in, or contiguous to, the County of York; and that various Goods and Merchandize are now laden and shipped, landed and discharged, on the North Side and Welt End of the said Dock, or Bason, lying in the said County of York, contrary to the Custom which hath heretofore obtained, by Means whereof many Inconveniencies and Disadvantages have, on that and other Accounts proceeding from the said Act, arisen, and are likely to happen, which might be prevented if the said Dock, or Bason, and the Banks, Shores, Quays, Wharfs, and landing Places of the fame, on the North Side and West End thereof, not extending above Twenty Yards in Breadth, should, as to the purposes of lading and shipping, landing and discharging Goods and Merchandize, but for no other Purpose whatever, be declared to be of and in the Town and County of the Town of Kingston upon Hull, and not in the County of York, and certain Doubts concerning the said Act be ex-plabed: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to effectuate the several Purposes above mentioned, and that the Petitioners may have such Relief b the Premises as the House shall think proper.

Birmingham A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Canal Birmingham Canal Navigation was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That an Act was passed in the Eighth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for making and maintaining a Navigable Cut, or Canal, from Birmingham to B and from thence to Au-therley, there to communicate with the Canal then making between the Rivers Secern and Trent, and for making Collateral Cuts up to several Coal Mines; and that another Act was pasted, in the Ninth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, to rectify a Mistake in the said first-mentioned Act, and to explain and amend the fame; and that the said Canal bath long since been

completed from certain Parts of the Town of Birmingham to Autherley, as have also the said Collateral Cuts in the said first Act particularly mentioned; and that there are several other Tracts of Land near to the said Canal and Collateral Cuts, wherein there are large and valuable Mines of Coal and Ironstone, and the extending the fai(l Canal, or Collateral Cuts, into such new Mines, with additional Collateral Cuts, as also extending the said Canal from or near Birmingham, to join the

Coventry Canal at or near Fazeley, may induce the

Proprietors of the Oxford and Coventry Canals to complete the same, and thereby open a Communication as well between the said Mines and the Mines upon the Line of the present Birmingham Canal, and the said Oxford and Coventry Canals, as also between the Counties of Bucks, Oxford, and Warwick, and the Ports of Bristol, Liverpool, and Hull; and that the said Company of Proprietors are willing, at their own Expence, to make and maintain the said Two Extensions of Canal and Collateral Cuts: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making and maintaining such Two Extensions of Canal, with Collateral Cuts, into the said Coal Mines, by such Ways and Means, in such Manner and Form, with such Powers, Privileges, and Authorities, and under and subject to such Rules, Regulations, and Restrictions, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the Petition . of the Company of Proprietors of the Birmingham Canal Navigation is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

A Petition of Thomas Lewin, Esquire, was presented Privilege — to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petition from Petitioner having, on the 2istof this Instant January, c^jJonln voluntarily surrendered himself to abide the Pleasure ° y' of the House, was, by their Order, committed to the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms, where he has continued a Prisoner ever since; and that, in Addition to the painful Restraints of Imprisonment, and the Detriment arising from thence to his private Concerns, much deranged by his late Absence from this Country, the Petitioner cannot but feel the deepest Concern at having drawn upon himself so severe a Mark of the Displeasure of the House; and that the Petitioner, impressed with the highest; Veneration for its Dignity and Authority, and of the implicit Obedience due so every Power acting under it, does not presume to vindicate his pall Conduct, or to arraign the Justice of that Punishment which is inflicted upon him for it,

'but humbly hopes that he shall be permitted to implore Forgiveness for a Default w'hich originated from no Motives difrepeftful to the House, or dishonourable in themselves; and that the Petitioner did not avoid an Examination, for the Purpose of withholding any Information of a public Nature, or relating to public TransaQions, which it was in his Power to give; and solemnly declares, that he has not, nor ever had, any Wish or Intention of that Kind; and that the precipitate Resolution which the Petitioner was induced to take, was the Result of a sudden Fear and Alarm; and he hopes, from the Indulgence of the

and that the Commissioners, in pursuance of the Powers vested in them by the said Acts, have expended very large Sums of Money in erecting a large Pier and Key at or near five Mouth of five said River, in deepening file Channel of the said Port, in making several necessary Alterations and Additions in the said Pier, and in making divers other Works for the Improvement and Security of the said Port, Haven, and River, whereby great Advantages have arisen to the Navigation of the said River; and that the East End of the said Pier, from the Force and Violence of the Sea and Land Floods, and the Badness of its Foundation, is at present in a ruinous State, and likely to fell down; and in case the same should fall into the River, the Petitioners apprehend it will be injurious to the Trade and Navigation of the said Port, especially as the Mouth of ithe River may by that Means be choked up, and the Passage of Strips and Vessels in and out of the said Harbour thereby totally prevented, to the great Prejudice and Obstruction of the Trade and Navigation of the said River, Port, and Haven; and that the Commissioners, for the avoiding thereof, have been advised by an able and experienced Engineer, and intended to have taken down a considerable Part of the said Pier, and to have rebuilt the same in a different Direction, so as that the Sea and Land Floods might not aft with such Violence thereon, and also be more beneficial to the Navigation of the said River, Port, and Haven, and, they had actually begun that Work, but the Money to arise from the Duties granted by the said Two last mentioned Acts, being insufficient for the Purpose of carrying on the said Work, they were thereby prevented from proceeding the rein, and the said Work, and other Works which are necessary to be made and effected at the Mouth and other Parts of the said River, to render the said Port and Harbour safe and commodious, cannot be proceeded in and carried on without further Duties being granted for that Purpose; and that the Expences of taking down and rebuilding that Part of the said Pier, and of such other Works, will, upon a moderate Computation, amount to 60,000l. and upwards; and that the Commissioners have borrowed Money on the Credit of the Duties payable by the said Acts, and are also indebted several Sums of Money on account of the Works that have been carried on in pursuance of the said Acts, and the Petitioners arc advii'ed that the Navigation of the said River, Port', and Haven, might be further improved and extended; Rotherhithe A Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, Overpaying, tic. seers of the Poor, and other principal Inhabitants of Saint Mary Rotherhithe, otherwise Redrijfe, in the County of Surrey, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in Behalf of themselves and the other Inhabitants of the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Streets, Lanes, Ways, and Passages, within the said Parish, are ill paved, cleansed, and lighted, and are also greatly incumbered with Posts, and annoyed with Signs, Spouts, Gutters, and other Obllruftions, whereby they are rendered incommodious, and in many Parts dangerous to the Inhabitants and to Passengers; and that there is no regular Watch in the said Parish, for Want whereof the Inhabitants, their Houses, and Property, are exposed to the Violence of Footpads, Housebreakers, and other Disturbers of the Peace; and that, if proper Powers were given to pave, cleanse, light, watch, and regulate the several Streets, Lanes, Ways, Passages, and Places, within the said Parish, and to remove all Annoyances and Obstructions, and to prevent the same for the future, it would tend greatly to the Health, Convenience, and Safety of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, and be of public Utility: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner, and with such Powers and Provisions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Coals used in A Petition of John Esquire, on Behalf of

Anglesey himself, and others, Owners, Proprietors, and Lessees, incs« of Copper and Lead Mines in the Isle of Anglesey, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That there are several considerable Mines of Copper and Lead in the said Me, and the Petitioner and other Persons who are concerned in railing Copper and Lead therefrom, are obliged, on account of the Want of Coals and other Fuel in the said Me, to carry their Copper and Lead Ores, at a very considerable Expence, to other Places at a great Distai\ce, where Coals pay no Duty, in order to be smelted; and that the heavy Expence which the Petitioner and others necessarily incur on account of the high Price of and Duty on Coals in the said Me, is a great Discouragement as well to the Lessees, Owners, and Proprietors, of the said Mines, as to other Persons who might become Adventurers therein; and that in the Progress of working the said Mines, they must necessarily go to such a Depth, that, from that Circumstance and the Situation of the Ore, it will be itnpoflible for the Water to be drawn and kept out of them without the Help of Fire Engines, in working of which great Quantities of Coals must be used, in procuring whereof the Lessees and Owners and Proprietors of Copper and Lead Mines in the said Me will be under the same Difficulties and Discouragement as in supplying themselves w’ith Coals for the Purpose of Smelting; and that, as an Encouragement for railing Tin and Copper Ores, a Drawback on the Duties on Coals consumed in smelting such Tin and Copper Ores in the Counties of Cornwall and Devon, was granted by an Act, made in the Ninth Year of Queen Anne, and allb a like Drawback on the Duties on Coals used in Fire Engines for draining Water out of the Mines of Tin and Copper within the County of Cornwall, was granted by an Act, made in the Fourteenth Year of King George the Second; and that the Petitioner apprehends, if the like Drawback was to be allowed for all Coals consumed in smelting of Copper and Lead Ores, and in working such Fire Engines, within the said Me, the Petitioner and other Persons would be enabled to work the Copper and Lead Mines in the said Me more effectually, as well to the Advantage of the Lessees, Owners, and Adventurers, as of the Public in general: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consuleration, and to give such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them to the House:

And it is referred to the Lord Bulkeley, Mr. Frederick Montagu, &c.: And they are to meet To morrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber: and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Bench Prison being so extensive, many Prisoners who have large Families frequently rent Houses, or Parts of Houses, or Lodgings ready furnished, therein, at the Rent of 10/. per Annum, or upwards, and others at lower Rents, all which making them liable to be rated to and to pay the Parish Rates and Taxes, they are thereby deemed to gain Settlements, and many of such Prisoners, their Families, and Servants, have become heavy Burthens upon the said Parish; and that the Families of Prisoners have frequently been sent from the said Prison of The Marshalsea, when lick or otherwise distressed, to the Overfoers of the Poor of the said Parish, to be by them supported, and when able, to be removed to their respective Places of Settlement, which brings on a heavy. and that the said Parish is burthened with a numerous Poor of their own; that the Inhabitants are chiefly Tenants at Rack Rent, and are very heavily taxed in all Respects, and in the Place called The Mint, and in Kent Street, which are large and fully inhabited, scarcely One-third Part of the Householders are able to pay any Rates or Taxes, and many of the Houses are let in single Rooms or Lodgings ready furnished, and frequently for a Angle Night, to Vagrants, Travellers, and poor Persons of every Description, which the said Parish is liable to by being the great Avenue to London and Portsmouth, Dover, and other Parts, by which Means Expence frequently falls upon the said Parish, and the Number of their casual Poor are thereby increased; and that the Inhabitants of the said Parish experience great Inconveniences from the whole Number of Overseers of the Poor being appointed at one and the same Time, because they are of Course at first coming into Office unacquainted not only with the proper Method of maintaining, regulating, and employing, the Poor in the Workhouse, but with the Characters and Circumstances of such of the poor Inhabitants as are upon the Lift for Relief without going into the Work-house; and the Petitioners conceive it would be advantageous to the said Parish if One Half of the Overseers were to be appointed at the usual Time, and the other Half in the Middle of the Year, each Party to be continued in Office for a Year, by which Means One Half will be in the Office Six Months, when the other Half are appointed; and that there being few Inhabitants in the said Parish of independent Fortunes, and most of the principal Housekeepers having served the Office of Overseers of the Poor, it is difficult to find Persons sufficient to serve that Office who can be expected to spare Time from their own Avocations to attend to the necessary Duties of that laborious Office, exclusive of the Business of collecting the Money upon the Poor Rates, which requires a more than ordinary Attention, great Part of the Inhabitants beings very poor, and frequently removing from one Part of the Parish to another, by which Means, and otherwise, without a strict Attendance, much Money is liable to be loft to the Parish; and the Petitioners apprehend it will occasion a Saving to the Parish to have a Power given

A Petition of the Merchants, Tradesmen, and Inhabitants of the Town and Borough of Southwark, in the County of Surrey, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the said Town and Borough is of great Antiquity, and a very large and extensive Trade is carried on therein; and that a Court of Record hath, for Time immemorial, been usually held in the said Town and Borough once every Week, for entering and carrying on the necessary Proceedings in bringing to Issue and Trial of Causes in all personal Actions arising within the Jurisdiction thereof; but that the Mode of Proceeding the rein, for the Recovery of Debts and Damages between Forty Shillings and Ten Pounds, is very dilatory, and the Expences attending the same are very burthensome to the Suitors of the said Court, by Means whereof many Persons now l'ubnait to the Loss of their just Debts; and that, if the Proceedings of the said Court were regulated and shortened, and the Creditor enabled to recover his Debt or Damages in a more summary Way, and the Expences attending the Prosecution of Suits in the said Court were reduced, the Petitioners apprehend the same would be of great Advantage to all Persons residing within the said Borough, and of public Utility: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purposes aforesaid, by such Ways and Means, and in such Manner, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of the Owners and Occupiers of Houses in the Parish of Saint James, within the Liberty of Westminster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That several Acts were made, in the Second, Third, Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for paving, cleansing, and lighting the Streets, Squares, Lanes, and other Places within the City and Liberty of Westminster, and Parts adjacent, and Power was thereby given to certain Commissioners to make Rates upon the Inhabitants for defraying the Expences thereof; and that, by an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, the Power of making Contracts for paving, cleansing, and lighting the Streets and other public Passages and Places within the respective Parishes in the said City and Liberty, and Parts adjacent, and of performing several other Matters relating thereto, and likewise the Power of raising Money for the Purposes aforesaid, were taken from the Commissioners appointed by the said Acts, and vested in & certain Number of the Inhabitants of such Parishes respectively, who are annually appointed by the Vestry to be Committee Men for those Purposes, but the Powers so vested in the said Committee Men are, in feme Cafes, subject to the Controul and Direction of the said Commissioners; and that the Paving of all the Streets and public Passages in the said Parish of Saint James hath, for some Time past, been completed under the Powers and Authorities granted by the said Acts, and a Debt of 26,650/. was on that Account contracted, and 23,318/. 15 s. Part thereof, ltill remains unpaid, and Hands charged upon the Estates of the Petitioners, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parish; and representing to the House, that the Controul and Jurisdiction of the said Commissioners over the Streets and other public Passages and Places within the said Parish, are not only unnecessary, but occasion a very considerable Annual Expence to the Petitioners, from which they do not receive the least Benefit; and that, if the Power and Jurisdiction of the said Commissioners, which any wife relate to the paving, cleansing, and lighting the Streets and other public Passages and Places within the said Parish of Saint James, were abolished, and proper Powers for paving, cleansing, and lighting the said Parish, were given to the Vestry and a Committee of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, in like Manner as was done by an Act of the last Session of Parliament, with respect to the Parish of Saint George, Hanover Square, the Petitioners apprehend the same would be better and more conveniently conducted, and at a much left Expence than at present: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purposes before-mentioned, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the feme, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Cedi Wray, Mr. Byng, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are Wapping the reunto subscribed, being Inhabitants of the Parish Poor, &c. of Saint John of Wapping, in the County of Middlesex, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That an Act was made in the last Session of Parliament, for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor of the Parish of Saint John of Wapping, in the County of Middlesex, and for providing a proper Workhouse and Burial Ground for the Use of the said Parish, and for opening certain Communications, and making certain Streets within the said Parish, and divers Persons are thereby appointed Trustees for carrying the same into Execution, and to be and continue such Trustees for Life, unless disqualified by the Means in the said Act mentioned; and that such Appointment of the said Trustees for Life, so far as relates to the Poor of the said Parish, may be attended with Inconveniences; but the Petitioners apprehend the same may be prevented, if Power is given to choose the Trustees for the Management of the Poor of the said Parish annually, in like Manner as is directed by an Act, made in the Sixteenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for better maintaining, regulating, and employing the Poor within the Parish of Saint George, in the County of Middlesex, and other Purposes; and that by the said first-recited Act it is enacted, that no Person, other than those intitled to be Trustees by virtue of their Offices, shall be capable of acting as a Trustee in the Execution of the said Act, unless such Person shall be Proprietor of, or occupy, a House or other Tenement which shall be charged towards the Rates for the Relief of the Poor at the Yearly Rent of 15 /. or upwards, nor be capable of acting as a Vestryman, unless such Person shall hold or occupy a House, or other Tenement, which shall be charged towards the Rates for the Relief of the Poor at the Yearly Rent of 10/. or upwards; but there is no Penalty inffifted on any Person acting as a Trustee, or a Vestryman, without being qualified as aforesaid, the Want of which, the Petitioners apprehend, will, in a great Degree, prevent such Disqualifications from having the Effect intended; and that, by the said first-recited Act, it is also enacted, that if any Person appointed, a Trustee for any of the Purposes therein mentioned, shall have any Share or Interest in any

(eers of the Poor, and other Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint Mary Whitechapel, in the County of Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Lane called Church Lane, in the Parishes of Saint Mary Whitechapel, Saint George, and the Hamlet of Mile End Old Town, in the County of Middlesex, is a great public Thoroughfare, and has Communication with l'everal Streets and Places leading from the River Thames, and into the great Turnpike Road called The Middlesex and Essex Turnpike Road, and Whitechapel High Street; and that the Inhabitants of the said Parish of Saint Mary Whitechapel, have expended large Sums of Money iu repairing and amending such Part of the said Lane as is within their Parish, notwithstanding the said Part is now in a ruinous Condition, dangerous for Carriages, and incommodious to Passengers, and if the same was properly paved and clean-led, and all Obstructions and Annoyances removed therefrom, it would be of great public Utility, and advantageous to the Inhabitants; and that there are several other Streets, Avenues, and Places, within the said Parish of Saint Mary Whitechapel, which are very ill paved, and greatly obstructed by Posts, Rails, and other Annoyances, and if the same were also properly paved, and all Obstructions and Annoyances removed, it would be of great Benefit to the Inhabitants, and all Persons passing through the lame; and that the Parish Church of Saint Mary Whitechapel being in very great need of an immediate and considerable Repair, the Petitioners have lately caused the said Church to be thoroughly repaired, the Expence whereof amounts to about 1,700l. and have already made a very considerable Assessment towards paying the Workmen employed in the said Repairs, but the same is not in anywise sufficient for that Purpose; and the making any further Assessments for immediately raising Money to defray the whole of the said Expence will be very burthensome and inconvenient to the Petitioners; and that, by an Act, passed in the Third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to enable the Parishioners to raise Money to defray the Expences of the Repairs of the said Parish Church, the Trustees appointed by the said Act were authorized to raise any Sum of Money, not exceeding i,"2oo/. for defraying the Expences of the then Repairs of the said Church; and that it will be a very great Easement and Benefit to the Petitioners, if they were now enabled to raise a Sum of Money for the Purpose of discharging the Remainder of the Expences of repairing the said Parish Church, and for paving and regulating the said Part of the said Lane, and the said several other Streets, Avenues, and Places, within the said Parish: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to empower the Petitioners to pave and regulate the said Part of the said Lane, and the said other Streets, Avenues, and Places, and to enable the Petitioners to raise Money for that Purpose, and for the Purpose of defraying the Remainder of the Expences of repairing the said Parish Church, by such Ways or Means, and under such Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Byng, Sir Wray,

tic.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Sir Cecil Wray reported from the Committee, to Leeds Road*, whom the Bill for continuing the Term, and altering and enlarging thfe Powers, of several Acts of Parliament therein mentioned, lb fef as the same relate to the repairing and amending of the Roads leading from Leeds, through Bradford and Horton, and through Bowling, and Wibsey, to Halifax, and also the Roads called Bawling lane and little Horton Lane, in the West Riding of the County of York, was committed; and to whom the Petition of several Freeholders and Inhabitants of the Villages of Bowling and Horton, in the Parish of Bradford, in the West Riding of the County of York, and the Neighbourhood thereof, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Freeholders and Inhabitants of the said Villages, and of the Neighbourhood thereof, was referred; That the Committee had considered the said Petition; and had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the feme to be true; and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report ter the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table:

the House, and read; Setting forth. That at the General Quarter Session of the Peace, held for the County of Northumberland, on the 6th of Febru 1777, before certain Justices of the Peace for the said County, the Petitioner proposed to the Court, that he would, for the Considerations in his laid Proposals specified, undertake to build a Stone Bridge across the River Tyne, opposite to the Town of Hexham, in the said County, of the Form and Dimensions therein described, the Whole to be executed in a substantial Manner, and according to a Plan to be delivered in by Mr. Smeaton, an eminent Engineer, and that the same should be built, and the other Works carried on, under his Direction and Inspection; and that the Petitioner further proposed to complete the said Bridge, and provide all necessary Materials-for the fame, over and above all the Timber,

Stone, Iron, and other Materials whatsoever, which had been prepared and provided by and at the Expence of the said County, for the Purpose of building a Bridge a little higher up the said River, upon receiving the Sum of 5,7001, from the said County, and being allowed all the said Timber, Stone, Iron, and other Materials, the said Sum to be paid by Instalments at stated Times; and that, at the said Quarter Session, the Petitioner’s Agent did in his Behalf propose and undertake to make a good and sufficient Road from the North End of the said Bridge, when built, to the Alemouth Turnpike Road, for the Sum of 400 /. such Road when made to be a public Road; and the Petitioner’s said Agent did also propose and undertake, that the Petitioner would enter into a Bond in the Sum of 9,100l.

to the said County, conditioned for building, making, finishing, and completing, the said Bridge and Road on or before the 25th Day of March 1780, and for upholding and maintaining the same respectively, for the Term of Seven Years, from the Time of their being completed, which laid Propiofals were, at the said Session, accepted of and agreed to by the Justices then present, 01 Behalf of the said County; and that, in pursuance of such Proposals and Undertakings, certain Articles of Agreement, bearing Date the 2d Day of June 1777, were entered into between Three of His Majesty’s Justices of the Peace for the said County and the Petitioner, for carrying the said Proposals and Undertakings into Execution, in Manner and on the Conditions above specified; and that, in consequence of an Order made by a Court of General Quarter Session for the said County, on the 14th of January 1778, that, for the future, no Part of the County Stock should be applied in ere€ting any new Bridge as a County Bridge in that County, without an express Act of Parliament for that Purpose, Application was made, and an Act whs passed in the Eighteenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for confirming the said Agreement with the Petitioner, and carrying the same into execution, and for making Roads and Avenues to the intended Bridge; and that, by the said Act, it was declared, that the said Bridge, when finished, should be deemed a County Bridge, and be supported and maintained for ever as such, after the Expiration of the said Term of Seven Years; and it-was further provided and declared, that the Roads or Avenues thereto should be deemed Part of the Turn-

pike Road, and be repaired as such; and that, pursuant to the Directions of the said Act, and the Terms of the said Agreement, the building of the said Bridge, and performing the other Works, were carried on under the Direction and Inspection of the said Mr. Smeaton, whose Authority and Instructions were to complete the feme in the most substantial and effectual Manner, which fas accordingly done, to the entire Satisfaction of the said Justices and the County Surveyor, and the said Bridge and Road were duly certified in January 1781, to be well and sufficiently finished and made; and that, on the nth Day of March 1782, the said new Bridge was, by the Violence of a Flood, forced down and destroyed, without its having previously suffered any apparent In-juty or Decay, and a full and careful Examination being had of what were the Causes of the Accident, it appeared to be the Opinion of able and experienced Engineers, that, from the Weakness of the Stratum, or Bed of the Rvier, now discovered and proved by this ' fatal Accident, any Bridge built thereon would be liable to be thrown down by the same extraordinary rapid Floods to which this River now appears to be liable; that although it might happen that a Bridge built there might be upheld during the said Term of Seven Years, which Term must of Necessity nearly expire before any Bridge could be built, yet it would be highly inexpedient to make the Attempt, as the Accidents to which a new Bridge will be liable are the same to which the former one was exposed, and which brought on its Destruction; and that, as there are no reasonable Expectations that a new Bridge would be permanent, the rebuilding thereof would not only be a fruitless Expence to the Petitioner, but might in the Event be burthensome and injurious to the County; and that these Circumstances were submitted by the Petitioner to the Consideration of the Justices of the Peace for the said County, at their General Quarter Session held on the 17th Day of July 1782, with an Offer on the Part of the Petitioner to pay into the public Stock of the County any Sum that should be judged reasonable, if it should be required, in order tint be might be discharged from the Security he had entered into, rather than be at the

fruidels Expence of attempting to rebuild the said Bridge, the Support of which, and the probable Charge of rebuilding the fame, would fall on the County; that the Justices appeared to be sensible of the Truth of the said Representation, and of the Inexpediency of an Attempt to rebuild the said Bridge, but conceived they had no Authority to bind the County, or to act in the Cafe, and that no Relief could be had for the County or the Petitioner but by the Aid of Parliament; and that the Petitioner being Owner of an Estate near the Site of the late Bridge, the Hopes of benefiting his Property and that of others in the like Situation, together with a With to accommodate the Public, and a firm Belief which he then entertained, that (although a former Attempt to build a Bridge near the Town of Hexham had failed of Success) a good and permanent Bridge might, by additional Skill and more liberal Expence, be coo-strufted, induced him to make his said Proposals, without any Expectation or View of Profit to arise from his Undertaking and Contraft, in fulfilling which he has actually expended more than the Sum paid him as aforesaid by the County: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that I.eave may be given to bring in a Bill for granting him such Relief, with respect to the said Articles of Agreement, as the Circumstances of his same may be found to merit and require, and to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of Richard Arkwright, of Cromford, in Arkwright’* the County of Derby, Cotton Manufacturer, was pre- Cotton fented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Macblne-Petitioner, after many Years intense Study and painful Application, and after a great Variety of repeated Experiments, invented about the Year 1768, a Machine or Machines for making Cotton into Yam in a more expeditious, as well as in a very different Manner, from any Invention that had preceded it; and in the Prosecution of his Experiments expended considerable Sums of Money, and in the Year 1769 obtained a Patent for his said Invention; and that the Petitioner, conceiving that his said Invention was capable of considerable Improvements, did, after several Years further Study and Alfiduity, improve the principles of his said Invention, and, after a large additional Expence incurred therein, brought th*e same to a greater Degree of Perfection, and also invented Machines for preparing the Cotton for spinning by a much leis expensive and much more expeditious Method than had been before pursued, for which Improvements and further Invention he also obtained a Patent in the Year 1775; and that the Petitioner has, with his Partners, in consequence of the said Patents, expended the Sum of 30,000l. and upwards in Buildings and other necessary Works, in order to carry the said Manufactory into complete Execution, over and above the Labour and Expence of instructing and training up many Thousand poor Persons, of different Ages as well as Sex, in a Knowledge of the said Manufactory; and that by the Introduction of the said Machines the Cotton is prepared and made into Yam with great Facility and Expedition, and the Twist or Thread is of a superior Nature and Excellency to any that was ever before produced: hence the Manufacturer is enabled to fell in Foreign Markets; the Callicoe Business, which promises to be of the greatest Importance to this Kingdom, has been introduced, many Thousand Persons are now, who were not before, employed in this Manufactory, and earn a comfortable Maintenance, and great and essential Benefit has of consequence resulted to the Public; and that the Petitioner has, together with his Partners, in the Course of carrying on and establishing his said Manufactory, luffcred Losses to the Amount of Four or Five thousand Pounds, by the Violence of riotous and ill-disposed Persons, who have burnt and destroyed his Buildings and other Works erected for the Purpose of carrying on the said Manufactory; and representing to the House, that the Legifla-ture has, in many Infiances, granted to Persons for a considerable Number of Years beyond the Term of their Letters Patent, an exclusive Right of exercising their Inventions, which the Petitioner submits, have been of much less public Utility and Advantage than the Inventions which he has produced; and therefore be has presumed to apply to the House, trusting that the Merit and Importance of his Inventions will be proved to be of such National Concern and Advantage, as to entitle him to the Assistance and Support of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to extend the Term granted by the First Patent in the Year 1769, so as to make the same expire with the Term granted by the Patent in the Year 1775, as feme Recom pence or Satisfaction for what, he humbly conceives, he may call his public Services and Sufferings, or that he may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Landowners, Trades-men, Manufacturers, and others, of the Counties of Gloucester, Wills, and the adjoining Counties, was pre-iented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That it appears from the Reports of various experienced Engineers, who have explored the Country between the Navigable Part of the River Isis and Severn, in the said County, that a Communication between those large and extensive trading Rivers, the Thames and Secern, by a Navigable Canal, is practicable; and it also appears, by Levels and correct Surveys since taken, that a Canal for the Navigation of Boats, Barges, and other Vessels, may be conveniently made from and out of a Navigable Part of the River Thames and at or near Leachlade, in the County of Gloucester, to or near Stroud, in the said County, there to join and communicate with the Stroud Canal Navigation, which passes into the River Severn, as also a Collateral Branch from or near Siddington, to or near the Town of Cirencester,

whereby the Two great Rivers will be united, and a Communication opened between the Port of London and the principal trading Towns in the Kingdom, by Means of the different Canals and Rivers communicating with the Severn, a Circumstance of infinite Advantage, as it will promote the Circulation of Trade, lower the Price of Carriage, improve the Landed Interest, be a great Relief to the Poor, tend to preserve the public Roads, and contribute every Way-to the public Welfare: And therefore praying. That Leave may by given to bring in a Bill for making and maintaining the said Canal and Collateral Branch, and also Railways and Roads of Communication to and with the fame, in such Manner, and under such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir William Guise, Mr. Elzoes, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.
