KrprdVnta- A Petition of the Citizens of Winchester, and the tiun m Far- Inhabitants of Saint Bartholomew Hyde, Saint John in foment. the East Soke, Saint Peters Saint Swith'ui,

and Saint Michael, the Suburbs of the said City, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners conceive it essentially necessary towards the Preservation of Public Liberty, that the Three Branches of the Legislature should maintain their several Privileges in a distinct, entire, and uninfluenced Manner; that the Petitioners think the Balance of Power, which ought ever to be kept even between these Three Branches, has been overturned, and loo much Influence thrown into the Scale of the Crown on one Hand, and the Lords on the other; and that the Petitioners are persuaded these Evils have originated from too long a Duration of Parliaments, and a very unequal Mode of Representation, both which are apparently favourable to Corruption, and notoriously productive of it; and that to remedy these Evils, the Petitioners wish to lee Parliaments of shorter Duration revived, and such a Mode of Representation as may be more equal and more conducive to the general Good established throughout the whole Kingdom; and that the Number of Citizens in the said City is Three thousand Four hundred, of whom Six hundred and Fifty at least are assessed to the Parish Rates, and actually bear Eighteen Parts in Twenty of the Burthens of all Parliamentary and Parochial Aids within the said City, and that the Inhabitants of the Suburbs are not less in Number than One thousand Five hundred, Three hundred of whom are assessed to their respective Parish Rates, futiain their Share with the Corporation and Citizens of Parliamentary Burthens within the City, and pay a far Vol. 39.

greater Part of all such Burthens than the Corporation do, yet the Two Members who represent the said ancient, large, and populous City, are elected by the Mayor and Corporation, confiding only of One hundred and Nineteen Voters, Thirty-eight whereof, and no more, being resident in the City (of whom some inhabit with their Parents, others are Lodgers, and many are not even liable to be rated at present) the Eighty-one non-resident Burgesses therefore, though nominated by and chosen under the supposed Influence of Members of the Legislature, and though mostly Strangers to the City, and altogether to its Interests, have virtually iu themselves the Power of Election, and the Citizens, in consequence, are not represented at all; deprived therefore, as the Petitioners are, of a due Share in the elective and repre-fentative Rights inherent in the Constitution of their Country, they humbly beg for a Participation of those Rights on any System which the Wisdom of the House may establish in the intended Parliamentary Reform.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Captain William Brerelon, late Governor of the City and District: of Caciti, and Commander of His Majesty’s Ships Rationed at The Philhpine Islands, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been intorined of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That an Expedition having been concerted against the Spanish Settlements, in the Island of Laconia, the same was undertaken by Troops composed of His Majesty’s 79th Regiment of Foot, and Europeans and Sepoys in the Service of the East India Company, uho were transported to the Island of Laconia, in His Majesty’s Squadron commanded by Vice Admiral Cornish, assisted by fbme Ships belonging to the Company, and, on the 6th of 1762, the City of Manila was taken by Storm, and the City of Caoitk surrendered without an Attack; and that the City of Manila, on the 2d of November following, was delivered up to certain Agents authorized by the East India Company to receive the same, in conformity to the Directions given by His Majesty to General Draper, who commanded the Land Forces employed on that Expedition; and that His Majesty, anxious to preserve the said Conquest, gave Directions to His Admirals and Generals to be assisting to the Officers of the East India Company in holding Possession thereof, until His Royal Will and Pleasure should be further signified, with regard to the future Disposition of the said Conquest, which was to depend entirely and absolutely upon His Majesty, and the Company not having sent more Officers and Servants on the Expedition than were necessary to take Charge of the City of Manila, and it being judged of great Importance, that a Sea Officer should command at Cavith (where the Naval Arsenals and Storehouses

were situatej the Petitioner was appointed Governor of the City and District of CavitS, by Vice Admiral Cornish, and remained there with His Majesty's Ships and Naval Forces under his Command, until the Restoration of the Conquest to the Spaniards, by the Treaty of Peace, which the Petitioner restored in pursuance of a Warrant for that Purpose, under His Majesty’s Sian Manual; and that the Petitioner, not having the Means of embarking the Troops after the Restoration of the Conquest, he fitted up Two old Spanish Ships, and transported the Garrisons to India; and that, during the Time the Petitioner was Governor of Cavite, he incurred very considerable Expence in carrying on the Public Service, and afterwards, upon his Deprature therefrom, he was under the Necessity of going to Batavia, where he resided Six Mouths, in hopes of being able to repair His Majesty’s Ship Falmouth, of which the Petitioner was Commander, but, upon repeated Surveys held upon the said Ship, it was found utterly impracticable to repair he^j, and he was obliged to leave her there, and take hi? Passage, and those of his Servants, to Europe, in a Dutch East Indiaman, which was attended with great Expence and Inconvenience; and that the Petitioner has also incurred

very heavy Expences by the Loft of Exchange oil Money taken up for the Use of His Majesty’s Sick Seamen and Troops employed on the Expedition, and for Costs and Damages of a Suit at Law, brought against him for Matters that were indispensably necessary in carrying on His Majesty’s Service, and several other Expences were incurred by the Petitioner during the Course of his Command in The Philippine Islands; and that the Petitioner has not yet received any Cotn-pensation for his said Diflburfements, but, on the contrary; has been at a considerable Expence in prosecuting several Memorials to the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, who are of Opinion he cannot be relieved but by the Justice and Wisdom of the Legislature:

And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and indemnify him for his said Expences and Disbursements, the detaining of which, for lo great a Length of Time, has been attended with great Injury to his private Fortune, acquired by a long and faithful Service to his King and Country.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Adam, Sir Adam Fer gusson, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber.

That a Stream of Water is brought into the said Town, by Means of Pipes, for the Use of the Inhabitants, which may be regulated so as to he much more useful and beneficial to them, and an additional Supply may be also brought in from certain Springs in the Neighbourhood, which would greatly increase the Benefit to the said Inhabitants; and that it would render the said Town, and also the Village of Tanshelf, which adjoins thereto, much more agreeable and commodious, if the same w'ere properly paved, lighted, and cleansed; and that there is a Charity School in the said Town, founded and endowed by various Subscriptions and Donations, and to which appertain divers Closes and Parcels of Landed Property, but the same is at present under no legal Regulation whatsoever, and the Inhabitants are desirous of putting the same under proper Regulations; and that there are also in the said Town and Village several Hospitals, and other charitable Institutions, which want better Regulation and Improvement in their several Foundations, Establishments and Revenues; and that qn Act of Parliament lately passed for an Inclosure and Division of a certaiq District of Ground called Pontefract Park, by virtue whereof a Pasture has been set out for the Use of the Inhabitants of the said Town and Village, and made Parcel of the said Town, and in the said Act are contained several Regulations for the Management of the said Pasture, but the same have been found by Experience to be defective, and to require Amendment: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the several Purposes above-mentioned, in such Manner, with such Powers, and under such Regulations and Restrifilions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Mettish Mr. &c.:

And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Hamlets, and Places, within the said Hundred, for railing Money for discharging the Interest of the principal Sum to be borrowed as aforesaid, and for defraying the Expences attending the Management, Support, and Maintenance, of the said Poor, and likewise for paying off the Principal Money authorized to be borrowed for the Purposes aforesaid, but the said Hates or Assessmenta are never to exceed in any one Year the Sum that had been annually rated, alfefied, or expended, for the Relief of the Poor within such Parishes, Hamlets, and Places respectively, upon an Average of Seven Years, to be reckoned from Easter 1767; and that, in pursuance of the Powers granted to the Petitioners by the said Act, they have purchased Ground, and erected proper and commodious Buildings thereon, for the reception and Employment of the said Poor, and have also borrowed a considerable Sum of Money upon the Credit and Security of the said Grounds and Buildings, and of the Rates or Assessments authorized to be made by them as aforesaid, which {till remains due; and the Petitioners find, that the Produce of the Rates or Assessments they are authorized to make, is insufficient to enable them to carry the said Act into Execution, and, unless they are authorized to raise some further Sums of Money, over and above the Produce of the said Rates or Afi’efimeots, the Principal Money so borrowed, and the Interest thereof, cannot be paid oftj and the Poor within the said Hundred supported and maintained: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enabling the Petitioners to carry the Purposes of the said Act into Execution, by such W ays and Means, and in such Manner, as the House shall think proper.

A Petition of William Mence, of Moorfields, Glove Mence’s Dyer, being offered to be presented to the House; Lodes by the

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Riotsinl780* Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioner being a Papist, became one of the Objects of the Outrages committed in the Month of June 1780, in and about the Metropolis, and his Loss amounting to more than 100l. he could derive no Benefit from the Vote which passed this House in the last Session of Parliament, for reimbursing such Sufferers by the said Riots whose Lois or Damage amounted to 100l. or less; and that the Petitioner’s same is lb circumstanced, that as to the chief Part of his Loss, the Statute of the First of George the First, called The Riot Act, affords him no Relief, for the Petitioner being out of Town when the Rioters sent a Message that they intended to pay him a Visit, his Servants thought it prudent to, and did, remove the chief of his Effects, amounting to 160 /. to the House of a Neighbour for greater Safety; and that on the 7th. of June the Rioters performed their Promise, in afiem-bling at, and beginning to pull down, his House, but being informed by some of the Bystanders of such previous Removal, they instantly repaired to the Place where they were deposited, carried them to a Fire, and there completely destroyed them; and that the Petitioner brought his Action in the Court of Common Pleas, with Intention to recover his whole Loss, but the Judge who tried the Cause was of Opinion, that the Goods being removed off the Premises previous to the Riot, and no Felony committed at the House where they were deposited, by " pulling down or demolishing,

" or beginning to pull down or demolish," as described in the above Act, lie certainly could not recover for those Goods, and the Jury thereforeonly found a Verdict for the Damages done to the Petitioner’s own House; and that the Petitioner having thus suffered by a public Calamity, his Servants having endeavoured to prevent the Mischief as much as lay in their Power, by previously removing the Goods oft’ the Premises, and the Petitioner having in vain uled his utmost Efforts to recover a Recom pence by Law, and not being in Circumstances to afford such a Loss, therefore prays the House to grant him the like Reconipence as was granted to the Sufferers whose Loss or Damage amouhted to 1001, or less, or such other Relief as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

of Draft. interested in the Exportation of Brass, 4’C. was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by the Acts of the 33d of Henry the Eighth, and the 2d and 3d of Edward the Sixth, the Exportation of Brass, 8$c. is prohibited under very severe Penalties; and that, for many Years pall, several Companies have been established in this Kingdom for the making of Brass,;

and that the above Laws being passed at so remote a Period, have been looked upon as obsolete, the Exportation of Brals having been constantly permitted, tl^at Article constituting a large Proportion of the Cargoes sent to the Coast of Africa, and many other Parts of the World; and that, some Months since, a considerable Seizure was made of Brass sold by some of the Petitioners for Export, and upon Application to the Commissioners of the Customs, they did not think themselves authorized, under the aforesaid Acts, to allow of the Exportation; and representing to the House, that from the large Capitals, and Numbers of Persons employed in the said Manufacture, it is an Object of considerable Consequence to the general Commerce of the Kingdom; and, as the Tenor of the above Acts is so incon-fiftent with the Interest of the British Manufacturer, therefore praying for the Repeal of the Prohibitory Clauses in the said Acts, or for such other Relief as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the

Table.

Lever's A Petition and Representation of Sir Ashton Lever,

Museum. Knight, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner, in the early Part of his Life, having a Turn for Natural History, began to collect Specimens of every Kind, and being flattered by his great Success, resolved to remove his Museum to the Vol. 39.

Metropolis, not doubting but he could make it, by its Pre-eminence over all other Collections, a national Honour; and that, notwithstanding the Difficulty and Expence of this Undertaking, he entered upon it with determined Spirit, and has pursued it in such a Manner as to have secured every capital Article that has offered itself, and by selecting out of some Hundred thousand Specimens, has actually formed a Collection superior to any Thing of the Kind in Europe, or perhaps to them all united, as it comprehends Subjects not to be found in any other Cabinet, with others more elegant in their Attitudes, and more perfect in their Preservation; and that the Petitioner has persevered in this Pursuit at a very great Expence, encouraged by a firm Belief that it might be rendered worthy the Attention of the Nation, in which he has been confirmed by the Opinion of Persons of the first Consequence, so that it is now grown too great a Concern for any Individual; and that, notwithstanding this Collection had been thus made, in hopes that it would have been purchased for the Use and Benefit of the Public, yet, from the critical Situation of the Times, it has been thought improper to apply for the Indulgence of Parliament in the Mode he intended otherwise to have done: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to authorize and impower the Petitioner, his Executors, Administra-. tors, and Assigns, to sell and dispose of the said Museum and Collection, and the several Pieces composing the lame, in such Manner as the Petitioner, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, shall think proper, without being liable or subject to any Penalty or Forfeiture imposed by any Act or Acts of Parliament against any Sale or Sales by Way of Lottery, or Lots, Tickets, Numbers, or Figures; and that such Sale or Sales lb to be made of the said Museum, and of the several Pieces composing the fame, by the Petitioner, his Executors, Administrators, or Assigns (before a Day in the Act to be specified) may be good and valid, any Law or Statute to the contrary thereof notwithstanding.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Chamberlains and Four-and- Alnwick twenty, and the rest of the Freemen of the Borough Inclosure. of Alnwick, in the County of Northumberland, and of the Widows of deceased Freemen, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, Was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Town of Almcick is an ancient Borough* consisting bf ancient Burgages or Borough Houses, for which there are certain small Burgage Rents, or Quit Rents, paid to the Duke of Northumberland, Lord of the Manor and Borough aforesaid; and that there are, within the said Borough, Ten Companies or Fraternities of Freemen, who are a Body corporate by Prescription, and are fcifed of certain ancient Estates within the said Manor and Borough; and the Management of the Business and Concerns of the said Freemen has, for Time immemorial, been performed by a fclcCfc Number of the Freemen, called Chamberlains and Four-and-twenty, amounting to Twenty-four Persons in the whole, Eight of whom have been annually returned by the said Chamberlains and Four-and-twenty, to the Court Leet Of the Lord of the said Manor, out of which Number Four Persons have usually been eleCled Chamberlains by the Lord’s Steward at thb said Court for the Year ensuing, and fwbrii before him to the due Execution of their Office; and that there is adjoining to the said Town or Bbrdugh, a large TraCl of Land, called Almcick Moor, situate within and Part of the said Manor of Alnwick, and, by virtue of certain Grants from the Lords of the said Manor, the said Freemen are entitled to Common of Pasture, and to divers other Privileges on the said

Moor, they paying to the Lord of the Manor Two Shillings per Annum for the Liberty of depasturing their Cattle thereon in the Fence Month; and that the said Freemen, or such of them as have been resident in the Town or Parish of Alnwick, have actually enjoyed such Right of Common, and other Privileges, over the whole of the said Moor, until the Time of making the Inclosures therefrom, and the Widows of Freemen, as well as the said Freemen themselves, resident in the said Town, have allb uniformly enjoyed the said Right of Common and other Privileges; and that long after the making of the said Grants, and for some Time past, divers Parcels of the said Moor have from Time to Time been inclosed therefrom, and cultivated by the Chamberlains and Four-and-twenty, and some of the said Freemen, but without the Conient of the Lord of the said Manor and the rest of the said Freemen of Alnwick; and that the Lord and Lady of the said Manor and Borough for the Time being, by certain Articles of Agreement, bearing Date the 6th Day of March 1762, did consent that the said Inclosures should be established to the said Freemen and Widows, and should continue to be let to Farm for their Benefit, and also to grant to them certain Privileges therein mentioned, and did likewise agree to such other Matters as are in the said Articles contained; and that the Rents and Profits of the said Inclosiires respectively, have from Time to Time been received by the said Chamberlains and Four-and-twenty, and have, or ought to have, been applied for the Use of the said Freemen, and the Widows of Freemen deceased; and that the said Duke of Northumberland, being desirous of shewing further Favour and Regard towards the said Freemen of Almcick, hath consented to permit an Improvement

on other Parts of the said Moor, and to grant certain Privileges for that Purpose, as well for the Accommodation of the said Freemen, as for the ornamenting that Part of the Country; and the said Chamberlain and Four-and-twenty, with the rest of the said Freemen, are desirous that the same should be carried into effectual Execution; and that divers Disputes have arisen, touching the Application of the Rents and Profits arising from the said several Inclosures, as also of the Rents and Profits of the said ancient Estates, and other the Properties or Revenues of the said Freemen; for Remedy whereof, divers of the said Freemen, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the said Freemen (except the Members of the Four-and-twenty) and also divers of the Widows of deceased Freemen, residing within the said Borough, have filed a Bill in Chancery against the said Chamberlains and Four-and-twenty, for the Time being, praying a Discovery and an Account of the Matters therein mentioned, and also that the Rights and Interests of the said Freemen resident in the said Borough, to their laid Estates, Properties, and Privileges, might be established, and that proper Directions might be given for the future Enjoyment thereof; and that divers Disputes have also arisen among the Petitioners, the said Freemen of Alnwick, touching the Government and Conllitu-

tion of the said Corporation; and the Petitioners are desirous of putting an End to such Litigations and Disputes, as well touching the Revenues of the said Corporation, as the Government and Constitution thereof, and that the Affairs of the said Freemen, particularly with respect to the Revenue belonging to them, should in future be subjected to certain Regulations, which, the Petitioners apprehend, will greatly conduce to secure to the Freemen of the said Town, the Benefit of the several Grants made to them by the Lords of the said Manor, and of the other Properties, Rights, and Privileges belonging to the said Freemen, and that the Articles of Agree-06

ment entered into as aforesaid, should in Part be effectually established and confirmed, and also that such further Improvements of the said Moor, as have been proposed by the said Duke of Northumberland, should be made, and that there is no Free School within the said Borough, for the Education of the Children of the Freemen (except a very inconsiderable Charity School, at which some of the Children of the poorer Sort of Freemen are taught to read) and it would tend greatly to the Benefit of the Freemen to have such a Free School instituted, and to have Part of the Revenues of the said Corporation appropriated for the Support of the lame, and for building a new' School and School House for that Purpose, and to have certain Regulations elta-blished touching the Choice and Removal of such Schoolmaster, and for the good Order and Government of the said School: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, and for carrying the Intentions of the said Parties into effectual Execution.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Will Middleton, Sir Thomas Clavering, See.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons,

Papers, and Records.

and that the Trustees lb deemed to be disqualified, are, amongst others, nearly all the Gentlemen of Property and Consequence in the Counties of Dorset and Hants, for that of Eighty-three Trustees named in the said Act, who are now living, and either reside or have considerable Estates in those Counties, Seventy-three at least come within the Description of those disqualified as aforesaid; and that the Petitioners, and the said other Trustees, have incurred their present Disqualification, either by being unacquainted with their Appointment as Trustees for executing the said Act, till after the Time limited for their taking on themselves the Trull was elapsed, or by not being apprized that their desisting to act for a certain Length of Time, would render them incapable of ever acting in future; A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Dealers in Tea, in the City of Bristol.

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are greatly injured in their Trade, not being on an equal Footing with those resident in and near London, by reason of an Act made in the Twenty-first Year of His present Majesty, whereby it is enacted, that no Tea exceeding Forty Pounds Weight (not being in the original Chest in which the same was imported by the East India Company) at any Time dirtfted to the same Person, shall be removed from any Place in the Kingdom, not being within the Limits of the Weekly Bills of Mortality, to any other Place out of the said Limits not within the Place from which the same shall be so removed, upod Pain of being forfeited; and, by another Act, made in the Twenty-second Year of His Majesty’s Reign, the Quantity is limited to Twenty Pounds Weight; and that the City of Bristol is the principal Market for the greatest Part of Wales, and the Vessels that come from Cardigan arrive but Once in Three or Four Months; from Haverfordwest Once in a Month, from Pembroke Once in a Month or Six Weeks, from Tenby, Swansea, and Neath, Once in Six Weeks or Two Months, and from Newton btit Once in Two Months, so that they cannot take a sufficient Quantity to supply the Demands from one Voyage to another; and although a Vessel arrives from ry Fortnight,

that Place and the Country round it cannot now be sufficiently supplied, notwithstanding the Petitioners may have a Sufficiency in their Warehouses, by Means whereof great Encouragement is given to Smugglers; and that, in the Counties of Somerset, Gloucester, and Wilts, where there are several Carriers, the Shopkeeper who may want about Eighty or One hundred Pounds Weight of Tea, mull send to several Wholesale Dealers, and be' a 1 the extra: Expence of several Packages, and employ many Carriers, when One may take the Whole; and a Shopkeeper may have Occasion for Eighty or One hundred Pounds Weight of Tea of divers Sorts, but not know how to dispense With Sixty or Seventy Pounds Weight of Green Tea, or Three or Four hundred Weight of Bobea Tea, which the Chests from the India House Vo l.39.

usually contain, and there being but One Carrier to several Places where those Shopkeepers reside, they cannot be supplied; and that it often happens that a Tea Dealer has Orders given him for Six or Eight different Sorts of Tea, and according to the Act, he can only fend Two or Three Pounds Weight of each; and that in case the before-mentioned Clauses are not repealed, the Trade of the Petitioners will be almost annihilated, and Smuggling of Necessity be greatly encouraged: And therefore praying the House to repeal such Parts of the before-mentioned Statutes as are so prejudicial to the Petitioners.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

and the Petitioners apprehend that the paving, cleansing, and lighting the said Street may be more conveniently done, if such Part thereof as lies within the said Parish of Saint Mary le Strand be put under the Direction and Management of the same Persons as the other Part of the said Street, lying within the said Parish of Saint Martin in the Fields,

A Petition of the Grocers and Tea Dealers in the Rtmoval of City of Norwich, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Tea. was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That by an Act passed in the Twenty-first Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for repealing the Duties payable upon Chocolate made in Great Britain, and for granting certain Inland Duties upon Cocoa Nuts in lieu thereof; for the better and more effectual securing the Revenue of Excise, and of the Inland Duties under the Management of the Commissioners of Excise, and for preventing Frauds therein, and other Purposes, it is enacted, that no Tea exceeding Forty Pounds Weight (not being in the original Chest in which the same was imported by the East India Company) at any one Time, directed to the same Person, shall be removed from any Place in this Kingdom, not being within the Limits of the Weekly Bills of Mortality, or of the chief Office of Excise in London, to any other Place out of the said Limits, not within the Place from which the same shall be so removed, upon Pain of being forfeited; and, by another Act, passed in the Twenty-second Year of His laid Majesty’s Reign, the Quantity is limited to Twenty Pounds Weight; and that although 1 the Intent of the said Acts appear to have been the Prevention of Smuggling, yet, the Petitioners apprehend, they obviously tend to promote, instead of preventing it; and as Tea is an Article of almost univerlal Consumption in this Kingdom, and for which there is consequently a general and large Demand, the Opportunities of Conveyance from Place to Place, in many Parts of the Kingdom, cannot, under the Restrictions of the said Acts, be frequent enough to supply the necessary Demand; and, if the legal Dealers in the Country are restrained from supplying their Customers with as much Tea as they may want, it will be an additional Inducement to Retailers and Consumers to buy it of Smugglers; and that the Opportunities of Conveyance to many of the Towns and Villages in the County of Norfolk, from the City of Norwich (which is the principal Market for Tea for the whole County) come only once a Week, and to some of them still seldomer, and therefore the Restrictions alluded to must affect the Tea Dealers in the said City and County in a very considerable Degree; and that, even where the Opportunities of Conveyance are frequent enough to supply the usual Demand for Tea, still it is a Hardship upon the fair Dealer, that the Quantity he may have Occasion for, must be sent in several Packages, and by several Carriers: And therefore praying, That lb much of the aforesaid Acts as respects the Conveyance of Tea from Place to Place, not being within the Limits aforesaid, may be repealed.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his Majesty King George the First, intituled, "An Act for making the River Douglas, alias Asland, navigable from the " River Ribble, to IVig, in the County Palatine of Lancasterand also, an Act passed in the Tenth

Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled,

" An Act for making and maintaining a navigable Cut,

" or Canal, from Leeds Bridge, in the County of York,

11 to The North Lady's Walk, in Liverpool, in the County " Palatine of Lancaster, and from thence to the River Mersey," were read: And,

Mr. John Hardy, Law Clerk to the Company of Proprietors of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal, being examined, informed your Committee, That in pursuance of the said lirft-mentioned Act, the River Douglas hath been made navigable; and, in pursuance of the second-mentioned Act, a considerable Part of that Canal, to the Extent of Sixty Miles, hath been made, and is now navigable, to the great Benefit and Advantage of the adjacent Countries and the Public.

That the Company of Proprietors of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal, finding it efl'ential to their Interests to be possessed of the Right of Navigation on the said River Douglas, they agreed with the Proprietors thereof for the complete Purchase of it, and are accordingly now the Owners of that Navigation — That a considerable Part of the Purchase Money has been paid, but that there is a Balance yet undischarged, which the Company of Proprietors of the Leeds and Canal find

themselves unable to provide for without the Aid of Parliament.

That the Powers of the said Act of the Sixth Year of King George the First, have proved insufficient for effecting the Purposes thereby intended, and feme of the Provisions thereof are incompatible with the Pro-Vo l, 39.

T73

visions contained in the said Act of the Tenth Year of His present Majesty, particularly with respect to the Tenure of the Property, which is Part Freehold and Part Leasehold, in the Douglas Navigation, and all Personal Estate in the Leeds and Liverpool Canal; and that it would be for the Benefit of the Whole, that all the Shares should be made of the Nature of Personal Estate.

That in order to complete and preserve the Navigation of the said River, it is necessary that feme further Powers should be granted, particularly with respect to the Choice of new Commissioners — to varying the Tolls — punching Persons destroying the Works — weighing Boats, and making Bye Laws.

That the Powers of the said Act of the Tenth of His present Majesty also want Amendment, Addition, and Alteration; and the Sanction of Parliament is requisite for confirming the Purchase of the said River Douglas Navigation.

And being further examined, he said, That the Company of Proprietors of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal have incurred a Debt of above lb,000l. the greater Part of which Sum hath been expended in the Improvement of the said River Douglas; and that about the Stun of 4,000l. is wanted to complete the Purchase of that Navigation — That in order to Secure the Discharge of the said Debt, and the Balance of the said Purchase Money, it is expedient and necessary, that a Sufficient Sum should be borrowed on the Credit of the Tonnage Duties granted by the said Acts of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave lie given to bring in a Bill for altering and enlarging the Powers of an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of King George the First, for making the River Douglas, alias navigable

Duncombe and Sir Cecil Wrey do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Representa- A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town of Lament!'81" bridge, whose Names are thereunder signed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the present disproportioned and unequal Representation of the Commons of this Realm appears to be in no Instance more remarkable than in that of the Privileges of Election exercised in great Towns, by a finall Proportion of the Inhabitants, to the Exclusion of the rest, who cannot without Regret feel themselves defiitute of the first of Constitutional Rights, a Share in the Election of those who are chosen to represent them: Under these Circum-liances, the Petitioners desire to state to this Honourable House, that the Two Members of Parliament to represent the Town of Cambridge, are elected by One hundred and Eighty Free Burgesses of the Corporation, of which not more than One hundred are resident; and that the Number of Inhabitants in the said Town is by Computation Seven thousand, of which about Twelve hundred are assessed to the Parish Rates; to the Wisdom and Justice of this Honourable House the Petitioners therefore respectfully apply, praying that their Petition may be taken into Consideration, and such Relief granted as is agreeable to the Confiitutional Principles of Representation.

and that the Petitioner is Owner of a certain Tra6l of Low Ground called Arram Carr, containing upwards of 300 Acres, and also of divers other Parcels of Low Ground situate in the Township of Arram, and within the Petitioner’s Manor of Lee-conjieid, in the said East Riding, which Low Grounds are overflowed with Water, and incapable of Improvement in their present State; and that the Petitioner’s said Grounds are upon the same I-evel with, and do nearly adjoin upon, the said Tracts of Open Ground proposed to be drained by the intended Bill, and the proposed Course and Outfall of the said intended Drainage are the only ones which the Nature of the Country is capable of for draining the Petitioner’s said Low Grounds, and would effectually drain the fame; and that the Petitioner’s Agent attended a Meeting of the Proprietors interested in the said proposed Drainage, held at Hull, on the 25th Day of January last, for the Purpose of signing the said Petition, and did apply and propose to have the Petitioner’s said Grounds included in the said proposed Drainage, upon the Terms of paying a proportionable Share of the Expence thereof; but several of the Proprietors then present objected thereto, on account of the Petitioner’s said Grounds not being included in the Notices which had been given pursuant to the Standing Order of the House, and that the Petitioner, residing at a great Distance from his said Estate, was not apprized of the said intended Application to the House early enough to cause such Notice to be given within the Time required by the said Standing Order: And therefore praying, That Provision may be made in the said intended Bill, for draining his said Grounds, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Mr. Ord reported from the Committee, who were appointed to enquire what Laws are expired, or near expiring, and to report their.Opinion, from Time to Time, to the House, which of them are fit to be revived or continued, That the Committee had made a further Enquiry; and had come to One other Resolution; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered'it in at the Clerks Table: Where the Resolution of the Committee was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for the better Regulation of Laftage and Ballastage in the River Thames, which was to continue in Force from the lft Day of June 1733, for Five Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty, was further continued from the Expiration thereof for Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act, made in the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of his said* late Majesty, was further continued from the Expiration thereof for Eleven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act, made in the Thirty-second Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty, was amended, and further continued until the 24th Day of June 1770, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty King George the Third, was further continued from the Expiration thereof for Eleven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

The laid Resolution being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

MR. Dempster reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of John Esquire,

was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same was read; and is as followeth; v

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for compelling John J Esquire, to return " into this Kingdom, and for restraining him, in case of " his Return, from going out of this Kingdom for a " limited Time; and for discovering his Estate and " Effects, and preventing the transporting or alienating " of the lame," was read: And,

The Agent for Mr. Whiteh delivered in to Your Committee, a Particular and Inventory of all the real and personal Estate, which Mr. was possessed of upon the ill of April 1781, or any Time after, with

I&3

an Account of the Manner in which the same had been disposed of; which Particular and Inventory is hereunto annexed: Then

Mr. Whitehill was called, who informed your Committee, that he left this Kingdom in November 1781.

And being asked, Whether he was at that Time under any Apprehension from his private Creditors? he said. He knew they might call on him, and he had it not in his Power to comply with their Demands if they had done so; that he had not at that Time Property in England nearly equal to his Debts, but he since has had remitted to him from Abroad between 20 and 30,000l.

And being asked, Whether he was in perfect Health when he lett this Kingdom? he said, No, far from it, being very much afflicted with the Gout.

And being asked, If he was able at that Time, to find Sureties to the Amount of the Sum required by Act of Parliament ? he said, He believed he should have found great Difficulty, he did not think he could have procured Suretiek immediately; that these Apprehcn-fions remained upon his Mind during the Time he was Abroad; and if Bail to that Amount had been procured, it would moll likely have brought his Creditors upon him.

And being asked, Whether the Bulk of his Fortune was then in India? he answered, Yes, and still is.

And being asked, If the Particular and Inventory, which had been delivered in to the Committee, was a full and true State of his Affairs ? he said, It was.

The PARTICULAR and INVENTORY of me John Whitehill, Esquire, according to the bed of my Knowledge and Belief, of all and Angular the Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, Goods, Chattels, Debts, and personal Estate whatsoever, in Europe, the East Indie, China, or elsewhere, which I the said John Whitehill

was seized or possessed of, or entitled to in my own Right, and which any other Person or Persons was or were foiled or possessed of, or in Trull for me, or to or for my Use or Benefit, upon the ill Day of 1781, or at any Time after (my Wearing Apparel, and the Furniture of any House or Houses belonging to me the said John Whitehill excepted) and an Account of the Manner in which the same hath been disposed of.

In the Year 1777, I purchased the Lease of a House, with the Appurtenances, situate in Queen Anne Street TVest, in the Parish of St.Mary le Bone, in the County of Middlesex, for the Sum of 4,800l. and the same was by Indenture of Assignment, bearing Date the 2d Day of June 1777, made between Sir Henry Peyton, of the First Part, Sir Patrick Blake, of the Second Part, and me the said John Whitehill, of the Third Part, in Consideration of the said Sum of 4,800l. by me paid to the said Sir Patrick Blake, assigned to me for the Remainder of a Term of Ninety-six Years and an Half, wanting Ten Days.

In June 1777, I mortgaged the said House, with the Appurtenances, for the Sum of 4,500l. to General Joseph Smith, and during my Residence in India, in the Year 1780, having an Intention of promoting a Marriage betw een One of my Nieces and Thomas Lewin, Esquire, my Secretary at Fort St. George, in India, I did promiseto give him the said House, and the Furniture therein, freed and discharged from the Principal and Interest due to the said General Smith on the said Mortgage; and the said Mr. Lewin having, in my Absence, as my Attorney, been called upon by the said General Smith for the said Principal and Interest, he did thereupon pay to the said General Smith the Sum of 5,157/. 15s. 5 d.the Amount thereof, and an Assignment of the said Mortgage was thereon made and executed by the said General Smith to Mr. Lewin, in February 1782, which Assignment has not yet been executed by me, though I think myself bound in honour to execute the same in pursuance of my said Promise.

I have no Right Title, or Interest, nor hath any other Person or Persons whomsoever in Trull for me, any Right, Title, or Interest in or to any other House or Houses, Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments in Europe, the East Julies, or China, or in any other Place whatsoever, except the Estate in Tobago herein after mentioned.

Admiral Darby reported from the Committee to whom the Petition of Stephen Drew, of Stoketon, in the County of Cornwall, and William Dunsterville, of Plymouth, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth, viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, intituled, "An Act for cleansing, preserving, and maintaining the Harbour of

uter, lying near Plymouth, in the county of;

" and for the cleansing and keeping clean the Pool, " commonly called Sutton Pool, lying in Plymouth " aforesaid," was read; whereby it was enacted, That Benjamin Joules, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, should, at his and their own proper Costs, dear and cleaofe the said Harbour of Catwater, and tire said Pool, called Sutton Pool, in Manner therein particularly mentioned, and under the Direction of certain Supervisors therein named; and that he and they should, from the 25th of March 1710, have the foie ballasting and unballafiing of all Ships and Vessels in the Harbours and Waters, called Plymouth Sound, Hammoaze, Catzvater, and Sutton Pool, or within the Road between Saint Nicholas Island and the main

Land; to bold the said foie Privilege of ballasting and unballafiing for Seventy-one Years; and the said Act ascertains what Rates should be paid for ballasting and unballafiing, and was to continue in Force for Seventy-three Years — And

Mr. John Bud informed your Committee, That certain Shoals and great Banks of Sand, which have been caused in the said Harbour of Catwater, by the Tides and Violence of Storms, have not been removed and carried away, nor the Water flowing over 4he Middle Bank or Middle Ground deepened, according to the Directions of the said Act; and that the Supervisors thereby appointed have, not of late Years inspected, supervised, or given any Directions whatsoever in relation to the Undertaking of the said Benjamin Joules, and the Performance and Execution thereof, nor made any Orders relating thereto.

And the Witness further said, That the said Harbour of Catwater, is separated and divided from the Sea, called Plymouth Sound, by a Peninsula, or small Neck of Land, called Mount-Batton Field, which was formerly fenced and secured on the West Part thereof towards Plymouth Sound, by a strong Wall, long since destroyed and beat down by the Violence of the Winds and Seas, by which great Quantities of the Soil of the said Peninsula have been washed away; and unless the said Wall be rebuilt, there is great Reason to believe, that by the high Tides and Violence of Storms, a thorough Breach will be made from Plymouth Sound through the said Peninsula, into the said Harbour of Catwater, which will entirely ruin and render unfit the said Harbour for any Ships or Vessels to be or lie therein. — Then

Mr. Drezo, the Petitioner, informed your Committee, That he and Mr. Dunsterville have made Proposals for undertaking, at their own Costs and Charges, to deepen and cleanse the said Harbour, and to keep clear and cleanse the fame; and also to rebuild the said Wall at Mount Bat ton, and secure the said Peninsula or Neck of Land from being washed or destroyed, upon receiving such Encouragement, and under such Regulations, as to Parliament dial I seem meet; and that the Expence of building the said Wall will amount to 4,500l.; the other Works will be an Annual Expence — Then

Mr. John Bidcock, a Builder, was called, who said,

e.

He would undertake to build the said Wall for the above Sum; the Dimensions of which is proposed to be 320 Feet in length; the Height above the Beach 15 Feet; and to be 7 Feet thick at Top, and 11 at the Bottom.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for cleansing, clearing, and rendering more safe and commodious, the Harbour of Catwater, within the Port of Plymouth, in the County of Devon: And that Admiral Darby, Sir Frederick Leman Rogers, Mr. Parker, and Mr. Rolle, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Two Acts, passed in the Twenty-first and Twenty-second Years of His present Majesty, wherein the Sum of 20,000l. was granted towards rebuilding His Majesty’s Gaol of Newgate, in the City of London, were read: And,

George Dance, Esquire, Surveyor to the City of London, being examined, said, That the said Gaol of Nezigate being under the immediate Care and Direction of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the City of London, they have proceeded with all possible Dispatch to lay out the Money so granted by Parliament, in fitting up and providing different Apartments for the Reception of Prisoners, whereby the middle Quadrangle (which is now occupied as a Prison for Felons) with the Chapel and Lodge, is finished, the North, or Debtors Quadrangle, is also very nearly finished, and will be fit to receive Prisoners on or before Lady Day next.

That a spacious Infirmary is built and finiftied, the Cells for condemned Prisoners substantially repaired and improved, and a defective Part thereof rebuilt; the Press Yard paved, and the Passage for conveying the Prisoners to the Sessions House arched over, in order to prevent Escapes.

That in the Prosecution of this Business, there has been expended the Sum of 18,105/. 10 9 (includ-

A Petition of the Gentry, Clergy, Freeholders, and Inhabitants of the Town of Lyme Regis, in the County of Dorset, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Inequality of the present State of Representation, though derived from a Variety of concurrent Causes, appears to the Petitioners to be m no Instance more remarkable than in that of the Privileges of Election exercised in Towns by a very small Proportion of the Inhabitants, to the Exclusion of the rest, who feel themselves destitute of the first Constitutional Rights, a Share in the Electron of those who are chosen to represent them; and that the Two Representatives for Lyme are elected by the Corporation, consisting of a Mayor and Fifteen capital Burgesses, and a few Honorary Freemen, most of whom live at very considerable Distances from the Town; and that the Town of Lyme is an ancient and well-inhabited Town, consisting of more than Six hundred Inhabitants, of whom upwards of One hundred are regularly assessed to the Parish Rates; to the Wisdom and Justice of the House, the Petitioners therefore respectfully apply, praying that their Petition may be taken into Consideration, and such Relief granted in the Premises, as shall appear best adapted to the State and Circumstances of the Town, agreeable to the Principles of Representation.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Richard Whitworth and Mr. Benjamin Grazebroo/c, Surveyors, being examined, said, That they have explored the Country between the Navigable Part of the River Isis and Severn, and find that a Communication between those large and extensive Trading Rivers the Thames and Severn, by a Navigable Canal, is practicable.

That it appears, by Levels and correct Surveys which they have since taken, that a Navigable Canal may be conveniently made from and out of a Navigable Part of the River Thames and Isis, at or near Leachlade, in the County of Gloucester, to or near Stroud, in the said County, there to communicate with the Stroud Canal Navigation, which passes into the River Severn; as also, a Collateral Branch from or near Siddington to or near the Town of Cirencester, whereby the Two great Rivers will be united, and a Communication opened between the Port of London, and the principal Trading Towns in the Kingdom by Means of the different Canals and Rivers communicating with the Severn.

And the Witnesses added, That the above Work will be attended with great public Utility, by promoting the Circulation of Trade, lowering the Price of Carriage, improving the Landed Interest, and will be a great Relief to the Poor, and tend to preserve the public Roads.

0 in the several Counties of Stafford, Derby, Leicester,

Nottingham, and Lincoln, and interested in die Navigation of the River Trent, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Navigation Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth 5 viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Vol. 35).

Act, made in the Tenth and Eleventh Years of King William the Third, intituled, "An Act for making " and keeping the River Trent, in the Counties of " Leicester, Derby, and Stafford, Navigable," was read; tod

Mr. fVHham Jessop, Engineer, being examined, said.

That the Navigation of the said River is greatly obstructed by Shoals, and other Impediments — That he had made a Survey of it, and found Sixty-seven Shallows, of which there are Twelve Fords.

And being asked. What Depth were those Shallows ? he said, Upon the Shoal at Holme Ford, Seventeen Inches in the dry Seaibn; at Fiskerton, Twenty-seven Inches; at Hoveringham, Twenty-seven Inches; at Gunthorpe, Nineteen Inches; at Burton, Thirty-two Inches; at Stoke, Twenty-five Inches; at Church, Nineteen Inches; at Eighteen Inches;

at Chilwell, Twenty-nine Inches; at Thrumpton, Twenty-

nine Inches; at Moses’s Mouth, Thirty Inches; at Sawley, Seventeen Inches. — Being asked, If it was practicable to make those Fords of a proper Depth? he laid, It was. — And being asked, What was the Depth of Water he proposed in those Fords which are not navigable ? he said he meant to allow Eighteen Inches moveable Water; which Deepening might be done according to the Estimate. — Being asked, What Burthen a Vessel must be to carry Eighteen Inches Water? he said, When new, and in good Condition, and of the largest Size now used upon the Trent, they will carry Twenty-four Tons; but when old. Twenty-two Tons — That Ten Tons could not pass the Fords at present — That the Shoals have less Water upon them than the Fords — That he has made Two Ellimates. — And being asked, What was the Subject of the other Estimate ? he said. To make it capable of carrying Vessels drawing Two Feet of Water — That the Amount of that Estimate was 7,064/. and an Annual Ekpence of 1,330/. — That the Amount of the Estimate annexed to the Petition is 4,431/- and an Annual Expence of 795/. — And being asked, What Tonnage would that carry? he laid, Under similar Circumstances, Vessels of Thirty-six Tons. — And being asked, What Burthens do the Vessels bear which are now used upon the River ? he said. Probably they will carry Forty Tons. — Being asked, What is the shalloweft of all the Shallows? he said. He thought on Dunham Rack, which is Eight Tenths of a Foot. — And being asked, Supposing the Profit to answer the Expence, and not taking the Fords into Consideration, would a greater Depth of Water than Eighteen Inches be more beneficial? he said, It would. — Being asked, How many Fords exceed Twenty-four Inches in Depth ? he said. Seven out of Twelve — That Thirty-two Inches was the greatest Depth of any of those Fords — That the least of the other Five, which do nbt exceed Twenty-four Inches, is Seventeen Inches deep — That be means to make the Channel of the River nowhere less than Thirty Feet in Breadth; but in many Parts he means to allow more. — And being asked, Whether the River was capable of a greater Depth than Eighteen Inches ? he said, It was capable of being made any Depth at a greater Expence. — And being asked, Whether he conceived any Inconvenience would arise from deepening the Fords to the Depth of Twenty-five or Twenty-six Inches ? he said, If he was a Land Owner, he would prefer a Ford of Twenty-four Inches, flatted even at Bottom, to an uncertain one of Eighteen Inches. — And being asked, Whether Carriages and Horses muke a Difficulty of fording at Thirty Inches deep? he said, He believes not. — Being asked. Whether he proposed making any1 Side Cuts ? he said. No.

And the Witness being further examined, said, That at present, Boats and Vessels navigating upon the said River are haled by Men; but that if Power was given

Earl of Pembroke's

Estates.

Birmingham

Canal.

given to hale them with Horses, it would save One Half of the Expence, and the Navigation on the said River would be attended with greater Expedition and Convenience. — And he added, That the Attainment of those Objects would complete the Communication with the Port of Hull, and greatly tend to the Encouragement and Increase of Trade carried on in the Neighbourhood of the said River, and consequently be of public Utility.

Mr. Houghton being again examined, said, That the extending of such Canal and Collateral Cuts up to the Mines mentioned by the other Witness, with additional Collateral Cuts, and also extending the said Canal from or near the Town of Birmingham, to join the Coventry Canal at or near Fazelcy, in the Parish of Tarmorth, in the County of Stafford, may be a Means of inducing the Proprietors of the O.iford and Coventry Canals to complete the lame, and thereby form a Communication between the said Mines and other Mines on the Line of the present Birmingham Canal, and the said Oxford and Coventry Canals;. as also between the Counties of Buckingham, Oxford, Northampton, and Warwick, and the Ports of Bi'istol, Liverpool, and Hull; which would be productive of great commercial Advantages to those Counties, and the Public in general.

Mr. Bull being again examined, said, He had had many Years Experience in making Canals, and particularly for Fifteen Years as principal Engineer to the O xford and Coventry Canals — That it is very practicable to make the Extensions of Canal and Collateral Cuts specified and described in the Plans annexed to the said Petitions; and that a Supply of Water, amply sufficient for the Purposes of a complete and useful Navigation, will easily be procured and kept up.

Your Committee then examined John Smeaton, Esquire, who said he had seen the w hole Tract of the Country through which the said Extensions of Canal and Collateral Cuts are intended to be made, and very carefully examined the Supplies of Water that may be procured for their Use; the Result of which Examination was, a full Assurance, in his Opinion, that there must be Plenty of Water to be had for the Purposes of Navigation on the said Extensions of Canal and Collateral Cuts; and that, if the Demand for Water should be greater in the Course of Time, by Means of an Increase of Trade thereon, the greater will of course be the Quantity of Water to be procured from the Mines, beyond what will be necessary for the Supply of the Extensions' and Collateral Cuts.

To prove the Allegations of the last mentioned Petition,

John Meredith, Esquire, Agent for the said Company of Proprietors, being examined, said, That the Company are willing and desirous to undertake the making of the Extensions of Canal and Collateral Cuts above-mentioned, as specified in the Plans annexed to their said Petition; and that the Individuals who have signed the said last mentioned Petition, are very considerable Proprietors of the present Birmingham Canal.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Richard Whitworth, Surveyor, being examined, said, That the Navigation of the said River is much impeded, and many Delays in Trade occasioned, for Want of a proper Towing rath to hale their Vessels with Horles, which would be done with more Expedition, and at Half the Expence of the present Method of drawing by Men — And added. That the Lessees of the said Navigation are willing to make Compensation for the Property necessary for the above Purpose.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for empowering Persons navigating Vessels upon the River Trent, between a Place called Wilden Ferry, in the Counties of Derby and Leicester, or one of them, "and the Town of Burton upon Trent, in the County of Stafford, to hale the same with Horses: And that the Lord Lewisham, Sir JohWrottesley, and Mr. Gilbert, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Freeholders and principal Inha- Re prefen ta-bitants in the North West Division of the County of tion in L’ar-Devon, whose Names are thereunder written, was pre- lament, fented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners beg Leave to call the Attention of the House to Two Subjects of Reformation, which the Petitioners conceive essential to the Preservation of the Constitution; one of them relates to the present Duration of Parliament, the other to the Mode of elefiting the Representatives of the People; and that the Petitioners learn, from a late Resolution of the Commons, " That the Influence of the Crown hath " increased, is increasing, and ought to be diminished;" and gratefully acknowledge the Reform already begun in the Expenditure of the public Money, and consider it as a happy Prelude towards completing and confirming a Purpose, the Necessity of which so high an Authority hath so wifely and forcibly pointed out, and which, the Petitioners apprehend, can only be effected by shortening the Term for which Representatives are elected, and reforming the Mode of their Election: When the Number and Qualification of the Electors shall have been regulated and improved by the Wisdom of the Legislature, the best and most independent Men of the Country will be called into its Service by the disinterested Voice of the Nation: Such Men will be above the Reach of that Influence, whose baneful Effects the Petitioners have long felt, and much lamented; and that the more frequent Occasions upon which Representatives must account for their Conduct, will either keep them firm to their Duty, or enable Electors to dismiss them more speedily from a Trust which they may have betrayed; and that the Petitioners do not presume to dictate how far the Remedy they petition for should be extended, dr in what Form it should be applied, but complain of an Evil that they feel, and only point out the Cause from which it manifestly arises: It is, however, with great Concern that the Petitioners fee Boroughs, very inconsiderable in themselves, using every Measure still to lessen the Numbers of their Electors, and exclude Persons of Weight and Property, by which Means Venality is become so flagrant and enormous, and the Object of Temptation so alluring and irresistible, that Self-Interest too frequently prevails over general Benefit;

REPORT on the Estimate of the Ordnance, for the Year 1783.

The Estimate for the Ordnance* which I have the Honour to lay before this Honourable House, being very different from those which it has been customary to present, I think it my Duty to submit the Grounds upon which I have thought necessary to deviate from the Plan of former Estimates.

The Two main Objects of Estimates seem to be,

lft, To know what will be the whole Amount of the Expence for the' Year.

2ndly, To have a Distribution of that Expence under distinct Articles.

But the Estimates of the Ordnance, as hitherto presented, do not appear to me to answer either of these Ends.

The Arrangement of Ordnance Estimates has been very properly made under Three Heads;

The

UNPROVIDED,

ORDINARY,

AND

EXTRAORDINARY.

The Unprovided is not properly an Estimate, but an Account of Debt incurred in the preceding Year without the Authority of Parliament; and consequently ought to consist only of such very few Articles as could not be foreseen, but which Emergencies made necessary to provide.

The Ordinary and Extraordinary form the Estimate for the enfiling Year.

The Ordinary should contain a true Account of the whole Establilliment and Expences that are of a permanent Nature, and likely to occur every Year.

The Extraordinary should contain a Computation of such Expences as are Temporary, together with the probable Cost of New Works.

To what Degree the Estimates hitherto delivered have been correct Materials to shew the whole Expence necessary to be provided, will be seen by comparing the Ordinary and Extraordinary for feme Years palt, with the Exceedings that appeared in every subsequent Year under the Head of Unprovided.

If the Ordinary and Extraordinary had been formed upon just Calculations, the Exceedings under the Head of Unprovided in a subsequent Year could have been but trilling; whereas it appears that for the last Seven Years the Unprovided has upon an Average exceeded, by 116,924/. 8s. 4 d.in each Year, both the Ordinary and Extraordinary put together; so that in Fadfc the Requisition to Parliament has every Year been considerably leis than Half the Sum really wanted.

But even this subsequent Charge of Unprovided by no means closes the Account: as a Statement of Debt, it ought to state the Whole of the Debt; but it does no such Thing: A large Arrear of Undischarged Debentures remains behind till the End of the War, when there appears a vast Debt, of which Parliament has not had the least Knowledge, either as to its Extent or Causes, although it has been continually accruing, whilst Estimates and incomplete Accounts of Debts have been Yearly presented.

This Debt at the Close of the last War was 595,423/. 2 s.Sd. — It is now near Three Times that Sum.

Besides these Defects in the general Statements of the Ordnance Estimates, they are equally deficient in giving either a distinct or genuine Account of the Articles that are stated.

Vox.. 39.

One Article in the Ordinary is called, 4‘ the Ordi- Report on " nary of Office, comprising Repairs of Storehouses, Ordnance " Magazines, Barracks, Platforms, Carriages, Stores 1,1iniategfor Garrisons, Rents, Salaries, and Incident Charge So strange a Mixture of heterogeneous Matter feeir.s rather to confuse than explain, and moreover is not a genuine Account of their Cost, which appears to have constantly and considerably exceeded the Charge delivered to Parliament. This Charge in the Estimates has uniformly, for many Years, been identically the same Sum of 36,092/. Js. 6d. although the Expence of Office has been increasing, although Repairs and Incident Charges mult from their Nature be continually varying, and in Fact the actual Expenditure has been 69»395/-

From these Observations it appears, that the 'Whole of the Estimate on the former Plan cannot be satisfactory; Charges are made under various Heads for Money, but the Articles for which it is voted have no specific Relation to the real Expenditure. A grols Surh is obtained for Land Service, which, together with tba/t received for Sea Service, forms an aggregate Fund, from whence various Expences, very different from those in the Estimate, are in Part defrayed; and what can heft wait accumulates as a Debt, hereafter to appear in one lumping Sum before Parliament, in the shape of Outstanding Debentures, unaccompanied with any Account to shew how it has been incurred, or how the Money has been actually employed.

The present Estimate endeavours to avoid these Defects. I-t begins by stating the actual Debt, made up as correctly as could be collected, amounting tb L7-24.503/- *</

It next states, under the Head of Unprovided, the Exceedings in 1782 beyond the Grants of Parliament, which, from the Deficiency of last Year's Estimate, were unavoidable; but notwithstanding the vast Demand so ' Gibraltar, they have been lb kept within Bounds, as b by 80,464/. 12#. \od. leis than they were the Year lx lore.

The Distribution of this Expenditure in the Unprovided, formerly made under the Head of the several Articles supplied, is now arranged under the Head of Places where the same has been incurred, which it is presumed will appear more distinct. The whole of this Article amounts to 819,259/. 2 swhich when paid will reduce the Debt to 905,244/. 8s.: And this,

from the most accurate Calculations which the Office could produce, closes the Account, and, it is believed, leaves no Arrear whatever behind.

The Ordinary of the present Estimate brings forward the whole Establishment of Office of every Kind, and divides it, with much greater Accuracy than heretofore, under the distinct Head Of Places Where the Expences Were incurred. It amounts to 233,3631. 6 11 d.

Under this Head it may be proper to observe, that various Salaries in the Civil Establishment have received an Augmentation of 1,973/. 16 s. 4 since last Year, in order to give competent Incomes to the Persons employed in lieu of Perquisites, private Fees, and private Agencies, all which are now entirely abolished. But this Increase of 1,973/. 165. 4 dhas, by the Savings made in consequence of new Regulations for the Cdn-duct of Proofs of Powder and Ordnance, and by restraining the Expence of Coach Hire, Messages, and other Articles, been reduced to 964/. 155. 3 in present; and when the Salaries of sundry Offices now suppressed, amounting to 1,170/. 7*. 6 which are to cease with the present Possessors, shall fall in, there will be no Excess, but a Saving of 205/. 12 3d.

The Corps of Engineers composed entirely of Officers, which forms another Branch of the Ordinary, it is lup-poled will be thought necessary to be kept up.

Report on Ordnance Estimates,

The Royal Regiment of Artillery, immediately before the War, consisted of Four Battalions of Eight Marching Companies and Two Invalid Companies each; since which, each Battalion has beai augmented, One to Eleven, and the Three others to Ten Marching Companies, and the Invalids have been formed into a separate Battalion, also confuting of Ten Companies. The Establishment now proposed, leaves the same Number of Battalions and Companies, except One, but reduces One Officer and 48 Men Company from the War Establishment of last Year. The Reduction of Men will be amongst the Matrofles only, preserving the Serjeants, Corporals, Bombardiers, and Gunners, who are the best Men, and many of w hom would be entitled to Pensions on their Discharge. 'l'his Reduction will produce a Saving of 37.917/. 8 s. 4per Annum, which will take place in July next; and a further Saving of 9,976/. 135. 4 d.will be made by supplying the Vacancies of Serjeants, Corporals, Bombardiers, and Gunners, with Alatiofles only, till the Establishment of each Company is reduced to 2 Serjeants, 2 Corporals, 3 Bombardiers, 53 Matrofles, and 2 Drummers.

It is further proposed, as fit Men can be found, to employ a considerable Part of the Regiment as Artificers and Labourers in the Laboratory, in making Gun Carriages, and in other Works at Woolziich, and the Out Ports, giving them only Half of what is now paid for such Business; w hereby it is computed that a Saving from Twelve to Fifteen thousand Pounds a Year may be made; the Duty will be more regularly performed; and the Regiment w ill have a Body of Artificers, always much wanted on Service.

The Superannuated Lift is a great but unavoidable Expence; a Variety of Pensions and ulelels Offices, which appeared in different Articles, are now brought all together under this, and they will cease with the present Possessors. But the greatest Part of this Expence is owing to the necessary Consequence of a long M ar and severe Service operating on a large Establishment.

The Extraordinary amounts to 397,249 /. 5 s. 11 This Charge may be divided under the following general Heads; viz.

£. d.

The Remains of the War - - 189,646 8 11

Common Incidents - - - - 54,827 7 11

Fortifications Abroad - - - 19,100-----

Fortifications in Great Britain - 101,192 11 9

Buildings in Great Britain - - 32,482 17 4

397.249 5 1,1

The First of these will entirely cease with this Year, and the Second will probably be considerably diminished.

The Fortifications Abroad may increase.

The Fortifications at Home depend upon the System that may be adopted. At the close of the last War, the few Field Works that had been thrown up, were totally neglected, and suffered to go to Ruin; the Consequence of which was, an immense fedden Expence at the breaking out of this War. An opposite Extreme of fortifying every where, has been since pursued.

It is at present proposed to confine future Works to the principal Dock Yards. It is computed, that to render Portsmouth and Plymouth complete, will require or 500,000l., which, at 50,000l. per Annum, will be done in Eight or Ten Years. The Sum of 46,384/. 135. 3d.is a Iked in the present Elii mate for

New Works. The other Sums for Fortifications me only for Repairs and Improvements of Old Works, and to finish such Works in various Places as are nearly done, or may be in feme Degree completed at a final! additional Expence, without which, that already laid out would be entirely thrown away.

The Buildings, confuting chiefly of Magazines and Storehouses, are unavoidable.

Every Expence that is probable to occur, is now brought forward in the Estimate, and it is hoped and believed, that, under proper Restraints, it will be found sufficient to answer every Purpose, w ithout b ing obliged to recur to Parliament next Year for any Aid under the Head of Unprovided, unless Services totally unforelecn may arile.

The Expence of Sea Service must remain uncertain until it can be entirely fepurated from the Land Service: To make this Distribution, will require much Time and Arrangement, and feme additional Buildings. But when this desirable Object is attained, the Expence of Sea Service may, as well as that for Land Service, be al’cer-tained with Precision, and the Debt on that Account (if any) will appear.

In Addition to this Estimate, there fcems wanting an Account to (howr how the Money granted has been afiiually applied, towards the Services for which it was voted. Such an Account for last Year will shortly be laid before Parliament; but for the lleafens above stated, cannot be so accurate this Year, as it hereafter may be made.

It is earnestly hoped that Provision will immediately be made for discharging, in feme certain Period, the Debt of the Ordnance, which now fe greatly depreciates the Value of Debentures, and renders all Contracts depending on such uncertain Payment so disadvantageous to Government.

When this Debt is put into a regular Course of Payment, all future Bargains may immediately be made with ready Money, which has been found by Experience to produce, in many Instances, a Saving of from 20/. to 30 /. per Cent.

A farther Benefit will arise to the Public from the Method of dealing by open Contract, as will appear by the considerable Reduction of Price made even under the Diladvantages of the present Mode of Payment, in the following Articles; Viz.

A Petition of the Freeholders of the County of Representa-Derby, was presented to the House, and read; Setting tion in Par-forth, That the Petitioners, sensible of the original liament‘ Excellency of the Constitution of this Country, most ardently wish to have it maintained upon the genuine Principles on which it was founded; and that it is necessary to the Welfare of the People, that the Commons House of Parliament should have a common Interest with the Nation, and that, in the present State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, the House of Commons do not sufficiently speak the Sense of the People: And therefore praying the House to take into their most serious Consideration the present inadequate State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, and to apply such Remedy to this great and alarming Evil, as to the House may seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

!Mr. Alderman Harley reported from the Committee, Regulating to whom the Petition of several Dyers of Cloth, Bays, the Dying and other Woollen Goods, within the Counties of Trade. dlesex and Surrey, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Dyers of Cloths, Bays, and Woollen Goods, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of King George the First, intituled, "An Act for preventing Frauds and Abuses in the Dying Trade," was read, by which it appeared, fhat all Persons are restrained from buying Cloths, Bays, fend other Woollen Goods, as or for Mather or Woaded Blacks, with any other Ingredients than such as are particularly mentioned in the said Act; and also from using any Logwood in dying of Cloths, Bays, or other Woollen :Goods, as or for Blue, under certain Penalties therein mentioned; and the Company of Dyers of London are authorized to appoint Persons to be Searchers, who are impowered to enter the Shops and Warehoilfes of all Persons using the Trade of Dyers of Woollen Goods within the City of London, and the Distance of Ten Miles thereof; and the like Authority to appoint Searchers is given to the Justices of the Peace at their respective Quarter Sessions, within the several other Parts of the Kingdom. Then

Mr. Edward Seward, being examined, said. That though the Company of Dyers are impowered by the said Act to appoint Searchers, they have of late Years neglected so to do — -That many Frauds and Abuses have been 'committed by Persons using the Trade of Dyers of Woollen Goods, by using Ingredients which are prohibited by the said Act, to the Great Diferedit of the ManufacturCs, and the Prejudice of the fair Trader — That since the passing of the said Act, great Improvements' have been made in the dying of Blacks; and it is found, by Experience, that feme of the Ingredients directed to be used by the said Act, are improper-for that Purpose — That it is necessary ’ forae Alterations should be made in the said Act, touching the Ingredients to be used in the dying of Blacks;
