A Petition of the Gentry, Clergy, Traders, and other Inhabitants, of the Town of Saint Edmund's Bury, in the County of Suffolk, was preferred to the House and read; Setting forth, That the Inequality of the present State of Representation, though derived from a Variety of concurrent Causes, appears to the Petitioners to be in no Instance more remarkable than in that of the Privileges of Election exercised in great Towns by a very small Proportion of the Inhabitants, to the Exclusion of the relt, who, content as they might be without the peculiar Privileges annexed to Corporations, cannot at the same time, without Regret, feel themselves destitute of the First of Constitutional Rights, a Share in the Election of those who are chosen to represent them; and that the Two Representatives for Bury are elected by a Corporation, under a Charter from King James the First, consisting, when full, of One Alderman, or First Magistrate, Twelve capital Burgesses, and Twenty-four of the Common Council, the Vacancies being supplied by Election, made according to the Charter by the Corporate Body only; and tie at the Town of Bury is an ancient and well-inhabited Town, conlifting of more than Six thousand Inhabitants, of whom Five hundred and upwards are regularly assessed to the Parish Rates: To the Wisdom and Justice of the House the Petitioners therefore respectfully apply, praying that their Petition may be taken into Consideration, and such Relief granted in the Premises, as shall appear belt adapted to the State and Circumstances of the Town, agreeably to the Constitutional Principles of Repre-fentation.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Motion w’as made, and the Question being proposed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty our most humble Thanks for having been graciously pleased to lay before us, the Articles of the different Treaties which His Majesty has concluded, and to allure his Majesty that we have confujered them with the most lerious Attention.

To express the great Satisfaction and Gratitude with which we perceive that His Majesty, in the Exercise of the Powers which were intruded to Him, has concluded Provisional Articles with the States of North Amei'ica on such Principles as must, we trust, lay the Foundation of perfect Reconciliation and Friendship with that Country.

That, impressed with these Sentiments, we cannot forbear particularly to lay before His Majesty, our earnest With and just Expectation that the several States of North America will, in (the amplest and most satisfa<5lory Manner, carry into Execution those Measures which the Congress is so solemnly bound by the Treaty to recommend, in' favour of such Persons as have , suffered for the Part they have taken in the War, a Circumstance to which we anxiously look as tending to cement that Good-will and Affefition which we trust will uniformly mark the future Intercourse between us.

And to allure His Majesty, that we are sensible of His wife and paternal Care for the Welfare and Happiness of His Subjects in relieving them from a long and burthensome War, and restoring the Blessings and Advantages of Peace, by the Preliminary Articles agreed upon with the Courts of France and Spain.

To allure His Majesty, that we indulge the most

sanguine

17" — 190 Februarii. A. 1783.

sanguine Hopes, that His Subjects of Great Britain and Ireland will successfully apply their Attention to culti* vate and improve by every possible Means their domestic Resources.

That with these Views we shall apply ourselves to a Revision of our Commercial Laws on the most liberal Principles, and in a Manner adapted to the present Situation of Affairs, for the Purpose of extending our Trade and Navigation on the surest Grounds, and diligently providing for the Maintenance of our Naval Power, which can alone ensure the Prosperity of these Kingdoms.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out from the Words " and to " assure His Majesty, that" in the First Paragraph, to the End of the Question, in order to insert these Words, " His faithful Commons will proceed to consider the same with that serious and full Attention " which a Subject of such Importance to the present " and future Interests of His Majesty’s Dominions " deserves: That, in the mean Time, they entertain " the fullest Confidence in His Majesty’s paternal " Care, that He will concert with His Parliament " such Measures as may be expedient for extending " the Commerce of His Majesty’s Subjects. That " whatever may be the Sentiments of His faithful " Commons on the Result of their Investigation of " the Terms of Pacification, they beg Leave to assure " His Majesty of their firm and unalterable Resolution. " to adhere inviolably to the several Articles for which " the Public Faith is pledged, and to maintain the " Blessings of Peace, so necessary to His Majesty’s " Subjects, and the general Happiness of Mankind," instead thereof.

And the Question being put. That the Words proposed to be left out Hand Part of the Question;

The House divided.

And the Question being proposed, That the Words " His faithful Commons will proceed to consider the " same with that serious and full Attention which a " Subject of such Importance to the present and future Interests of His Majesty’s Dominions deserves: " That, in the mean Time, they entertain the fullest " Confidence in His Majesty’s paternal Care, that " He will concert with His Parliament such Measures as may be expedient for extending the Commerce of His Majesty’s Subjects. That whatever " may be the Sentiments of His faithful Commons " on the Result of their Investigation of the Terms " of Pacification, they beg Leave to assure His Majesty of their firm and unalterable Resolution to " adhere inviolably to the several Articles for which (< the Public Faith is pledged, and to maintain the Blessings of Peace, so necessary to His Majesty’s * Subjects, and the general Happiness of Mankind," be inserted instead thereof;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the said proposed Amendment, by inferring, after the Words " Commerce of His Majesty’s Subjects," these Words, " and His Majesty’s faithful Commons feel that it " would be superfluous to express to His Majesty the " Regards due from this Nation to every Description " of Men, who, with the Risque of their Lives, and " the Sacrifice of their Properties, have distinguistied " their Loyalty, and Fidelity during a long and calamitous W'ar."

And the Question being put, That those Words be there inserted;

It was rtfoived in the Affirmative.

Then the said proposed Amendment, so amended, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Then the main Question, so amended, being put;

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty our most humble Thanks, for having been graciously pleased to lay before us the Articles of the different Treaties which His Majesty has concluded; and to assure His Majesty, that His faithful Commons will proceed to consider the same with that serious and full Attention which a Subject of such Importance to the present and future Interests of His Majesty’s Dominions deserves: That, in the mean Time, they entertain the fullest Confidence in His Majesty’s paternal Care, that He will concert with His Parliament such Measures as may be expedient for extending the Commerce of His Majesty’s Subjects: And His Majesty’s faithful Commons feel, that it would be superfluous to express to His Majesty the Regards due from this Nation to every Description of Men, who, with the Risque of their Lives, and the Sacrifice of their Properties, have distinguished their Loyalty and Fidelity during a long and calamitous War.

That whatever may be the Sentiments of His faithful Commons on the Result of their Investigation of the Terms of Pacification, they beg Leave to assure His Majesty of their firm and unalterable Resolution to adhere inviolably to the several Articles for which the Public Faith is pledged, and to maintain the Blessings of Peace, so necessary to His Majesty’s Subjects, and the general Happiness of Mankind.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty’s most Honourable Privy Council.

Ordered, That all Committees have Leave to fit, Committees, notwithstanding any Adjournment of the House.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

And the House having continued to fit till near Eight of the Clock on Tuesday Morning;

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Mom- Supply, ing, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

THE Lord Althorpe reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, and other principal Inhabitants, of Saint Mary Rotherhithe, otherwise Redriffe, in the County of , whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in Behalf of themselves and the other Inhabitants of the said Parish, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Blackburn being examined, said, He was well acquainted with the Parish of Rotherhithe — That the Streets, Lanes, and other Places, within the said Parish, are ill-paved, cleansed, and lighted, and are also greatly incumbered with Potts, and annoyed with Signs, Spouts, and Gutters, and other Obstructions, whereby they are rendered incommodious, and in many Parts dangerous to the Inhabitants, and others, resorting thereto.

And the Witness produced to your Committee, a Calculation he had made of the original Expence of paving, lighting, watching, and cleansing, the said Pa-rith, which amounts to 5,580/.: And he added, that it is proposed to borrow that Sum by Life Annuities, not exceeding 10/. per Cent.; which, in a few Years, inuft fink — That the Interest of the Money borrowed, together with the Annual Expence of repairing the Pavements, and cleansing, lighting, and watching, the said Parish, will amount to 1,585/.; and that it is proposed to make a Rate in the Parish not exceeding -is. 3 d.in the Pound, which, allowing for every Deficiency, will exceed the Sum wanted by about tool, a Year — Then Mr. Henry Mills, an Inhabitant of the Parish, was examined, who confirmed Mr. Blackburn's Evidence with respefit to the State of the Pavements, and Obstructions in the Streets; and he further said, that there is no regular Watch kept in the said Parish, except such as is paid by private Subscription; and that there are no Lamps in the lower Part of the Town, nor any but private ones in the upper Part. — That he was born in the Parish, and remembers about 40 or 50 Years ago, there was hardly a Cart kept in the Town, and that now there are more than Fifty employed in a Day, besides many Coaches — That if the Parish was properly paved, cleansed, lighted, and watched, it would be of great Benefit to the Inhabitants and Persons resorting thereto, who are at present exposed to the Violence of Footpads, House-breakers, and other Disturbers of the Public Peace; and that there are not at present sufficient Powers for those Purposes.

William Wells, Esquire, and Mr. Peter confirmed the Whole of the foregoing Evidence, except the Calculation made by Mr. Blackburn — And Mr. Mestaer added, that the Parishes of and Shadwell, on the opposite Side of the River, have been very iquch improved since Powers were granted for paving, lighting, and watching the fame.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for better paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching the Streets, Lanes, Yards, Courts, Alleys, and Paffeges, within the Parish of Saint Mary at Rotherhithe, Vol. 39.

otherwise Redriffe, in the County of Surrey, and for removing and preventing Nuisances and Annoyances therein: And that the Lord Althorpe and Sir Joseph Mawbey do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Byng reported from the Committee, to whom Wapping the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are Poor> &c-thereunto subscribed, being Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint John of Wapping, in the County of Middlesex, on Behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabit' ants of the said Parish, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Twenty-first Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor of the Parish of Saint John of Wapping, in the County of Middlesex, and for providing a proper Workhouse and Burial Ground for the Use of the said Parish; and for opening certain Communications, and making certain Streets within the said Parish: and also,

An Act, passed in the Sixteenth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for the better maintaining, regulating, and employing the Poor within the Parish of Saint George, in the County of Middlesex, and for cleansing and lighting the Squares, Streets, Lanes,

Alleys, Courts, Yards, and other open Passages and Places; and for keeping and regulating a nightly Watch within such Parts of the said Parish as are not within the Liberty of the Tower of London, were read: And

Mr. Andrew Burt being examined, said, That the Provision in the said First-mentioned Act contained, with respect to the Nomination of Trustees (their Appointment being for Life, so far as relates to the Poor,; may be attended with Inconveniences, and that it would lie for the Advantage of the Parish if Power were given to choose Trustees for the Management of the Poor Annually, as is done by virtue of the said Second-mentioned Act in the Parish of Saint George — That the Pow'ers of the said Act for Relief of the Poor in Saint John of Wapping, have been found defective in other Respects, and particularly with regard to the Qualification of Trustees, there being no Penalty on Persons acting who are not qualified as the Act directs — That the Clause restraining Persons from acting as Trustees while they hold any Place of Profit, or have any Contract under the Act, is also without any Penalty; and that other Powers and Provisions thereof require Amendment and Alteration.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for amending an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor of the Parish of Saint John of Wapping, in the County of Middlesex; and for providing a proper Workhouse and Burial Ground for the Use of the said Parish; and for opening certain Communications, and making certain Streets, within the said Parish: And that Mr.

Byng and Mr. Alderman Wilkes do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Representa- A Petition of the Resident Burgesses of the Borough tion m Par- of Derby, in the County of Derby, and of the Inha-liament bitants, Housekeepers in the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners deem the Representation of the People of England in Parliament to be in general very disproprotionate, and particularly that of the Borough of Derby, for there are near Twelve thousand Inhabitants in the said Borough, about Two thousand of which are Vol. 39-

Housekeepers, and ho more than Four hundred and Thirty are Burgesses, and do now vote for Members to serve in Parliament for ’ the said Borough; and that the said Members were formerly chosen by the said Burgesses, who had obtained their Franchise by Birth or Servitude, but of late Years the Corporation have tflade great Numbers of Honorary Burgesses for the said Borough, merely to serve Election Purposes, Confiding of People who have no Interest or Property within the said Borough (as will appear by the Lift annexed to the Petition) the greatest Part of whom never come near it, except to be made Burgesses, or to vote at Elections; and that the said Non-resident Honorary Burgesses are now so numerous as to overturn and totally destroy the Franchise of the said Resident Burgesses: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, end to adopt such Measures, as that a more equal Representation in general may take place, and the Right of Election for the said Borough in future may be in the Resident Burgesses, and the Inhabitants paying Scotland Lot only.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Penruddock reported from the Committee to whom the Bill for dividing and allotting in Severalty the Open and Common Fields and Downs, Common Meadows, Common Pastures, and Commonable Places, within the Parish of Heytesbury, in the County of was committed; and to whom the Petition of the Right honourable Thomas Lord Viscount Weymouth, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Bills of Inclosure, had been complied with; and that the Committee had considered the said Petition, and had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Parties concerned had given their Consent to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee (except the Owners of 87 Acres and Three Roods of Land, and of Two Common Right Houses, who refuted to give their Consent to the Bill; and that the Whole of the Lands intended to be divided and allotted, contains 3,552 Acres, or thereabouts, and there are 134 Common Right Houses; and that no Person ap|>eared before the Committee to oppose the Bill) and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Mr. Anderson Pelham presented to the House, according to Order, a Bill for the more easy and speedy Recovery of Small Debts, within the Wapentakes of Yarbrough and Bradley Hare(except the Parish of Laccby) and within the Wapentakes o and Manley, and Pai ifh of Kir ton, in the Hundred of Corringham, in the County of Lincoln: And the fatne was received; and read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

Memorandum:

By an Act, pafl’cd in the Year 1781, intituled, "An Act for establishing an Agreement with the United " Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies, &c." the East India Company are required to pay a certain Sum of Money, which is specified in the said Act, in Proportion to the Number of Troops sent, or to be sent, to the East Indies, on the Requisition of the said Company.

This Sum the said Company claim, under the Words of the Act, a Right of paying in the East Indies only; and as it will benecefiaryto provide for the Subsistence of the Recruiting Companies remaining in Great Britain, there will be wanting at present for this Purpose the Sum of Fifteen thousand and Seventy-four Pounds Ten Shillings, which it will be necessary to vote on Account of the said Estimate.

War-Office,

24th February 1783.

Were severally presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, sensible of the original Excellency of the Constitution of this Country, most ardently wish to have it maintained upon the genuine Principles on which it was founded; and that it is necessary to the Welfare of the People, that the Commons House of Parliament should have a common Interest with the Nation; and that, in the present State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, the House of Commons do not sufficiently speak the Voice of the People: And therefore praying the House to take into their most serious

Vol. 39.

Consideration the present inadequate State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, and to apply such Remedy to this great and alarming Evil, as to the House may seem meet;

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Free- Representa-holders of the County of Carnarvon, was also presented |!on ln to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Peti- Iame,t' tioners consider the British Constitution, as originally framed, the most perfect System of good Government that can possibly exist, being admirably calculated to promote the Ease and Happiness of the Subject; and that the Alterations which have been introduced into that Constitution are inimical to those free Principles on which it is founded; and that the extreme Inequality in the Representation of the People, the long Duration of Parliament, and the very expensive Mode of Election for Representatives, are Measures fundamentally wrong, and Grievances of alarming Tendency: And therefore entreating the House to take the same into their most serious Consideration, and to apply such Remedy to thele great Constitutional Evils, as to the House shall seem meet.

Sir Richard Hotham reported from the Committee, st. George’* to whom the Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, (Southwark) Overseers of foe Poor, and other Inhabitants, of the Parish of Saint George the Martyr, in the Borough of Southxcaiic, and County of Surrey, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Francis Vincent being examined, laid, That the King's Bench Prison, the Prison of His Majesty’s Court, called The Marshalsea, the Common Gaol of the County of

Surrey, called 'The New Goal, and the House of Correction for the said County, called New Bridewell, are all situate within the said Parish of Saint George the Martyr, and that the Rules of the King's Bench Prison extend over the Whole of the said Parish, except the South Side of White Street, the East Side of Kent Street, and Kent Street Road — That the Rules of the King's Bench Prison being so extensive, many Prisoners, who have large Families, frequently rent Houses, or Parts of Houses, or Lodgings ready furnished, therein, at the Rate of 10 per Annum, or upwards, and others at lower Rents; all which making them liable to be rated to and to pay the Parish Rates and Taxes, they are thereby deemed to gain Settlements; and many of such Prisoners, their Families, and Servants, have become heavy and grievous Burthens upon the said Parish. — And he gave the following Instances:

A Prisoner having the Rules of the King’s Bench, rented and lived in a Lodging, ready furnKhed, at Twenty Guineas a Year, where he continued during the Time he was a Prisoner, which was upwards of u Year — That his Widow was font from the Parish of Saint Edmund the King, London, to Saint George South-nark, as the Place of her Settlement, gained by the above renting of a Lodging, by virtue of an Order of Removal of 23d August 1781; against which Ordev Saint George’s Parish appealed: And the Sessions in London determined foe above Renting to be a Settle-men, and fixed the Pauper in Saint George's Parish,

where

where the was maintained till Hie died, in the Wdrk-house.

Mr. John Griffith confirmed the Whole of the above Evidence. And

Mrs. Elizabeth Bayley being examined, confirmed the Evidence of the Widow being in the Workhouse, and dying the re.

Mr. Vincent being further examined, said, That another Prisoner in* the King's Bench Prison gained a Settlement, by renting a House in the Mint; upon whose Death his Widow and One Child were sent to the Workhouse, where Hie was delivered of another Child, which was sent out to nurse at the Expence of the Parish.

Which Evidence was confirmed by Mr. Samuel Carter and Mrs. Elizabeth Bay ley.

Mr. Vincent then said, That another Prisoner in the King's Bench rented and lived in a House in Mint Street, at 14/. per Annum.And

Mr. Carter added, That the Prisoner being taken ill, and having a Wife and Five Children, the Wife applied to the Parish of Saint George for Relief — That the Parish relieved the Man and his Farpily, at a heavy Expence; and that the Prisoner is dead; and the Family is now relieved by the Parish.

Mr. Vincent then said. That another Person having been committed to the King's Bench Prison (where he ,fti|l remains) his Wife and Five small Children followed him, and took a Lodging in the Rules; and being dif-trelled, applied to the Parish of Saint George for Relief, which was given to him: And Inquiry being made after the Man’s Settlement, it appeared to be in the Parish of Saint Margaret, Westminster; to which Place the Wife and Family were removed: But the Parish of Saint JMargaret have appealed against the Order of Removal, and it is not yet determined; which Litigation will be a great Expence to the Parish.

That another Person was a Prisoner in the Rules of the King's Bench, from the 3d of March 1779 till he was discharged in 1782; and that a Woman, who lived with him as a Servant, being delivered of a Baltard Child, applied to the Parish Officers for Assistance; and although the Officers got some trifling Sums of Money from the reputed Fattier towards the Maintenance of the Child, yet the Parish were considerably out of Pocket on that Account.

Mr. James Sherrard being then examined, said, That a Servant to another Prisoner was admitted into the Workhouse, and was there delivered of a Bastard Child; and being afterwards ill, was lent to the Hospital, from whence lhe was returned to the Workhouse, where the continued some Months; all at the Expence of the Parish.

Which Evidence was confirmed to your Committee by Mrs. Bayley, who further said. That another Servant of the last mentioned Prisoner applied for Relief for a Bastard Child; which was given her, and her Child lent to Nurse, where it continued some Months, till its Death.

Mr. John Griffith being then further examined, said, That a Woman, who had been a Servant to a Prisoner in the King's Bench Prison, was sent from Saint Paul's Cray to the Parish, as having gained a Settlement by living as a Yearly hired Servant with the Prisoner in the Rules of the King's Bench — That being with Child, (he was delivered in the Workhouse, and taken care of at the Expence of the Parish.

Which Evidence was confirmed by Mrs. Bayley.

Mr. Carter then informed your Committee, That another Woman was admitted into the Workhouse, lhe having gained a Settlement in the Parish by living as a Yearly hired Servant with a Prisoner in the Rules of the King's Bench Prison — And the Witness concluded, by saying. That there are many other Instances similar to the above; which can be proved by several Persons a ho have served the Office of Overseer.

With respefit to the Marshalsea Prison;

Mr. Vincent said, That Families of Prisoners have frequently been lent from that Prison when lick, or otherwise distressed, to the Parish to be relieved; which has been given; and when able, they have been removed to their respefilive Places of Settlement; by Means whereof an heavy Expence has been incurred by the Parish:

And as an Instance, Mr. James Hedger said, That a Servant to a Prisoner in the being deprived

of her Senses, the Officers of the Parish were obliged to take her out of the Prison; and as no Place of Settlement could be found, lhe was admitted into the Workhouse, and afterwards sent to Bethlem Hospital, and there kept a Year at the Expence of the Parish.

Then, to prove that frequent Applications are made to the Officers of the Parish from the County Gaol and House of Correction, for Relief and Support for miserable Objects of Prisoners, and for Children born there, and for removing them to their respective Settlements.

Mr. Vincent and Mr. Carter laid, That a Woman being charged with Felony, was committed to the County Gaol, and was delivered of a Baltard Child in the Prison — That lhe was afterwards convicted of the Felony, and removed to the House of Correction, where lhe was delivered of another Ballard; both which Children were sent to the Workhouse of Saint George's Parish, and taken care of till the Mother’s Settlement could be found, and then removed to penshall, in the County of York, at the Expence of the Parish.

And Mr. Hedger then said, That an Insane Person was sent by Order of Two Juliices, to the County Gaol, where he continued a few Days; and then being found to be furiously mad, he was sent, by Order of the Magistrates, to the Parish Workhouse; and continuing very bad, and having neither Money nor Friends, and the Place of his Settlement not being known, he was sent at the Parish Expence to Bethlem Hospital, where he continued a Year, and was afterwards placed by the Parish in a private Madhouse, at 8 a Week; and, with much Trouble and Expence, the Place of his Settlement being found to be in Carmarthenshire, in South Wales, he was lent there at the Expence of the Parish.

And Mr. Samuel Carter, Mr. James Hedger, Mr. John Griffith, and Mr. Richard Smith, being then examined, severally said. That the Parish of Saint George confilts chiefly of Tenants at Rack Rents, and who are heavily taxed — That, in the Mint and Kent Street, many of the Householders are too poor to pay Rates or Taxes — That a great Number of the Houses are lett in single Rooms, and ready-furnillied Lodgings, to Weekly Tenants, who cannot be rated to the Poor, 8$c.; and many Vagrants, Travellers, and other poor Persons, are hhrboured there, which brings a heavy Expence on the Parish.

Then Mr. Smith, Mr. Hedger, and Mr. Griffith, further said, That the Inhabitants of the said Parish experience great Inconvenience, from the whole Number of Overseers of the Poor being appointed at one and the same Time, because they are of course, at first coming into Office, unacquainted not only with the proper Method of maintaining, regulating, and employing, the Poor in the Workhouse, but with the Characters and Circumstances of such of the poor Inhabitants as are upon the Lift for Relief, without going into the Workhouse; and that it would be advantageous to the Parish if One'Half of the Overseers were to be appointed at the usual Time, and the other Half in the Middle of the Year; each Party to continue in Office One Year.

And the same Witnesses further said, That there being few Inhabitants of the said Parish of independent

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Edward Codd, Deputy Town Clerk of Hull, being examined, said, That the Common Gaol of the said Town and County is a very old and ruinous Building, of small Dimensions — That it is ill-contrived and inconvenient; and being situate in a confined Place, and the Middle of the Town, without any Outlet or open Ground adjacent to it, is prejudicial to the Health of the Prisoners, and insufficient for their safe Custody — That the same has been presented as such by the Grand Jury, at the Assizes held for the said Town and County; and that it will be beneficial to the Prisoners, the Town, and the Public, to take down the said Gaol, and build another in a more eligible Situation — That Estimates have been made of the Expence of such a Work; from which it appears that the same might be done in a proper Manner for about 2,500l. including the Purchase of a competent Quantity of Land for the Scite and Outlets — That, from the Increase of Population in the Parish of The Holy Trinity, in the said Town, the Burial Ground is become too small for the Interment of the Dead; that the Parishioners suffer much Inconvenience and Annoyance therefrom; and that it is very ne-efissary a proper Piece of Ground should be provided for an additional Cemetery for the Use of the Parish; and that it is expedient that the necessary Powers for railing Money for that Purpose, and the building of a new Gaol, should be granted by Parliament — That in the said Town, and the Liberties and PrecinQs thereof, many Hackney Coaches and Chairs are kept; but the Persons who drive or carry them not being under any Regulation or immediate Controul, either with respect to Fares or Behaviour, the Inhabitants do not derive Vol. 39.

so much Benefit and Convenience therefrom as they might do if they were properly managed and regulated —

That the said Town, Liberties, and PrecinQs, are in extreme Want of sufficient Powers, Rules, and Re-ftriQions, in the various Articles of internal Police, particularly with respect; to Spouts, Signs, Gutters, Chopping Blocks, Stalls, the llaughtering of Cattle, and other Nuisances and Annoyances committed and existing in the Streets; with respect: to the ConstruQion of the Wheels of Trucks, to driving Carriages on the Pavement, the Manner of removing the Filth and Dung, and throwing the same into the Water, and the Standing of Stalls in the Streets at other Times, besides the Market Days.

To prove the Allegations of that Part of the Petition which relates to the Haven of the said Town, an Act, passed in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making public Quays in the said Town; for making a Dock for the Accommodation of Vessels using the Port; and other Purposes, was read. — And the Witness being further examined, laid, That the Haven of the Town and Port of Kingston upon Hull, in which Goods and Merchandize have been accustomed to be laden and shipped, landed and discharged, lies within the Town and County of the Town of Kingston upon Hull — That, by virtue of the said Act of Parliament, a Dock or Bason for the Reception and Accommodation of Ships and Vessels hath been provided, and is now in Use; the South and East Ends whereof are in or contiguous to the said Town or County of the Town of Kingston upon Hull-, and the North and West Sides thereof are in or contiguous to the County of York —

A Petition of several Noblemen, and the humble Petition' of several other Persons who are Owners of the Rivers Trent, Tame, and Anker, in the Counties of Stafford, Derby, and Warwick; and of the Merchants, Traders, and other Inhabitants of the Borough of Tamworth, in the Counties of Stafford and Warwick,

and of the Town of Burton upon Trent, in the said County of Stafford, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal, with Collateral Cuts, from certain Coal Alines in the Liberty of in the

Parish of Wolverhampton, and in the several Parishes of Sedgeley, Tipton otherwise Tibbington, Wednesbury, and Westbromwich, in the County of Stafford, to or

near Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, and from thence to communicate with the Coventry Canal, at or near Fazeley, in the Parish of Tamworth, in the said County of Stafford, and all'o of the Bill to enable the Proprietors of the Birmingham Canal Navigation to make and maintain an Extension of Canal from a Place near Riders Green, in the Parish of Westbronncich, to Broadwater Fire Engine, and to make Six small Collateral Cuts from the same to lead to several Coal Alines, and also an Extension of Canal from or near the Town of Birmingham, to join the Coventry Canal at or near Fazeley, in the Parish of Tamworth, with a Collateral Branch to the lower Part of the said Town of Birmingham; and Setting forth, That it appears, by Surveys and Levels taken, that the Rivers Trent and Tame may, at an easy Expence, be made navigable from the Town of Burton upon Trent to the Town of Tamworth, and from thence to or near Fishers Mills, in the Parish of Middleton, in the County of Warwick and also, That the River Anker may be made navigable from the said Town of Tamworth, at its Junction with the 'River Tame, to or near Filand Bridge, in the County of Warwick; and that a Cut or Canal may be conveniently made from thence to communicate with the Coventry Canal, already completed to Atherstone; and also, That a Communication may be conveniently made from the River Trent to the Canal between the Rivers Trent and Mersey, at or near Wichnover, in the County of Stafford; and alledging, That the making the said Rivers navigable with the aforesaid Cuts or Canals, will be done at much less Expence than extending the said Canal from Fishers Mills to Fazeley, as intended by the said Bills, and completing the Coventry Canal from Atherstone to Fradley Heath, the Place of its intended Junction

with the Canal from The Trent to The Mersey; and that it will also be attended with a Saving to the Public of a large Quantity of rich and valuable Land, which would be taken and used for the said Canals, and every Communication, intended by the said Bills, will be effected; and that, if the said Bills, or either of them, should pass into a Law in their present Form, the Petitioners and the Public at large will be greatly injured: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, against such Part or Parts of the said Bills, or either of them, as may affect the Interest of the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the Bill to enable the Proprietors of the Birmingham Canal Navigation to make and maintain an Extension of Canal, from a Place near Riders Green, in the Parish of Westbromwich, to Broadimter Fire Engine, and to make Six small Collateral Cuts from the same, to lead to several Coal Mines; and also, an Extension of Canal, from or near the Town of Birmingham, to join the Coventry Canal at or near Fazeley, in the Parish of Tamworth, with a Collateral Branch to the lower Part of the said Town of Birmingham, is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, il they think lit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the Alayor, Burgesses, and principal Copper Coin. Tradesmen and Inhabitants, of the Borough of Devizes, in the County of Wilts, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners find themselves greatly aggrieved by the present Circulation of base and counterfeit Copper Coin, the Quantity of which has of late lb much increased as to become highly injurious to the Commercial Interests of the Nation; and that the Petitioners have done all in their Power to put a Stop to such Circulation, but find themselves unable to do it effectually without the Interference of the House; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the evil of which they complain is chiefly owing to a Defect in the Laws for preventing the coining and circulating such bale and counterfeit Copper Aloney, and, unless some more effectual Remedy be forthwith applied, the Consequence may be still more detrimental to the Public: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their most lerious Consideration; and that the Petitioners may have such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie ’ upon the Table.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Sheriffs, and Common Council, of the City of Gloucester, in Council assembled, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners consider the British Constitution, as originally framed, the most perfect Syf-tem of good Government that can possibly exist, being admirably calculated to promote the Ease and Happiness of the Subject; and that the Alterations which have been introduced into that Constitution are inimical to those free Principles on which it is founded; and that the extreme Inequality in the Representation of the People, the long Duration of Parliaments, and the very expensive Mode of Election for Representatives, are Measures fundamentally wrong, and Grievances of an alarming Tendency; and therefore entreating the House to take the same into their most serious Consideration, and apply such Remedy to those great Constitutional Evils as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders of Liverpool, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Application mentioned in the lad preceding Petition; end letting forth, that the said Richard Arkzvright hath already obtained every Advantage which the Laws in being have provided for the Encouragement of new Inventions, and, by the Emoluments arising from this exclusive Grant, hath, as the Petitioners are informed, and believe, realized such a Fortune as every unprejudiced Person tnuft allow to be an ample Compensation for the most happy Efforts of Genius; and that the Interposition of the Legislature to grant still greater Rewards, and such as are unwarrantable by any Statute now in being, might, as the Petitioners apprehend, give Stability to a dangerous Monopoly, and prove highly prejudicial to the Manufactures, Commerce, and Navigation of this Land, by leaving to all other Kingdoms the unlimited Use of Machines, which would in England alone be thereby confined to the arbitrary Disposal of One Man only: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pals into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Free- R fenta-holders, of the County of Somerset, was presented to the tion in Par-House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners liamenu conceiving that a System of Corruption, subversive of the natural Rights of Britons, has, by flow, but too sure Steps, crept into the Representation of the People of thele Kingdoms, and considering that an equal Representation in Parliament is their Birthright, congenial with, and inseparable from, the Constitution, in all due Deference, but in full Confidence, implore the Interposition of the House, to restore to them the Exercise of that Right which has been the Glory and Boast of their Ancestors; and that it is only through the Medium of an uncorrupt, uninfluenced, and equal Representation, that the Voice of the People can be truly heard, and through such a Medium only can their Liberties be protected, or their Purses constitutionally opened: And therefore praying, That the House will take such effectual Measures to remedy this growing Evil, as a free People may, with a full Assurance in an honest Cause, humbly hope for, and the House may in their Wifdorn think fit to grant.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Sir William Middleton reported from the'Committee, to whom the Petition of Henry Errington, of Sandoe, in the County of Northumberland, Esquire, was referred; That the Committee had examined die Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House and he read the Report in his _ Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, paised in the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for building "a Stone Bridge across the River Tyne, opposite the " Town of Hexham, in the County of Northumberland, u and for making proper Roads and Avenues to and

Martii. L783.

" from the same,’* was fead, whereby it appeared, that certain Articles of Agreement were therein recited and confirmed, authorizing the Petitioner to build the said Bridge, under the Conditions mentioned in the said Articles.

And it appeared, by an authenticated Copy of a Certificate, produced to your Committee, under the Hands of Three Justices of the Peace for the said County, dated the 9th January 1781, that the said Bridge and a Road to the same had been completed, according to the Terms and Conditions of the above-mentioned Articles of Agreement. Theri

Mr. John Donkin being examined; laid, That he had been 'employed by Mr. Smeaton, the Architect, to superintend the Works while the said Bridge was building, and after it was finished to visit and inspect it, from Time to Time, in order to observe and give Notice of its State, and to replace the loose Stones which were laid down to defend the Piers from the Force of the Current, in case of their being removed by Floods or otherwise — That on the 11th of March 1782, the said new Bridge was, by the Violence of a Flood, forced down and destroyed, without having previously suffered the least Derangement or Decay, as, on a careful Examination Ten Days before the Accident happened, fully appeared to him — That there had been a considerable Flood in the River about a Month before that, on the 11th of March, immediately after which he had inspected the Bridge in all its Parts, when he found, that so far from having been injured then by it, it had received Benefit, the Violence of the Stream having driven Sand and Gravel amongst the loose Stones at the Feet of the Piers, so as to render them more compact and serviceable.

And being asked, What he thought caused the Destruction of the Bridge? he said, There was an extraordinary Fall of Snow the Night before the Accident, which laid about a Foot thick on the even Ground — That it began fnowing at Nine o’Clock at Night, arid continued till One in the Morning, when a violent heavy Rain came on, attended with a very high Westerly Wind, to which concurring Circumstances he presumed the Accident might in feme Degree be attributed — That he perceived in the Morning a very extraordinary Flood in the River, which runs from Weil to East, which induced him to go iriimediately to look at the Bridge.

And being asked, Whether he could tell, by certain . Marks on the Bridge, how high the Water was above, and how high below it? he said. He observed the Water on the lower Side of the Bridge was only at the Bottom of the Impost, or the projecting Part of the Top of the Pier, and on the upper Side it was above the Height of what is called the Dombing.

And being asked, Whether he was under any Apprehension, when he observed the Flood at that Height, that the Bridge was in any Danger of giving way? he replied. He was not; so far from it, that he lent his Son over to examine the Land Arches at the South End of the Bridge, with Two or Three Melons, who were on it not above Five Minutes previous to its Fall.

And being further asked, What Symptoms or Appearances of Failure of any Kind he had observed ? he said, He perceived feme Particles of Lime fall from the Fourth Arch, about the Size of Chaff — -That the Lime coming from thence, and no where else, he pointed his Observations to that Part only — That the falling of the Lime continued to increase in Size and Quantity for about the Space of a Minute — That soon after he observed a Crack across the Bend of the Arch, towards the upper Side of the Bridge, which Crack gradually widened, and in about a Minute more the Splinters from the Stones, !on the plain Part of the Spandrel, between the Third and Fourth Arch,

s. were

Geo. III. 40 Martii. 467

were forced out to a considerable Distance; ih Two Minutes more, the Pillar between the Third and Fourth Arch, which he could perceive shake, gave way, and the Two Arches and a Pier fell together — That the whole Bridge (Two Arches excepted) was destroyed within about the Space of Half an Hour, and one other Arch fell in the Evening; and he concluded with saying, that having carefully examined the Bridge from Time to Time, he was certain there had not been any previous Failure in that Part which first gave way, or in any other Part whatever.

Mr. John Smeatmiy the Engineer employed in building the Bridge, confirmed the Evidence of Mr.

respecting the Cause of its Destruction; and said, that the Nature of Snow was like that of a Spunge, it drank in all the falling Water till it was perfectly Saturated, without letting any of it go, and, after it was perfectly saturated, it burst forth all together, like a broken Reservoir, both Rain and Snow at once; this likewise, aided by the Rain continuing to fall, produced lb great and sudden a Torrent, that, according to the Parts of the Bridge to which the Water arose, by Mr. Donkins Evidence, there would be a Fall of no left than Five Feet perpendicular, between the upper Side of the Bridge and the lower, which was in the Space of Twenty Feet; the Consequence of which, together with the natural Weakness of the Stratum of Gravel on which the Bridge was built, was that the Torrent, as he apprehended, had forced the Gravel out of its Place, or not only forced it out of its Place, but that the incumbent Weight of a Body of Water, of I*lve Feet in Thicknest above the Bridge, superior to what was to counterbalance it below, had actually forced down the whole Stratum of the Gravel into the soft Matter that lay beneath it, and caused the Bridge itself, bodily, to take a Heel up the Stream, in which Postion the Remains of it now ft.

The Witness being further examined, said, That could he have been allured, before he recommended it to Mr. Errington to build the Bridge, that there had been a Possibility of a Fall of Five Feet of Water taking place at the Bridge, by a Quantity of Water coming down the Channel of the Tyne, or even Half of it, he never would have advised him to have undertaken to build the Bridge at his Charge, nor would he have hazarded his Reputation as an Artist upon it; and yet he had been allured by the County Surveyor, who was also Surveyor of the Bridge under the Witness during the Time of its building, that from Observations he had made in a similar Manner with those made by Mr. Donkin, as above described, that there had been a Fall, amounting to Three Feet Nine Inches in a former Flood, without the Bridge fullering any Derangement whatever — That, although in the singular Instance of the Flood in the Year 1771, the Water role to a greater Height than it did in 1782, yet, as he apprehended the Circumstances of the Rife of Water in 1771 did not bring it down lb suddenly, and of conrfe not with such Velocity, he was of Opinion, that had this Bridge been handing at that Time, as the Fall of Water would have been greatly left, it would not have been injured by it — That the additional Velocity, occasioned by the additional Fall of Five Feet, would be upwards of One thousand Feet in a Minute.

And being asked, Whether in his Opinion it was expedient to attempt the building of another Bridge on the Site of that lately destroyed? he said, He thought not, because the same Causes would, in all Probability, produce the same Effefits, and that therefore whenever the same Combination of Circumstances should concur, the same Effects would follow — That the same Considerations that, if then known, would have deterred him from attempting it at firsty

Vol. 39.

would operate as powerfully hbw, and Would fee Hexham strengthened by the Experience of the late Accident. Bridg*.

- — That he apprehended the Situation and Circumstances of the River were nearly similar at the Place Where a former Bridge, that was forced down by at Flood, had stood, and those of the Place where the Bridge in Question stood. — That if he were to be asked, he would not attempt to build a' Bridge there at his own Rilk, nor would he advise any other Persons to build it, much left that any Undertaking should be entered into for its standing the Term of Seven Years.

And being atked, Whether Mr. Errington derived any Advantage from the Contraft, pursuant to the Estimate delivered in by the Witness? he said. That Mr. Errington declared, when he applied to him, he did not desire or expefit any Advantage from the Contract. — That he was inltru&ed by Mr. Errington to build the Bridge in as substantial a Way as it could be done, who added, that if it cost him feme Hundreds more he ihpuld not mind it, the Advantages to which he looked being only such as might arise from the Contiguity of the Bridge to his Estate.

Being atked, Whether the Public at large, within a certain Distance of the Town of Hexham, were not t be equally benefited with Mr. Errington ? lie said, He apprehended the making of the Road to join the Turnpike Road, which cost feme Hundred Pounds, made that Bridge as beneficial to the Public in the Place where it then stood as it could be if built any where else, and he apprehended the Public would be benefited by it as well as Mr. Errington.

And being atked, Whether Mr. Errington had not fulfilled his Contract as completely as he the Witness could do it? he replied, Yes, he could not do it better —

That he did not know of any Place in the Vicinity of the Town of Hexham, where a Bridge could be built with greater Safety than the Place where the Bridge in Question stood; and he added, that the Plan upon which it was built was the best he could devise —

That the Plan had been executed without Accident, one Instance excepted, in which the Works at feme of the Piers had been injured by a Flood, but that the Pier the most damaged by that Flood was by the last Flood the least damaged, although upon perceiving the Accident happening to these Piers that were damaged, further Works were added to the Whole of them, which occasioned an additional Expence of 600 /. or more.

And being asked. What would be the Expence, with the Materials of the Bridge lo destroyed, of rebuilding it? he said, He could not pretend to ascertain the Expence of rebuilding it; but, as an- Answer to the Scope of that Question, he could say, from the Accounts he had of the Situation of the Bridge, and the Materials belonging to it, that if the County, or any other Person, were desirous of trying another Experiment, there is a more valuable Preparation of Materials than Mr. Errington received from the County.

Mr. Donkin being again examined, informed your Committee, That Mr. Emngton received from the County the Sum of 5,700l. as specified in his Contract — That he expended that Money, and at least 300l.-more, exclusive of the 400l. paid for making the Road, the Whole of which was laid out, except between 20 /. or 30/.

And being asked, What was the Value of the Materials of the destroyed Bridge? he said, He could not ascertain it exactly, but he believed them to be worth-double the Materials that were delivered to Mr. Errington under the Agreement, those having turned out worfo’ than were expected.

A Petition of the United Company of Merchants of East India England trading to The East Indies, being offered to Affair*, be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners were incorporated by Charter, made for a valuable Consideration, whereby the whole, foie, and exclusive Trade to, in, and from The East Indies was granted to the Petitioners, with other Rights and Privileges, which have been confirmed by divers Acts of Parliament; and that, under the Authority of the Charters granted to the Petitioners, and the Faith of Acts of Parliament confirming the fame, the Petitioners raised a very large Sum of Money by Way of Capital, and have carried on the Trade to, in, and from The East Indies for above 80 Years, to the very great Emolument and Advantage of this Country; and that, till the Year 1745, the Petitioners were considered in India merely in the Character of Traders enjoying such Settlements or Factories, and Privileges of Trade, as were from Time to Time granted to them by the Princes of India, without having any Military

All the Petitioners Profits inbeyond a Dividend of 8/. per Cent, to the Proprietors, are to be divided between the Public and the Petitioners in the Proportion of Three'-fourths to the Public, and One-fourth to the Petitioners; and, according to the Letter of the said Act, this Profit may be computed on the Accounts of a single Year, without providing for the Reiinbursement of any Lois sustained in the preceding Year, the Whole of which is, by this Mode of Computation, thrown upon the Petitioners; and that this Appropriation of Profits, for the Time past and to come, ariles from an Idea of the Public being entitled, independent of the Petitioners, to the Territorial Revenues in India: The Petitioners do not acquiesce in this Claim, however they do not think it incumbent upon than at this Time to enter into a Difculfion of it, and the Question to which the Petitioners intreat the Attention of the House, is under what Condition Justice can require a Participation from the Company? The Petitioners rely, that the most strenuous Afferter of the Claim of the Public {much more those who will give a liberal Consideration to the Subject) must allow that the Indian Revenues, or any Part thereof, ought not to be wrested from the Petitioners without a Reimbursement of the Expences of Acquisition, to which the Petitioners must add, that the Situation of their Affairs, distressed at Home, and loaded with Debt Abroad, requires such a Reimbursement, or an adequate Recompence in lieu thereof; the Bond Debt, which the Petitoners now owe, in a great Measure arose from their Military Expences in India, or has been necessarily continued on that Account; independent of theie Expences, the Petitioners ordinary Mercantile Profits would have enabled them to have extmguished the Whole of their Bond Debt long before the Territories were acquired; and that the Petitioners Necessities, arising from the Want, of being reimbursed a Principal of above Three Millions and an Half, and an Interest increasing on such Principal to a much greater Amount, it is conceived will justify Hopes of receiving effectual Aid from the Public; whillt these Disbursements remain unpaid to the Petitioners, they must conceive they are within the Bounds of Moderation in thinking that the Payments of 2,169,000l. and 300,000l. for the LTfe of the Public, were made under mistaken Ideas of the Petitioners pecuniary Abilities, and they confidently hope and trust, that so much thereof will now be returned as may enable them to carry on their Affairs, at Ic-aft that the ’300,000 /. so lately advanced when the Petitioners were utterly unable to spare it, may be returned in Part of the Reimbursement of their Ex-

want to carry on their Affairs only to the lft of March 1784, upon the most correct Calculation they have been able to make, allowing for the fofe Arrival «f all their expected Ships within that Period, will be about 900,000l. without paying the said loo, oo0/. but what farther Supply the Demands upon the Petitioners, fub-sequent to that Period, may require, they are not at present able to ascertain; nor will the House be surprised at the pecuniary Difficulties in which the Petitioners are involved, when they are informed, that, in Addition to the Expences and other Losses necessarily attendant on a State of Hostility, the increased Charge of the Petitioners in the Article of Shipping alone, during an European War, exceeds the Annual Sum of 500,000 /.; in this Cafe, and in order to provide for all Events without reducing the Dividend, which must affect the Petitioners Credit, and consequently the Interest of the State iri their Commerce, the Petitioners would propose to the House, that they should be permitted to increase their Bond Debt, as their Occasions may require, to any Sum not exceeding their former Bond Debt, and to repay the same from their subsequent Profits before any Participation takes place, which Increase of Debt, as the Law now Hands, cannot be made, preserving the very moderate Dividend at present paid on their Stock; and that, although the Petitioners trust that a Recompence will be made to them for their Disbursements in acquiring the Territories, they do not wish to apply the same in Dividends beyond 8 /. per Cent, as long as they shall owe Money upon Bond exceeding 1,500,000l. nor after that Time to increase their Dividend beyond the Rate mentioned in the said Act of the Twenty-first of His present Majesty, until the present Bond Debt shall be wholly discharged; and that the Petitioners further hope, that the House will not only fee proper to vary the subsisting Agreement, but that the Term of the Agreement will be extended; so short a Term as Ten Years (whereof Two Years are now expired) is injurious to Public Credit, in promoting Speculations upon what may be the Terms of new Agreements; and the Affairs of the Petitioners, by means of short Terms, are kept in a continued State of Agitation; on the Part of the Public, the Petitioners conceive a long Term cannot be objected to, as the Public cannot polfibly ever require to be paid a greater Share than Three-fourths of the Profits of the Territories; and the Petitioners further beg Leave to submit to the House, that the Clause of the said Act of the Tw-enty-first of His present Majesty, which directs that the Payment of the Three-fourths of Profits appropriated to the Public shall be made on the First Day of May in every Year, should be varied; the September Sale, when the Petitioners Sales arse regular is always the largest, and it frequently happens, in the ordinary Course of the Compariy’s Affairs, independent of any uncommon or unforeseen Expences, that the Petitioners are obliged to borrow Money in the Summer Half Year to pay Duties, or for other Purposes, therefore the Payment to Government of the Public’s Share of Profits being fixed to be made on the First of May, is very inconvenient; Two Remedies may be applied, the first {and which appears to be the most eligible) is, out of the Surplus Profits to raise a joint Fund, to remain by way of Stock, not to be divided till the End of the Term of Participation; the other is, to give Liberty to the Lords of the Treasury to allow such Time for the Payment of the Public’s Share of Profits as the Company’s Affairs may appear to require: The Third Observation which arises on the said Act of the

A PETIT ION of the Gentlemen, Traders, wnden TVn-v Freeholders, Land Owners, and others, in the toOainfoo-' County of Stafford, whole Names are thereunto fob- rough Navi-{bribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting 8ation-forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that Application is making for a Bill to improve the Navigation of the River Trent from Wilden Ferry, in the County of Derby, to Gainsborough, in the County of Lincoln; and that the Petitioners are fully sensible of the extreme Necessity there is for such Improvement being made, the piefent State of that River being a grievous Impediment to the Trade and Commerce of the adjacent Counties, and of the Kingdom in general; and that the Petitioners are informed, the Depth of Water meant to be procured by the said intended Improvement is to be only 18 Inches, whereas they are clearly convinced that a less Depth than 24 Inches will be very inadequate to the Occasions . of the Public, and insufficient to accommodate the several Navigable Canals and Rivers communicating with The Trent: And therefore praying, That Provision may be made in the said Bill, for deepening the said River Trent to 24 Inches at the least, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, Manufacturers, Ditto.,) and other Inhabitants, of the Town of Manchester, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Application mentioned in the preceding Petition; and setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed the said Improvement is intended to be confined to a Depth of 18 Inches of Water, although a much greater Depth may be obtained at a moderate Expence, and they are clearly convinced a greater Depth will be necessary for the Occasions of the Public, and the Accommodation of the several Canals which open Communications between the interior Parts of the Kingdom and The And

therefore praying, That the Improvement of the said River may not be limited to so inadequate a Depth as 18 Inches, but that it may be extended to such Depth of Water, and executed in such Manner, as will be moil beneficial to the Public, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for improving the Navigation of the River Trent, from a Place called frilden Ferry, in the Counties of Der and Leicester, or one of them, to Gainsborough, in the County of Lincoln, and for impowering Persons navigating Vessels thereon to hale the feme with Hories, is committed.

to whom the Petition of the Guardians of the Poor, within the Hundred of Forehoe, in the County of Norfolk, under their Common Seal, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Sixteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor, within the Hundred of Forehoe, in the County of Norf olk, was read: And

The Honourable Henry Hobart being examined, said, That the Guardians of the Poor in the said Hundred have, by virtue of the Powers vested in them by the said Act, purchased Grounds, and erected proper and commodious Buildings thereon, for the Reception and Employment of the Poor — That they borrowed a very considerable Sum of Money on the Credit and Security of the said Grounds and Buildings, and of the Rates or Assessments authorized by the said Act to be made and laid — That the Money lo borrowed was the whole Sum that the Guardians were by the Act enabled to raise, end has been all expended — That besides that Sum, the Whole of which remains due, some further Debts have unavoidably been incurred — -That it is now found, that the - Rates or Assessments, which by the said Act the Guardians are empowered to make or lay, are inefficient; and, that unless they are enabled to raise a further Sum, over and above the Produce of the said Rates, some additional Buildings, which are quite necessary, cannot be erected, the Principal Money already borrowed cannot be paid off, nor the Interest regularly discharged, and the Poor within the said Hundred cannot be properly supported and maintained.

Sir John Wodehouse, Baronet, confirmed the Whole of the foregoing Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for rendering effectual an Act, made in the Sixteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor, within the Hundred of Forehoe, in the County of Norfolk: And that Sir Edward Astley, Mr. Coke of Norfolk, and Sir Harbord Harbord, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Setting forth, That the Borough of Penryn is a Borough by Prescripfion, and the Portreeve of the said Borough is the principal Officer within the lame, and presides at the Election of Members of Parliament for the said Borough, and is the Returning Officer on such Elections; and that, ever since the Time of Edward the Sixth, the said Borough has lent Members to Parliament, and the Right of Election is in the Inhabitants paying Scotland bearing Lot within the said Borough; and that the Portreeve of the said Borough is elected at a Court Leet held for that Purpose within One Month after Michaelmas, Yearly; and that King James the First created a Corporation within the said Borough, consisting of a Mayor and Aldermen, and Burgesses, but did not impower the said Mayor and Aldermen to el eft, or join in the Election of, Members to serve in Parliament; and that King James the Second, during the Subsistence of the First Corporation, granted a Charter of Incorporation to the said Borough, and thereby impowered the Mayor and Twenty-four Aldermen nominated by him, in and by the said Charter, to elect and return Two Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough; and that, notwithstanding the Grant of the said last mentioned Charter, the Mayor and Aldermen have never interfered, or pretended to interfere, in the Election of Members, save as herein after-mentioned; and that, from the Time of the Grant of the first-mentioned Charter, until the Year 1767, the Offices of Portreeve and Mayor were generally united in the feme Person, and therefore the Precepts from the Sheriff for the Election of Members during that Period were directed to the Mayor and Portreeve; and that, since the Year 1767, the Offices of Mayor and Portreeve have been held by separate and distinct Persons, and from that Time until the Year 1780, the Precepts on the General Elections, and on the several intermediate Vacancies for the said Borough, were directed by the Sheriff of the said County of Cornwall for the Time being to the Portreeve of the said Borough only; and that, on the General Election in the Year 1780, the Sheriff of the said County directed his Precept to the Mayor and Portreeve, but the Words " Mayor and " were afterwards struck out, yet the Mayor and some of the Aldermen and Burgesses of the said Borough in that Year presented a Petition to the House, complaining of the Election and Return made by the Portreeve, And, amongst other Things, complaining that William Crowgey, the Portreeve of the said Borough, took upon himself to act as Returning Officer at the said Election, without permitting the Mayor of the said Borough to join with hint therein, but the said Petition, not having been heard in the Session when it was presented, it was not returned in the next Session; and that, in the Month of December last, on the Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, in the room of John Rogers, Esquire, who had vacated his Seat, Mr.

Charles Rashleigh, the Undersheriff, and who afteft for John Coryton, Esquire, the Sheriff of the said County, directed his Precept to the Mayor and Portreeve, and refused, on having the Fasts herein before-mentioned Hated to him, to strike out the Words Mayor " and" in the said Precept; and although the Mayor of the said Borough did not interfere in the Elect/on,

not

nor claim a Right of being Presiding and Returning Officer jointly with the Portreeve, yet the- Petitioners apprehend, that such illegal Conduct of the said Undersheriff may in Time create a Precedent in Prejudice of the Petitioners Rights, and of the Constitution of the said Borough, and tend to create Disputes and Dillurbances therein: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Mayor, Freemen, and Inhabitants, of the City of Rochester, in the County of Kent, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, sensible of the Excellency of that Con-ltitution under which they have the Happiness to live, most ardently wish to have it maintained upon the true Principles on which it is founded; and that, by Length of Time and other Circumstances, the llepresentation of the Commons of Great Britain is become greatly unequal, and in consequence the House of Commons does not sufficiently speak the Voice of the People: And therefore praying the House to take into their most . serious Consideration the present inadequate State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, and to apply such Remedy to this great Constitutional Evil, as to the House may i’eem meet.

A Petition of the Freeholders, Salt Merchants, and others. Inhabitants of Lyming in the County of Southampton, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the State of Representution in that Borough has been for many Years, as the Petitioners apprehend, extremely inadequate and imperfect, being restricted to the Mayor and a small Number of Burgestes; and that the Number of legal Resident Electors in the said Town at present docs not amount (according to the heft Information the Petitioners can procure from the Senior Resident Burgess) to more than Six; and that the Petitioners being thus deprived, as they conceive, of their natural and constitutional Right, the Right of voting for Representatives in Parliament, find themselves constrained to implore the Interposition of the House, and to solicit such Relief in the Premises as to their Wisdom shall l’ecm meet and expedient.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

Rtpresenta- A Petition of the Inhabitants of Scarborough, in the bauient! ar" County of York, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth. That it is necessary to the Welfare of the People, that the Commons House of Parliament should have a common Interest with the Nation, and that, in the present State of the Representation of the People in Parliament, the House of Commons do not sufficiently speak the Scnfe of the People; and that the Inequality of the present State of Representation, though derived from a Variety of concurrent Causes, is in no Instance more grievous than in that of the Privileges of Election exercised in great Towns by a very small Proportion of the Inhabitants, to the Exclusion of the rest, who, content as they might be without the peculiar Privileges annexed to Corporations, cannot, at the same 'lime, without Regret, feci themselves destitute of the first of Couftitutional Rights, a Share in the Election of those who are chose to represent them; and Alledging, that the Two Representatives for Scarborough are elected by a Corporation consisting, when full, of Two Bailiffs, Two Coroners, Four Chartiber-

1 Jains, and Thirty-six Capital Burgesses, the Vacancies

being supplied by Election out of the Freemen at large, by Twelve of the Corporate Body only; and that by the . Operation of the Bill, passed in the fall Session of Parliament, for disqualifying certain Officers of the Revenue I from voting at Elections, the present Electors for Scar-

borough do not exceed Thirty-five, but the Inhabitants thereof amount to about Eight Thousand, of whom about Seven Hundred are regularly assessed to the Pa-Tiffi Rates: To the Wifdoni and Justice of the House the Petitioners therefore respectfully apply, praying that their Petition may be taken into Consideration, and such Relief granted on the Premises as shall appear most conducive to the general Welfare of the Community, and best adapted to the particular State and Circumstances of the Town of Scarborough, agreeable to the Consti-

A Petition of the Nobility, Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders of the County of Nottingham, was likewise presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That from whatever Causes the inadequate and disproprotionate Representation of the Commons of this Realm may have arisen, it is an Evil of a very high Magnitude, which has not been less injurious to the past, than it is dangerous to the future Interests of this Country, and which, the Petitioners trust, it will not be thought unworthy the Wifdoni and Virtue of the House to reform; to this Wifclom and Virtue the Petitioners respectfully confide the Reform; but it is their earnelt Petition that no Delay may be admitted in taking this Grievance into the serious Consideration of the House; at the same Time the Petitioners submit Vo l.
