A Petition of the Freeholders and Inhabitants of the Town and Liberties of the Borough of Portsmouth, in the County of Southampton, w as presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Borough of Portsmouth is a large and populous Place, containing about Twenty thousand Inhabitants, and, before January 1695, the Mode of electing Members to represent the said Borough in Parliament was by the Inhabitants thereof in general; and that the present Mode of electing l’uch Representatives is by the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of tire laid Borough, which Body Corporate do not conlilt of more than Eighty Persons, most of whom live in Parts of the Kingdom very distant from the said Borough, w ho come to Portsmouth on Occasion of such VoL.SU.

Elections, but seldom, if ever, at any other Times, which, the Petitioners think, is unconltitutional, and a very great Harbship on the Petitioners, as they conceive the Representatives of the said Borough, in the great Council of the Nation, (hoald be elected by Voters inhabiting the said Borough: And therefore the Petitioners hope the House will take their same into Consideration, and, in thele Times of National Reform, to procure that in future the Members to represent the Petitioners in Parliament,

shall be elected by the Majority of the Votes of the Inhabitants of the said Borough and Liberties, who pay to Church and Poor, or in such other Manner as to the House thall seem most proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

doaU used The Lord Bulkeley reported from the Committee, to wl, om the Petition of John Dawes, Esquire, on Behalf of himself and others, Owners, Proprietors, and Lessees of Copper and Lead Mines, in the lile of Anglesey, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed); viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Samuel More, Esquire, being examined, said, There are Two Mines of Copper in Anglesey, both of which he had seen, but had not any Interest in either — That the Ore is carried from those Mines to be smelted. the greater Part to St.Helens, near Liverpool, and some to Swansea, in Glamorganshire, because there is not Fuel in the

3 Hand for (melting it — That no Duty is paid 011 Coals at the Places to which the Ore is sent. — Being asked, If the Copper Ore of Cornwall is carried to the Coal Mines to be smelted ? he said, He believed great Part - of it is — That the Price of Coal in where the Ore is lent to be smelted, is 5 s. or 5 6 d. at

the Delivery at the Works, and on Ship-board at Sxvan-tea 48. 3 d.per Ton — That the Freight of Coals from Liverpool to Anglesey is near 6 s. per Ton, and from Swansea about 7 s.exclusive of Port Duties. — And being asked. Whether there is any Fire Engine yet erected in Anglesey?he said. It is Two Years and an Half since lie was there — That there is not, nor any Work for smelting Copper — That when he was there, the Mines were about Twenty Yards deep — That they are different from any Mines he had ever ieen, the Ore being all in one Mats, like Limestone and Gravel — That there are some Advantages in that, but which may hereafter turn out in some Degree to their Disad vantage, for as they have begun by opening a large Space, and will hereafter be obliged to fink Shafts, as is usual in Mining, the great Opening will serve as a Funnel to receive a large Quantity of Rain Water, and tend to fill up the Mine — That the Altitude of the Mountain, from the Level of the Island, may be about or under 200 Feet, and the Openings are very near the Summit of the Hill. — And being asked, In what Degree the Discouragement the Mines are laid to have suffered, has been hitherto felt? lie said, The Company themselves are the bell Judges of that. — Being asked, Whether they are near the Bottom of the Ore ? he said, That when he was there they were not near it. — And being asked. How loon his. Observation led him to think a Fire Engine would be necessary? he laid, He should imagine soon; that it depends much on Circumstances — That it rtiay be necessary directly, and may not for a considerable Time. — And being asked, If he had tried

07

the Ore? he said, He had, and all the Materials that come from the Mountain where it is raised — That the Ore in its raw' State is so poor, as not to produce on the Average One in Twenty. — And being asked, Whether he knew, that notwithstanding the Poorness of the Ore, the Work is exceedingly profitable? he said, He was not competent to speak to that, but it is under-Hood so to be — That he had always heard from the Parties themselves that it was.' — And being asked, Whether the Miners have an ealy Method of increasing the Value of the Ore, by burning it on the Grass when landed, without the Expence of Fuel? he laid, The Nature of the Ore is fuel), that it is very easily set on Fire, so as to be calcined in large Kilns, without much Expence of Fuel; but by being thus calcined in the open Air, a very great Proportion of the Metal itself is loft in the Operation, notwithstanding the Methods made qfe of to recover some of the Metal by Precipitation, by means of Iron Plates — That after this Calcination, he should suppose the Produce of the Ore is on the Average about Two in Twenty. — And being asked, Whether the Water follows in digging up the Ore from this Mass, as it does in other Mines ? he said. Not near in the same Proportion as it does when the Veins are small. — And being asked, What is the Altitude of the Mountain from the Level of the Sea ? he said, From 300 to 350 Feet, he believed, from that Part of the Mountain where they were at Work when he was there, and that Part of it next the Sea forms a bold Shore. — And being asked, What Stratum a Level from the High Water Mark to the Mine would go through? he said, He believed a hard Quartz, and not any Metals, for none appeared to him. — And being asked, If there are Adits from Mines in Cornwall of a3 great a Length as that which would be necessary for draining the Mines in Anglesey? he said, He believed there are. — And being asked, How the Water was got out of the Anglesey Mine when he was there? he said, By Horse Wheel, called a Whim. — And being asked, Whether, in case the Petitioners succeed, and the Drawback should be allowed, the Processes that would then be used by the Proprietors in linelting the Ore, would be more injurious to the circumjacent Country than the Processes now used? he laid, Certainly not — That they cannot be more injurious; and if they were, the Country is so ruined already, that it cannot be made worse. — And being asked, Whether the present Produce of the Ore will pay the Expence of an Act from the Mine, as he had described it? he said, It would not. — And being asked, What will be the Expence of an Adit? he said, Nobody can tell — That he took the common Average Price of making Adits to be Twelve Guineas a Yard, but it may be more. — And being asked, What is the Annual Produce of the Mine? he said, He did not know. — And being asked, Why he thought the Mine would not bear the Expence of an Adit? he said, Because, if the Ore continues as poor as it is now, the increasing Charge of railing it will be such, that it will not bear both Expences. — And being asked, What is the Average Proportion of the Produce of the Cornish Mines? he said, Two and on Half in Twenty — That the Standard Price of Copper may be said to be 801, per Ton. — And being asked, What, at that Price, is the Anglesey Ore, which produces One in Twenty, worth to the Proprietors ? he said, The general Rule for finding the Value of Ore is to multiply the Standard by the Product; from that Product to deduct 3/. for smelting Charges, which is univerl’ally allowed, and the Remainder will be the Value; which in the Instance of the Anglesey Ore, is Twenty Shillings per Ton — That by the same Mode of Calculation, the Ore, which produces Two and an Half in Twenty, is worth 7/. per Ton to the Proprietors; and that the great Increase of Value ariles

from the smelting Charges being only 3/. on feach Kind of Ore. — And being asked, What Proportion of the Metal is actually loft, after all the Processes of burning and smelting ? he said, About One Third.

Your Committee then examined Mr. Samuel liamson, Agent for the Owners of the Paris Mine, in the Isle of Anglesey; who being asked, By what Method the Water is raised from that Mine ? said, by a Horse Engine. — And being asked, Whetl>er they can go on working that Mine any longer, by draining it in that Mode? he said, That in the Winter of the Year 1781 the Water in the Mine increased so much, that the Workmen found it difficult to go on at all at the lower Bottoms — That this Winter it has baffled all the Power of the Horses and Men too, inso much that in many Places they could not get to the lower Bottoms at all, and in general did not raise near the Quantity they should otherwise have done — That they now employ a Change of Twelve Horses Two at a Time, the Wheel being perpetually going Day and Night, and that it most certainly is necessary to have a Fire Engine to keep the Mine clear of Water; and that it is not possible that any Number of Horses that could be used should answer the feme Purpose. — And being asked, Whether an Act would not answer all the Purposes of a Fire Engine, and at less Expence ? he said, That not being a Miner he could not tell. — And being a feed, What is the present Depth of the Mines ? he laid 36 Yards on their Side, and 40 at that belonging to the

Macclesfield Company. — -And being asked, Whether he thought it would be possible to carry on the Works in Anglesey, without some Relief is given, similar to that in Devonshire and Cornwall, with respect to the Drawback on Coals? he said. That considering the excessive Poor-ness of the Ore, the increasing Depth from which it is raised, and the Weight of Water, he thought they could not.

MR. Speaker acquainted the Housej That he had received, from Lieutenant General Boyd, the following Letter, in Return to the Thanks of this House, signified to him by Mr. Speaker, in Obedience to their Commands of the 1 -2th Day of December last.

Sir, Gibraltar, March 13th, 1783.

By His Majesty’s Frigate Thetis, which arrived here the 10th Instant, I was honoured with your most polite Letter of the 13th December, inclosing a Resolution of the House of Commons, in which I am named as an Officer of this Garrison worthy of their Thanks.

For this, in my Estimation one of the noblest Testimonials a British Officer can receive of his Service, I am to beg you would be pleased to offer the most cordial Acknowledgements of a worn-out Veteran; who has served Fifty-three Years, most of that Time Abroad, and who now only laments that from the rapid Progress of Age and Infirmities, he cannot hope to be of any further Service to his King and Country.

I am, Sir, with great Respect,

Your most obedient,

humble Servant,

Bob' Boyd.

Right honourable C. W. Comexva

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names Removal of are thereunto subscribed, Dealers in Tea, within the Tea.

City and County of the City of Exeter, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Twenty-first Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for repealing the Duties payable upon Chocolate made in Great Britain, and for granting certain Inland Duties upon Cocoa Nuts in lieu thereof; for the better and more effectual securing the Revenue of Excise, and of the Inland Duties under the Management of the Commissioners of Excise, and for preventing Frauds therein, and other Purposes; it is enacted, That all Tea seized by any Officer of the Customs, or for the Inland Duties upon Tea, for any Cause of Forfeiture in any Part of England, shall, before the same is fold, be deposited in some Warehouse to be appointed by the Commissioners of Excise and Customs in England, within the City of London, in order to be there publickly fold; which Clause the Petitioners conceive bath been attended with very pernicious Consequences to the Revenue and Fair Traders of the City of Exeter, and the Country adjacent; for, the Petitioners being now obliged to send to London for their Teas, and allow a Profit on what is bought there, which, together with the high Price of Carriage into the Country, hath occasioned the Price of Low Teas to come so high to the Consumer, that it hath almost put an entire Stop to any Tea being sold at the entered Shops as before the passing of the said Act, greatly reduced the Number of Retailers, and been very instrumental in promoting Smuggling; whereas, before the passing of the said Act, the Petitioners were able to supply themselves with Teas at the Custom Houses in and near Exeter, and render them on equal Terms with the London Traders, by which Means great Quantities were sold at the entered

Shops,

And the said Order was read accordingly.

And several Members, returned upon new Writs, having taken the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, and having delivered in to the Clerk of the House an Account of their Qualification, and taken and subscribed the Oath of Qualification, according to the Laws made for those Purposes;

The laid Bill was read a Second Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Thursday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

Sir James Lcwther reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers of an Act, made in the Second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty King George the Third, intituled, "An Act for widening, repairing, and amending, the Road " from Hesket, by Yewes Bridge, to Cockermouth; and " from thence by Lorton, over JVhinlatter, to Keswick,

" in the County of Cumberland -, and from Keswick,

" by Dummail Rays and Am to Kirby in Ken- " dall, in the County of Westmorland; and from -

garth's Cross, uear Kirby in Kendall aforesaid, to the

" Lake called Windermere, in the County of -

" land; and from Keswick aforesaid to the Town of " Penrith, in the County of Cumberland," was committed; That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingossed.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to Horsham the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ for Writ* the electing of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Horsham, the County of Sussev, in the room of James Wallace, Esquire, who, since his Election for the said Borough, hath accepted the Office of Attorney General to His Majesty.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Hett and Mr. Thomson:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to repeal so much of Two Acts, made in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, as prohibits Trade and Intercourse

with the United States of America; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Ireland — Act for removing and preventing all Doubts which have Legislative arisen, or might arise, concerning the exclusive Rights of the Parliament and Courts of Ireland, in Matters of Legislation and Judicature; and for preventing any Writ of Error, or Appeal, from any of His Majesty’s Courts in that Kingdom, from being received, heard, and adjudged, in any of His Majesty's Courts in the Kingdom of Great Britain;without any Amendment:

And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Newnham t* Act for amending and widening the Road from the St. Whites Passage or Ferry over the River Severn, at Newnham, Road‘ in the County of Gloucester, through the Parishes of Newnham and Little Dean, to a Place called Saint Whites, adjoining His Majesty’s Forest of Dean, in the said County; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act Sandon, Ac. to enlarge the Term and Powers of an Act, made in ®oa^* the Second Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for repairing, widening, and altering the Road from Sandon, in the County of Stafford, to Bullock Smithy, in the County of Chester; and from Hilderston to Draycott in the Moors, and from Wetley Rocks to Tean, in the said County of Stafford; w ithout any Amendment:

And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Staunton Act for dividing, inclosing, and improving a certain "P°" "[ye. Common, or Waste Ground, within the Parish of c,ncoure* Staunton upon Wye, in the County of Hertford, and for extinguishing the Right of Common upon certain inclosed Lands within the said Parish; without any Amendment.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

A Petition of John Buller, Esquire, w’as delivered in gajta(h at the Table, and read; Setting forth, That, at the late EleAioo. Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Saltash, in the County of Cornwall, the Petitioner, and Sir Grey Cooper, Baronet, were Candidates; and that Mr. Caleb Colton, the Mayor and Returning Officer for the said Borough, behaved himself with Partiality in favour of Sir Grey Cooper, by rejecting the Votes of several Persons who had an undoubted Right of voting at the said Election, and who tendered their Votes for the Petitioner, and by admitting on the Poll for the said Sir Grey Cooper, the Votes of several Persons who had no Right to vote, and ought to have been rejected; and that thereby a Majority of Votes was improperly received on the Poll for the said Sir Grey Cooper, and he was returned as duly elected, to the Prejudice of the Petitioner, and in Violation of the Rights and Privileges of the Electors of the said Borough of Saltash: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant to the Pe-tioner such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Confi- . deration upon Friday the 9th Day of May next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Seven-night, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

A Petition of the several Merchants and Manufacturers of Birmingham, Wolverhampton, Walsall, and

Bilslon, in the Counties of Warwick and Stafford, whole Names arc thereunto l’ubscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, and many other Perfops at the several Places before-mentioned, are extensively concerned in various Branches of Trade and Manufacture, wherein great Quantities of Copper and Lead are necessarily used; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Petition has been presented on Behalf of the Owners, Proprietors, and 'Lefices, of the Copper and Lead Mines in the Isle of Anglesey, itating the Inconveniencies they labour under for want of Coal and other Fuel in the said Isle, and that, by reason of the high Price of and Duties on Coals there, it will be impossible for them to work the said Mines without having the same Drawback of Duties on Coals carried Coastways as are granted in respect of the Coals consumed in Cornwall and Devonshire in draining the Mines, and fmelting the Copper and Tin Ores within those Counties; and Representing to the House, that the

Consumption of Copper and Lead in the different Branches of Manufacture within this Kingdom, and the Exportation thereof, has greatly increased within a few Years last past, and, since the Copper Mines in Anglesey have been discovered and worked, the Petitioners have been the better enabled to get a necessary Supply of Copper for their Manufactures, and at lower Prices than otherwise would have been the Cafe; and they have great Reason to fear that, if some Parliamentary Relief is not given to encourage the Working of the said Mines in Anglesey, so as to put them on ,the same Footing with the Copper Mines in Cornwall and Devonshire, and thereby prevent that Monopoly always attendant upon exclusive Privileges, the Owners and Lefl’ees of the said Anglesey Mines, by reason of the extreme Poverty of the Ores, and the increasing Depth of the Mines, together with the high Duties upon Coals imported into Anglesey, may be discouraged from prosecuting the said Mines, which will be very injurious to the Petitioners, and all other Persons concerned in any Branch of Manufacture, wherein Copper is used, and to the Public in general: And therefore praying the House to take into Consideration the same of the said Owners, Lessees and Proprietors, of the said Copper and Lead Mines in Anglesey, and to grant them such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for allowing a Drawback of the Duties upon Coals used in smelting Copper and Lead Ores, and in Fire Engines for draining Water out of the Copper and Lead Mines within the Isle of Anglesey, be read a Second Time.

The other Order of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Seven-night, resolve itself into a Committee of the w hole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That he had received from General Eliott and Major General La Motte the following Letters, in Return to the Thanks of this House, signified to them by Mr. Speaker, in Obedience to their Commands of the 12th Day of December last.

Gibraltar, March 18 th 1783.

Sir,

I mull intreat you to accept our grateful Acknowledgments for the high Satisfaction you are pleased to express in your Letter of 13th December 1782, received on the nth Instant by the Thetis Frigate, transmitting, in Obedience to the Commands of the House, the Two unanimous Resolutions respecting all who have served in the Defence of Gibraltar.

I have delivered to Lieutenant General Boyd, Major General De La Motte, and Major General Green, the several Inclosures addressed to them; and I have also communicated the Resolutions of the House to the whole Garrison.

We, the Officers, are highly sensible of the Honour conferred on us; the Sailors and Soldiers, I am confident, will receive the Honour done them with every Demonstration of Gratitude and Joy, as loon as it can be declared to them in suitable Military Form.

I have the Honour to be,

Sir,

Your most obedient, and

most humble Servant,

A. Eliott,

Right honourable Charles Wolfran Cornwall,

Sic. Si c.&c.

Gibraltar, 18th March 1783.

Sir,

I have the Honour to acknowledge the Receipt of your Letter of 13th December last, together with a Refutation of the House of Commons, ordering the Thanks of that House to be given to Lieutenant General Boyd,

Major General La Motte, Major General Green, Chief Engineer, to Sir Roger Curtis, and to the Officers,

Soldiers, and Sailors, lately employed in the Defence of Gibraltar.

I beg you will be pleased, Sir, to inform the House, that, for my Part, I have the highest Sense of the great Flonour the House of Commons of Great Britain has bestowed upon me by their Resolution.

I return you my particular Thanks, Sir, for the very polite Manner in which you have been pleased to communicate to me the said Resolution; and have the Honour to be, with the greatest Respect,

Sir,

Your most obedient and

most humble Servant,

A. De la Motte.

The Right honourable C. W.

Cornwall, Speaker to the House of Commons.

Mr. Ord, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolution which the Committee had direcded him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Sum of Twelve Millions be raised by Annuities j and the further Sum of Four hundred and Eighty thousand Pounds by a Lottery, in Manner following; that is to say:

That every Contributor to the said Twelve Millions shall, for every One hundred Pounds contributed and paid, be entitled to the Principal Sum of One hundred Pounds in Annuities, after the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum, to Commence from the Fifth Day of January, One thou fend Seven hundred and Eighty-three, and shall be added to, and made One Joint Stock with, the Three Pounds per Centum Annuities, consolidated by the Acts of the Twenty-fifth, Twenty-eighth, Twenty-ninth, Thirty-second, and Thirty-third Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, and by several subsequent A9s, and shall be payable and transferrable at the Bank of England, at the same Time, and in the same Manner, and subject. to the like Redemption by Parliament, as the said Three Pounds per Centum consolidated Annuities are payable and transferrable there.

That every Contributor shall also be entitled to the further Principal Sum of Twenty-five Pounds in Annuities, after the Rate of Four Pounds Centum, to commence from the Fifth Day of One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-three, and shall be added to, and made One Joint Stock with, certain

Vol. 30.

Annuities, after the Rate of Four Pounds per Cenlum, which were consolidated by the Atts of the Twentieth, Twenty-first, and Twenty-second Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, and be payable and transferrable at the Bank of England, at the feme Time, and in the same , Manner, and subject to the like Redemption by Parliament, as the said Four Pounds per Centum consolidated Annuities are payable and transferrable there.

That every such Contributor shall likewise be entitled to an Annuity of Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence per Centum, to commence from the Fifth Day of January, One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-three, and to continue for the Term of Seventy-seven Years, and then to cease, over and above the Principal Sums of One hundred Pounds, after the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum per Annum, and Twenty-five Pounds, after the Rate of Four Pounds per Centum per Annum, in respect of every One hundred Pounds to be contributed, and paid towards raising the said Sum of Twelve Millions; which Annuity of Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence per Centum lb to continue for Seventy-seven Years, shall be added to, and made One Joint Stock with, certain Annuities, payable at the Bank of England, which were granted for the several Terms of Ninety-nine, Ninety-eight, Eighty, and Seventy-eight Years, and were, by the Acts of the Fourth, Twentieth, and Twenty-second Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, consolidated and made One Joint Stock of Annuities, and shall be paid, payable, and transferrable at the feme Time, and in the same Manner, as the said Annuities so consolidated by the Acts of the Fourth, Twentieth, and Twenty-second Years of the Reign of His present Majesty are payable and transferrable at the said Bank of England.

That the several Annuities after the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum, Four Pounds per Centum, and Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence per Centum, so to be payable as aforesaid, shall be charged and chargeable upon, and payable out of, a Fund to be established in this Session of Parliament for Payment thereof, and for which the Sinking Fund shall be a collateral Security.

That every Contributor. towards raising the said Sum of Twelve Millions shall, for every One thousand Pounds contributed, be entitled to Four Tickets in a Lottery to consist of Forty-eight thousand Tickets, amounting to Four hundred and Eighty thousand Pounds, upon Payment of the further Sum of Ten Pounds for each Ticket, the said Four hundred and Eighty thousand Pounds to be distributed into Prizes for the Benefit of the Proprietors of the fortunate Tickets in the said Lottery, which shall be paid in Money, at the Bank of England, to such Proprietors, upon Demand, as loon after the First Day of March, One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-four, as Certificates can be prepared, without any Dedu6tion whatsoever.

That every Contributor shall, on or before. the Twenty-fourth Day of this Instant April, make a Deposit of Fifteen Pounds per Centum on such Sum as he or she shall chuse to subscribe, towards raising the said Sum of Twelve Millions, with the Chief Cashier or Cashiers of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, and also a Deposit of Fifteen Pounds per Centum with the said Cashier or Cashiers, in Part of the Monies to be contributed towards raising the said Sum of Four hundred and Eighty thousand Pounds by a Lottery, as a Security for making the future Payments respectively, on or before the Days or Times herein after mentioned; that is to say, On 12,000,000l. to be raised by Annuities.

A Petition of the Burgesses in the Royal Borough of Montrose, North Britain, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, in common with their Fellow Citizens in the other Royal Boroughs in Scotland, have no actual Representation in Parliament, as the Magistrates and Town Councils in the different Boroughs claim and exercise an exclusive Right of electing Repref'entatives in Parliament without the Con-lint or even Knowledge of their Fellow Burgesses; and that, to render the Situation of the Petitioners still more degrading, the Town Council, confiding only of Nineteen Persons, annually elect their Successors, or continue themselves in Office, without the Suffrage of one Burgess in the Town; and the Petitioners, having no Voice in the Choice of their Representatives, are debarred from the Rights of British Subjects, and having no Vote in the Election of their Magistrates, are deprived of the Rights of Free Members of the Corporation to which they belong; and that the Petitioners conceive the Safety and Prosperity of their Country will greatly depend on restoring the Confiitution to the Purity of its first Principles, in Compliance with the Willies of Thousands of their Fellow Subjects, whole Petitions lie on the Table; And therefore the Petitioners, in full Confidence of the Justice of the House, earnestly request that they will grant such lledress as they shall see fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

MR. Speaker acquainted the House, That he had received from Major General Green the following Letter, in Return to the Thanks of this House, signified to him by Mr. Speaker, in Obedience to their Commands of the 12th Day of December last.

Gibraltar, nth Ma1783-

Sir,

I had the Hopour, this Day, of receiving your Letter of the 13th December last, transmitting the rewith the Resolution of the Honourable House of Commons, which had passed the Day before, wherein their Thanks were given to certain Officers serving in this Garrison (among whom I have the Honour to be named) and to the Officers, Soldiers, and Sailors* lately employed in the Defence of Gibraltar.

Such a condescending Mark of Public Approbation, from the House of Commons of Great Britain, I deem to be one of the highest Rewards a British Subject could receive, for every contributing Endeavour of miue towards the Defence' of this Fortress.

Permit me to allure you, Sir, it did not fail of warming my natural and professional Feelings* in such a Manner, as I find myself extremely deficient in a due Style of Language properly to cxprcls, both in regard to its stimulating Effect, as well as that high Sense of Gratitude, and Acknowledgements, which I ‘hope for your Goodness to make acceptable to the House of Commons, for such an honourable Distinction conferred

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Tenants, and Occupiers of Lands and Tenements within the Town and County of the Town of Kingston u])on , whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending for building a new Gaol for the Town and County of the Town of Kingston upon Hull, and other Purposes; and that a Petition of several Owners, Proprietors, and Occupiers of Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments within the said Town and County; and also, a Petition of Christopher Sykes, Christopher Goulton, Henry Legat'd, John Bowman, and Bethel Robinson, Esquires, and others, have been presented to

Recruiting the Land Forces.

Supply.

Supply Bill: Lottery, dec.

Kingston upon Hull Gaol.

23 Geo. III. 290 dprilis. 397

the House, praying to be heard, by Counsel, against certain Parts of the said Bill; and Representing to the House, that the present Gaol in the Town of Kingston upon Hull is a very small, ancient, and decayed Building, and was erected for the Use of the said Town only, but that, since the several Towns, Villages, Hamlets, and Places now within the County of the Town of Kingston upon were separated from the County of York, the Gaol has been appropriated to the Use as well of the County of the Town of Kingston upon Hull, as of the said Town; and that the Populoufnels of the Town and County of Kingston Upon Hull having of late Years much increased, a larger Gaol is become necessary, and the Petitioners eonceive it is reasonable, that the Expence attending the same should be equally dilfufed among all the Persons who receive Benefit from it; and that, before the County of the Town of Kingston upon Hull was separated from the County of York, the Inhabitants thereof were liable to contribute towards the Charges of the Building and Support of the Castle or Gaol for die County of York, from which Expences they are now wholly exempted;, and ,that although the Inhabitants of the County as well as of the Town of Kingston upon Hull have an equal Advantage from the present Gao), and will have the like Interest in the New Gaol which is proposed to be erected, yet the Proportion of the Expence which the County of the Town of Kingston upon Hull will become liable to contribute towards the building such New Gaol will not exceed One Fourth Part thereof; and that the Necessity of having a larger, more commodious, lafe, and healthy Gaol for the Town and County of the Towm of Kingston upon Hull is an Object of so great Importance, and of such public Utility, and the Expence attending the fame, when raised in the Manner proposed by the Bill, by an AffeOment not exceeding Four Pence in the Pound Rent in any One Year, will be so ealy and inconsiderable a Charge upon the several Persons interested, that it has been adopted by the said Bill, in Preference to the Method prescribed by the Statute of the Eleventh and Twelfth of King William the Third, for impowering Justices of the Peace to raise Money by a County Rate for building or repairing Gaols: And therefore praying, That the said Bill now depending in the House may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the Bill for building a new Gaol for the Town and County of the Town of Kingston upon Hull', for purchasing an additional Burial Ground for the Use of the Parish of The Holy Trinity, in the said Town, and for railing Money for’ those Purposes; for ascertaining the Fares of Hackney Coachmen and Chairmen, and regulating their Behaviour; for preventing Annoyances within the said Town, and Liberties and Precincts thereof; for explaining an Act, made in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making and establishing Public Quays or Wharfs at Kingston upon Hull', and for other Purposes, is committed.

And the Counsel for Sir Thomas Rumbold proceeded further in his Defence; and having proposed to produce Evidence in order to shew, that, notwithstanding the Orders given to Lord Macartney to fend the Committee of Circuit, yet that it was impracticable in a State of War so to do; and that no Censure of the Company has passed in consequence of its not having been done;

The Counsel for and against the Bill were directed to withdraw.

It passed in the Negative.

And the Counsel for Sir Thomas Rumbold proceeded further in his Defence.

And then the Counsel for and against the Bill were again directed to withdraw.

A Petition of the Five incorporated Trades of the Burgh of Dumbarton, and of the Merchants, Here-tors, and other residing Burgesses of the said Burgh thereto subscribing, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Magistrates and Town Council of the said Burgh, in whom the Government thereof is vested, conliit of a Provost, Two Baillics, Dean of Guild, and Treasurer, and Ten Common Council; and, by the present Mode, the Petitioners have no Voice in the Election of the said Magistrates and Council, they Annually electing themselves; and that this Mode of Election the Petitioners conceive to be unconstitutional, and not only repugnant to those natural Rights, which, as British Subjects, they have a Title to enjoy, but a violent Infringement on their Privileges as free Burgesses; that it not only tends to keep the same Set of Men in Office during Life, but of late has been the Means of their introducing amongst them, as Members of their Council, Persons not residing in the Bunfe, nor anyways connected with it, whereby Vo L. SO.

its true Interests have been neglected, its Revenue lost or misapplied, and the whole Administration of it rendered only subservient to particular Views of Interest or Fastion; and that the Magistrates and Common Council thus self-elected, are in Use to chuse from amongst themselves a Delegate to meet with the Delegates from the other Burghs in the District, and cleft a Burgess to represent them in Parliament; and the Petitioners having no Voice in the Choice of the said Delegate, have no Representation in Parliament: And therefore praying.

That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill declaratory of the Petitioners Rights as free Burgesses, and for vesting in the free Residing Burgesses of the said Burgh the Power of electing the Magistracy and Town Council thereof, as well as the Delegate to meet with the Delegates from the other Burghs in the District, for chusing a Burgess to represent them in Parliament, or to give the Petitioners such other Relief in the Premises as to tho House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of The Tower Hamlets, not represented in Parliament, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That The Tower Hamlets form a very large and populous' District, wherein a great and extensive Trade is carried on, and are Annually charged considerably more to the Land Tax than several Counties that now fend Members to Parliament; and that there are Thousands of Copyholders, Leaseholders, and Householders, within The Tower Hamlets, who contribute largely to the Burthens of the State, but are, as the Law now stands, deprived of their Right of voting for the Choice of the Representatives by whom those Burthens are imposed, and are therefore, as they conceive, altogether unrcpresented in Parliament; and that the Petitioners are impressed with a deep Sense of the original Excellence of the British Constitution, and cannot but consider the present unequal Representation of the Commons of this Realm as a most alarming Grievance, that calls aloud for immediate Redress, and beg Leave to express their Apprehensions to the House, that no effectual Reform can take Place, unless the Right of voting for the Choice of Representatives in Parliament is extended, agreeably to the genuine Spirit of the Constitution of this Country: And therefore praying the House to take their same into serious Consideration, and to grant them such Relief, and apply such Remedy to the present disproportioned and inadequate Representation of the People in Parliament, as to the House shall fcem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Merchants and Manufacturers in and Coals used near the Town of Birmingham, who are materially interested in the Price of Copper, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, that a Bill is depending to allow the Exportation of Coals, Duty-free, for the Use of the Copper Works in the Island of Anglesey, or for allowing the Duties payable on the Coals used in those Works to be drawn back; and that, in consequence of the Copper Ores of Anglesey being raised at ai less Expence than any others, the Proprietors can afford to fell their Copper at a lower Rate, and have therefore much reduced the Price of that Commodity; and the Petitioners conceive, that any Encouragement which may be given to those Works, is not only adding to the great Advantages which they already derive from Nature over other Mines where the Ores are got with more Difficulty, and the Number of People employed considerably greater, but may also in the End prove highly injurious to the Public, by enabling the Proprietors of the Anglesey Mines to reduce the Price of Copper, so as to prevent other Adventurers from working the deep Mines which at present produce the greatest Part of the Copper Ores, whereby the Copper Trade would be thrown into a few Hands, Competition would in a great Measure cease, and such Prices might be fixed upon Copper as would materially affect the Manufactures of the Town and Neighbourhood of Birmingham, in which the Petitioners are deeply interested; and the Petitioners are also assured, that English Copper is now fold in most Foreign Markets cheaper than any other Copper, and they conceive, that any further Abatement of the Price in those Markets is unnecessary, and would be giving away the natural Riches of this Country to Foreigners at an under Value: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for allowing a Drawback of the Duties upon Coals used in smelting Copper and Lead Ores, and in Fire Engines for draining Water out of the Copper and Lead Mines, within the Ifie of Anglesey was committed.

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petitions.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Five Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into She Glasses, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Nine* Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of John Buller, Esquire, being drawn, he required to be excused from serving on the said Select Committee, on Account of his being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards; and having at the Table verified the same upon Oath, he was excused accordingly.

And the Name of One other Member, then present, was drawn, who was not objected to.

And the Name of John Anstruther, Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee by the Counsel for the Petitioners, and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Thirty-nine other Members then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, ‘ the Names of Two other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside with the Names of those who were absent from the House, on account of their being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards, which they had before verified upon Oath.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members, lb drawn as aforesaid, and not excused or set aside, being complete;

The Counsel for the Sitting Member nominated the Right honourable William Eden to serve on the said Select Committee.

And Lists of the said Forty-nine Names were delivered by the Clerk to the said Counsel.

And the Door of the House being opened;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides withdrew.

A Message by Mr. Quarme, Yeoman Ulher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Com- Royal Assent million, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts to Bill*, agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

A Petition of the Committee of the Company of Mer- African chants trading to Africa, being offered to be presented to Company, the House;

Lord John Cavendish, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of die House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;'

Setting forth, That the Petitioners have laid before the House an Account of the Money granted in the Year 1781, examined and passed by the- Cursitor Baron of the Exchequer, as required by an Act, of the Twenty-third of George the Second, intituled, "An Act for " extending and improving the Trade to Africa f and that they have invested the Money, granted in 1782, for the Support and Maintenance of the Forts and Settlements on the said Coast; and that the said Forts and

Settlements

4^4 I 6* Mai 1783.

Settlements were delivered to the Petitioners in a very ruinous Condition by the Royal African Company, and the Sums annually granted by Parliament for their support and Maintenance being nearly expended in the Civil and Military Establishments, and in the neccfl'ary contingent Charges, there remained little or nothing for the Purpose of Repairs, so that several of them Hill continue in a very defenccless State} and that fundrv Abuses having been alledged to exist in the Conduct of the Officers employed by the Petitioners on the Coast of Africa, and more particularly in the Management of the public Money committed to their Care, the Peti-. tioners thought proper, in the Year 1779, to suspend their Governor in Chief and the Council at Cape Coast Castle, and to appoint certain Commissioners to examine in Africa into the Conduct and Accounts of the Officers, from the Beginning of the Year 1770; and, the said Commissioners having made their Report upon the Accounts of Richard Miles, Esquire, Governor of Cape Coast Castle, and the Petitioners having themselves like-wife gone through a very long and most careful Examination of the said Accounts, they find, in Confirmation of the Report of the Commissioners, that the Sum of 5,544/. 94'. $d. Company’s Pay, equal to about 3,465/. Sterling, is due to the said Richard which they are not at present in any Condition to pay, without the Affifiance of the House; and that there are several other Sums of Money claimed by the said Officers, which the Petitioners cannot at present decide upon, the Commissioners not having reported upon the Accounts on which they are founded; and that the Petitioners, by Advices from Africa, find that a very considerable Expence has been incurred by the Hostilities on that Coast between the Subjects of this Country and of the States General of the United Provinces, for which no Provision has been made, but having received'no particular Accounts of the said Expenditure, they cannot at present ascertain the exact Amount; and that the Petitioners, being sensible of the great Regard fheu n by the House for the British Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa, therefore pray the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Sum as may be necessary for the effectual Support and Maintenance of the Forts and Settlements in Africa, for the Payment of the Debt already ascertained to be due to Richard Allies, Esquire, and for discharging such Debts as shall appear to have been incurred by the Dutch War, and likewise such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do li6 upon the Table.

Mr. Ord, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it w as referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Rel'olutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: W'here the same w'ere read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Stamp Duties now charged upon every Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which any Inland Bill of Exchange, Promissory Note, or other Note, payable otherwise than upon Demand, shall be ingrossed, written, or printed, do cease, determine, and be no longer paid or payable.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Stamp Duty of Six Pence be laid upon every Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which any Foreign or Inland Bill of Exchange, Promissory Note, or other Note, shall be ingrossed, written, or printed, where the Sum expressed therein, or made payable thereby, shall not amount to the Sum of Fifty Pounds.

Resolved, That it is, the Opinion of this Committee, That a Stamp Duty of One Shilling be laid upon every Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which any Bill of Exchange, Promissory Note, or other Note, shall be ingrossed, written, or printed, where the Sum expressed therein, or made payable thereby, shall amount to the Sum of Fifty Pounds, or upwards.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, a Stamp Duty of Two Pence be charged upon every Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which any Receipt, or other Discharge, given upon the Payment of Money amounting to Two Pounds, and not amounting to the Sum of Twenty Pounds, shall be ingrossed, written, or printed, every such Receipt to be charged with the said Duty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, a Stamp Duty of Four Pence be charged upon every Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which any Receipt, or other Discharge, given upon the Payment of Money amounting to the Sum of Twenty Pounds and upwards, shall be ingrossed, written, or printed, every such Receipt to be charged with the said Duty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Stamp Duty of Two Shillings and Six Pence be laid upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingrossed, written, or printed, any Receipt or other Discharge for any Legacy left by any Will or other Testamentary Instrument, or for any Share or Part of a Personal Estate divided by Force of the Statute of Distributions, or the Custom of any Province or Place, the Amount whereof shall not exceed the Value of Vol. 39.

Twenty Pounds; and where the Amouilt shall exceed the Value of Twenty Pounds, and not amount to-One hundred Pounds, an additional Stamp Duty of Eive Shillings; and where the Amount thereof shall be of the Value of One hundred Pounds, an additional Stamp Duty of Twenty Shillings; and a like additional Stamp Duty be charged upon every further Sum of One hundred Pounds, so left by any Will or other Testamentary Instrument, or for any Share or Part of a Personal Estate divided by Force of the Statute of Distributions, or the Custom of any Province or Place.

Resolved, That is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Stamp Duty of Twenty Shillings be laid upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingrossed, written, or printed, any Probate of a Will or Letters of Administration for any Estate of or above the Value of One hundred Pounds; and a further additional Duty of Twenty Shillings where the Estate is of or above the Value of Three hundred Pounds; and a further additional Duty of Twenty Shillings where the Estate is of or above the Value of Six hundred Pounds; and a further additional Duty of Twenty Shillings where the Estate is of or above the Value of One thousand Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Stamp Duty of One Shilling be laid upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingrossed, written, or printed, in Great Britain, any Indenture, Lease, or other Deed, for which a Stamp Duty of One Shilling and Six Pence is payable, by virtue of an Act made in the Seventeenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty (except Bonds given as Security for the Payment of any Sum or Sums of Money).

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee;-That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Stamp Duty of Five Shillings be laid upon every Skin or Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which any Bond shall be ingrossed, written, or printed, given as Security for any Sum of Money, the Amount whereof shall exceed One hundred Pounds; and an additional Stamp Duty of Ten Shillings where the Amount thereof shall be of the Value of Five hundred Pounds or upwards.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Stamp Duty of Six Pence be charged upon every Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, upon which shall be ingrossed or written any Original Writ (except such Original' upon which a Writ of Capias issues) Subpoena, Bill of Middlesex, Latitat, Writ of Capias Quo Minus, Writ of Dedimus Potestatem, to take Answers, examine Witnesses, or appoint Guardians, or any other Writ whatsoever, or any other Process or Mandate theft shall issue out or pass the Seals of any the Courts at Westminster, Courts of the Great Sessions in Wales, Courts in the Counties Palatine, or any other Court whatsoever holding Plea, where the Debt or Damage doth amouflt to Forty Shillings or above, or the Thing in Demand is of that Value (Writs of Covenant for levying Fines, Writs of Entry for fuflcring Common Recoveries, and Writs of Habeas Corpus, always excepted).

Article 1.

That Widows of Commission and Warrant Officers of the Royal Navy shall be reputed proper Objects of the Charity, whose Annual Incomes, arising from their Real and Personal Estates, or otherwise, do not amount to the following Sums; viz.

Ancl that where any such Widow is possessed of, or interested in, any Sum of Money, the Annual Income and Produce thereof shall be computed and deemed as Annually yielding; Three Pounds per Centum, and no more. , .

<’ - - '

’ '* ’ 2.

That to avoid Partiality and Favour in the Distribution of the Charity, Widows of Officers of the same Rank shall have an equal Allowance, the Proportion of which shall be fixed Annually by the Court of Assistants, according to their Discretion; and that, in order thereunto, the said Court may distribute Annually such Part of the Monies arising by the said Charity among the Widows, as they think proper; and to lay out such other Part thereof in South Sea Annuities, or. other Government Securities, as to them shall seem meet, for raising a Capital Stock for the general Benefit of the Charity, where the Application is not particularly directed by the Donors.

1 3-

That in the Distribution of Allowances to poor Widows, the same be proportionate to one another, with respect to the Sum each is to receive, according to the following Division; viz.

Widows of Commission and Warrant Officers Navy Officer* of the Royal Navy, that died on the Widow*.

and has left

the Bearer C. B. a Widow; and (according to the best Information we can get from others, and do really believe ourselves) is not possessed of a. clear Annual Income to the Value of: And therefore (he appears to ys to be entitled to the Benefit of the said Charity, under their Direction.

Besides which, the Widow is to make Affidavit that her Annual Income is not better than is expressed in the said Certificate; and that she was legally married (naming the Time, when and the Place where) to the Officer in whose Right the claims the Benefit of the Charity.

8.

That if the Widow resides in any other Part of His Majesty’s Dominions, a Certificate of the like Nature is to be signed by the Minister of the Parish, a Justice of the Peace, and Two or more Officers of the Navy, who are best acquainted with her Circumstances; and (he is to make such Affidavit as is before mentioned.

.9-

That all Widows applying for the Benefit of the Charity are to make Affidavit that they are unmarried.

The Widow of a Captain or Commander shall receive a Sum One Third more than the Widow of a Lieutenant or Master.

The Widow of a Lieutenant or Master shall receive a Sum One Third more than the Widow of a Boatswain, Gunner, Carpenter, Purser, Surgeon, Second Master of a Yacht, or Master of a Naval Velltl, warranted by the Navy Board.

4-

That Widows admitted to an Annual Allowance from the Charity, shall begin to enjoy it from the l irst Day of the Month following the Decease of their Husbands, provided they apply within Twelve Months for the fame; other wise, from the Time of their Application.

5-

That if any Widow admitted to the Charity marries again, her Allowance from thenceforth shall cease.

6.

That, in order to prevent Abuses, no Widow shall -be admitted to the Benefit of the Charity who has not been married for the Space of Twelve Months to the Officer by whose Right she claims the fame, unless the said Officer was killed or drowned in the Sea Service; and if any Officer marries after the Age of Seventy Years, his Widow shall be deemed unqualified to receive the Charity.

7-

That if the Widow of an Officer lives in the Neighbourhood of any of His Majesty’s Dock Yards, the Commissioners of the Navy residing the re, and some of the principal Officers of the Yard, or the said Officers of the Yard where there is no Commissioner, shall inform themselves thoroughly of the Circumstances of the deceased; and being satisfied that the Widow comes within the Rules of the Charity, shall sign and give her the following Certificate gratis; viz.

These are to certify the Court Of Assistants for managing the Charity for Relief of poor Vol. 59.

1°.

That Widows admitted to the Charity shall, Once in every Year, at the Time that shall he appointed, bring to the Court of Assistants their Affidavits, containing a particular State of their Circumstances, and that they continue unmarried.

n.

That Widows of Masters and Surgeons are to apply to the Navy Office, and receive from thence a Certificate of the Quality of their Husbands in the Navy, which shall be given them gratis, before they apply to the Court of Assistants to be admitted to the Charity.

12.

That no Officer or Servant employed in the Business or Service of this Charity, shall receive any Salary,

Reward, or other Gratuity, for his Pains or Service in the Affairs of the said Charity; but that the whole Business thereof shall be transafited gratis.

Copper Coin. A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Borough of Portsmouth was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Circulation of Counterfeit Halfpence hath increased to a Degree greatly prejudicial to Trade, and oppressive to the Poor, a Traffick being carried on between many Towns, particularly the said Borough and the Metropolis, for the sole Purpose of promoting such Circulation; and that the Laws already in Force to prevent the making or circulating Counterfeit Copper Coin have been found unequal to remedy this Grievance: And therefore praying the House to take the same into Consideration, and that speedy and effectual Measures may be adopted for Redress of an Evil not less rapid in its Progress, than injurious in its Consequences, to the Public in general, and to the Inhabitants of the said Borough in particular.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Stanley reported front the Committee, to whom the Petition of George Slut now and Company, of Dundalk, in the County of Lou th, and Kingdom of Ireland, Linen Manufacturers, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the ClerkV Table: Where the same was read; and is as iolloweth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, your Committee examined Mr. Sharrow himself, who, by his said Petition, states. That he has discovered and brought to Perfection a Process for making useful Cotton of Refule Flax; and that he is willing to dilclofe the whole Method of preparing it, lb that the same may become of general Use in the Cotton Manufactories, on receiving such Satisfaction to himself and Company for their Labour and Application, and the Expence they have incurred in prosecuting these Experiments, as this House shall judge adequate. — And he produced to your Committee several Samples of the Refule Flax,- called Hirds and Backings, and of the factitious Cotton produced from it, which he said had been made by him by the Process he had invented and brought to Perfection. — . He also said. That several Attempts have, from Time. to Time, and at different Places, been made to produce Cotton similar to his, from the same Material, without Success — That the Material costs from One Penny to Three Halfpence per Pound. — And being asked. Whether he would undertake to find Sureties for his making Fifty Tons of Cotton a Year, for Seven Years, like that he produced to your Committee, and of which he had before given in a Sample to the Committee of Trade at Manchester, at a Price not exceeding Six Pence per Pound ? he said, He w'ould give Security for lb doing as long as the raw Material shall not exceed in Price Three Halfpence per Pound; and that, if such raw Material should rife in Price, he would engage to make the Fifty Tons a Year, for the above-mentioned Term, at a Rate bearing the fair Proportion, according to' his present Proposal of Four Pence Halfpenny per Pound for the Charge of manufacturing.

He then produced to your Committee, Pieces of Vol. 39.

Stripes, Cheques, and Fustians, made by Mr. Birch, a very principal Manufacturer at Manchester; all of which were wholly, or in Part, of the factitious Cotton made by Mr. Sharrow; who, being further examined, said,

That the Sorts of Goods then produced were heretofore made with the Tin'keyCotton, the average Price of which is about One Shilling per Pound — That the Cotton

he makes will also be a complete Substitute for the real Cotton in Wicks for Candles, and most, if not all, other Articles in which the latter is now used.

Your Committee then examined Mr. Peter Drink-water, a principal Manufacturer, and One of the Committee of Trade, at Manchester; who, being desired to inspect the several Samples and Specimens produced by Mr. Sharrow, laid, He thought the Use of the factitious Cotton made by Mr. Sharrow's Process, will be very beneficial to the Cotton and Liuen Manufacturers of the Kingdom, as it will in general be a very good Substitute for Turkey Cotton in all low-priced Goods.

— Being (lttiin a Piece of dyed Fultiaii, One Part of which w as made of real Turkey, and the other of Mr.

Sharrow & factitious Cotton, and asked if he could distinguish one Part from the other? he, after examining it, said, He could not engage so to do. — -And being1 asked, Whether the factitious Cotton will take a good Dye ? he said, It was capable of receiving a richer Dye than Linen, and altogether as good, in all common Articles, as real Cotton will. — And he concluded with saying, That, on the Whole, be was of Opinion, that the making of Mr. Sharrow's Discovery public will be

productive of considerable Advantage to the Linen and Cotton Manufactures of the Kingdom, in many material Points.

Your Committee- then examined Mr. Thomas , a Tallow Chandler in Holborn, who produced some Candles, which he laid he made the Night before with Wicks of Mr. Sharrow's factitious Cotton — That he had tried them against some Candles, made at the same Time, with Wicks of real Turkey Cotton; and was of Opinion, the Wick made with factitious Cotton was equally as good as the other — That a small Part of the Candle Wicks used in England is imported from Turkey in Yarn; but that the Generality of the Article is imported raw, and spun here — That, if the factitious Cotton can be produced for Six Pence per Pound, Candle Wicks may be made of it for Fourteen Pence per Pound — That the Price of Candle Wick' Yarn has not been less than.

Two Shillings per Pound for Ten Years past; and that during the War it was as high as Three Shillings.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

And it appeared to your Committee, that by virtue of the said Commission, and in pursuance of the said Order and Instructions, he took upon himself the Government of the said Castle, Town, and District, on the 14th of November 1762, and that he continued to

exercise the Office of Lieutenant Governor until the ift of April 1764, the Day on which the Conquest on the Philippine Islands was delivered over by him to the Agents of the King of Spain, in obedience to an Order under His Majesty’s Royal Sign Manual, directed to the Commander in Chief of His Ships at the said Islands; and that during that Period he was at very considerable Expence, amounting to upwards of Fourteen hundred Pounds.

The said Order under His Majesty’s Royal' Sign Manual for evacuating the Conquest, and also the Order from Rear Admiral Cornish, dated 21st of August 1763, to concert Measures with the Commanding Officer of the King’s Troops, and the India Company’s Governor and Council at Manilla, for the Removal of the King’s and Company’s Troops from thence as early as possible, and the Confutations of the t'oth 4764, held ip

consequence thereof, were also read; and by the said Consultations it appeared, that there were only Two of His Majesty’s Ships, Two of the Company’s Ships, and ft Spanish Ship called The Siatn, which Ships could only carry 1,160 Men, to transport about 1,500 Men, exclu-five of the Company’s Civil Servants and Domestics, from thence to India.

And it further appeared to your Committee, That it being impracticable to transport the said Men in Five Ships, another old Spanish Ship was fitted up by Captain j Prereton, without any ExpenCe to the Public, to

assist in removing the Garril’on; and that, after a difficult and tedious Passage, he put into the Port of Batavia, in a very distrefi’ed State, having incurred a further very heavy Expence in the Passage, to the Amount of at least 20O /.; and that by this his Conduct he rendered a very essentiai Service to the Public, iri removing the Troops from Manilla, by fitting up the Two Spanish Ships, when other Ships could not be procured.

It also appeared to your Committee, That the Falmouth was in a very leaky Condition on her Departure from the Bay of Manilla, and upon her Arrival at Batavia repeated Surveys wvere held upon her by the Carpenters belonging to her, as likewise by those of the Princess Augusta, the Duke of Richmond, and the Duke of Gloucester, East India Company’s Ships then riding

in that Port; the Result of which was, that it was totally impracticable to repair her so as to go to Sea again; and that by many unavoidable Delays he was detained on Shore at Batavia for more than Six Months, and put to the additional Expence of more than 400l.

And it appeared to your Committee, that during Captain Breretohs Detention at , a very general

Sickness prevailed among the Seamen and Soldiers, and that it became necessary to establish an Hospital on Shore, and that he was obliged to take up Money for defraying Hospital Expences. — And by the Contracts produced to your Committee it appeared, that he contracted for the Maintenance and Cure of the Men at the Rate of Two Shillings per Man per Diem, the usual and accustomed Rate in that Country — -That the Money he lo took up was charged to him at the Rate of Five Shillings per Rix Dollar; but those Dollars, when offered in Payment, could be received after the Rate of only Four Shillings each, the then Rate of Exchange at that Place, upon which there was incurred a Loss of One Shilling upon each Dollar; and by a Certificate under the Haud of his Agent, it ap-Vol. 39.

peared, that upon passing his Accounts at the Navy and BreretoB’s Victualling Boards, for Expences incurred at the same Expences at Time, the said Loss of Exchange was allowed; but upon Cav, te* the Hospital Accounts being presented to the (’ommissioners of Sick and Hurt for their Inflection and Examination, they objected to the Allowance of the One Shilling Loss of Exchange, alledging, that the Contracts made by hirn being for Two Shillings per Man per Diem, and not for Half a Rix Dollar, therefore they were of Opinion, that the Loss of One Shilling per Rix Dollar ought to fall upon himself; and that the Loss accruing to him on this Head amounted to the Sum of 513/.

And it further appeared to your Committee, That His Majesty’s Ship Falmouth being in the Condition before Hated, so as to render it impossible for her to put to Sea, Captain Brereton acquainted the Secretary of the Admiralty thereof by a Letter, dated the 8th of November 1764, and that he, after providing Passage for and other wise disposing of her Complement of Men, was under the Necessity of taking a Passage to Europe, for himself and some of his petty Officers and Servants, in a Dutch East Indiamen, which he procured with great Difficulty; and it likewise appeared to your Committee, That the Money he disbursed for Ship Room and Victualling amounted to 3501, more than he was allowed by the Navy Board, who, as it appeared by a Certificate under the Hand of his Agent, paid him only personal Pay for himself and Servants, from the Time he left Batavia to his Arrival in England, and which, if allowed him, will not be any additional Expence to the Public, so far as respects the Victualling; as the Victualling at the King’s Expence ceased from the Time the Ship was rendered unfit for Service.

Upon the Evidence of Mr. Birch, Captain Brere-torfs Attorney, if appeared that an Action was brought against Captain Brereton by Charles Peter Saulnier, Commander of an armed Vessel under his Command, for an Assault and false Imprisonment, in taking him out of his Ship and detaining him on board the Falmouth; and that it appeared in Evidence upon the Trial of this Action, that Saulnier was going off with the Ship, without Leave, and disobeying the Signals for bringing his Vessel to, was taken and brought before Captain Brereton, as the Commander in Chief, and there detained to answei1 for his Conduct, and another Person put in Command of the Vessel; and that Admiral Cornish, in giving his Evidence at the said Trial, declared, that had Captain Brereton done otherwise than he did, that he would not have done his Duty, and that, as his Admiral, he should have called him to a Court Martial; but the Jury thought proper to give a Verdict against him for 400l. Damages, with Colts; and that such.

Costs on Taxation amounted to 84/. and which, with his own Costs, and the Expences paid to Witnesses, some of whom were brought from France and other distant Parts, could not amount, in his Opinion, to left than 6001.

And Captain Brereton assured your Committee, That he has never received any Allowance or Compensation whatsoever for the said Expenditures and Disbursements, or any Part thereof, making all together the full Sum of 3,4631, besides the total Loss of Interest upon so large a Sum, the greatest Part of which he has been in Disburse for Twenty Years, and the Whole for more than Seventeen Years.

Mr. Pulteney, according to Order, reported from the

Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Report which, upon the

28th Day of May last, was made from the Select Committee appointed to take into Consideration an Act, made in the Twenty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for further regulating and ascertaining the Importation and Exportal ion of Corn and Grain w’ithin several Ports " and Places therein mentioned," and to report the [Matter thereof, as it shall appear to them, to the House; the Resolutions which the Committee had di-rested him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as* folio weth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That His Majesty should be enabled, by and with the Advice of the Privy Council, to allow the Importation of Corn for a Time, not exceeding Four Months, from the 3d Day of September next, into the several Counties of Perth, Kincardine, Aberdeen, Inverness, Ross, Naime, Cromartie, Argyle, Forfar, Banff, Sutherland, Caithness, Elgin, Dunbarton, Orkney, and , under certain

Restrictions and Limitations.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Commissioners of the Land Tax of the said Counties be enabled to levy a Sum, nqt exceeding Fourteen Pounds Scots, on every Hundred Pound of the valued Rent of the said Counties, and to apply the same to the Relief of such of the Inhabitants as are or shall be reduced to Poverty by the Failure of last Year’s Crop, and the Scarcity and High Price of Com occasioned thereby.

The laid Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Air. Pulteney also acquainted the House, That he was directed by the Committee to move the House; That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to acquaint His Majesty, that this House, in consequence, of His Majesty’s Aloft Gracious Speech from the Throne, has bellowed constant Attention to the Scarcity and high Price of Corn; and that, notwithstanding the several salutary Laws already made in the present

Vo i„ 39.

Session of Parliament for the Relief of the Poor, the ElTcfts of the Scarcity and high Price of Corn are still severely felt by many of His Majesty’s idyal Subjects:

That it appears, from Evidence brought before this House, that the Inhabitants of The , and

Northern Parts of Scotland in particular, have futfered most severely from the Lateneis of the l.ilt Harvest, whereby their Corn while green was covered with Snow, and in many Places was not gathered in till the Alonth of December, apd then in a very bad Condition; that the Crop of Potatoes, on which the said Inhabitants principally depend for Support, was also destroyed by the Frost; that many of the said Inhabitants, being thereby reduced to Indigence, w ill either be conltrained to migrate, or exposed to the Danger of perishing for Want of Food, unless timely Measures he devised for their Relief; that the Distresses occasioned by Famine being generally most extreme in the Summer Alonths immediately preceding the new Harvest, when' this House may not be fitting, most humbly to beseech His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased tp give such Directions, as may tend most effectually to avert the Evils that are to be apprehended from the above calamitous State of the Northern Parts of Scotland; and to affine His Majesty, that this House will make good, out of the First Aids that shall be granted by Parliament, such Expences as tliall be incurred by His Majesty, in relieving the Aiifery to which His Majesty’s unhappy Subjects may be reduced by this most deplorable Calamity.

And Mr. Pulteney moved the House accordingly.
