A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and Exportation Tradelineno {Wolverhampton, in the County of Stafford, cf brass. was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,

That the Brass Manufactory of the said Town and its Environs is now brought into great Perfection, and Numbers of Persons are employed therein, and their Families supported thereby; and that the Petitioners observe a Bill is ordered to be brought into the House, to repeal the Acts of the 33d of Henry the Eighth, and the 2d and 3d of Edward the Sixth, in order to allow the free Exportation of Brass; and Alledging, that frequent Attempts having heretofore been made to establish similar Manufactures in different Parts of Europe, and other Foreign States, should such Bill be passed into a Law, and the Exportation of Brass take place, the Brass Manufactory must thereby be very materially injured, and Numbers of His Majesty’s Subjects, and their Families, be unemployed, and rendered useless to Society; and that the Manufacturers have already felt great Injury from the Exportation of Ingot Brass, contrary to Law, arid in order to preserve such Art in its present Perfection, every Sort and Quality of English Brass is absolutely necessary to be used by the Makers of all or some of the great Variety of Articles produced by this excellent Composition, and consequently the Exportation of any one Quality must advance the Price of the Whole, to the great Prejudice of the general Trade, and Foreign Manufactories may be thereby encouraged and established to rival, if not exceed, those of His Majesty’s Subjects at Home: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to prevent such Bill passing into a Law.

A Petition of sundry Merchants and Manufacturers Ditto, in the Town of Birmingham, on Behalf of themselves and others, was also presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the 6th of February last, that a Petition was presented, in order to obtain a Repeal of certain Laws prohibiting the Exportation of Brass, but, as no Proceedings appeared thereon, the Petitioners flat- tered themselves that the Attempt was relinquished; yet after the Expiration of Four Months, at this late Period of the Session, the Promoters of the Petition have moved to bring on the Merits of it, and have refused to allow a Discussion of that important Subject to remain until the next Session of Parliament, when the Petitioners hope to be better prepared to explain the Injury which the Repeal of the old Laws may occasion to the Manufactures of the Town and Neighbourhood of Birmingham, that are exported to a considerable Amount, and employ a great Number of Men, Women, and Children; and Representing to the House, that frequent Attempts have been made to erect similar Manufactures to those of the said Town in different Parts of Europe', and that the Excellence of some of our Articles depends upon Brass of very different Qualities, arid fortunately for this Country, there are several Sorts of Brass that are peculiarly adapted to the different Branches of our Manufactures, so that the Sort which is suitable for one Article is

6 E improper

by

Supply Bill;

Stamp

Duties.

11° Junii. A. 1783.

improper for another; and the Petitioners have Reason to believe the Knowledge of adapting the various Sorts of English Brass to different Articles in our Manufactures, is not yet known to Foreigners; but that if free Liberty is given to export Brass, every Maker may be induced to discover the peculiar Uses of his Sort, and produce very disagreeable Consequences to our Manufactures; and that Brass Makers in different Provinces of this Kingdom have not succeeded in making the Sorts of Brass made in other Provinces; and one great Company of Brass Makers have not succeeded in making Brass suitable for this Market, though they have professed an earned Desire to do fb; and the Petitioners apprehend there never has been such a Quantity of Brass exported as to render it a national Object, and there is not a Probability of any such Quantity being exported, though so much may be as to raise a ruinous Competition to our Manufactures: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and, before they authorize such Brass to be exported, which Foreigners particularly describe as proper to make our Manufactures, that it may be examined whether it is probable the national Profits, that may arise from the Exportation of Brass, are such as to be put in Competition with the National Loss that may be occasioned by exporting the Brass which is suitable for our Manufactures; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the Petition for repealing those Laws which prohibit the Exportation of Brass.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until a Bill be brought m upon the Two First of the Resolutions reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of permitting the Exportation of Brass from this Kingdom.

And the said Petition was read; Taking Notice of the Bill for repealing an £Ct, made in the Twenty-second Year of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for charging a Stamp Duty upon Inland Bills " of Exchange, Promissory Notes, or other Notes,

" payable otherwise than upon Demand," and for granting new Stamp Duties on Bills of Exchange, Promissory and other Notes, and also Stamp Duties on Receipts; and Setting forth, That there are certain Clauses and Provisions contained in the said Bill, which, the Petitioners apprehend, in case the same should pass into a Law, will be very injurious to the Manufactures, Trade, and Commerce of this Kingdom: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Clauses and Provisions, and that they may have such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the several Persons, whole Names are thereunto fubl’cribed, being Maltsters and Brewers

Vo l.39.

Junii 475

residing within the District of Poole, in the County of Dorset, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by the Statute of the Twelfth of Queen Anne, and by the several Annual Malt Acts, the Officers of His Majesty’s Excise are authorized to compound with any Person inclined to make Malt to be consumed in his ow>n Family only, for the Duties of such Malt at certain Rates for every Head which at any Time, during the Continuance of such Competition, shall be of the Family of the Persons compounding, and such Persons whilst compounding, are not to have their Houses, Out-houses, or Malt-houses, surveyed or searched by the Excise Officers; and that the aforesaid Powers have for foveral Years last past been productive of numerous Frauds, to the great Loss of the Revenue, and the Injury of the fair Trader, many Persons in divers Parts of the Kingdom, and particularly in the Counties of Dorset and Hants, under Colour of making Malt for the Use of their own Families, having made very large Quantities for Sale; and that, in the District of Poole, there are no less than Twelve Maltsters, whose Houses a few Years since were regularly entered and surveyed, and who made Malt for public Sale, that are now become Compounders; that the Quantity of Malt made at such Houses, when so entered and surveyed, was, upon an Average, about Three thousand Quarters Annually, such Houses being, generally worked only Five or Six Months in the Year, but since they have been compounded for, the Petitioners are well allured that the Owners continue to make Malt in them at least Ten Months out of the Twelve, and, on a very moderate Computation, at least Five thousand Quarters are Annually made at such Houses; and that the number of Heads compounded for by the said Twelve Persons is Eighty only, and the Competition, paid by them per Head is Thirteen Shillings and One Penny Halfpenny, amounting in the whole to no more than 52/. 10 s. whereas the Duty of Five thousand Quarters of Malt, as paid by the fair Trader, amounts to 2,625/. or thereabouts, so that, within the District of Poole only, the Annual Loss which the Revenue suffers from such Compositions is, at a very moderate Estimate, upwards of 2,500l.; and that a Person very lately made near Twenty Quarters of Malt, Weekly, under a Composition for Three Heads only, and Two of the Persons so compounded for were Water Di inkers; and that the Laws in being for preventing of such Frauds are very inadequate for that Purpose, that the Penalties laid on Compounders who shall fell, exchange, barter, or deliver out any Malt to, or allow it to be made in their Houses for, any other Person, or shall foil Malt Liquor, or have more Persons in their Family than compounded for, are 5 /. and 20 s. per Bushel for the Malt fold; but such Compounders remove their Malt privately in the Night-time, and by other Arts and Contrivances elude the Vigilance of the Excise Officers, and make it extremely difficult to prove the actual Sale of such Malt, and to convict them in the said Penalties; as a Proof whereof, the Petitioners beg Leave to observe, that, in the Course of several Years, during which these Practices have been carried on, there have been only Two Convictions, and those in the Penaly of 95/. only, in the whole of the before-mentioned District; and that the Security in which these Frauds are practised tends every Day to increase the Evil, and the Petitioners are persuaded, that, if some effectual Remedy be not soon applied, the Number of Compounders will be considerably enlarged, and the Temptation it holds out will induce many who are at present fair Traders to become Compounders; and the Petitioners conceive that such Frauds cannot effectually be prevented unless the before-mentioned Powers given to the Officers of Excise to compound

for

Fees, See. of Public Offices.

A Petition of the Merchants and Manufacturers of Exportation the Town of Walsall, in the County of Stafford, oh of Draft. Behalf of themselves and others, was presentfed to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners bhferve, by the Votes of the 6 th of February last, that a Petition was presented, in order to obtain a Repeal of certain Acts made in the Thirty-third Year of Henry the Eighth, and the Second and Third of Edward the Sixth, prohibiting the Exportation of Brafe; and Alledging, That the Trade and Manufactures of the said Town (which is very populous) principally consist in the manufacturing of Buckles, and various Other Sorts of Brass Goods, by which the greater Part of the Inhabitants are employed arid supported, and the greatest Part of such Goods are exported to Foreign Markets; and that the Excellence Of various of our Articles depends upon Brals of very different Sorts, and there are sundry Sorts of Brals that are peculiarly adapted to the different Branches of our Manufactures, so that the Sort which is suitable for one Article is improper for. another; and that the Knowledge of adapting the Various Sorts of English Brals to different Articles in our Manufactures is not yet known to Foreigners, but that if free Liberty is giveh to export Brass, every Maker thereof may be induced to discover the peculiar Excellence of his Sort to Foreigners, and thereby enable them to make and manufacture the Goods that are now made and manufactured here, which will tend to the Destruction of the Trade of the said Town, and the Ruin of the Manufacturers: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that the Repeal of the Prohibitory Clauses in the said Acts may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, uiitil the Bill to repeal certain Acts, made in the Thirty-third Year of the Reign of King Henry the Eighth, and the Second and Third Years of King Edicard the Sixth, so far as they prohibit the Exportation of Brals from this Kingdom, or carrying the same Coastwise, and for laying a Duty upon Brass exported from Great Britain, be read a Second Time.

Lever'* Mr. Gascoyne, Junior, reported from the Commit-

Mufeuni. tee, to whom the Petition and Representation of Sir Ashton Lexer, Knight, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition and Representation; and had directed him to report the Vox.. 39.

fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the feme was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition and Representation, Mr. Thomas Waring being examined, said, He had been Manager and Superintendent of the Collection of Natural and Artificial Curiosities belonging to Sir Ashton Lexer, ever since it was brought to London, in the Year 1775 — That Sir Ashton had been diligently employed, for Twelve Years before that Time, in forming his Collection — That it consists of Natural Productions and Curiosities of Art, and that the various Specimens and Articles are in Number upwards of 26,000 — That this Number has been selected from more than 150,000 that have been in Sir Ashton Lexers own Possession, exclusive of a great Number procured from Foreign Cabinets — That this Collection is the most extensive and valuable of any in England, and contains many Articles not to be found in any other — That, according to his Judgment, Sir Ashton mull have expended at least 40,000l. in making his Collection, and that it may probably have cost him nearer 50,000l. — That he has from Time to Time received considerable Presents of curious Things, but that the preparing those Articles for public Inspection has put him to considerable Expence — That if the Collection shall be kept in a Place proper for its Reception, and due Care and Attention be given to it, the Articles may be preserved for Ages in their present beautiful and perfect State j and that the Expences of keeping it at Leicester House, where it now is, amounts Annually to about i,2oo/. of which 660/. is paid for House Rent and Taxes. — And being asked, How the Public are admitted to the Sight of the Collection ? he said, On paying a certain Sum for each Person’s Admission, and that the Money collected by those Means has amounted, from the opening of it in February 1775 to the present Time, to about the Gross Sum of 12,000l.

Mr. Thomas Tenant being then examined, said, He had been upwards of Twenty Years a Collector of Subjects of Natural History — That he had seen all the Cabinets of Curiosities, both public and private ones, of any Note, in Holland, France, and Portugal, at Brussels, Dresden, Brunswick, and Vienna — That he had also seen the Spanish Cabinet whilst collecting in land — That he had never seen any Collection more rare, more curious, or more instructive, than Sir Ashton Lever's, nor any that can be compared with it — That his exceeds all others in the Beauty and Preservation of the numerous Articles it contains, which are better selected than any he had seen elsewhere. — And being asked, Whether he had heard of any Commissions to purchaseany of the Articles in Sir Ashton Lever's Collection ? he said, That an Idea being entertained Abroad, that the Collection is to be sold, he had Commissions to buy a great Number of the Articles for private Cabinets. — And being further examined, he said, That in his Opinion this Collection is of such Value and Rarity, as to be an Object of National Attention, and worth being purchased by the Public. And he concluded with saying, That if a Sovereign Prince were to endeavour at forming such a Collection, it could not be done in less than Twenty Years, nor ever be made so extensive and complete, there being many Specimens in this that could not be procured at any Expence.

A Member present, Mr. Baron Dimsdale, then informed your Committee, That he had seen the Cabinets of Curiosities at Moscow and St. which are esteemed very curious and valuable, and that they are not to be compared with Sir Ashton Lexer's Collection.

Mr. John Church being then examined, feid, He

had

484 16° Junti. A. 1783.

had amused himself many Years in collecting Natural Curiolities — That he had seen all the Collections in England of any Note, and that the whole of them put together would not form one so rare and valuable as that now at Leicester House — That the Articles there are in complete Beauty and Preservation — That he had taken great Pains to form an Eftiraate of their Value, ascertained by the Prices he had known similar Articles fell for at public Sales, of otherwise; and that, according to his Calculation, the Value of the Whole to be sold is upwards of 53»oooo /.- — That in this Valuation he includes the Cafes and other Matters connected with the Articles as now exhibited — That he did not believe such another Collection could be made in a Man’s Life; and many Articles are so rare, they could not be procured at all; and that, if the same proper Care be continued to be taken of the Collection as is now, he thought the Arti-

cles in it would preserve their Beauty for Ages. And he concluded with saying, That in his Opinion Sir Ashton Levers Collection is well worthy the Attention of the Public, to fdve it from being dispersed again, by the present Possessor being obliged, or being induced, to part with it to Individuals, which would be a Discredit to this Country.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Henry Phillips, of Knightsbridge, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That Sir Gilbet't Elliot, some Time since, presented a Petition to Parliament, praying a Reward for the Petitioner’s Discovery of an Invention of a Powder for the Preservation of all dry Provisions on board His Majesty’s Ships from Weevils, <§c. and brought in a Bill for that Purpose, which passed the House of Commons; but the Hoofe of Lords rejected it, until further Certificates of the Succcfs of the Petitioners Invention should be procured, and which are now laid before the House of Lords; and that the Reason why the Petitioner could not prefer his Petition sooner is, because he was not possessed of a sufficient Number of Certificates to make him confident that the Utility of his Powder would fully appear to the Satisfaction of both Houses of Parliament: And therefore requeuing, That his Petition for Relief may be now received.

A Petition of the several Wholefele Dealers in Tea, in the Town of Kingston upon Hull, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and other Dealers in Tea, who reside without the Limits of the Weekly Bills of Mortality, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act passed in the Twenty-first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, no Tea above Forty Pounds Weight (not being in the original Chest in which it was imported by the East India Company, and then continuing in the same State in which it was imported) at any one Time, directed to any one Person, shall be removed from one Place to another,* out of the Limits aforesaid, under the Penalty of Forfeiture; and, by on Act passed in the following Year, the Quantity of Tea so to be removed is not to exceed Twenty Pounds Weight; and that the Petitioners, and other Wholesale Dealers in Tea, in many Cities, and great Towns without the Limits of the Weekly Bills of Mortality, have frequently fold large Parcels of Tea, from Fifty to an Hundred Pounds Weight, and upwards, at one Time, but are at present deprived of a great Part of that Trade, and are apprehensive that they shall sustain a much greater Loss by being deprived of the Whole of it, if the Prohibition of the said Acts be permitted to continue, which restrains them from lending their Tea in those large Quantities, and obliges them to fend the same in small Parcels at different Times, and by different Conveyances, the Persons with whom they deal being unable to buy Tea in the original Cheka in which it is imported; and that, whilst the Petitioners, and other Wholesale Dealers in Tea who relide without the Weekly Bills of Mortality, suffer so great a Rcltraint on their Trade, the Dealers in Tea in the City of London enjoy an unlimited

Privilege of fending Tea to their Correspondents in any Quantity, and in any Package j and that the Petitioners are sensible of their Duty to submit to any Regulations which may be thought expedient to prevent illicit Practices in Trade, yet they do not conceive that the Restrictions established by the above-mentioned Acts on the Trade of the Petitioners, can in the final left Degree conduce to the Improvement of the Revenue, the Benefit of the Fair Trader, or be attended with any general good Effect; but, on the contrary, that the Continuance of those Restrictions will cause a very considerable Diminution of the Trade of the Wholesale Tea Dealers in the Country, and divert the Channel of Trada from them wholly to the Dealers in Tea in the City of London, or to Smugglers who travel the Country: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to make such Provision for the Relief of the Petitioners as the Nature of their same requires, and may be confident with the Safety and Improvement of the Revenue, and the general Advantage of the Trade of the Kingdom.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Right honourable John Sidney Earl Limitation of of Leicestet' (most usually called John Sidney) respecting of the Bill now depending in the House, for the further Limitation of Writs of Right, and for the further Amendment of the Law, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioner lays claim at Law to several considerable Estates in Kent, Middlesex', Sussex, and South Wales, to the Amount of Five or Six thousand Pounds per Annum, as the only Son and Heir of the Right honourable Joceline and Elizabeth Sidney,

Earl and Countess of Leicester, deceased; and that the Petitioner’s said Father and Mother both died when he was an Infant, the said Earl in the Year 1743, when the Petitioner was about Five Years old, upon whose Dc-cease the said Dignity, Name, Stile, and Title of Earl of Leicester, devolved to the Petitioner; and the said Countels died in the Year 1747, when the Petitioner was about the Age of Nine Years; and that the Petitioner’s said Father was of the Established Church of England, and his Mother a Roman Catholic, and most greatly bigotted to that Religion; that the unlawfully endeavoured to secrete the Petitioner from the World, under the Name of Sharpe, in order to bring him up in the Principles of that Religion, with Intent afterwards of fending him Abroad to some of the Romish Seminaries, there to take up Holy Orders, which illegal Secretion and Intentions have, in a great Measure, been the Cause of his Misfortunes; and that on the Death of the said Earl Joceline, the Petitioner’s Two Cousins on his Father’s Side, Lady Mary Sherard, deceased.

Wife of Sir Broxcnlow Sherard, since also deceased, seized upon all the Petitioner’s Real Estates, under Pretence that he was a Baltard, and not born in lawful Matrimony; and on the Death of the said Countess, the Petitioner’s Aunt, Maty Morgan, deceased, who was the Petitioner’s Mother’s Sifter, and the Wife of Charles Morgan, Gentleman, since also deceased, seized upon all the Petitioner’s Maternal Estates, under the like Pretence; and that the Petitioner being deprived of all his Estates, and thus rendered entirely destitute in his Infancy by his own Relations, had it not in his Power when he came of Age, which was in the Year 1759, to contend for the Recovery of such Estates, of to support Suits at Law against his powerful Adversaries then in Possession of them, nor within Twenty Years after he came of Age, which Time expired in the Year 1779, whereby he is now deprived of the common Remedy of bringing Ejectments at Law for the Recovery of the Possession of such Estates, and is now under the absolute Necessity of bringing Writs of Right as the only legal Remedy for the Recovery of Inch his Paternal and Maternal Estates, and which Right, as it now stands under the present Statute Law, does not

6 K cease

494 29° J 178 j.

cease or expire till the Year 1803, which is Sixty Years from the Death of his said Father; and that, being now possessed of foine small Property, he has lately brought a Writ of Right against Elizabeth , Widow, for the Recovery of Place, Park,

and Premises, in the County of Kent, being Part only of the said Real Estates of the said deceased Earl, at the Trial of which Action, before Lord Chief Justice Loughborough, and the other Judges of the Court of Common Pleas, the said Elizabeth Perry set up an old Will of the Petitioner’s Father, the said Earl Joceline, under which no Possession of such Estates had eves gone, which Will was intended to have been made in Favour of his natural Daughter, but the Validity of which (he herself had formerly contested, both with respect to the Insanity of the said Earl, and the Informality of such Will at the Time of die Execution, and had thereby got Possession of such Premises during the Petitioner’s Infancy, under Pretence that (he was a Co-heiress at Law to such Estates; which several inequitable Circumstances have compelled the Petitioner to go into the High Court of Equity respecting such Penshurst Estates, and in which Court he is now proceeding with all possible Dispatch against the said Elizabeth Perry; and that the several other Parts of the Estates of the said deceased Earl and Countefe are in the Possession of many other Persons, but the Right of Property belongs to the Petitioner, and for the Recovery of which he has no other legal Remedy (the Possession being gone) but by Writs of Right, or by Bill in Equity (founded on such Right of Property) and against whom he intends to proceed with all pof-lible Dispatch; but, as Bills in Equity must be filed for the Discovery of great Part of the Premises, and of the Alienation of them, it will inevitably be a Work of a considerable Length of Time, according to the usual. Course of Chancery Causes, and impracticable to be accomplished by the First Day of November next, which is the utmost Time allowed for bringing Writs of Right, or other real Action, in the said Bill now depending in the House; and therefore, should such Bill pals into a Law in its present Form, the Petitioner conceives it will (without any Judicial Determination in the Courts ot Law of the Legality of the Petitioner’s Claim) tend in itself in a great Measure, if not altogether, to deprive the Petitioner of such his just Right (now m esse) of recovering his Paternal and Maternal Estates; and should that unfortunate same happen, it is most probable be never could otherwise possess but little Property to support the great Dignity of Peerage (the rewarded Achievements of his Ancestors): And therefore praying the House to take his same into their Consideration, that such Bill may not pass into a Law in its present Form, but that all such Right as he may now have to proceed by Writ of Right, or other real Action, or in the High Court of Chancery, for Relief (grounded on such real Action or Actions) may be saved, protected, and defended, the same as if no such Act of Limitation bad ever been made; or that the Petitioner may be heard, by bim-self or Couniel, respecting the fame, or have such other Relief, in such Manner and Form, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the further Limitation of Writs of Right, and for the further Amendment of the Law, is recommitted; and that the Petitioner be heard, by himself or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the said Bill, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

A Petition of the Agents of His Majesty’s Loyal Subjects late belonging to the several Provinces of New Hampshire, Massachuset'sBay, Rhode Island, New

York, New Jersey, Pensylvama, Maryland, Virginia, Vo L.39.

North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia, on Behalf of themselves and the said Loyal Subjects, being offered to be presented to the House;

Lord John Cavendish, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recomr mends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then

L*oo£ie

496 20° JuniA. 1783.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That, at the Commencement of the late War in America, great Numbers of the Inhabitants, and amongst them some of the first Characters, Fortune, and Consequence, were actuated by the purest Principles of Loyalty to their Sovereign, by a grateful Sense of the Happiness they enjoyed under the British Government, and by an Abhorrence of every Measure which tended to destroy the Union between Great Britain and her Colonies; and, impressed with this just Sense of their Duty as Subjects, they either openly opposed, or steadily refused, during the whole Progress of the Contest, to join in the Measures which have since unfortunately terminated in a Dismemberment of the Empire; and that, - notwithstanding many Allurements held out to seduce them from their Allegiance, and a Variety of Losses and Distress sustained in consequence of their Loyalty, their Zeal for restoring the Authority of the Crown, and preferring the Union between the Two Countries, remained not only undiminished, but was greatly stimulated by the Hopes of Protection and Relief, founded on a Series of Acts and Resolutions of the British Parliament, on a Proclamation published in His Majesty’s Name at St. James's, on a Variety of other Proclamations and Declarations published in America by His Majesty’s Commissioners and Generals acting under the Authority of Parliament, and on many Letters from His Majesty’s confidential Servants, calling on the Loyalists to assist in fopprefling the Rebellion, and giving the moll solemn Assurances that they might depend, at all Events, on I Its Majesty’s Paternal Regard and Protection; and that, repoling the fullest Confidence in thel'e Royal and National Assurances, many Thousands, who were attached to the Government of Great ,joined

His Majesty’s Troops, and inrolled in His Service; and, by the Evacuation of Boston, Philadelphia, Rhode Island, Nexc Jersey, Virginia, Georgia, South Carolina, and North Carolina, many of the principal Inhabitants, who had taken an open and decided Part, in Obedience to the Calls of their Sovereign, were obliged to abandon their Families and Estates, and to seek an Alylum in the King’s Garrisons, or in some other Part of His Dominions; and that these unfortunate Men, in consequence of their Fidelity to the Crown, have been attainted, and their Estates confiscated, by Laws passed by the Legislatures of the several American States; that there were others who, on the same Account, suffered under those Laws an ignominious Death; others who fell in the Service of their Country, leaving their helpless Widows, and Orphans destitute of the Means of Subsistence; and others, a very respectable Number of Military and Civil Officers, Clergy, and Professional Men, at present in a distressed Situation, who can never be reinstated in their Offices or Professions; and that they conceive, as the Preservation of a Part of the Empire has, by the Events of War, been rendered impossible, the Losses liiftained, and the Sacrifices made by the State for the Public Safety of the Property of Individuals, who have been solemnly called upon by their Sovereign, and have particularly distinguished themselves by their Zeal in the Common Cause, ought, by the Principles of Natural Justice, and the fundamental Laws of the British Government, to be equitably distributed among, and borne by, the whole Society: And therefore praying the House to take their same into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as their peculiarly hard and distressing Situation may appear to merit, and permit them to be heard, by Counsel,. at the Bar of the House, should it be found necessary.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Message from Lord John Cavendish acquainted the House, That the King — he had a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to or 0 ney. House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered); and is as followed); viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty, having taken into His Royal Consideration the many eminent and signal Services performed by George Badges Rodney Lord Rodney, Vice Admiral of England, and One of the Admirals of the White, his Conduct in The West Indies in Three several Engagements, in the Months of April and Alay 1780, with a superior French Fleet, under the Command of the Count de Guichen, and his great and glorious Victories over the Spanish Fleet, on the 16di Day of January 1780, on his Voyage to the Relief of the Gurrifon of and over the French Fleet in The West Indies, on the 12th of April 1782, not only highly honourable to himself, but greatly beneficial to His Majesty’s Kingdoms; and being desirous to bestow upon the said George Brydges Rodney Lord Rodney feme considerable and lading Mark of His Royal Favour, as a Testimony of His Majesty’s Approbation of the said Services, and for this Purpose to give and grant unto the said George Brydges Rodney Lord Rodney, and to the Two next succceding Heirs Male of the Body of the said George Brydges Rodney Lord Rodney, to whom the Title of Lord Rodney shall defeend, for and during their Lives, a nett Annuity of Two thousand Pounds per Annum’, but His Majesty, not having it in His Power to grant an Annuity to that Amount, or to extend the Effect of the said Grant beyond the Term of His own Life, recommends it to His faithful Commons, to consider of a proper Method of enabling His Majesty to grant the lame, and of extending, securing, and settling such Annuity to the said George Brydges Rodney Lord Rodney, and to the Two next Persons on whom the Title of Lord Rodney shall defeend, in such Manner as shall be thought -moll effectual for the Benefit of the said George Brydges Rodney Lord Rodney, and his Family.

R. ’

Resolved, That this House will. Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to take His Majesty’s said Most Gracious Message into Consideration.

THE Hoofe being informed that Mr. Nectoe and Mr. Drummond, Two of the Commissioners for

examining, taking, and dating, the Public Accounts of the Kingdom, attended at the Door; they were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House, pursuant to the Directions of an Act of Parliament,

A Tenth Report of the Commissioners appointed to examine, take, and date, the Public Accounts of the Kingdom.

And then they withdrew.

And the Title of the said Report was read.

And the said Report was also read.

The said Report is as followeth;

To the Honourable the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled.

The Tenth Report of the Commissioners appointed to examine, take, and date, the Public Accounts of the Kingdom.

THE Examination into the Manner of passing the Accounts of the Paymader General of His Majesty’s Forces, in the Office of the Auditor of the Impred, led us necedarily to enquire into the Mode in use of paying the Army, and of keeping the Army Accounts in the Pay Office. Several Observations occurred to us in the Progress of that Enquiry, and many Regulations, which, in our Judgment, appeared fit and expedient to be established: Some of them we have inserted in our lad Report, and submitted to the Wisdom of the Legislature: There are other Subjects connected with both these Offices, as well as other Matter of Observation and Regulation, that demand our Attention.

The Paymaster General issues Money to Two Persons, who are Public Annual Accountants — the Paymader of the Widows Pensions, and the Agent for the Out Pensioners of Chelsea Hospital — to the former, in his official Capacity of Paymader General of the Forces; to the latter, as TreaiTurer of the Hospital: He issues lidewife to R^imental Agents, and to various Persons employed in the Army Expenditure, Sums for which they become accountable: All theie furnished Matter of Enquiry.

Wei applied ourselves fird to the Office of the Paymader of the Widows Pensions, and required from the Auditors of the Impred the lad declared Account of the Receiver and Paymader of His Majesty’s Royal Bounty ^o the Widows of Officers who were killed or died in the Service, with the Materials from which that Account was noafje out. We obtained, likewise, from the iSecretary at War, a Copy of His Majesty’s Orders and Instructions to be observed in the Payment of that Bounty.

The Return to us from the Auditors Office, in consequence of this Requisition, was the Account of the Honourable Henry Eduard Fox, Receiver and Pay-

mader of the Pensions to Widows, for Two Years, ending the 24th of December 1779, and passed the 29th of April 1782, with a Book of Account, and an Establishment for each Year, and with the Certificates, Affidavits, and Receipts of the Persons receiving.

The Book of Accounts confids of all the Receipts and Payments of the Year: The Edablidiment contains the Names' of, and the' Sums payable to, the Ob-jfefts of this Boiinty, with the King’s*Wafthni prefixed, directing the Payment

The Examinations of John Powell, Esquire, latfe De- N#a. puty Paymader 6f these Pensions, of John Lloyd, Esquire, n* 3. late Deputy Auditor of the Imptedi who passed this Account, and of Mr. John Davie, and Mr. Keen Sta- N° 4. hies, the Clerks employed in the Payments, supplied us N° 5. with Knowledge of the Manner in whith the Business of this Office is conducted, and the Accounts are paised.

The Office of Receiver and Paymader of the Widows Pensions, is held by Letters Patent for Life, to be executed by- himself or Deputy. Upon Inspection of those by which the Office is now holden, we find it is granted to " Henry Edward Fox for his Life; and from and " after the Death, Surrender, Forfeiture, or other t)etermination of that Edate, to John Powell, Esquire,

<l his Executors, Administrators, and Affighs, during " the Life of Charles James Fox." This Office is executed entirely by the Deputy and Clerks; the Principal never interfering in any Part of the Business. The whole Office is merely miniderial; paying certain Sums to certain Persons, upon Production of proper formal Affidavits and Certificates: It confids of Four Persons, the Paymader, the Deputy, add Two Clerks; it is executed at the War Office by the Two Clerks; One a Clerk in the War Office, appointed by the Secretary at War; the other a Clerk in the Pay Office, appointed by the Deputy Paymader of the Pensions.

The Fund appropriated for this Service, is compounded of Sums taken from the Pay of the several Regiments , and Corps upon the Edablidiment, and of the Marines. The Deputy Paymader of the Pensions applies for Money out of this Fund, from Time to Time, to the Paymader General of the Forces, and to the . Paymader of the Marines: He supplies, occasionally, the Clerk he employs to make the Payments, with such Portions of it, as he thinks may be wanted. The Payments are made every Four Months} and the Pay Clerk attends for an entire Week at the Beginning of a Payment, and on every Wednesday afterwards, and pays the Widows pursuant to the Edablidiment. To entitle herself to receive, each Widow must, if die receives in Person, produce an Affidavit of her Widowhood, and that die has not any other Pension or Allowance from Government; if (he receives by Attorney, he mud produce the like Affidavit, and a Certificate of her being alive, and a Widow.

Hence it appears, that the Manner of passing this Account, by the Auditor of the Impred, is very simple!

- The Charge in the official Account confids of the Balance remaining on the lad Account, and the Sums received from the Paymader General of the Forces, and from the Paymader of the Marines, during the Period of the Account: These Suras are verified by the Certificate of the proper Officer in each Office. The Discharge contains the Payments, for the Allowance of which, the Edablidiment, the Affidavit, the Certificate, and the Acquittance of each Person, or her Assignee or Attorney, are the Vouchers. After the Account is examined, and the Balance agreed, the official Book of Account is signed, and the Truth of the Account, attested upon Oath by the Deputy Paymader of the Pensions, before the Deputy Auditor of the Impred. AH the Sums being received, and the Payments made by the Deputy, the Deputy, and not the Principal, is the Person who pafles and lwears to the Account. That Account, which is drawn up by the Auditor, is neither signed nor sworn to by the Accountant; nbr is it declared, orpafled through any of the Exchequer Offices;

One Part of it is delivered to the Accountant; and is declared, by His Majesty’s Indruftions, to be, without any other Formality, his final Discharge and Quietus; the Duplicate remains in the Auditors Office.

The Emoluments accruing to the Officers in the Office of the Paymaster of the Widows Pensions, are these: The Auditor of the Imprest is directed, by His Majesty’s Orders and Instructions relative to this Office, to allow the Paymaster Twelve Pence for every Twenty Shillings received and paid by him, for his Expence. Care, and Trouble in the Service; not to be deducted out of the Pensions, but to be allowed him in his Discharge out of the Money he receives for the £’6l Service: This Sum, in the Account before us, is One thousand Three hundred Sixty-two Pounds and One 631. o. o. Penny; that is, Six hundred Eighty-one Pounds for each of these Years.

The Deputy Paymaster is allowed by the King’s Warrant One hundred Pounds a Year, for his extraordinary Trouble and Care in paying the Widows Pensions, and in stating and settling the Accounts; and he receives, by Custom, from the Auditor of the Imprest, One Third of the Sum inserted and allowed in the Discharge for the Fees and Disbursements for stating, examining, and passing the Accounts: This Sum, in the Account before us, is One hundred Sixty-five Pounds; of which One Third is Fifty-five Pounds; that is, Twenty-seven Pounds Ten Shillings a Year; which makes the Profit to the Deputy, One hundred Twenty-seven Pounds Ten Shillings a Year. These Emoluments to the Paymaster, and his Deputy, amount-8c8. 10. a ing to Eight hundred and Eight Pounds Ten Shillings a Year, are a Charge upon the Public.

The Two Clerks are paid in a different Manner. The War Office Clerk has a Salary of Ninety-two Pounds a Year from the Secretary at War, besides which he receives a Moiety of Two Kinds of customary Payments from the Widows; each pays Two Guineas when ffie first receives her Pension; and at the Rate of Six Shillings a Year, that is, Two Shillings for each Four Months Payment afterwards. These Two Fees are equally divided between the Two Clerks; and the Moiety of them, together with the odd Pence, forms the Whole of the Profit accruing to the Pay Office Clerk from this Employment.

The Office of Paymaster of the Widows Pensions appears to us, from this Description, to be an unnecessary Office. The Public derives from it no Utility whatever; it is a perfect Sinecure; and the Office of the Deputy is not much more: He only serves as a Channel, and that not wanted, to convey the Money for this Service from the Paymasters of the Forces and Marines to the Pay Clerk, whose Attendance is Three entire Weeks, and one Day in every other Week in the Year.

The Payment of this Bounty is an Army Service; it is made out of Money voted for Army Services, and by a Clerk in the Pay Office. If the Measure of voting upon Estimate a distintt Fund for this Service should be adopted, the Whole must be issued from the Exchequer to the Bank, and placed to the Account of the Paymaster General of the Forces. What then forbids that the Whole of this Business should be transacted at the Pay Office by a single Clerk, to be appointed to that particular Branch ? These Pensions may all be paid, as many of them are now, and as the other Army Payments are required by Att of Parliament, to be made, by Drafts upon the Bank; and the Accounts of the Payments for this Service may be incorporated and passed with the other Accounts of the Paymaster General of the Forces.

The proper Payment for this Clerk is a Salary only. The Acceptance of any Fee, Gratuity,' or

other Reward, ought to be strictly prohibited. It is not for the Honour of Government, that His Majesty’s Bounty should be curtailed by Gratuities and Fees of Office: No Part is to be intercepted; it should pals to the Object as liberally and as entire as it flows from the Royal Beneficence.

Since then these Pensions may be paid without the Intervention of so many Officers, and at a much less Expence to the Public, that Principle of public Oeconomy pointed out to us as the Rule to direct our Judgment, a Principle this Nation feels most sensibly the Necessity of attending to, leads us to be of Opinion, that the Office of Paymaster of the Widows Pensions is a useless and unnecessary Expence to the Public, and ought, therefore, no longer to be suffered to subsist; and that all the Business of this Office should be transferred to the Pay Office of the Army.

The other Officer, who accounts Annually for the Money issued to him by the Paymaster General of the Forces, is the Agent for the Out Pensioners of Chelsea Hospital. William Brummell, Esquire, who N* * holds this Office, and Charles , Esquire, who N° 13*

atts for the Deputy Treasurer of the Hospital, gave us an Account in what Manner this Business is transacted.

The Office of Agent for the Out Pensioners of Chelsea Hospital was created by the Att of the 28th of George the lid, Chapter the lit, for the Purpose of receiving the Money for this Service from the Treasurer of the Hospital (that is, from the Paymaster General of the Forces) and of paying or remitting it to the Out Pensioners. The Fund is a Sum voted Annually by Parliament upon Estimate.

Twice in the Year a Requisition is sent by the Secretary and Register of the Hospital to the Treasurer, stating the Number of Out Pensioners, and the Sums to be advanced them for the succeeding Half Year.

After the Treasurer has received Money from the Exchequer, a Warrant issues from the Board of Commissioners for the Government of the Hospital, signed by Three or more of them, to the Treasurer, requiring him to issue to the Agent for the Out Pensioners, such Sums as shall be due to them for the Six Months ensuing.

In consequence of this Warrant, the Treasurer issues to his Deputy such a Sum as he thinks proper. A Lift of the Out Pensioners is made out every Half Year by the Secretary and Register, and transmitted to the Agent: He copies it, and applies to the Deputy Treasurer; who issues to him upon Account such a Sum as, in his Judgment, will be sufficient to satisfy the Payment of that Lift, retaining out of it Twelve Pence in the Pound, according to the Directions of the Att of Parliament.

There are Three Sorts of Out Pensioners; the common Men, who are paid Five Pence a Day; the Nine-penny Men, who have Nine Pence; and the Letter Men, who have One Shilling; but from all these Payments the Twelve Pence in the Pound is de-dutted: They are all paid Half-Yearly, Six Months in Advance, and are dispersed over Great Britain and Ireland, and a few of them live in the Itlands of Guernsey and Jersey, consequently it becomes necessary for this Officer to employ Deputies and Agents, in various Parts, to assist him in transacting this Business. His last settled Account, transmitted to us by the Auditor of the Imprest, was declared before the Chancellor of the Exchequer upon the 28th of June 1781; it is for One Year ending the 24th of December 1775; and comprehends the Payment of about Fifteen thousand Nine hundred Pensioners.

The total Charge upon him, in that Year, is One hundred and Twelve thousand Four hundred and £. 111,44 6-

As the Fund for this Service is a specific Sum voted every Year by Parliament, which passes from the Exchequer through the Hands of the Treasurer to his Deputy, and from him to the Agent who distributes it, we traced its Progress through tliele several Channels.

We extracted from the Votes of the House of Commons the Grunts for the Out Pensioners, from the Year N° 14. 1775 to the Year 1782 inclusive: We procured from the Pay Office of the Army, an Account of the Gross N° 15. Sums received by the Paymaster General of the Forces, for this Service, from the Exchequer: We learned from the Deputy Treasurer what Portions of those Sums had been issued to him by his Principal, and what Portions he had issued to the Agent during the same Period; and N° 16. from the Agent we received an Account of his Gross Receipts and Payments every Year, from 1775 to 1780: And that the State of these Sums, as they passed to the different Officers, may appear at one View, we have brought them together into One Account; K# 17. which (hews what Portion of each Sum (topped in each Stage of its Progress; and what Proportion the Total of the Balances, unapplied in the Possession of these Ollicers, at the End of each Year, bore to the Sum voted.

The Surplus in the Hands of the Deputy Treasurer arises in Part from the Savings out of the Poundage: This, like the rest of the Sums granted for Army Services, is made liable to a Deduction of Twelve Pence in the Pound, to be applied in the Manner which His. Majesty shall, by Warrant under His Royal Sign Manual, direct. This Deduction, is not blended with the Army Poundage: A distinct Account is kept of it; and it has been applied to the Annual Payments of One thousand Pounds Salary to the Agent; and of Two Allowances, Six hundred Pounds to the Deputy Treasurer, and Three hundred Pounds to the Secretary; together. One thousand Nine hundred Pounds a Year. No other Payments appear to have been made out of it; and therefore this Fund has far exceeded the Charges upon it.

So much of the Savings as accrued to the 24th of December 1773, was paid back to the Paymaster General of the Forces: So much of them as accrued from j that Time to the 24th of December 1780, amounting

*,64$. a. 7. to Twenty-two thousand Six hundred Forty-five Pounds Two Shillings and Seven Pence was, in October last, pursuant to His Majesty’s Warrant, paid into the Exchequer, to be applied towards the Supply of the Year 1782. The Balance of this Deduction, remaining in the Ilahds of the Deputy Treasurer upon the 24th j,o*i. jj. i{. of December last, was Three thousand and Ttfenfy-one Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Two Pence Halfpenny: But as the Money, applicable to the general Service of the Hospital, is not paid by Government at the Time it becomes due, the Deputy Treasurer, having received nothing for that Service to a later Period than the 24th of June last, has been obliged to apply Part of this Balance in defraying the current Expences of the llospital.

The same Reasons upon which the Abolition of the Army Poundage is grounded, weigh equally against Vol. 39.

keeping up this Deduction: It is of no Utility; it Tenth serves only to generate a Balance in the Hands of an Report Officer, for no other Purpose than that of paying it on l>ubl,c back again when required by proper Authority. Nei- ccoulU*-ther the Salaries, nor any other Service, to which this Poundage is now applicable, require the Existence of any such Fund: They may all be defrayed out of the grols Sum voted for the Service. The Sum estimated for the Payment of the Out Pensioners may, as it is wanted, be issued to the Agent by the Draft of the Treasurer upon the Bank; and the Agent will continue to pay them the same Sums they receive at this Day.

The Issues to the Agent seem to have been more abundant than was necessary. The average Balance iu his Hands, for the Four first Years in his Account, was Four thousand Nine hundred Ninety-nine Pounds 4>999- >4-Fourteen Shillings: In the Year 1780 it was reduced to One thousand Six hundred Fifty-seven Pounds Nine 1,6s7‘ 9‘ Shillings and Two Pence. As this may be presumed to have been a Sum sufficient for the Demands of the Service, it is probable the Issues of the former Years exeeeded what the Service required; and it is expedient that future Issues (liould be calculated with greater Exactness.

The Regimental Agents are a Class of Men who receive Money from the Paymaster General of the Forces, for which they are accountable, not before the Auditor of the Imprest, but to the Secretary at War.

This Money is placed by every Agent to an Account kept for each Regiment and Corps to which he is*

Agent, called in the Cavalry, The Stock Purle, and in the Infantry, The Non-effective Fund. It consists of die Non-effective Subsistence of each Regiment and Corps issued to him by the Paymaster General, either under the Head of Subsistence, or in the Clearings: A Part of it is called The Vacant Subsistence-winch is described in His Majesty’s Warrant for regulating the Non-effective Fund, annexed to our last Report, to arise " where a Vacancy happens between " the Days whereon each Captain usually receives " the Subsistence of his Company." The Purposes ta which this Fund is to be applied are directed by that Warrant.

That the Public might be informed of the present State of this Fund, we required from every Agent an Account of the Balances of the Stock Purse of the Cavalry, and of the Non-effective Fund of the Infantry, belonging to each Regiment, Troop, and Company, including the Guards, Invalids, Militia, and Fencibles, of which they are or have been Agents, remaining in their Hands, Custody, or Power, at die Time when the Accounts were severally made up. We have inserted in the Appendix the Returns made to this Requisition; N° 1*. in which we have distinguished the Agents who have Money in their Hands, from those who have none; and where an Agent to different Regiments has Balances in his Hands upon the Non-effective Accounts of some, and has disbursed more than he has received upon the Non-effeflive Accounts of others, we have inserted in a Second Column the Balance due to him on the latter Account, and in a Third Column die Difference of the Two Balances, as (howing the real Sum of Public Money remaining in his Hands upon the Balance of his Non-effective Accounts taken together: But some of them informed us, that they had advanced other considerable Sums in the Payment of Contingent Bills, and of Extraordinaries, on Account of many of die Regiments and Corps; which Payments they could not include in these Returns, because they are not such Charges a3 are allowed by the King’s Warrant to be brought against the Non-effefitive Funds; yet until these Sums are repaid to them by Government, they are a Diminution

Account* The Total Sum of Non-effective Money, in the Hands of all the Regimental Agents taken collectively, and for C i.<i. which they are accountable, appears by the Schedule *3- 7i of their Returns, to be One hundred Twenty-three thousand Four hundred Sixteen Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Seven Pence Halfpenny; an important Sum, of which the Public has a Right to expect from the Office intrusted with the Power, a speedy Examination and Adjustment.

Should the Regulations, suggested in our last Report, of abolishing the Warrant Men, and issuing the Subsistence according to Muster, be adopted, the only Supply for the Non-effective Fund will be the vacant Subsistence, and the Non-effective Subsistence that may be casually issued, when a Vacancy happens between the Return of the Muster and the Issue of the Subsistence; but this will not be sufficient to carry on the Recruiting Service, which requires a Sum in Advance, ready for immediate Application. To supply this Deficiency we have suggested the Creation of a specific Fund, to be voted Annually, and a distinct Account to be kept of the Issues.

An-Examination every Year into the State of this recruiting Fund in the Hands of each Agent, will be the Means of keeping it within its proper Bounds; and a punctual Payment, by Government, of Services as soon as they are incurred, will take away every Pretence for having in his Hands more Money than is necessary for the Service.

The Public Accountants are numerous; and as the Public is deeply mterested in preventing the Accumulation of Balances in their Hands, it would be a useful and necessary Regulation, that in all Cases where Money is issued from Time to Time upon Account, to carry on a Service that has Continuance, the Officers intrusted with the Direction of the Issue should be enjoined, as a Duty upon every Issue, to examine into the State of the Money remaining in the Hands of the Accountant, and the Demands it is subject to, and to regulate the Sum to be issued accordingly: By these Means the Service will be supplied with no more than it wants, and that Tendency which every Balance has to increase, will be checked.

The remaining Class are the Army Sub-Accountants, or those Persons who receive Money on Account from the Paymaster General of the Forces for Extraordinary Services of the Army. At the End of every Year’s Account of a Paymaster General is added a List of the Insupers of the Year; and to his final Account is annexed a List of the Insupers during the whole Time of his being in Office. All the Persons thus set Insuper remain accountable to the Public for the Sums set opposite their Names, until they are cleared by the Auditor of the Imprest; and in order to their being cleared and obtaining their Quietus, they must pass their Accounts in his Office, except in One particular Instance, that is, where the Service has been performed Abroad, and the Account has been ’allowed by the Director General of Control, and signed by a Commissary General, and the Balance paid by the Deputy Pay-tnafter General, pursuant to a Warrant of the Commander in Chief. Upon the Production of this Warrant by the Paymaster General, with the stated Account annexed, so allowed and signed as his Voucher for the Payment of that Balance, the Auditor will clear the Insuper, though the Account has not been passed byhimself; but in every other Cafe, passing the Account in the Office of the Auditor is essential to obtaining the Quietus.

The farther we proceeded in our Investigation of the Army Accounts, the greater we found the Increase

of this Insuper Account We thought it a Part of our Duty to examine into its present State as far as we were able.

The Result from these Lifts is, that under the Head of Issues for the Extraordinary Services of the Army, between the Year 1746 and the 6th of May last, Six i, hundred Sixty-four Persons remain at this Day accountable to the Public for the Sum of Thirty-eight Millions Nine hundred Thirty-three thousand Nine hundred and Twenty Pounds Sixteen Shillings; and of them Six Persons only for the Sum of Four Millions Two hundred Fourteen thousand Four hundred Eighty-seven Pounds: And, according to the present Course of the Exchequer, every one of them must pals his Accounts of the whole Sura he has received before the Auditors of the Imprest, or he cannot have his Quietus.

It is equally expedient for the Public, and for the Persons concerned, that the State of this Insuper Account should be made known. Whoever of these Accountants are, upon the Balance of their Accounts, indebted to the Public, should pay such Debts; if the Public are indebted to them, they should be paid; if their Accounts are even, they ought to be quieted; if, through Ignorance or Delusion, they think themselves secure, they ought to be warned that prerogative Process hangs over their Persons and Estates; and the longer they delay palTing their Accounts, the greater Difficulty they will find in avoiding it.

That Persons, intrusted to such an Extent should continue so long without being called to Account, and bting so deeply interested, should not long ago anxiously have pressed to have their Accounts adjusted, was a Difficulty that seemed not easily reconcileable with public Attention or common Prudence: The Examination of One of these Accountants might throw some Light upon the Subject.

We examined Mr. Bacon relative to the Circum- N* 3®» stances of these Payments. The First was a Claim by him upon the Treasury, for having, pursuant to an Agreement, supplied for a certain Time certain Articles to the Troops in the Isle of Man: The Treasury referred this Claim to the Controllers of the Army Accounts; and upon their Report, granted him the Warrant for the Payment of the Sum that appeared to be due to him: The other was a stated Account, confiding of various specific Sums paid to him from Time to Time, by Warrants, either upon the Exchequer or the Paymaster General of the Forces, for Services performed pursuant to a Contract with the Treasury, for supplying Negroes for the Use of the ceded Islands.

These Sums were not Imprefts, but directed to be made without Account. Upon Production of proper Certificates of the Execution, this Account was settled by the Treasury; the Balance struck, and paid to him by that Warrant.

As the First of these Payments was mad<f to him in consequence of the Report of the Controller of the Army Accounts, and the Second as the Balance of a stated settled Account, Mr. Bacon considered them as Accounts completely adjusted: He did not conceive himself any longer responsible, or fabjefil to render any other Account for the Sums he had received in consequence of these Two Engagements.

It is more than probable, that many of the Persons in these Lifts are in the like Situation. Satisfied that their Accounts with the Public are finally settled, they rest perfectly secure from being ever called to Account again; and yet the Names of all the Persons in the Lists of Lord Chatham and Lord Darlington, have.

Twice a Year, for several Years, been issued with the Writs of Distringas ad computandum to the Sheriffs of London and Middlesex", and, had that Process been executed, Issues must have been returned upon them all for neglecting to bring in their Accounts.

Mr. Bacons Two Accounts having been settled, one by the Controller of the Army Accounts, the other by the Treasury, we examined Sir John Dick, Baronet, n° 31. one of the Controllers of the Army Accounts, and John Martin Leake, Esquire, one of the Clerks of the Trea- N°3*. fury, relative to the Examinations given to Accounts of this Description in their Offices.

All the Issues for the Army Extraordinaries ought regularly to be examined by the Controller of the Accounts of the Army, but in some Cafes, as where the Agreement is to furnish Articles upon Commission, or where the Vouchers of an Account, stating the Performance of a Contract, are competent, and require no Reference, they have been examined by a

Clerk.

l

Tenth Report on Public Accounts,

528 2° Julii. A. 1783.

Clerk of the Treasury, and Payments have been directed to be made in consequence of that Examination, without any other Reference, and without Account.

Every Contract with the Treasury is entered in the Controllers Office. Where it is an Agreement only by a Minute made at the Treasury Board, either a Copy of that Minute is brought to the Controllers Office to be entered, 'or the Controller has Recourse to the original Minute when necessary. Every Account or Claim grounded upon the Contract or Agreement, is generally referred, with the Vouchers and other necef-l’ary Instruments, by the Lords of the Treasury, to the Controller, for his Examination and Opinion: He compares the Articles in the Account with the Terms of the Contraft or Treasury Minute, and with their correspondent Vouchers; he examines the Computations and Caftings, and requires the Certificate of the proper Officer, of the faithful Execution of the Contracts in every Part; he corrects the Errors in the Account; he states his Doubts, and reports his Opinion to the Lords of the Treasury, who form their Judgment upon his Report, and direct Payments accordingly.

Issues directed by the Treasury upon these Contracts, may be either previous to the Execution of any Part of the Contract, or in consequence of either a Part or the Whole having been performed: The First is without the Intervention of the Controller or the Treasury Clerk, and must be upon Account: The other Two are in consequence of the Reference to One of them, and may be directed to be made either upon or without Account; but they are usually upon Account. Hence we may collect the Situation in which the Sub-Accountants under our Consideration may at present stand. To some of them, the Sums they are charged with may have been issued on Account, and no Examination whatever had of the Expenditure. To others, Sums may have been issued, either upon, or without Account, in consequence of the Reports of the Controller of the Army Accounts, or of the Examinations of the Clerks of the Treasury; and the Auditors of the Imprest have seen Reason, according to the Rules of their Office, to let them all Inluper, though some of the Warrants may have been silent, or have even directed the Issues to be made without Account. There can be no Doubt that those Persons, whose Accounts have never been examined, are bound to pass tfiem: But those to whom Payments have been made in consequence of Accounts examined and approved by Officers duly authorized, stand upon a different Ground. If such an Examination be liable to no Suspicion of Careleffhefs, Partiality, or Collusion; if it has such Credit as to warrant the actual Payment of the Demand, any farther Check seems to be unnecessary. The Auditor follows exactly the Steps of the Controller: He re-computes, re-casts, and re-examines the same or similar Vouchers. It is true, he may correct the Errors of the Controller, as the latter has corrected his Errors; for the Statements of the Auditor have been referred to and corrected by the Controller; but if the Possibility of Error were a Ground for Re-examination, Checks would be endless. If Two Persons competent in Accounts do their Duty; if each examines, and they both agree, the Probability is they are both right, for it is highly improbable they should both err exactly alike; and, therefore, if an Office for the Examination of Accounts be faithfully executed, there is no Necessity for the Interpolation of any other Office by way of Check.

The passing these Accounts in the Office of the Auditor is not only useless, but attended with very considerable Expence, and the Public pays it. The Fees paid for passing an Account of Extraordinaries in the Office of the Auditor, are in proportion to the Length and Period of the Account, and the Trouble 02

it gives to the Office. Where the Account comprehends a Number of Years, the Auditor is paid from Ten Pounds to Twenty-five Pounds for each Year of the Account. All the Fees for passing a short Account through all the Exchequer Offices, amount to about Forty Pounds, and a long one to One hundred Twenty Pounds. Estimating the Expence of passing the Accounts of Six hundred Sixty-four Inlupers (the Number in these Lifts) in the Auditor's Office, one with another, at a Medium of Eighty Pounds each, it will amount to Fifty-three thousand One hundred and Twenty Pounds; £-53. a Sura to be paid for Business unnecessary, and which ought, especialiy in the present State of its Finances, to be laved to the Public.

It will hot be difficult to distinguish which of these Accounts have been examined, and which not. The Controller keeps Entries of all his Reports in his Office. The Treasury can certainly with Ease find out what Accounts have been settled by their Clerks; and by the Publication of these Lists of Insupers, they who are alive, and the Representatives of those who are dead, will fee the Sums for which they stand Accountable to the Public: It nearly concerns them all to examine into the State of their Accounts, and to be ready to produce them when called upon by proper Authority.

We are of Opinion, That all these Lists of Sub-Accountants should forthwith undergo a Scrutiny in the Treasury, and in the Office of the Controller of the Accounts of the Army; that such of the Persons therein named, or the Representatives of those who are dead, whose Accounts have been either imperfectly or not at all examined, should be compelled to produce their Accounts in the Office of the Controller of the Accounts of the Army, in order for their Examination; and that those Persons, whose Accounts shall appear to have been sufficiently examined, either by the Controller or the Clerks of the Treasury, should be relieved from the Necessity of passing their Accounts in the Office of the Auditor of the Imprest, and should, by special Warrants to be granted for that Purpose, have their Insupere cleared in the final Accounts of the Paymasters General of the Forces, from whom they received the Sums with which they stand charged, and be enabled to obtain their Quietus.

The next Subject to which we directed our Attention, was the State of the Accounts of the Paymasters General of the Forces in the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest. The Account we had been examining, was the last declared Account of a Paymaster General of the Forces, and of the Year 1767 — only One Account more of a subsequent Year, which is that of Mr. Cooke and Mr. Thomas Toumhend, ending 24th of June 1768, has been declared. An Arrear of Fourteen Years, in the Accounts of an Office so important and of so exten-five a public Expenditure, was a Subject that called for Enquiry.

Hence appears the present State of the Debt due to the Public from the Representatives of Lord

Holland, as Paymaster General of the Forces. The Public have, at all Events, an undoubted Right to 94,736. 6.10. the Sum of Ninety-four thousand Seven hundred Thirty-six Pounds Six Shillings and Ten Pence; and therefore, in Obedience to the Act that regulates our Conduct, we report it as oui; Opinion, that the Representatives of Lord Holland ought, without Delay, to pay into the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, upon the Terms mentioned in the Act of the 21st of 94,716. 6.10. jj8 present Majesty, Chapter 48th, the Sum of Ninety-four thousand Seven hundred Thirty-six Pounds Six Shillings and Ten Pence, to be applied to the Service of the Public; and as it is highly expedient, as well for the Quiet of the Persons interested, as for the Satisfaction of the Public, that an Account so long depending, and of so remote a Period, should be brought to a Conclusion, we are of Opinion the doubtful Articles should forthwith be examined and decided upon, and the Balance (truck between the Public and the Accountant, and this Account be presented for Declaration.

In the States of the Accounts of the Paymasters General of the Forces, in the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest, the Accounts (landing next after the final Account of Lord , are those of the Right

honourable Richard Rigby. It appears from these States, that Two of his Accounts, the one for Half a Year ending the 24th of December 1768, the other for the next Year ending the 24th of December 1769, are balanced and attested. An Objection made by the Auditors, relative to Omissions in the Civil List Deduction, retards their Declaration. Since the 16th of Nan:ember 1780, Four more Accounts of the Four Succeeding Years have been delivered into the Auditor’s Office: They are under Examination, and in different Stages towards their Completion. The Auditor docs not appear to have received any Account from the Pay Office of a Year subsequent to that of 1773. He proceeds upon the Pay Office Accounts as soon as they are sent to him. When Objections arise from Mistakes, Omissions, Articles that require Explanation, or Want of Vouchers, those Objections are transmitted to the Pay Office to be corrected, explained, or supplied. Answers are returned, sometimes shortly after the Observations are sent, sometimes not until long after; and the Auditor is retarded in completing the Accounts for Want of a regular Attention to his Applications. The first Step must certainly be taken by the Pay Office, that is, the Delivery of the Account to the Auditor, with the Vouchers. By the Dates of the Delivery, as they are stated by him, they have not been sent to him until long after the Year of the Account has been elapsed. The Accounts of the Years 1768 and 1769 were not delivered until Ten Years after. We do not, therefore, find that the Imputation of Delay lies in the Office of the Auditor. The Pay Office seems lately to have been more attentive to this N# 48. Duty: We fee by their Lift of Accounts delivered into the Office of the Auditor, that Five Accounts, down to the Year 1769, were delivered in the Year 1779; Two for the Years 1770 and 1771, in the Year 1780; and Two for the Years 1772 and 1773, in the Year 1782.

Considering the Account, as drawn up in the Pay Office for the Purpose of being examined and checked in another Office, there seem to be in the State, in which it is transmitted to the Auditor, feme Defects that require Correction. The Entries of many of the Articles are without Dates and Authorities: These are Vo 1. 39.

the distinguishing Marks of similar Articles, and the Tenth Omission of them tends to confound the Auditor, and Report may be the Means of Fraud or Concealment. Every "

Article both of Receipt and Payment should be entered, ccounts* with its Date and the Authority which directs it, in the Account of the Year in which the Sum is actually received and paid. It is not the Account of the Year it purports to be, unless it comprehends all the known Receipts and Payments of that Year. Can any good Realbn be assigned, why Sums, received by the Deputies and entered in the Books of those Deputies in the Pay Office, in the Year 1758, (liould be left out of their proper Place, the Account of the Year 1758 (which was not delivered to the Auditor until 1768) and continue to be omitted in every Succeeding Account, until the last of that Paymaster General, the Account of the Year 176.5, and not even there inserted until the Year 1782 ? Twenty-four Years after they were entered as Charges upon that Paymaster General in the Books of the Office.

The Account is sent to the Auditor, with Blanks for Sums in the Body of it: After he has examined it as far as he is able, it is taken back again to the Pay Office, the Blanks filled up, and Corrections and Additions made to it at their Pleasure, without the Knowledge of the Auditor; and this, frequently in the Progress of the Examination. This Practice is inconvenient and dangerous: It increases the Trouble of the Officer; it confounds the Articles he has examined with those he has not; Alterations may be made in the former to the Prejudice of the Public, and pass unobserved by the Auditor. We are of Opinion that the Account, w hen once delivered to the Auditor, ought to remain in his Office until it is completed, and all Additions and Corrections after the Delivery be made at his Office, and with his Privity.

There are feme Articles in the voluntary Charge, of whose Accuracy the Auditor cannot judge for want of sufficient Materials: These are Profit on Exchange and Remittances, some of the Payments to the Deputies, and feme Of the Stoppages. The Vouchers produced to the Auditor for these Charges, are Accounts made up and signed by the Accountant of the Pay Office.

A voluntary Charge is an Admission of the Receipt of a Sum on Account, as far as it goes; but it may be erroneous or defective, or Sums received may be suppressed; and the Account of an Officer in the same Office can be no Check by which such Errors may be discovered. The Auditor should be fumiffied with the same Materials from which the Accountant col-lefts the Charge. Had not Peter Taylor's own Account of Profit and Loft by Exchange been at last produced to the Auditor, the Error of Eight thousand £.8,577.13.10. Five hundred Seventy-seven Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Ten Pence had never been brought in Question, and the Right of the Public might have been (0 far violated.

In the Account of the Additions to the Charge in Lord Holland's final Account, returned to us from the Pay Office, is the Sum of Four Thousand Pounds, received of Major Gates by Mr. Mort a Deputy Paymaster: This Sum had been issued to him by Warrant from General Monckton; and consequently Major Gates must be set Insuper for that Sum in the Account of Lord Holland. Major Gates paid it back to Mr.

Mortier, who gave him a Receipt for it: Unlefe Major Gates pafles his Account of this Sum in the Office of the Auditor (an Event not very probable) this Receipt, which is the only Evidence to charge Mr. Mortier, can never appear against him; and consequently this Sum might have dept in the Hands of the Deputy, or, upon his charging himself with it, in the Hands of the Paymaster General, without being discovered by the Auditor. We are, therefore, of Opinion, that no Money should be paid into the Hands of the

Paymaster
