Paymaster General, or his Deputy, unless by Warrant; and that a Cony or Extract of such Warrant, if it proceeds from a (Commander in Chief, should be transmitted to the Treasury, as the Evidence of the Charge upon the Paymaster General of the Forces.

The Business of the Auditor of the Imprest, to be collected from his Commission, is, to audit the Accounts of most of the Receivers, and of all the Officers and Persons entrusted with the Expenditure of the Public Revenue. Possibly this Office might formerly have been able to accomplish this Duty; but such has been the Increase of the Revenue within these few Years, that the Accounts are grown to a Number, Magnitude, and Extent, greatly beyond what could have been fore-seen. The Accounts, which at this Day remain for the Audit of the Exchequer, are Seventy-four Millions, the Issues of Twenty-one Years, for the Navy Service; Fifty-eight Millions, the Issues of Eighteen Years, for the Army Service; near Thirty-nine Millions ifftied to Sub-Accountants; together, One hundred Seventy-one Millions; the Receipts and Issues of all the Provisions for the Support of the Land Forces in America and the West Indies during the late War: All these Accounts must be passed. The Public have a Right and good Cause to demand it. If, according to the present Constitution of the Exchequer, they can be passed no where but in the Office of the Auditor, that Constitution should be altered. Such of the Accounts as may appear the most proper to be removed, should be transferred from his Office to such other Offices as may, from their peculiar Circumstances, and the Relation they bear to the Subject Matter of the Accounts, be presumed to be the belt qualified for the Examination of them.

Wherever an Office is instituted for the Purpose of examining and controlling Accounts previous to their Examination by the Auditor, and that Office is so formed as to answer the Use intended, and the Officers do their Duty, it seems to us to render any subsequent Examination superfluous, and an unnecessary Expence to the Public. Upon this Principle we suggested the Exemption of the Accounts of the Treasurer of the Navy from the Jurisdiction of the Auditor. The same Principle leads us to relieve him from the Accounts of the Army. Parts of these Accounts, and those very considerable, — the Execution of the Contracts, and the Expenditure of the Extraordinaries, — according to the present Usage, pass the Office of the Controller of the Army Accounts previous to their Examination by the Auditor. As far as appears to us, the Examinations by the Controller are sufficient, and consequently those of the Auditor may be dispensed with. If the Office of the Controller is so constituted, that these Species of Accounts may safely rest upon his Examination (and the Treasury rely so much upon it, that they direct Payments upon his Reports without waiting for the Confirmation of the Auditor) he must be equally qualified to pass the rest of the Accounts of the Army: The latter are not more difficult than the former; nor does it require greater Talents to examine the one than the other.

Though the Business of the Controller is at present confined to these particular Branches, yet he seems to have been originally intended for a more extensive Employment. By his Commission, in the 2d Year of Queen Anne, he is created Controller of all Accounts relating to the Forces; and, by the last Instructions for the Conduct of the Office, dated 28th of 1704, be is to keep an Account of all Monies issued to the Paymaster General of the Forces, and to take Care he is charged therewith.

The Time seems to be come, when the State of the Business in the Office of the Auditor renders it necessary to carry into Execution the Intention of Queen Anne in the Institution of this Office, and to extend its

Duty to all the Accounts of the Army. The Two Offices of Controller and Paymaster General are lb unconnected and independent of each other, that the first may be with Safety placed as a Check upon the other. One entire Species of Public Expenditure will be the Employment of One Office; which, though but one Species of Expenditure, is yet, from the Number and Variety of its Branches, and from the long Arrears suffered to be incurred, fully sufficient to engage the continual Labour of any One Office for a Time not easily to be defined. Should the Treasury be dissatisfied with the Report of the Controller, upon any particular Account or Article, or require farther Information, it will continue to be, as it is now, in their Power to refer it to the Auditor for his Examination and Opinion.

For these Reasons we are of Opinion, that the auditing the Accounts of the Paymaster General of the Forces should be transferred from the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest to that of the Controller of the Accounts of the Army; that the Pay Office of the Army should complete such Accounts of the Paymaster General of the Forces, as have been already delivered into the Office of the Auditor, and that the Auditor should proceed without Delay to finish and pass such Accounts; and that all Army Accounts, subsequent to those already delivered into the Office of the Auditors, and all future Accounts of Paymasters General of the Forces, should be sent to the Office of the Controller of the Accounts of the Army, and be examined and audited by him, and inrolled in the Office of the King’s Remembrancer in the Exchequer.

We required from the Auditor of the Imprest, a List of the Fees on passing the Account of the Year 1767 (the Year that had been under our Examination) with the Rate at which such Fees were taken. We required, likewise, from the Controller of the Accounts of the Army, an Account of the Salaries, Fees, and Gratuities, received by the Officers and Clerks in his Office. From the State of the Fees returned to us by the Auditor, it appears that he is paid at the Rate of Ten Shillings a Year for every Troop and Company, and a Fee of One hundred and Fifty Pounds a Year for the Account of the Paymaster General, and of Seventy Pounds a Year for the Account of the Treasurer of Chelsea Hospital. The Deputy had One hundred Guineas, and the Clerks Fifty-four Pounds Twelve Shillings. The Amount of all the Fees, for these Two Accounts of the Year 1767, payable to the Auditor, was Seven hundred and Six Pounds Nine Shillings and Ten Pence; and of those payable for passing them through the Exchequer Offices, One hundred Thirty-eight Pounds Nine Shillings.

In the Office of the Controller of the Accounts of the Army, the Two Controllers have each a Salary of Seven hundred Forty-nine Pounds Nineteen Shillings and One Penny, reduced, by the Army Deductions and the Land Tax, to nett Five hundred Fifty-eight Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Eight Pence a Year. They have no other Emolument, except such Saving as may be made out of their contingent Allowance. The Secretary and Clerks received, until very lately, Salaries, Fees, and Gratuities, which, in the Year 1781, amounted to the nett Sum of Three thousand One hundred Ninety-three Pounds Nine Shillings and Four Pence: But this Mode of Payment has been changed to an Allowance of One Eighth per Cent. upon the Sum contained in the Account, in lieu of Fees and Gratuities: This is allowed the Contractor in his Account, and is consequendy a Charge upon the Public.

Should the auditing the Accounts of the Paymaster General of the Forces be transferred to this Office, it will be a Saving to the Public of feme Part, though not the Whole, of the Expence now incurred in the

N° 2.

The Examination of John Porvell, Esquire; taken upon Oath, the 2d, 11th, and 15th of April 1783.

THIS Examinant faith, That he was, until very lately, Deputy to the Honourable Ilenr) Eduard , Paymaster of the Widows Pensions: lie had been in that Office before, and ever since, the Year 1771.

The Business of this Office is carried on at the War Office by Two Persons; the one employed by the Secretary at War, the other by the Deputy Paymaster; the Principal has not, as he believes, ever executed any Part of it; he has been for feme Years in North America.

He received for this Service Sums upon Account from the Pay Office of the Army, and from the Marine Pay Office, and applied for them Two or Three Times a Year to the Army Pay Office, and occasionally to the Marine Pay Office.

The Sums for this Service arise from the Allowance to Widows voted upon the Establishment. This Fund, in Time of War, produces more than is wanted for the Service; and in Time of Peace it has produced, as he believes, sufficient for the Service.

The Account kept of the Issues for this Service, in the Pay Office, specifies out of what Year’s Produce the Sum is issued; and during the Time of the same Paymaster General, the full Produce of each Year is generally received from the Pay Office before any Ift'uc is made out of the Produce of the succeeding Year.

The Annual Produce has so far exceeded the Demands for the Service, that in the Year 1780, the Produce for the Years 1775, 1776, 1777, 1778, and 1779, amounting to One hundred Thirteen thousand Nine hundred Ninety-eight Pounds Seven Shillings and Four Pence, was applied by Parliament in Aid of the Extraordinaries incurred between the 31st of January 1779 and the lft of February 1780, and not provided for by Parliament.

The Payments are made every Four Months, upon an Establishment made out every Year by the Secretary at War; the Widow, to entitle herself to Payment, must produce, by herself or her Agent, her Affidavit of her being the Widow of the Officer, and that ffie is not otherwise provided for by Government, and give a Receipt for the Money: The Establishment,

with the Affidavit and Receipt, is his Voucher to the Auditor of the Imprest. The Account for the Year 1780 is in the Office of Lord and 1781 in

the Office of Lord Sondes.

This Examinant further faith. That the Account signed by him, dated 25th of March 1783, and delivered to this Board, contains, to the best of his Knowledge and Belief, a true Account of the Sums received and paid by him for the Years therein mentioned, except that the Sum of Thirty-four thousand and Sixty-three Pounds Eleven Shillings, inserted in the Column of Payments for the Year 1781, contains the Sum of Twenty thousand Seven hundred Sixty-nine Pounds Twelve Shillings and Six Pence, paid back by him to the Paymaster General of the Forces; which was Part of the Savings upon this Service applied by Parliament the preceding Year: That the Balance in his Hands, on Account of the Widows Pensions, upon the 24th of December last, was Twenty-four thousand Three hundred Fifty-two Pounds Two Shillings and Six Pence: That he received, the 4th of February last, for the Marine Widows, One thousand Six hundred Eighty-nine Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Three Pence: That he has paid to the Widows, since the 25th of December last, Four thousand Six hundred Ninety-one Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Sevenpence; and on the 21st of March last, to Mr. Moore, the present Deputy Paymaster, pursuant to a Letter from the Secretary at War, dated the 19th of March, Twenty-one thousand Pounds; which leaves a Balance in his Hands of Three hundred Fifty Pounds Five Shillings and Two Pence only.

The Examination of John , Esquire; taken upon Oath, the 7th and llth of April 1783.

This Examinant faith, that he was Deputy Auditor of the Imprest to Lewis Lord Sondes, and made up the Account of the Honourable Hcmy Edxeard Far, Receiver and Paymaster of His Majesty’s Royal Bounty to the Widows of Officers, for Two Years, ending the 24th December 1779.

It has been usual, ever since he has been Deputy, which is about Twenty Years, to make up there, Accounts for Two Years together.

The Deputy Paymaster of these Pensions has been, for many Years, an Officer in the Pay Office; and the Deputy has always pafi’cd the Account, and not the Principal.

The Deputy Paymaster fends to the Auditor’s Office, Pay Office Certificates of the Sums that have been ifl'ued to him; and a Book of Account comprehending all his Receipts and Payments for the Two Years, with the Establishment for each Year; and the Certificates and Attestation of each Widow, of her Marriage, Widowhood, and not being otherwise provided for by Government; and the Acquittance of the Person receiving. The Pay Office Certificates are the Vouchers for the Charge; the Establishments, with the Certificates and Receipts, are the Vouchers for the Discharge: After the Account is examined, and the Balance agreed upon with the Accountant, he tigns an Abstract of the whole Account, inserted at the End of the Book of Account, and swears to the Truth of it before the Deputy Auditor. This is the Form of parting an Account of a Paymaster 9f the Widows Pensions; it is not declared before the Chancellor of the Exchequer, nor is Vol. 39-

it passed through the Exchequer Offices; The Duplicate Tenth of the official Account remains in the Office of the Report Auditor, the other Part is delivered to the Accountant, °" i>ubl‘c

1 . Accounts.

and is his Quietus.

The Fees allowed for making up this Account for the Years 1778 and 1779 were, a Poundage of One Shilling on the Sum paid and allowed, amounting to One thousand Three hundred Sixty-two Pounds and One Penny; to John Powell, Esquire, for his extraordinary Trouble, by Warrant, Two hundred Pounds; for the usual Fees and Disbursements paid for stating, examining, and parting this Account, One hundred Sixty-five Pounds: Of this last Sum Mr. Powell received One Third Part, as had been usual, and the rest was for the Use of the Auditor.

John Lloyd.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Sam! Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond.

N 4-

The Examination of Mr. John Davies; taken upon Oath, the 15th of April 1783.

This Examinant faith, That he is a Clerk in the War Office, and has been for above Twenty Years employed in the Payment of the Widows Pensions: He is appointed by the Secretary at War. This Business is tranla&ed by himself, and by One more Clerk, who does not belong to the War Office, but is appointed by the Deputy Paymaster of the Widows Pensions. It is his Business to keep the Books, and to make out the Establishments, the Warrants, the Certificates, the Affidavits, and the Receipts. He fees the Payments made, and witnesses the Receipts. The Business of the other Clerk is, to bring the Money from the Deputy Paymaster of the Widows, and to pay to them the Sums due for their Pensions.

For this Business he receives from the Secretary at War a Salary of Ninety-two Pounds a Year; and each Widow, when Hie first receives her Pension, pays by Custom Two Guineas, and at the Rate of Six Shillings a Year afterwards; which last Sums are equally divided between him and the other Clerk. He does not receive, for the Execution of this Office, any other Fee or Emolument whatever, except that he has occasionally, once in a few Years, accepted a Present of a few Guineas.

John Davies.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Geo. Drummond.

N* 5.

The Examination of Mr. Keene Stables; taken upon Oath, 15th April 1783.

This Examinant faith, That he is a Clerk in the Pay Office, and also employed in the Payment of the Widows Pensions; he was appointed by the Deputy Paymaster of the Widows Pensions. It is his Business to Pay the Pensions to the Widows, for which Purpose he received Money from the Deputy Paymaster.

The Widows are paid every Four Months. At the Beginning of a Payment he attends for a whole Week j and every Wednesday in the succeeding Weeks, are Days of Payment. At the Beginning he applies for and receives from the Deputy Paymaster Two thousand Pounds; and when that Sum is exhausted, he

applies,

applies, from Time to Time, for such a Sum as he thinks will be wanted. He pays the Widows fomedmes in Caih, and sometimes by Drafts. He also makes out the Book containing the Account of the Payments for this Service, which is delivered into the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest, when the Deputy Paymaster pafles his Accounts there. The Deputy Paymalier transacts no Part of the Business hirnfel^ except supplying the Money.

He receives no Salary for the Execution of this Office,

nor any Fee or Emolument, except from the Widows; One Guinea upon their being put upon the Establish-ment, and a Shilling for each Four Months, and the odd Pence, amounting in the Whole to about One hundred and Ten Pounds a Year.

K. Stables.

The Examination of Willum Brumme//, - Esquire; taken upon Oath, the 8th and 1 ith April 1783.

This Examinant faith, That he is Agent for paying the Out Petitioners of Chelsea Hospital, and \yas appointed in the Year 1774.

This Office is created by the Act of the a 8th . of George the Second, Chapter the First; and the Officer is appointed by a Sign Manual, couotersigned by the Lords of the Treasury.

, The Fund for this Service is YPtfid Annually, and received by the Paymaster General of the Forces, as Treasurer of Chelsea Hospital, and by him issued to his Deputy Treasurer. A Lift is made out every Half Year, by the Secretary and Register of the Hot-pita!, of all the Out Pensioners. This Lift is sent to the Agent for the Out Pensioners, who makes a Gopy of it, and then applies to the Deputy Treasurer lor Money to pay that Lift; the Deputy Treasurer advances to him upon Account, upon giving a -Receipt, such a Sum as he thinks will be sufficent for that Half Year’s Payment, retaining the Deduction of One Shilling in the Pound, pursuant to the Directions of the Act.

\Vhere Persons are admitted Out Pensioners by the Board of Commissioners, they issue a Warrant to the Treasurer, with a List ofluch Persons annexed, directing him to pay to the Agent fuqh Sums of Moqey as are d,ue to them, from the Day of their Admission: The Agent calculates the Sum due upon the Warrant, and receivefit of the Deputy Treasurer.

Where an Out Pensioner is admitted into the House, or sent into a Garrison, he returns back to the Agent so much as he has received in Advance from the Time of his Admission to the next Payment. A Number of Pensioners are continually discharged from the different Garrjfons in Great Britain, Guernsey, and ana

from the House, who are re-admitted Out Pensioners, and immediately paid their Pensions in Advance, by the Agent, for the Remainder o_f the current Half Year. ITe then delivers a List of |uch Pensioners, as aforesaid, discharged, to the Secretary and Register, who makes out a Warrant, which is laid before the Commissioners; and when signed by them, they direct the Treasurer to issue the Amount thereof to the Agent.

Out Pensioners who, having been resident Aoroad, apply upon their Return Home for their Arrears of Pension 'due to them, and being left off the Warrant for Non-appearance, the ^Qmmissioners restore them, and direct me Agent to pay the fiune. They are then put upon what is called tj Supplemental Warrant, the Amount of which the Commissioners direct the Treasurer to pay the Agent: By no' other Means than thele does the Agent receive Money for this Service.

The Out Pensioners are comprehended in Three Lifts — The common Out Pensioners, who are paid Five Pence a Day; The Nine Ij’enoy Men, who are paid Nine Pence; and, The Letter Men, who are paid One Shilling a Day: They are ^11 paiq Half Yearly, Six Months in Advance.

~ These Out Pensioners ar^ dispersed over Great Britain and Ireland, and a few of thpm in Guernsey and Jersey: Thofein Great Britain are paid by his Deputies and the Collectors oL Excite; those in Ireland, and in Guernsey and Jersey, by Deputies.

The last declared Account, the Agent to the*Out Pensioners, is for One Year, ending 24th December 1775: The dumber in that Year was about Fifteen, thousand Nine hundred.

For the Execution of this Office, he receives only a Salary of One thousand Pounds a Year, payable out of the Poundage; out of which he pays, for TaXos,

04

Seventy-five Pounds; for Deputies, Clerks, Contingencies of Office, and Fees to Auditors, not allowed in the Account, Five hundred Forty-three Pounds; which reduces his clear Receipt to Three hundred Eighty-twa Pounds a Year.

-Accounts- for Three -Years more have been-lent to the Office of the Auditors near a Year ago, and are now ready for Declaration; Two Years more will be ready-to be delivered in to the Auditors in about Three Months. From the Difficulty of procuring and adjusting the Vouchers, the Accounts are not made up in the Office to a later Period than the End of the Year 1780.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott, -SamtBeachcroft, Geo. Drummond,

N* 13.

The Examination of Charles Esquire; taken

upon Oath, 5th and 8th May 1783.

This Examinant faith, That he is employed by the 'Honourable Frederick Vane, the Deputy Treasurer of Chelsea Hospital, to transact for him the Business of that Office. The Deputy Treasurer.receives from the Paymaster ‘General of the Forces, and pays over to the Agent, the Sums "for the Out Pensioners; every Six Mouffis the iSecretary and Register of the Hospital fends to the Deputy Treasurer a Requisition, containing the Number of Out Pensioners, and the Sums to be advanced, to them for the succeeding Half Year: After the Requisition p Warrant issues from the Board of Commissioners for the Affairs of the Hospital, signed by Three, or more of them, directed to the Treasurer of the Hospital, requiring him to issue to the Agent for the Out (Pensioners fqch Sums AS Avail be due to them for the Six Months ensuing. In consequence of this Warrant, the Treasurer issues to his Deputy such a Sum as he thinks proper; and the Deputy, upon the Requisition. of the Agent, advances to him stich Sums upon Account as he thinks will satisfy the Lift.

Jhp Deputy stops out of the Sums issued to the Agent the Twelve Pence in the Pound, as directed by the Act of Parliament; a distinct Account is kept of this Deduction, which remains in his Hands for the following Purposes — the Payment of the Salary to the Agent, and Allowances; to the Deputy Treasurer Six hundred Pounds a Year; and to the Secretary Three hundred Pounds a Year; and such other Payments as may be directed by the King’s Warrants, which have amounted to a very inconsiderable Sqm. The Savings from this Deduction, from the 34th of December 1773 (to which Time the Balance was paid to the Paymaster General of the Forces) to the 24th of December 1780, amounted to Twenty-three thousand Six hundred Forty-five Pounds Two Shillings and Seven Pence; and was in last

paid back into the Exchequer, pursuant to the King’s Warrant, to be applied towards the Supply for the Year >782. The Balance of that Deduction, on the Payments made to the Agent down to the 24th December 1782, amounts to Three thousand and Twenty-one Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Two Pence Halfpenny, out of which he was obliged to advance various Sums for the current Expences of the Hospital, having only received the Sums for that Service down to the 24th of June last.

Cha' Harris.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Geo. Dnimmond.

Mem4".

The Supers on that Part of the Paymaster General’s Account executed by Paris Taylor, Esquire, his late Deputy in Germany, are not included in the foregoing Total of Arrears, being not settled.

The Paymaster General has surcharged himself with the Value of several Bills of Exchange, to a very great Amount, drawn by the Marquis of Granby and others, on Messrs. Pye and Cruikshank, in Favour of Peter Taylor, Esquire, his Deputy, in Germany; but the said Pye and Cruikshank have not delivered any Account to the Auditors.

The Paymaster General has also surcharged himself with very large Sums of Money received from Messrs. Thomlinson, Colebrooke, Nesbitt, and Hanbury, and their Account is under Examination at Auditor s

Office.

The Commissioners of Public Accounts.

We hereby certify, That we have compared this Lift with the Lift of the Persons at this Time remaining Insuper in the final Account of Henry Lord Holland; and find them to agree, and that none of the Insupers therein mentioned have been cleared by the Auditor. A Sum of 4,000l. set Insuper on Horatio Gates in the Year 1760, we presume will be cleared. The Paymaster General having charged himself with receiving, of Brigadier General MonckUm, a Sum issued to Major Horatio Gates, of 4,000l.; which Article, being without Time when received of Brigadier General Monckton, or by what Authority it w as paid to Horatio Gates, is included in Observations transmitted from this Office to the Accountant.

Auditor’s Office, Lord Sondes,} Jos. Hughes, 1 n y A Jit

The Examination of Anthony Bacon, Esquire; taken upon Oath, the 20th of February 1783.

This Examinant faith, That some Time, as he believes, in the Year 1764, he entered into a ContraQ with the Lords of the Treasury, for supplying Negroes for the Life of the new ceded Islands.

Upon Production to the Lords of the Treasury of Accounts of the Services performed, and of Certificates signed, either by the Commander in Chief, or by the Commissioners for the Sale of Lands in those Islands, or by the Surveyors, that l'uch Services were performed; and upon a Reference of the Accounts and Certificates to some of their Clerks for Examination; he received, from Time to Time, the Amount of the Accounts from the Exchequer, pursuant to Warrants obtained for that Purpose; except that Three of thele Payments were made to him by the Paymaster General of the Forces; thele Sums were Payments for Services performed, and not imprested to him.

In the Year 1768 the Balance due to him on this Contract being settled by the like Means, he obtained from the Lords of the Treasury a Warrant, dated 20th of December 17G8, directed to the Paymaster General of the Forces, to pay him the Sum of One thousand and Eighty-three Pounds Ten Shillings and Four Pence, being the Balance of that Account, without Deduction, and without Account.

This Examinant further faith, That he entered into an Agreement with the Lords of the Treasury, to furnish Bread, Candles, Coals, and Straw, to the Troops in the Isle of Man: He delivered to them an Account of the

Execution of this Agreement, with the incidental Charges: This Account was referred to the Controller of the Army Accounts: Upon his Report, he obtained the King's Warrant, dated the 10th of February 1767, directed to the Paymaster General, for the Payment of One thousand One hundred and Four Pounds Six Shillings and Ten Pence; being the Sum due to him on that Account; which Sum he received of the Paymaster General, and endorsed his Name upon the Warrant: The Words of this Warrant are, upon Account, to satisfy and discharge the like Sum due to him; but he has always considered this Account as completely settled, and that it was unnecessary to pass any other Account of this Agreement.

Antho. Bacon.

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Rich11 Neavc,

Sami Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

K# 31.

The Examination of Sir John Dick, Baronet; taken upon Oath, the 16th, 19th, and 2ill May 1783.

This Examinant faith, That he is one of the Controllers of the Accounts of the Army: This Office is executed by Two Controllers, a Secretary, and Four Clerks: It is granted by Letters Patent, during Pleasure.

The first Commission appears to bear Date the 10th of June, in the Second Year of Queen Anne. The first Set of InstruQions for the ConduQ of the Office, are dated the 26th of June 1703; and the other Instructions, which are the last, are dated 28th of Vol. 39.

1704. At this Day the foie Business of the Office is to Tenth examine and report upon the Accounts referred to them

r . 1 m /* on x ublic

from the Treasury. Account8.

After a Contrail for Army Services is executed at the Treasury, it is sent to the Office of the Controllers of the Army Accounts, to be there registered. Every Account or Demand by the ContraQor upon the Treasury, in consequence of his having executed this ContraQ, either in the Whole or in Part, is transmitted by the Treasury to the Controllers^ with a Letter from the Secretary, referring to them the Examination and Consideration of the Demand or Account, and directing them to report their Opinion thereon.

Where the Agreement is made by a Minute of the Treasury Board, either a Copy of that Minute is sent to the Controllers, or they have Recourse to the Minute itself entered at the Treasury, when necessary. The Contractor annexes to his Account all the necessary Vouchers; if he omits any, they are required of him.

The Controller first examines, and fees that the Account agrees with the Terms of the ContraQ; he compares every Article with its respective Voucher; the Computations and Caftings are examined, and a Certificate, by the proper Officer, of the faithful Execution of every Part of the ContraQ:, must be produced.

Where a Demand appears to be agreeable to the ContraQ, and each Article is proved by a proper Voucher, the Controller recommends the Payment in his Report to the Treasury: Where there are Errors,’ he correQs them; where there are Doubts, he states them specially, and refers the Determination of them to the Treasury. The Vouchers ase generally returned with the Report to the Treasury; such as it may be necessary to have Recourse to afterwards, are retained in the Office.

All the Issues for the Army Extraordirtaries ought properly to be examined by the Controllers of the Army Accounts.

Where a ContraQ is entered into for supplying Armies or Garrisons Abroad with Provisions, it is the Business of the Controllers of the Army Accounts, upon a Reference from the Treasury, to examine the Delivery of these Provisions into the King’s Stores: The Storekeeper, who receives them, ought to transmit, from Time to Time, to the Treasury, an Account of what they receive into the King’s Stores, and of what they delivered on board the Ships, specifying their Destination:

After they are delivered to the Comraiflaries, it is their Duty to transmit to the Treasury, an Account of what they receive, and what they issue, with the proper Vouchers; and it is the Business of the Controllers, upon a Reference from the Treasury, to examine these Accounts. The Controllers have no Power of aQing but upon a Reference from the Treasury; nor have they any discretionary Power, where a Voucher is wanting, of admitting an Article of Payment upon any other Evidence

Where an Agreement is made with the Treasury to furnish Articles upon Commission, the Person who engages must produce the Orders of the Treasury, and if he fumifhe3 the Articles himself, must produce Certificates of the Quantity, Quality, and Price; if he purchases, he must produce the Agreement or ContraQ.

All ContraQs are entered into the Controllers Office, with the Reports of the Controllers upon the References, and the Warrants issued in consequence of those Reports.

Several Statements of Accounts made by the Auditors of the Imprest, have been referred lately to the Controllers, for their Examination and Report; and Errors in them have been correQed.

The Controllers are paid, by a Salary out of the Army Poundage, Seven hundred Fifty Pounds a Year

each,

Report cm Public Accounts.

656 20 Julii. . 1783.

each, subject to various Deductions, which reduce it to about five hundred Fifty-eight Pounds a Year; and they have no Fees or Gratuities whatever, except what may be saved out of the contingent Allowance. The Emoluments of the Secretary and Clerks confided, until lately, of Salaries, F’ecs, and Gratuities; they are now allowed One Eighth per Cent, upon the Gross Sum contained in the Account, in lieu of Fees and Gratuities; which Sum is allowed to the Person whose Account it is, and is paid by the Public.

John Dick.

N* 32

The Examination of John Martin Leake, Esquire; taken upon Oath, the 3d March 1783*

This Examinant faith, That he is now a Clerk of the Treasury, and has been so for near Twenty Years. There are Two Forms by which the Lords of the Treasury enter into Contracts or Agreements for the Performance of Services; the one is by Indenture of Two Parts, the one Part executed by the Person contracting, the other Part by Three or more Lords of the Treasury; the other Form is a Minute of the Treasury Board, to which the Person contracting agrees, either by a Memorial previously presented by him to the Treasury, or by his being present when the Minute is made. It is the Business of the contracting Party, if it is necessary, to enter his Contract, or a Copy of the Minute, in those Offices where he is either to be paid or to pass his Accounts.. In some Contracts the Contractor receives Money upon Account, previous to the Execution of any Part of the Contract; in other Contracts he receives Payments froip Time to Time, in consequence of the Part Execution of his Contract, and, as far as be has executed it. Ip both these Cafes, where the Contract or. Agreement is for Army So-vices, the Treasury usually refer to the Controller of the Army Accounts, the Vouchers, Certificates, or Accounts produced by the Contractors in support of their Claim for Payments. If, upon the Repqrt of the Controller, Money appears to be due to him, and there is qo Reason to withhold the Payment, the Treasury prqcure the Warrant for the Payment, which Payment is in general Upon Recount. Where the Payment has been made upon an Agreement for furnishing Articles on Commission at a Sum per Cent, the Account has been examined iometimes by a Clerk of the Treasury, and sometimes by the Controller of the Army Accounts, and the Payments have been made by Warrants without Account. In Mr. Bacon's Coptract for supplying Negroes in the ceded islands, the Payments were made to him from Time to Time without Account, and, as he believes, without Reference; the Reason of which seems to be, that the Vouchers were competent and required no Reference.

John Martin Leake.

T. Anguish,

Rich4Neave,

Sant! Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond.

N* 35.

The Examination of Joseph , Esquire;

> taken upon* Oath, the 27th, 28th, and 30th May 1783.

This Examinant faith, That Lord Holland's final Account is not yet closed, nor is the Balance (truck; no Additions have been made to the Charge since the Three Articles added by Mr. Colbome, 12th last; one Article was added to the Discharge last Week, upon Production of a Tally for Twenty thoii-sand Pounds paid into the Exchequer by Mr. Powell in March last: In the Copy of the Additions made to the final Account of Lord Holland, transmitted from Lord Sondes’s Office to this Board, dated the 11th of February, the Two last Articles, amounting to One thousand Three hundred Sixty-eight Pounds Nine Shillings and Three Pence, are those which the Auditor pointed out as Errors in the Account to be added to the Charge.

I.ord Holland is charged in his final Account, with a Sum of Twenty-nine thousand Six hundred Fifty-six Pounds Eleven Shillings and One Penny, of Profit on Exchange of Money, made by Peter Taylor, his Deputy in Gennany. In order to enable the Auditor

to examine this Sum of Profit, a Book was produced to him some Time about Christmas last, as he believes, by Mr. Colbome, dated the 12th of May 1764, and ligned, as it appears, by P. Taylor, intituled, Account of Profit and Lois to the Public in all " Payments made by P. Taylor, Deputy Paymaster " in Germany," Lpon examining that Book, the

Auditor has discovered various Errors, to the Amount of Eight thousand Five hundred Seventy-seven Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Ten Pence, in Favour of the Public; which Sum remains yet to be added to the Charge of Loid Holland. The Auditor’s Observations

on this Account were lent to Mr. Powell 23d of February; some of the Articles have been examined by Mr. Colbome on the Part of Mr. Powell, and found to agree with the Auditor’s Computation; the others have not yet been checked by the Pay Office; until that is done, which the Auditor waits for, he cannot add it to the Charge against Lord Holland.

In the Pay Office Book of Account sent to the Auditor, there are frequently Blanks left in the Body of the Account, for Sums not then ascertained, which Blanks are afterwards filled up from' Time to Time, when the Book is returned to the Pay Office.

Lord Holland's final Account being ready to be closed, and waiting only for Mr. Powell's striking the Balance and attesting the Account, the Deputy Auditors, upon the 27th of November last, wrote to him, to inform him that they had Lord Sondes’s Direction to acquaint the Treasury with it; and upon the 30th of November they wrote to the Secretary of the Treasury, informing him, that it was ready for Declaration, if the Book of Account was closed and attested; and that the Balance due to the Public from the Estate of Lord Holland, was then Sixty-eight thousand and Eight Pounds Six Shillings and Six Pence TVr- This Balance includes the Two Articles, amounting to One thousand Three hundred Sixty-eight Pounds Nine Shillings and Three Pence, pointed out by the Auditor as Errors in the Account. The Book of Account was taken from the Auditor’s Office about Christmas, in order to have those Two Articles inserted. The Book was returned soon after Christmas to the Auditor, with Additions inserted in the Charge, amounting to Forty-eight thousand Seven hundred Ninety-nine Pounds Ten Shillings and Eleven Pence, without the Privity of the Auditor, and the Two Articles directed to be inserted by the Auditor were entered the last in the Charge; at the same Time a Receipt for Two thousand Eight hundred Forty-five Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Ten Pence, was produced to the Auditor, to be allowed as an Article in the Discharge. The Allowance of this Sum is now under the Consideration of the Treasury, Three Articles, amounting to Seven hundred Seventy-four Pounds Seven Shillings and Three Pence, have been since added to the Charge, in consequence of Lord Sondes's Letter to Mr. Powell, dated 10th February 1783, which makes the Balance now due from the Estate of Lord Holland < to the Public Ninety-seven thousand Five hundred Eighty-two Pounds Four Shillings and Eight Pence; and if the Article under the Consideration of the Treasury is allowed, it will reduce this Balance to Ninety-four thousand Seven hundred Thirty-six Pounds Six Shillings and Ten Pence ,* and if the Errors discovered in the Profit and Loss Account are just, it will increase this Balance to One hundred and Three thousand Three hundred and Fourteen Pounds and Eight Pence.

Jos. Hughes.

T. Anguish,

N* 37-

The Examination of Mr. John taken

upon Oath, /2th February 1783.

This Examinant faith, That he is an Assistant in the Office of the Paymaster General of the Forces, and has been almost the foie Person employed in making up the Accounts of Lord Holland. That, to the bell of his Recollection and Belief, about the latter End of November or the Beginning of December last, he took from the Office of Lord Sondes, by the Direction either of Mr. Powell or Mr. the final Book

of Account of Lord HolLind, as Paymaster General of the Forces, in order to add certain Articles to the Charge. Some Time after he had brought this Book to the Pay Office, he entered in the Charge several additional Articles; these Articles he had himself some Years before selected from the Ledger Accounts of Ixtrd Holland, and by the same Direction lie then inserted them in the Charge. He has, at several Periods, entered Additions to the Charge in this Account Book: He was governed, as to the Articles he entered at each Time, by the Directions he received. He several Years ago shewed to Mr. Powell all the Articles he had collected as Charges upon Lord Holland, except Two Articles of Profits on Remittances; all these have since, at different Times, been inserted in the Account. Three more Articles were this Morning added to the Charge, and he believes the Charge is now complete.

He does not recollect, nor did he make any Minutes or Memorandums of, the particular Times when he inserted the Additions in this Book of Account.

N* 44-

Gentlemen,

My Mind is extremely distressed, by having received Information that it is under Consideration, whether a criminal Prosecution shall not be commenced against me, on Account of my Examination upon Oath, taken in your Office on the 20th and 26th and the

9th, 12th, 15th, 19th, and 28th March 1781. In that Situation, I must entreat my further Examination may be deferred, until I shall be relieved, by Authority, from any Apprehension of such criminal Prosecution, left Questions should be put, the Answers to which may tend to accuse myself, which ought not to be done. If I can be affined that no such Prosecution is meditated, and that none such shall be commenced, I will readily submit fully to answer such Questions as you shall be pleased to put

I am, with great Respefit, Gentlemen,

Y our most obedient March 7th, 1783. and most humble Servant,

Jit Powell.

To the Commissioners of Public Accounts.

N° 45.

Extra6t of Minute of the Treasury, of the 22d of February 1783, on Mr. Powell's Examination -

My Lords are pleased to direct a full State of the same to be prepared by the Solicitor to this Board, from the Minutes of this Day, the 14th and the 15th Instant; and that the fame, with the several Accounts delivered in, be laid before the Attorney and Solicitor General as soon as possible, for their Opinions, to know whether any, and what further Proceedings ought to be had in this Business.

The above is a true Extract, Treasury Chambers,! John Martin Leake.

8th March 1783. J

And the Directions contained therein have been communicated to the Solicitor of the Treasury.

J. M. Leake.

N*46.

The Examination ef Mr. John taken upon

Oath, 17th March 1783.

This Examinant faith, That the Deputy Paymasters Abroad return from Time to Time to the Pay Office

in London, as Opportunities offer, generally within a few Tenth Months, an Account of their Receipts and Payments, Report made up to the Date of their Account, and usually with °n Publ'c their Vouchers. These Accounts are immediately exa- ecou* mined in the Office with the Vouchers, and then entered in the Books of the Accounts of the several Deputies:

The Parts of the Account that relate to the SubsistencC, are posted soon afterwards into the Ledger, to the separate Accounts of the Regiments; the Parts that consist of Extraordinaries, are entered in a Book containing the American Extraordinaries only; these Articles are entered in this Book of Extraordinaries at different Times, as the Business of the Office will permit; they must be entered before the Account of the Year, in which the Warrants bear Date, is made out for the ' Auditor. The Sum Total of the Year’s Extraordinaries is then carried to the Account of the Deputy Paymaster in the Ledger.

He has examined the Articles stated in the Account of the Additions made to the final Account of the late Lord Holland, since the 5th of October last, with the Books of the Deputy Paymaster in the Office; and he finds that all the Articles, importing to be Sums received and gained by the Deputy Paymasters therein mentioned, are severally entered as Charges upon them in the respective Books of those Deputies; and, as he believes, they were entered soon after the Accounts themselves were received at the Office. These Articles are posted separately to the Account of each Deputy in the Ledger, when the Account is made up for the Auditor.

He believes the Deputy Paymasters, Mr. Mortier, Mr.

Porter, Mr. Barrow, Mr. Nicolls, and Major Wrightson, are dead, and all their Accounts, except Mr. Barrow's, have been long since made up. He assisted in making out the Two Articles of Profit on Remittances; that on Subsistence, as he believes, about the Year 1764, under the Direction of Mr. Nicolls, the then Accountant of the Pay Office; and that on the Extraordinaries, about Five or Six Years ago, under the Direction of Mr. Powell.

The Articles that compose the Lift of the Stoppages, are taken from the Accounts of the Deputies, as they are returned to the Pay Office, and entered in their separate Books of Account, and were posted into the Ledger previous to the Year 1772, when the final Account of Lord Holland was sent to the Office of the Auditor of the Imprest.

Jit Colbome.

T. Anguish,

RichfNeave,

Sam> Beachcrofi,

Geo. Drummond.

N* 49-

ANNE R.

Whereas by Letters Patents under the Great Seal of England, lately passed, We have erected the Office of Comptroller of all Accounts relating to Our Forces (those Forces in Ireland excepted) with Directions therein, amongst other Things, That the said Comptrollers shall observe such Instructions as they shall from Time to Time receive from Us, under Our Royal Sign Manual: Our Will and Pleasure now is, and We do hereby direct and command, That the following Instructions be duly observed by the Comptrollers of the said Accounts, now and for the Time being, until We signify Our Pleasure to the contrary; that is to say,

lit. The said Comptrollers are to take and keep an Account of all the Monies which shall be issued at the Exchequer, or otherwise, to the respective Paymasters for the said Forces, and to take Care that they be duly charged therewith; for which Purpose all Orders for issuing Monies to the said Paymasters, are to be entered with the said Comptrollers.

2. The said Comptrollers are to take and keep an Account of all Arms, Provisions, Tents, and other Things, which shall be delivered out of Her Majesty’s Stores to the Use of any of the Regiments, Troops, or Companies; and (in Cafes where any Deduction is to be made for them, or any of them) they are to take Care that the Value thereof be duly charged to the Account of such Regiment, Troop, or Company.

3. The General having approved and sealed the Patterns for Clothing, the Colonels are to contract for the said Clothing, and then exhibit to the Comptrollers the said Contracts; which are to specify the Quantities, Qualities, and Prices of each Particular. The said Colonels, or their Agents, are like wife to exhibit to the Comptrollers the Debt owing on the Off-reckonings the 24th of February 1703; from which Day this Rule shall commence. The Comptrollers are likewise to take Care that the Clothes for the Army in England be furnished according to the Contracts and Patterns (for which, as to the Troops Abroad, the Certificate of the Captain General, or of such Person or Persons as shall be appointed by him, is to suffice); and that the Clothing do not exceed the Off-reckonings: And if any Regiment is in Debt, the Debt is to be funk Annually as much as the Service will bear; and the Observations how the Debt decreales are to be represented from Time to Time, by the Comptrollers, to the General and Lord High Treasurer, or Commissioners of the Treasury, for the Tune being. The Comptrollers being satisfied that the Contracts have been performed according to the Patterns, shall certify the feme respectively to the Pay -masters; without which they are not to comply with any Assignment for the Payment thereof.

4th. Iney are, by themselves or their Agents, to in-spe€t all the Mutters and Mutter Rolls to be taken of the said Forces, or any of them, and the Computations of Pay made thereupon; and to settle Methods in relation thereunto, as may best obviate all Frauds and Abuses concerning the Mutters; and on every Mutter to certify the Respites and Causes thereof to the General or Commander in Chief of Our Forces, and to Our High Treasurer, or Commissioners of our Treasury, for the Time being.

5th. They are to inspefit the Regimental Accounts kept by the respective Paymasters of Our Forces, and

to

i^-

33 Geo. III. a0 Julii. 671

to take Care that there be no Error therein, either to the Prejudice of Us, or any of Our Officers or Soldiers.

6th. They are to keep an exact Account of all Deductions from Our Forces for Poundage, and for One Day’s Pay in the Year, and of all other Matters and Things, which ought to compose the voluntary Charge in the Account of the said Paymasters, to be Annually passed in the Exchequer; so that they may be able to attest the same before the said Account be declared.

7th. They are to take and keep an Account of all Payments which shall be made by the Paymasters to the Colonels, Agents, Clothiers, -or others, and to examine the Vouchers for the fame; and also to esquire, from Time to Time, whether the Money received by the Colonels, or their Agents, for Subsistence and Clearings, be justly and duly paid over to the Captains; for which the Colonels, or their Agents, shall produce Certificates, or Efficient Vouchers, from the respective Captains, to the Comptrollers, Once every Year for the Troops Abroad.

8th. They are likewise to enquire and satisfy thera-selves, from Time to Time, concerning the Performance of all Matters and Things required to be performed by the respective Paymasters and Muster-malters, or any other Officers, by the late Act, intituled, "An Act for " punishing Officers and Soldiers who shall mutiny or

" desert Her Majesty’s Service in or Ireland;

" and for punishing false Musters; and for better Payment of Quarters in England; " and to take particular Care that the Muster Rolls be immediately closed at the Quarters or Garrisons; and that the Parchment Roll be transmitted by the Deputy Cominiflary directly to the Paymasters Office, to prevent any Alteration after such Clonng.

9th. They are, from Time to Time, to exhibit to Us, and to Our General and Commander in Chief of Our Forces, and to Our High Treasurer of , or Commissioners of the Treasury, for the Time being, ail Defaults which shall occur to them in Relation to Our said Forces, or any of them.

10th, and lastly. The said Comptrollers are to observe all such farther Orders, Rules, and Instructions, as they shall or may from Time to Time receive from Us, or from the General or Commander in Chief of Our Forces, or from Our Lord High Treasurer of England, or Commissioners of the Treasury, for the Time being, in relation to their Office, and for the better Government in the fame. Dated at St. James's, the 28th Day of April 1704, in the Third Year of Our Reign.

By Her Majesty’s Command,

Godolphin.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Hett and Mr. Thomson:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repealing an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of His prel'cnt Majesty, intituled, "An Act for repealing the Act, made in the last Session of " Parliament, intituled, "An Act for vesting the Fort " of Senegal, and its Dependencies, in the Company " of Merchants trading to Africa and to vest, as well " the said Fort and its Dependencies, as all other the " British Forts and Settlements upon the Coast of " Africa, lying between the Port of Sallee and Cape " Rouge, together with all the Property, Estate, and " Effects of the Company of Merchants trading to " Africa, in or upon the said Forts, Settlements, and " their Dependencies, in His Majesty, and for securing, " extending, and improving the Trade to Africa and for vesting James Fort, in the River Gambia, and its Dependencies, and all other the British Forts and Settlements between the Port of Sallee and Cape Rouge, in the Company of Merchants trading to Africa, and for securing and regulating die Trade to without any Amendment: And aUb,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for taking away from the Commissioners of Excise in England and Scotland the Power of compounding with Persons making Malt not to fell, but to be consumed in their own private Families; without any Amendment; And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for making Compenl'ation to the Proprietors of certain Messuages, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, in the County of Kent, purchased in pursuance of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, to vest certain Messuages, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, in Trustees, for the better securing His Majesty’s Docks, Ships, and Stores, at Portsmouth and Chatham; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for paving and regulating Church Lane, in and near the Parishes of Saint Mary, Whitechapel, and Saint George, in the County of Middlesex, and several other Streets, Avenues, and Places, within the same Parish of Saint Mary, Whitechapel, and preventing Annoyances therein; and for enabling the Inhabitants of the said Parish of Saint Mary, Whitechapel, to raise Money to defray the Expences incurred in repairing the Parish Church; without any Amendment: And also,

The Ixirds have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting certain Messuages, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, in Trustees, for the further securing His Majesty’s Docks, Ships, and Stores at and for the more safe and convenient carrying on His Majesty’s Gunpowder Works and Mills near the Town of Eavcrsham; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for ascertaining and collecting the Poors Rate, and for better regulating the Poor in the Parish of Saint Mary, Lambeth, in the County of Surrey; and for other Purposes therein mentioned; with some Amendments; to which Amendments the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table

A Petition of the Council and Assembly of Antigua, Antigua fre« was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, Port*. That the llland of Antigua has been visited for many Years past, by the Hand of Providence, with a most alarming Continuance of dry Seasons,- whereby the Industry of the Sugar Planters has met with few or no Returns, and the Interests of the Merchants in the said Island, and also in Great Britain, have been equally affected; and that the Fire which happened in the Town of Saint John in the Year 1769, and the Hurricane of the Year 1772, occasioned the Destruction of a very considerable Part of the Buildings in the said Island, which were only in a finall Degree repaired when the unhappy Rupture took Place between Great Britain and Ama-ica, and totally deprived the Petitioners of the Means of completing such Repairs; and that the Interruption of Commerce between the West India Islands and the Continent of North America, during the Continuance of o 1 the

23 Geo. III. 8° Julii.

the late War, has in a great Measure contributed to the general Distress, in as much as such a Separation from the great Source of Supplies rendered, from the great Scarcity of Provisions and Necessaries, and the exorbitant Prices consequent thereto, the Purchase of such Provisions and Necessaries almost as ruinous as the Want of them; and that the Inhabitants of the said Island had not repaired the Devastation of the dreadful Fire of 1769, and the Hurricane of 1772, when a second Fire broke out in the said Town of Saint John, in the Month of April 1782, which consumed One-half of the most valuable Buildings and ' Warehouses, with the Stores and Merchandizes therein; and that the Petitioners have borne this Repetition of Misfortune with Fortitude and Perseverance, but at length constrained by their Apprehensions that the said Colony will experience, as it were, a general Bankruptcy, from its Poverty and general Loss of Credit, they have ventured by their Representatives to petition the House to extend the Freedom of Trade to the several Ports of Saint John and Parham, as one of the Means of saving the Colony from Ruin: And therefore praying the House to take their distressed Condition into Consideration, and to pass a Bill for making Saint John and Parham free Ports, with an express Prohibition nevertheless of the Importation of all Sugar, Rum, and Molasses, from any Foreign Country, and under such other Rcitriftious as to the House may l'cem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Motion w-as made, and the Question being proposed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, representing to His Majesty,.that it appears that large Sums of Money which have at different Times, and many of them very long fihee, been issued for public Services to Sub-Accountants, amounting in the Whole to above Forty-four Millions, have not yet been accounted for before the Auditors of the Imprest; and that, although many of them may have been otherwise accounted for in the Course of Office, yet others, to a very large Amount, have not been accounted for at all: That it appears to this House to be of the utmost Importance, that all public Accounts should be brought forward with as little 'Delay as possible; and that therefore they do humbly beseech His Majesty, to be graciously pleased to give Directions, that the most effectual Measures should be taken to enquire concerning the Persons to whom the said Sums have been issued, or their legal Reprc-fentatives, and particularly those to whom Money has been issued in the Course of the late expensive War, and to take Measures, in all Cases \yhere there shall appear to be sufficient Ground, to compel them, in due Course of Law, to account for the fame; and that this House will, in due Time, co-operate in such Measures as may, on full Deliberation, appear to be proper, in order to prevent the like Delays for the future.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Words " it appears" and inlerting the Words " this House having Reason to " believe" instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Words "it appears " stand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put, That the Words " this House having Reason to believe" be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Words " amounting in the " Whole to above Forty-four Millions."

And the Question being put, That those Words stand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

Then the main Question, so amended, being put;

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, representing to His Majesty, that thi9 House having Reason to believe that large Sums of Money which have, at different Times, and many of them very long since, been issued for Public Services to Sub-Accountants, have not yet been accounted for before the Auditors of the Imprest; and that, although many of them may have been otherwise accounted for in the Course of Office, yet others, to a very large Amount, have not been accounted for at all: That it appears to this House to be of the utmost Importance, that all Public Accounts should be brought forward with as little Delay as possible; and that therefore they do humbly beseech His Majesty, to be graciously pleased to give Directions that the most effectual Measures should be taken to enquire concerning the Persons to whom the said Sums have been issued, or their legal Representatives, and particularly those to whom Money has been issued in the Course of the late expensive War, and to

Levying Mr. Dempster reported from the Committee who were

Ueguneot in appointed to consider of the State of the Fucts relating Switzerland. levying of the Regiment on the Borders of

East India Company, and to report the same to the House; That the Committee had considered the Facts respecting the levying of the said Regiment, and had directed him to report a State thereof, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth j riz.

Your Committee apprehending the most important Point for their Enquiry was, Whether Colonel Ershine's Regiment was to be raised as a Corps belonging , lolcly to the East India Company, or as a Corps to be taken, when raised, into His Majesty’s Service, and to be lent by His Majesty to the said Company, did, on this SubjtCt, hope to obtain satisfactory Information from the Right honourable Lord and for that Purpose directed his Lordship to be w aited on, and reqm fti-d to attend your Committee; but his Lordship exuding himself on account of his Attendance on his Majesty, your Committee had then Rccourse to the Evidence of Leonard Morse, Secretary to his Lordship at the Tune the levying of Colonel Ershine?)Regiment was under the Consideration of the Cabinet; who, attending according to Order, produced a Correspondence between his Lordship and Colonel Ershine, by which it appeared, that before the 12th of January 1781, Colonel Ershine had made Propofuls unto His Majesty, for raising a Corps of SwissChalfeurs, for the general Purposes of the War. — On these Proposals certain Difficulties having aril’cn, they were difcull'ed in His Majesty’s Cabinet, at divers Times, till the 12th of following; the

Result of which was, transferring the Matter to the East India Company, with whom they find, from

Sruling certain Papers produced from the East India oule, as well as from the said Correljtondence, that Colonel Ershine, on the 27th of April, signed the identical Proposals lie had made to Government, according to the Desire of Lord Amherst, the then Commander in Chief.

In Colonel ErLine's Letter to Lord , dated April the 30th, he desired his Lordship hunihly to thank His Majesty for deigning to take him into His Service, to which he should be devoted for the rest of his Life.

And Mr. Morse being examined, said, That he uiuicrstood, at the Time, that the Troops which were to be raised by Colonel Ershine, agreeably to his Proposals, were intended to be lent by Government to the East India Company; that he understood so from Conversdtions that hap|>cned at the Time, and from Arrangements that took place, both before and since, reljncting Troops lent by Government to the East India Company; and he was the more confirmed in this Opinion from his Knowledge of the Footing on which the other German Troops stand, those Mr. Morse informed your Committee were raised at the Expence of the East India Company, but are understood to be in His Majesty s Service, and only lent by His Majesty to the said Company.

Y’oi- Jl).

And in further Confirmation of the Evidence given by the said Leonard Morse, your Committee find, from a Letter entered upon the Proceedings of the Committee of Secrecy of the East Indict Company, 'written by General Calllaud, of Date 7th September 1781; and

also, from the Articles of Agreement, that the German Regiments raised about the same Time, and now lerv-ing in the East Indies, are actually in His Majesty’s Service, and only lent by His Majesty to the East India Company.

And your Committee, from a Minute of the Secret Committee of the Court of Directors, dated April the 4th, 1781, find, that the East India Company made Application to Government for 2,000 Foreign Troops; and from the Evidence of William Decaynes, Esquire, who was examined to this Point, they also find that Government offered to supply the Company either with the Troops proposed to be raised by Colonel Ershine, or with the Troops of German Princes.

They also find, from the Minutes of the said Secret -Committee, That a Note was received by Laurence Sulivan, Esquire, the then Chairman of the

Court of - Directors, requiring him to attend His Majesty’s' Servants at Lord Hillsborough's Office the next Morning, being the 23d of April 1781; and the said Mr. Sulivan being examined, said, That he had attended accordingly, in confluence of that Note, and that he then, for the First Time, heard of the Troops that were proposed by Colonel Ershine; that Colonel Ershine had waited on him by the Defiie of Lord Amherst, about Two Hours after his Return Home; and that he had said to Colonel Ershine, at that First Meeting with him, that as it was not he who had dilculfed the Business with him, he supposed it was Lord Amherst who would sign with Colonel Ershine; that when he received Colonel Letter, lay-

ing, that Lord Amherst, for Reasons that Colonel-Ershine had explained to him (Mr. Sulivan) the Day before, he understood the Meaning thereof to be, that Ibme political Reasons rendered it improper for Lord Amherst to sign the Propofuls — That, upon the Receipt of this Letter, he came out to Colonel and

told him, that though he had no Doubt of his Authority to write that Letter, he could not sign with him until either he or Sir William James, the tiien Deputy Chairman, had seen Lord Amherst; and that Sir William James having seen his Lordship, he (Mr. Sulivan) had signed the Proposals the next Day, being the 27th of April 1781, without any further Discussion.

Your Committee were also desirous of examining Sir William James; but, upon Enquiry, they found he had let out for Portsmouth, and was not to return to London for some time.

And your Committee found that Colonel Erskine left a Copy of the Letter he was authorized to write by Lord Amherst with Mr. Morse, his Lordship’s Secretary; and it does not appear that his Lordship said or wrote any Thing in Contradiction to it, or to diminish it’s intended Effect.

William Frazer, Esquire, being then examined, Your Committee found from his Evidence, that Colonel Erskine bad been furnished with Letters by Lord Stoj'mont, the then Secretary of State, to Sir Robert Murray Keith, His Majesty’s Minister at Vienna, and Mr. Heathcote, His Majesty’s Minister at Bonne, which he carried with him; but that Copies of them were not to be found among the Papers in the Office; and he produced the Copies of a subsequent Letter wrote by Lord so Sir Robert

Murray Keith, and of that Minister’s Answer; From the said last mentioned Letters it appeared, that His Majesty’s Orders were lent to Sir Robert Murray Keith, to aflt Passage for Colonel s Regiment,

And yonr Committee having examined Lieutenant Curtat, they found from his Evidence that he was induced to accept a Commission in this Regiment by Colonel Erskine's telling him, and other Officers, that though his Agreement was signed with the East India Company, it was to be in the Service of His Majesty, as soon as raised, and he produced a Letter fioin Colonel Erskinehiinself in proof thereof.

Lieutenant Colonel Stopford being then examined, said, That he always understood from Colonel Erskine, during tiic Course of this Business, with which he was acquainted nearly from the Beginning, that the Troops he proposed to raise were to be for the Service of His Majesty; and that he understood, when tlrefe Proposals were accepted, that though the Regiment was to be raised in the Name of the East India Company, it was, when raised, to be in the Service of His Majesty; and he was thereby induced to give a larger Sum for his Commission than he would have done if he had supposed the Regiment was only to be in the Service of the East India Company.

Tire Honourable Captain John Cunningham being tljen examined, said. That he was Captain in His Majesty’s 14th Regiment of Dragoons, when Colonel s

Proposals ter railing a Regiment were accepted; that he quitted that Regiment in order to become eldest Captain in Colonel Erskine's Regiment, not imagining he could thereby be luppoled to have quitted His Majesty’s Service.

Colonel Erskine then produced a Copy of a Paper which had been distributed by him throughout land, and on the Borders thereof, whereby it appeared, that the Officers were allured of their being entitled to Half Pay in case the Regiment should be broke.

And it appearing also material to your Committee, to be informed how far Colonel Erskine had l'ucceeded in tailing the Regiment agreeable to his Proposals, your Committee find that Colonel Erskine agreed to have the Men ready to be tendered for Muster on the 27th Day of August: that his Agreement was signed 27th 1781.

That unforefren Delays, after signing his Agreement, retarded Colonel Erskine's Departure for Germany for a full Month — That those Delays proceeded from the forms Colonel Erskine had to go through at the India House.

That, from the Proceedings of the Secret Committee of Directors, it appears, That Major Tonne was sent by the India Company to muster the said Regiment — That he did not arrive at Shaffhausen till the 16th of August', that Colonel Erskine, then at Studgard, did not receive Intelligence of Major Toone's Arrival till the 23d, and had it not in his Power to join Major Toone till the 30th, but that he had written to Major Toone the 25th August — That he had 850 Men ready for Muster — That Colonel Erskine, on his joining Major Toone on the 30th August, proposed to him immediately to muster the 850 Men — Thai to his inexpressible Surprize, as well as Mortification, Major Toone informed him, that his Orders were positive not to muster a Angle Man after the 27th August.

That these Instiuctions and Orders to Major Toone appeared the more extraordinary to your Committee, as they are informed it is seldom or never customary to keep Officers so strictly to a Day, who are engaged in fuel) Service, and industriously employed in the Pro-feention of it; and yet the Instructions which Major Toone carried with him from the Company, bear, " You are not to muster or receive any Men which shall not " be raised and ready for mustering at on or

" before tiic said 271I1 Day of Augustand in the

Letter which the Company wrote Mr. Erskine, dated 4th August 1781, and which Major Toone carried with him, there is this remarkable Paragraph, " Conformable " to the Contract on our Parts, we have appointed " Captain SwinneyToone, the Bearer of this Letter,

" to examine the Men, and have given him full " Directions thereon, with a Copy of the Contract; we " trust and hope that the whole Battalion will be " complete and ready to be mustered by the 27th of " this Month, agreeable to the Contract, but no Men " can be received after that Time."

And your Committee find from the said Proceedings of the said Secret Committee, dated the 14th September 1781, that Major Toone wrote for further Instructions, to know whether he should accept and muster these Men, which the Secret Committee ordered him not to do; and that on the 17th of September, though they w’ould not accept the Men Colonel Erskine had already raised, they gave an additional Bounty of 40 Shillings per Man for the railing of a Regiment of Hanoverians, whom it was represented to them could not be raised without such additional Bounty.

Colonel Erskine then exhibited authenticated Copies of his Regimental Books, which were seized at Rhineau, his principal Rendezvous; whereby it appeared, that 47.5 Recruits had joined him there, out of and that Lieutenant Alt, and all the Papers belonging to the Regiment, had been seized by the AbbC of Rhineau, Sovereign of that Place, upon various Pretences; and that the said Lieutenant Alt remained in Custody, and the Papers were detained until Colonel Erskine should pay the Sum of 500l.

Lieutenant Curtat being again examined, said, That of these 475 Men that had joined at Rhineau, 216 had been seized by the Cantons of Zurich and Berne, in the Free and Imperial Town of St200 by the Regency of Stockart, belonging to Austria; but it did not appear what became of the rest.

Colonel Erskine produced to your Committee, a Translation of a Treaty or Convention with the Duke of IVirtemberg, certified to be conformable to the Original by Mr. De Moshiem, His Majesty’s Electoral Minister at the Court of that Prince; whereby it appeared, that 650 Men were made over unto Colonel Erskine, and entered into the Pay of the East India Company, on the . 23d of August 1781.

And your Committee found, from the Answers given in Writing by Major Toone, now gone to the East Indies, to certain Queries put to him by Colonel Erskine, that the Duke of IVion the 18th of September, seized and dispersed the Men his Serene Highness had furnished Colonel Erskine with, many of whom Major Toone had seen wandering in the Country. — And it appears, from a Letter in the Proceedings of the Secret Committee, from Captain who was sent

to muster the Hanoverians, that the First Battalion of that Regiment had been negotiating with the Duke of IVirtemberg for the same Troops, but w’ould only pay Five Pounds per Man for them; and from the Treaty between the Duke of IVirtemberg and Colonel Erskine, it appears, that Colonel Erskine paid Ten Guineas per Man.

Colonel Erskine then informed the Committee, That his Papers being seized at Rhineau, he could not give so exa Gta State of his Expences as he wished; but he produced to your Committee certain Accounts and Papers, by which, and the Testimony of different Officers, who were examined, it appears, that he had expended in the Service ,£,6,187. 4- which he had

received from the East India Company; 5,100l. which he had received for the Commissions of different Officers; and 2,700l. of his own; — and that he ltands engaged for the Payment of 500l. for the Liberation

of Lieutenant Alt; 575 I to Colonel for

Pay advanced to his Officers Abroad; and 751, on Account of Major Muller: And he allured your Committee, that he was considerably in Debt besides, on Account of the Regiment.

Lieutenant Curtat being again examined, said, That it conlifted with his Knowledge, that all such of the Officers of this Corps as were Subjects to the Canton of Berne, and were discovered, were banished their Country, and fined to considerable Amounts, for having entered into the Service of Great Britain — That he himl'clf was banished Six Years, and fined, both upon his own Account, and upon that of Lieutenant Muret, whom he was falsely alledged to have enticed into the Service — That he, the Witness, was, at the Time he entered into His Majesty’s Service, Adjutant of the Militia at Lausanne, and enjoyed Civil Employments, which brought him an Income of considerable Amount.

Captain Muller being then examined said, That his Father, who was Major of Department in the Service of the Canton of Berne, loft his Employment, was banished for Ten Years, and fined 425 Guineas, on Account of his having alfifted Colonel in the

railing of his Corps — That be understood his Father engaged in that llufiness, not only because it was to procure the Witness his Commission, but also because lie w as to receive 1,500l. from Colonel Erskine, if it succeeded — That the State of Berne seized his Father’s Estate for the Payment of the Fine; upon which some Creditors came upon him, and the Estate was fold for One Third less than the Value — That since his Father’s Lois of his Estate and his Employment, neither he nor his Family, consisting of himself, a Wife, and Three Daughters, have any Means of Support — That he himself was lent over by his Family to Colonel Erskine, to take Charge of his Education until he should go to India, the East India Company having, in confi-

deration of the Lofics his Family had sustained in their Service, appointed him a Cadet, instead of confirming his First Commission. — And Captain Muller produced several original Letters, written by Colonel Erskine to his Father, on thcle Matters.

Lieutenant Colonel SlopJ'ordbeing again examined, said, That though he is 1,470/. in Disburse in the Business, he is satisfied that Colonel Erskine has expended it in the Service of the Regiment, and has taken as much Care of his Interest as of his own,

The Honourable Captain Cunningham being again examined, said, He had paid Colonel Erskine 500 /. for his Commission, which, he is satisfied, was expended in the Service of the Regiment; and that he has, at various Times, advanced Colonpl Erskine different Sums of Money, knowing him to be in great Distress; and he is satisfied that the Sum he had received from the East India Company, by Award, is very inadequate to relieve him from the Distress in which he has been involved, in consequence of having raised this Regiment.

And it appears, from the Tcliimony of the Foreign Officers-w ho were examined by your Committee, That Colonel Erskine has discharged his Duty to them, by flip porting them by every Means in his Power. And all the Officers examined concurred in declaring, that Colonel Erskine had behaved to them in the most honourable Manner.

" and to the Foreign Officers concerned in the Levy " of this Corps, the actual Expences they have incurred; and many of the latter having fullered by " Exile and Prison, in consequence of the Part they " had taken in this Business; I have had reasons to " know, that the utmost Distress has thereby fallen " upon them. How far they are to be considered a3 " under the immediate Protection, or appertaining " properly to the Government here, is not for me to " decide; but their Losses and Sufferings, from their " having forfeited their Fortunes, and, in many Cales,

" their Liberties, by Engagements taken for the National Ufc and Service, seem to render them, in Point " of Humanity, as well as of the Honour of this " Country, highly entitled to Favour and Retribution.

" Whether the Circumstances authorize the putting " them on the Establishment of Half Pay, having formally taken their Engagements with the East India " Company, I cannot say; but, in some Shape, the " Government here seem to me to be strongly called " upon to save them from the absolute Ruin they appear " to be threatened with."

Praters.

THE House being met, pursuant to the last Parliament Prorogation; and Mr. Speaker being in the further pro-Country; rogue

A Message was brought from the Lords, by Mr.

Quarme, Yeoman Ulher of the Black Rod:

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The advanced Season of the Year requires some Remission front your long and laborious Attention to the Public Service. The Exigencies of that Service may oblige Me to call you together again at an early Period; and 1 persuade Myself, from My uniform Experience of your Affection to Me, and your Zeal for the Public Good, that you will chearfully submit to a temporary Inconvenience, for the permanent Advantage of your Country.

The Consideration of the Affairs of the East Indies will require to be resumed as early as possible; and to be pursued with a serious and unremitting Attention.

I expected to have had the Satisfaction of acquainting you, before the End of the Session, that the Terms of Pacification were definitively settled: But the complicated State of the Business in Difeuflion has unavoidably protracted the Negociation. I have, however, every Reason to believe, from the Dispositions shewn by the several Powers concerned, that they are perfectly well inclined to such a Conclusion as may secure the Blessings of Peace, so much and so equally to be desired by all Parties.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I thank you for the Supplies you have so liberally granted for the Public Service; for facilitating My Arrangements towards a separate Establishment for the Prince of Wales; and for enabling Me, without any new Burthen on My People, to discharge the Debt which remained on My Civii Lift.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I earnestly recommend to you an Attention towards promoting among My People, in your several Countries, that Spirit of Order, Regularity, and Industry, which is the true Source of Revenue and Power in this Nation; and without which, all Regulations for the Improvement of the one, or the Increase of the other, will have no Effect

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission, desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House, in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly the House, with the Clerk, went up to the House of Peers: Where the Commission was read, for the further proroguing of the Parliament until' Thursday the 16th Day of October next: And the Parliament was accordingly prorogued until Thursday he 16th Day of October next
