Since the Year 1719 to the present Time, where the Annuities have been created, either from the Sum subscribed, or from a Lottery convertible into Annuities, this Allowance has been at the Rate of Eight hundred and Five Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Ten Pence Million, the Rate craved in the Memorial before us, except in the Year 1742. By the Act of that Year, the Fifteenth of George the Second, Chapter the Nineteenth, for raising Eight hundred thousand Pounds by Annuities, the Commissioners of the Treasury are empowered to allow the Cashier, out of the Contribution Money, Five hundred Pounds, for his Pains and Trouble in receiving and accounting for the fame; and by a Warrant, dated the 22d ot J 1743. transmitted to us from the Treasury. that Sum was allowed him. But where the Receipt of the Contributions has been attended with any additional or unusual Trouble or Expence, the Bank have been allowed at a higher Rate: In the Year 1747 they were allowed One thousand Pounds per Million.

The Bank appear to have received Contributions to Lotteries earlier than the Year 1714, which was their I'irit Year of receiving Contributions to Annuities: In 1710 and 1711 they received the Contributions to Two Lotteries of One Million Five hundred thousand Pounds each; and, in the following Year, to Two Lotteries of One Million Eight hundred thousand Pounds each: These are the first entered in the Manu-feript Book above-mentioned; and it is there fiated, that they were allowed, as to the Two first, for their Pains and Service in receiving, paying, and accounting for the Monies received, and for all their Charges and Expences in performing this Service (the Charges of parting the Accounts excepted) Two thousand Three hundred and Eighty Pounds Twelve Shillings and Nine Pence; for the Two latter they were allowed One thousand Two hundred and Fifty Pounds each.

The Receipt of these Contributions is attended with dittereut Degrees of Trouble and Expence. The Number of Tickets and Subscribers varies in different Lotteries: In the most simple, the whole Business is the Receipt of the Money, the Payment of it into the Exchequer, and the Payment of the Certificates of the fortunate Tickets; in others, it is attended either with the Creation or Redemption of Annuities: Hence the Allowance to the Bank for this Service has varied, according to these Circumstances, from One thousand Pounds, the Sum craved in the Memorial before us, to Two thousand Pounds, the Sum allowed them in the Years 1772, 1774, and 1775.

From this Enquiry into the Subjtft 6f these Bank and South Sea House Account, it appears that, exclusive of the Sums paid every Year in Annuities to their Creditors, the Public incur Two other Kinds of Annual Expences, in Consequence of the Debts they contract: The one is, Payments to the Public Companies for transacting the Annuities they have granted, called the Charges of Management; the other is, Feed and other Charges, at the several Public Offices, incidental to the Issue of the Money for the Payment; and to the auditing and passing the Accounts of these Annuities. As the Money for defraying the First of these Expences is issued from the Exchequer, usually, with the Annuities themselves; that we might have the Annual Amount of it before us at One View, and be likewise enabled to state the present Debt of this Nation, with all its attendant Expences (the most important of the Public Accounts) we procured from the Auditor of the Exchequer an Account of all the Public Debts standing out at the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, upon the 5th of July last, with the Annual Interest, and other Charges payable for the fame, distinguishing the Interest from the Charges. In this Account the Charges of Management of the Debt therein stated, which is the present Subject of our Attention, amount to One hundred and Twenty-four thousand Three hundred and Sixty-nine Pounds Three' Shillings and One Penny, exclusive of Three hundred and Sixty Pounds allowed for the Management of the Annuities of the Year 1726, and of the Sum to be claimed for the Loan of the present Year; which, at the same Rate, upon Fifteen Millions perpetual Annuities, and Eighty thousand Pounds a Year long Annuities, is Nine thousand Five hundred and Sixty-two Pounds Ten Shillings: The Addition of these Two Sums makes the Total of this Charge for the present Year One hundred and Thirty-four thousand Two hundred and Ninety-one Pounds Thirteen Shillings and One Penny. As the Public Debt has increased, this Expence has increased with it; and as by far the greatest Part of the Annuities have been transacted at the Bank, their Share in this Allowance is great in Proportion; it will amount this Year to One hundred and Twelve thousand Two hundred and Fifty-two Pounds Four Sniffings and Four Pence, exclusive of the Four thousand Pounds, Part of the One hundred thousand Pounds originally granted to them; which, being allotted by the Proprietors as a Compensation to their Governor, Deputy, and Directors, is not considered as an Allowance for Management; it is therefore included in the Column of Annual Interest, in the State of the Publid Debt. This Allowance is intended as a RecOmpence to the Public Companies for their Trouble, and the Expences they incur for Buildings, Clerks, Stationary, and Variods other Contingencies, and as a Compensation for the Losses they are liable to fultairt. The Business for which this Sum is intended to be the Compensation, is the Examination of the Dividend and other Warrants; comparing them with their correspondent Entries in the Lilts; calling up the Items; reducing the Account into the official Form } and ingrossing it.

It is true, in general, that w:here Money is issued from the Exchequer, to be applied to certain Public Purposes, an Account should be passed of that Money, that the Public may know and be satisfied as to the Application; but Circumstances may create Exceptions to this, as well as to every other general Rule: The Trust may be so well guarded by the Mode of Execution, as to render a Misapplication or Abuse hardly practicable; or the Expence of taking the Account may be so heavy, as to outweigh every possible Advantage to be derived from it.

A Sum equal to a Half Year’s Annuity is iffiicd from the Exchequer to the Bank, to be divided among the Proprietors of that Annuity, in Proportion to the Interest of each in the Capital; the making this Division is the Trust which the Bank engage to execute: The Manner ift which they execute it, we learn from the Information of Mr. William Edwards, Deputy Accountant of the Bank.

When the Transfer Books of any Annuity are (hut, for the Payment of the Dividend, the Share of every Proprietor in the Capital Stock is extracted from his Account in the Ledger, and set opposite to his Name; a Dividend Warrant is filled up for-each Proprietor, with his Share in the Capital, and Annuity attending it: A Dividend Book is formed, comprehending the Name of every Proprietor, the Folio of his Account in the Ledger, his Share in the Capital and Annuity, and the Number of his Warrant: A Duplicate is made of this Dividend Book: The Original, Duplicate and Warrants, are all compared together: That the Warrants may be correct, and correspond with the Dividend Books, they undergo various Formalities, and Examinations by different Clerks; and, after being signed by the proper Officer, they are deposited in the Office where the Annuity is transafited, until the Proprietors apply for Payment. The Person receiving it signs the Dividend Book, opposite the Name of the Proprietor, and the Receipt at the Bottom of the Warrant, which is witnessed by the Clerk who delivers it. The Teller pays it, enters it in his Book, and cancels it; after which it is entered in a Caffi Book in the Dividend Warrant Office, and in the Check Ledger in the Check Office; where all the paid Warrants are ranged in numerical Order, and the Total of them compared with the Total of the unpaid Lift made out at the Annuity Office: From thence they are transmitted to the Auditor of the Imprest.

This Transaction is Ample; — the Division of a certain Sum among a Number of Persons, in Proportion to their Interests. Many Persons are employed in this Division; and it seems well fenced against Fraud or Error. The Company can misapply no Part of this Money, for the whole Annuity is distributed in the Dividend Warrants; and the Entries of the Shares in the Dividend Books, which are transcribed into the Warrants, are call up, to see that they comprehend the Whole. Whatever Abuse or Error may be committed, must immediately affect the Proprietor; as by forging a Receipt, or obtaining it from him by Fraud, or refusing him Payment, or by an erroneous Calculation of his Share; but against these the Auditor’s Examination is no Security: The injured Proprietor must apply to the Company for Relief; and, if refused, he has his legal Remedy. These Circumstances cannot come before the Auditor; All he requires is a formal Receipt for every Payment;

Since then this Trust reposed in the Public Companies, being simple in its Nature, and guarded in its Execution, is not, as appears to us, open to Abuse; nor the Public Money iiiued for this Service liable to Misapplication; we arc of Opinion, that the Public derives no Benefit whatever from the Examination of the llank and South Sat Annuities in the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest; and consequently, that such Examination ouuht to be discontinued, as a heavy and unnecessary Expence to the Public. Wc are warranted in this Opinion by Usage in a ftmilar Instance: No Account of the Oid und New South Annuities is rendered at the Exchequer: Being originally Part of the Capital South Sea Stock, they were, as such, exempt from Account: The Annuities paid by Government upon all the Capital trading Stocks, the Bank, the South Sea, and the East India Stock, are itlued from the Exchequer without Account: The ltculon Items to be this; — the Annuity is granted to the Company in their collective Capacity, as a Body Corporate, and paid to them as One entire l)ebt to One Person: After the Officer appointed by them has received it, Government has no more to do with it; it iies upon those to whom the Company have intruded the Direction and Management of their Affairs, to take Care that a just Division of it is made among their Members: But upon the Separation of the Old and New Annuities from the Capital Stock, the Proprietors of those E'unds no longer continued Members of the Company: They quitted all Share both in the Direction and the Profits: They became distinct Bodies of Men, like the Proprietors of any other Government Security: The proportional Shares of the original Annuity, which they became entitled to upon the Separation, continued to be iiiued, and are now issued from the Exchequer to the Company, blended with the Stock Annuity; but the Acts expressly iav, those Shares fliull be issued in Trust for the Proprietors; and therefore, from the Time of the Separation, the Company became responiihle to Government for the Payment of thcle Annuities, just as the Governor and Company of the Bank of England stand at this Time responsible for the Payment of the Dividends upon any Capital they transact; and the Money for such Payment ought, in Couliftency, to have been issued from the Exchequer, by Way of Imprest and on Account; and yet, ever since the Y'ear 172 2,the Sum of Three hundred and Filty-seven thousand Two hundred and Twenty-four Pounds Two Shillings, the present Annuity attending the Old South Sea Annuities; The Duty, however, and Business of the Cashier ought, in our Opinion, to be continued without Alteration. It is expedient that Government should not be ignorant of the Annual State of these Accounts; and therefore the Cashier of each Company should, every Year, transmit to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, an Account Current, similar to that now transmitted by them to the Auditors of the Imprest, containing the Receipts and Payments of all the Annuities transa&ed by them, including the Old and New South Sea Annuities, with the Balance of the unclaimed Dividends and Stock remaining in their Hands, signed by the Cashier, and attelted' by him on Oath, before a Baron of the Exchequer.

We have suggested the Exemption of these Accounts from the Jurilcli&ion of the Auditors of the Imprest, as a Regulation proper and necessary to be carried into immediate Execution: We do not mean to violate, in the slightest Degree, any Right veiled in an Officer by virtue of his Office. The Principles which secure the Rights of private Property are sacred, and to be preserved inviolate: they are Land Marks to be considered as immoveable: But the Public

have their Rights also; Rights equally sacred, and as freely to be exercised. — That we may pursue the Line of Justice, without invading the Rights of the Subjefit on the one Hand, or sacrificing those of the Public on the other, it becomes necessary for us to endeavour to develope these official Rights, and define, if we can, their precise Boundaries. If a use-leis and expensive Office cannot be suppressed, nor the Redundancies of an Office curtailed, be the Necessi-ties of the State every so urgent, without intrenching upon the Right of the Pufll-ffor, and violating the Public Faith, the Evil must be endured, until the Power of the Legislature can, without the Imputation of Injuliice, be exerted for the Relief of the State.

The Principle which gives Existence to, and governs every Public Office, is the Benefit of the State. Government requires that various Branches of Business should be tranlafiled, and Persons must be found to tranl'aft them. The Acceptance of a Public Office implies an Engagement to do the Business, and a Right to a Compensation: The Officer has Powers delegated to him necessary for the Execution; but he has no other Right than to the Reward of his Labour: He has no Right to any specific Quantity of Business; that Quantity must fluctuate according to Circumstances, or may be regulated by the Convenience of the State: If the Good of the Community requires a Diminution or Annihilation of the Business of his Office, or the transferring it elsewhere, the Officer cannot oppose to the Regulation, the Diminution or Annihilation of his Profits; because not the Emolument of the Officer, but the Advantage of the Public, was the Object of the Institution: To suppose in him a Right to make such an Objection, would be to suppole the Office created for his Benefit; that is, to iuppole it to originate in a Violation of Public Trust, an Abuse of Power, and an Offence against the State. Where Law or Usage has annexed Terms to the Grant, which limit the Right of the executive Power to relume or take it away, the Reason leems to be the Expedience of leaving the Officer in the Exercise of the Duties of his Office, independent of the Influence of that Power, which might otherwise, at Pleasure, remove him: But w hen it is no longer for Public Convenience that such Duties should be exerdfed, or when the Exercise of them becomes an unnecessary Expence to the Public, it would be an Inverlion of the Principle that governs such Establish-

ments, to suffer that private Emolument, which was no Motive for the Inl’titution, to prevent or retard the Abolition of them. It matters not what the Duration or Condition of the littered may he, whether for Life or Years, during pood Behaviour, or Pleasure; all are equally subject to that governing Principle for the Sake of which it was created; the Good of the Public: Hence, in every proposed of-

ficial Regulation, the Advantage or Disadvantage of the Officer can never be properly a Subject of Difcussion; the only Question is. Whether the Necessity or Good of the State actually requires it r This decides the Propriety of the Regulation; and the Determination of it belongs only to the Supreme Power that watches over the Public Good, for its Improvement as well as Protection. The Regulation we have here suggested affects the Auditors of the Imprest, by a Diminution of their Business, and consequently of their Profits; It is necessary therefore to examine particularly, whether it interferes with any Right veiled in that Officer by virtue of his Office. We have procured, and inserted in the Appendix, a Copy of the lad Patent for the Grant of this Office, omitting the Recital of the then subsisting Patents: This Patent

describes his Office, with its Objects and Emoluments. The Power of auditing the Bank and South Sea House Accounts seems to be derived from the general Words of " auditing and determining all Accounts of all Persons whatsoever, being accountable for any Sums received by the Name of Imprest." The Blue, therefore, by Way of Impred, is the Circumstance that gives the Auditor the Power to examine the Expenditure. Whether a Sum shall be issued by Way of Imprest, or not, depends upon the Authority that directs the Blue; which is either the Royal Sign Manual, or an Act of Parliament; and, consequently, the Exercise of this Power of auditing mud depend upon the Will and Pleasure either of the Crown, or the Legislature.

The Office of the Auditors of the Impred existed before the Mode of borrowing upon Funds was tirft adopted. Upon the Creation of Annuities the Legislature thought proper to direct, that the Money to be issued for the Payment of them should be accounted for according to the due Course of the Exchequer; and thereby gave the Auditors a new Object. Should the Legislature fee good Reason for altering the Mode of Blue; should they find by Experience that the Examination of the Accounts by the Auditors of the Imprest is unnecessary; or the Advantage of it in no Degree adequate to the Expence; can there be a Doubt of their having a Right, without Insultice, to take from them again that Object, and to direct the Blue for the future to be without Account ?

There is another Limitation also, upon the Power of the Auditor, inserted in his Patent; that is, the Consent of the Treasury: He is " to audit and detcrmine, by and with the Advice, Authority, and " Conicnt, of the High Treasurer of Britain,

" or the Connnifiiooers of the Treasury, Chancellor " and Under Treasurer of the Exchequer, for the " Time being." This necefl’arily implies a Power in the Treasury, if they fee Realbn, to withhold their Assent; and, consequently, renders the Exercise of the Power of the Auditor dependant upon their Discretion. If this Mode of Reasoning be solidandconclusive; if the Propriety of continuing an Office, or particular Branches of the Business of an Office, be tried by the Advantage it produces to the Community; if the Officer ean have no Right in his Office, independent of the Public Good; we suggest the Infringement of no private Right, when wc deliver it as our Opinion, that the Money for the Annuities payable at the Bank of England, and South Sea House, ought for the future to be issued without

Account from the Exchequer: Anti we have not violated any private Right, by luggefting the Necessity of an immediate Abolition of useless and expensive Offices, and Reduction of unnecessary and redundant Expc'nces; convinced as we are, by the irrefil'tible Evidence of the State of the National Debt exhibited to us, of the absolute and indispensable Necessity of an immediate Attention to every practicable Retrenchment.

This Account of the Public Debt being transmitted to ns from the Exchequer in the ufuui official Form, required l'oine Explanation; with which we were supplied by the Examination of Mr. John Hugh son. Clerk of the Debentures in the Office of the Auditor of the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer.

The Sums inserted in the Column under the Head of Principal Debt, opposite to the First, Second, Third, and Fifth Articles of Annuities payable at the Exchequer, are the Purchase Money originally paid for them into the Exchequer. This Purchase Money does not seem to us to constitute a Part of the Public Debt; the Public are in no Event bound to pay it: They are bound to pay the Annuities purchased with these Sums, for the Duration of the Terms, and the Existence of the Lives for which they were granted; but upon the Expiration of the Annuities, either by Effluftion of Time, Qr Death, the Debt i3 at an End; an Event that has happened, as to the Second Article of Annuities for Lives with the Benefit of Survivor-ship, since the 5th of July last, the Date of the Account.

This Annuity is now expired, by the Death of the last Nominee; and therefore we have omitted this Article, as well as those other Principal Sums, in our State of the Public Debt. , d

All these Debts may be classed under Two Heads,

The Redeemable, and, The Irredeemable; the first, are those which the Legislature, pursuing the Forms and Terms specified in the Acts that created them, may redeem, without the Content of the Proprietors; the latter, are those which, being granted for certain specified Periods, cannot be redeemed without the Consent of the Proprietors: In the Creation of feme of the first, the Right of Redemption is restrained, in favour of the Subscribers, until after a limited Period.

It is expedient that the true State of the National Debt should be disclosed to the Public; every Subject ought to know it, for every Subject is interested in it. This Debt is swelled to a Magnitude that requires the united Efforts of the ablest Heads and purelt Hearts, to suggest the proper and effectual Means of Reduction. The Nation calls for the Aid of all its Members to co-operate with Government, and to combine in carrying into Execution such Measures as shall be adopted, for the Attainment of so indif-penfable an End: This Aid the Subject is bound to give to the State, by every other Obligation, as 3vell as by the Duty he owes to his Country; and, with such general Aid, the Difficulties, great as they appear, will, we trust, be found not insurmountable.

A Plan must be formed for the Reduction of this Debt, and that without Delay; now, in the favourable Moments of Peace. The Evil does not admit of Procrastination, Palliatives, or Expedients: It presses on, and must be met with Force and Firm-ness. The Right of the Public Creditor to his Debt, must be preserved inviolate: His Security rests upon the 1‘olid Foundation, never to be shaken, in Parliamentary National Faith.

The obvious Means of Reduction is the Creation of a Fund, to be appropriated, and invariably applied, under proper Direction, in the gradual Diminution of the Debt: This Fund must be the Surplus of the Annual Income, above the Annual Expences of the State, to be obtained and increased by the Extension and Improvement of the Sources of Revenue, and by a frugal Administration of the Produce. To accomplish the first of these docs not, in many Instances, depend lolely upon the Will and Power of the State:

To open new or enlarge old Channels of Commerce, to set up new or improve old Branches of Manufacture, often require the Concurrence of other Nations, and of other Bodies of Men: But Frugality in the Management of the Revenue, the Object to which the Act by which we are constituted has pointed our Attention, is within the Reach of every Government.

It needs no Concurrence or Assistance from without:

It possesses in itself full, absolute, and uncontrouled Powers, to regulate the Management of every Article of its Revenue: It can quicken the Passage of a Tax or Duty into the Public Colfers: It can direct it from thence, without Delay, to the Purpose for Which it is intended: It can abolish useless Offices; cut oft’ superfluous and unnecessary Expences; anil reduce

those that nro necessary within certain and reasonable Limits: It ran cad i!s Officers to account; and reclaim the Sams of Public Money, either detained in their Hands, or converted to their own life: It can correct every A bulb, and infufc a Sprit of Oecotiomy ti.rou^h every Pranch of the Receipt and Expenditure of the Revenue* What can bo done, the Support of Public Credit, the Preservation of National Honour, and the Justice due to the Public Creditor, demand fho dd he done: — It must be done, or serious Con-Icnucnces a ill cufie.

Where die Resources of a Country are so extensive, so various, and productive, a Spirit of Frugality, uni-v erf ill y diffused and kept alive, cannot but be attended with the mult powerful Eftcfts. The Subjects of this King loin arc opulent, generous, and publie-spirited: Let the 1 )litivlfe» of their Country be fairly laid before them; and let that Interest they and their Posterity have in this Confutation he appealed to, and they will contribute ciiccriully and liberally to her Relief.

Tin* Subject inuft place Confidence in the Integrity and W illlom of the CJuvei iiment: He should have no Doubt but his Contributions to the Public Service find their Wiv, undiminiiheil, without Deviation or Delay, to their proper Object: And let him no more feck for Shifts and Subtleties to evade the Payment of those Duties and Taxes which the Wisdom of the Ix'gillatme have deemed the moll eligible, and which the Neccfiities of the Stale fully justify.

Let Public Benevolence take the Lead of private Inttrclt. Example may produce much; and must begin Ibmcwhere. An extraordinary and unprecedented Conjuncture in the Finances of a Country may require extraordinary and unprecedented Efforts. Every Man may dedicate a Portion of his Income, or some Share of his Atlluence, according to his Faculties, to this great National Object: Let the Produce of i'uch a general Exertion be wifely directed, and faithfully applied; and this Debt, enormous as it is, will begin to melt away: And ever Man who contributes to so great a Work will feel the Consolation resulting from the Discharge of the most important of his Duties, by having allilted in relieving Public Di furls, restoring Public Credit, and averting a National Calamity.

When all the Half Yearly Abstracts have been examined, and the Observations answered, the Account is formed in the Auditor’s Office, and the Chief Cashier fends to the Auditor’s Office the Account Current for the Two Years. The Auditor examines his Account of the Charge and Discharge with the Account Current sent from the Bank. He does not recollect any Instance of an Error in the Account Current.

When the Account Current has been examined, and the Balance agreed, the Deputy Auditor attends the Cashier to a Baron or the Cursitor Baron of the Exchequer, when the Cashier signs and swears to the Account Current; which is brought back to and remains in the Auditor’s Office. The Account formed in the Auditor’s Office is then drawn out, and ingrafted upon Parchment and Paper. Both are presented for Declaration by the Deputy Auditor: Neither the Cashier, nor any other Person from the Bank, attends the Declaration. When declared, the Parchment Part is lent to the King’s Remembrancer, and the Paper Part remains in the Auditor’s Officer.

The Account Current, from the 5th of 1777 to the 5th July 1779, was delivered into the Auditor’s Office the 14th of March 1782; and the Account of the Cashier of the Bank was declared on the 2Qtti Junt 1782.

End of the Year, a Memorial is presented by the Court of Directors of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, to the Lords Commissioners of the

Treasury, stating, That in pursuance of an Act for raising a certain Sutn of Money by Annuities and Lottery, for the Service of the Year, there hath been received, at the Bank, the full Sum raised for the Service of the Year; and also, stating the Sum paid by them, on that Account, into the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer, and the Sum allowed for Interest, by the said Act, to such of the Contributors as advanced their Money previous to the Times appointed for paying the fame; and praying to be allowed to retain a certain Sum for the Use and Benefit of the Governor and Company of the Bank of , for the Service, Pains, and Labour, of their Officers employed in receiving, paying, and accounting for the said Money; and a certain Sum for the Lottery, in Proportion to former Allowances for the like Services: and also, praying the Allowance of the Annual Sums for the Services respecting the Annuities granted by the said Act, agreeable to former Allowances.

Annexed to this Memorial, anti agreeing the rewith, is an Account of the Contributions for the Sum raised by Annuities and Lottery, for the Service of the Year, made up at the Bank, and ligned by the Chief Cashier. This Memorial is referred by the Lords of the Treasury to the Auditors of the Imprest, to examine the fame, and report thereupon. The Memorial for the Year 1781 was so referred, on the 18th of December 1781. The Receipt of this Memorial and Account from the Treasury, is the First official Notice to the Auditor of the Contribution Account.

The Memorial and Account being thus referred, the Chief Cashier of the Bank fends to the Auditor’s Office the Tallies for, and a List of, the Sums paid into the Exchequer; and a Book, containing an Account of the Particulars of the Interest paid at the Bank to the Contributors prcvioully advancing their Money. The Articles of Interest are examined, to see that they are properly computed. The Contribution Account is then formed in the Auditor’s Office: the Charge confilts only of Two Articles; namely, the grols Sum received for Annuities, and the grols Sum received for the Lottery Tickets.

The Discharge conlifts of the Money paid into the Exchequer, appearing by the Tallies; the Money paid to the Contributors for Interest; and the Allowances to the Bank.

When the Account is ingrafted, the Paper Part is lent to the Tally Joiners, to have the Tallies joined, examined with the Discharge, and certified. The Account being returned, with the Deputy Chamberlain’s Certificate thereon, mentioning the Number of

7 O

Tallies and the Sum, and that they were reecived and joined, the Chief Cashier attests either the Account annexed to the Memorial, or the Account of the Interest paid to the Contributors; and the Auditors make their Report on the Memorial and Account to the Lords of the Treasury. This Report on the Memorial and Account of the Year 1781, was made on the 11th of June 1782. The Lords of the Treasury then sign a Warrant, addressed to the Auditors, authorizing and directing them to make the Allowances: The Account is presented by the Deputy Auditors, at the ext Declaration of Accounts, to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and is then declared, and the Parchment Part lent to the King’s Remembrancer.

Each Impi.Xt Roll produced to the Auditor, to warrant the Charge in the Bank Annuity Account, contains the Dividend for the Half Year, on each Species of Annuities, and the Charges of Management to the Bank for that Half Year.

The luit Iniprcft Rolls inserted in the Charge, arc for the Sum received from the Exchequer, to reimburse the Bank the Fees and Charges allowed in the preceding Account. The only Accounts, to the best

of his Recollection, that are examined by both Offices jointly, are the Accounts of the Bank, and of the South Sea Annuities of the Year 1751. Such has been the Custom of the Office ever since he knew it. The Fees for auditing and making up these Accounts, are equally divided between both Offices.

It appears from Papers and Accounts in the Office or Lord Mountstuart, that the Rate of One hundred Pounds a Year per Million, paid to the Auditors of the Imprest, for examining Accounts of this Kind, is very ancient: — it is allowed by Lord Treasurer Godolphin, in the Year 1704, as appears by a Warrant in the Office; and has been, as he believes, allowed ever since. The Rate of Fifty Pounds Million, for examining the Lottery Accounts, appears to have been allowed to the Auditors prior to the Year 1751; and it appears, from Accounts in the Office, that for-, merly the Allowances varied, and were generally above the Rate of Fifty Pounds a Million.

N° 4.

The Examination of Mr. John Walker', taken upon Oath, the 2ilt, 22d, 30th, and 31st July 1783.

This Examinant faith, That he is Second Clerk in the Office of Lord Sondes, One of the Auditors of the Imprest: He has been in the Office above Twenty-

four Years: He was employed, on the Part of Lord Sondes, in examining and drawing up a Part of the Account of the Chief Cashier of the Bank of for Two Years, ending the 5U1 July 1779. Mr. nard Cobbe was employed, as he believes, on the Part of the other Auditor, to examine and draw up the other Part of this Account. The Chief Cashier of the Bank fends to the Auditor’s Office the following Materials, from which the Account is drawn up: A Lift, containng the Names of all the Proprietors in the Capital Stock of each Fund, the Share of each, and the proportional Annuity attending it, with the Number upon each W arrant: another Lift, containing those Warrants inserted in the above-mentioned Lift, which remain at that Time unpaid, described by their respective Numbers, and the Sums due thereon for Interest: a Third Lift, containing the

Arrears of former Dividends credited in that Account, together with tile Dividend Warrants themselves: and when there is a Lottery, the Prizes of which are paid in Call), the Chief Cashier fends a List of the Certificates he has paid, with the Number and Amount of each, and the Certificates themselves.

The Business of this Account is divided between the Two Auditors. In Lord s Office are examined the whole Charge, the Three Cents of the Year 1726, the Three per Cents consolidated, and the Certificates for Prizes in the Lottery: the other Funds, in the Year’s Account, are examined in the Office of Lord Mountstuart.

Each Account contains the Receipts and Payments of Two Years, and comprehends Four Dividends upon the Annuities. After the Lift of Warrants, and the Warrants themselves, are delivered into the Office, the Auditor’s Clerk examines each Warrant, lees that the Receipt is properly ligned and attested; he compares the Number, the Name of the Proprietor, the Share of the Stock, and the Annuity due upon it, with the

2± Geo. III. 5° Decemb 785

the Entry of the Warrant upon the Lift; and if it agrees, marks it off upon the Lift.

The Total of the Annuity when call up, if right, must agree with the Total of the Annuity due upon the Total of the Capital. The unpaid Lift i9 compared with the Entry of those Warrants, in the above Lift, which are not marked as paid: The Total of this Lift, together with the Saving from the Total of the Fractions not paid by the Bank, a^ l)cing too finall, being deducted from the Total in the l'irft Lift, the Bank has Credit for the Remainder.

The Lilt of Arrears is compared, in like Manner, with the Warrants for those Payments. The Lift of Lottery Certificates is compared with the Certificates, to see that the Number and Sum agrees; and the Certificate is endorsed by the Person to whom it is made payable: the Bank has Credit for the Amount of each Lift. After this Examination, the Imprest Certificates having been delivered into the Office, that Part of the Account examined in this Office is drawn up in the official Form, and ingrossed; and after the other Part of the Account, examined in the other Office, is drawn up and ingrossed, the Two Parts are joined together, and form One Account. An Account Current, containing all the Receipts, Payments, Fees, and Allowances, with the Arrears, having been produced to the Auditor, he casts up the Sums upon the several Imprelt Rolls; and, adding to that Total the Arrears on the preceding Account, compares the compound Sum with the Total of the Charge upon the Account Current After this Account Current is signed und attested upon Oath, before a Baron of the Exchequer, by the Chief Cashier, the Account is completed, and presented for Declaration.

The Cathicr is charged with the Sums contained in the Imprest Roils; he is discharged by his actual Payments comprehended in his Account; he is allowed the Charges of Management retained by him, and the Fees paid by him for auditing and passing these Accounts.

The total Sum of Payments upon each Species of Annuities, for which the Chief Cashier has Credit in the ingrossed Account, consists of the Arrears of former Dividends, the Payments on the Four Dividends in the Time of the Account, and the Auditor’s Fee for the Time of the Account upon that Species of Annuity.

N# 6.

The Examination of Abraham El’quire,

Chief Cashier of the Bank of England; taken upon Oath, lft, 5th, 8th, and 13th August

1783.

This Examinant laith. That he is Chief Cashier of the Bank of England; as such, he palfes, every Two Years, in the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest, an Account comprehending the Sums received from the Exchequer, and the Sums paid during the Period of the Account The Payments are the Dividends upon the Annuities payable at the Bank, and the Principal and Dividends of the Annuities paid off, and the Certificates for Prizes; together with the Charges of Management, the Auditor’s and other official Fees.

Soon after each Day on which the Interest becomes due, the Exchequer issues to the Bank the full Sums due, at that Time, for Interest on the several Species of Annuities payable at that Time, and generally with the Charges of Management added to each Sum of Interest. Every Year the Auditors apply to the Bank for the Fees due to them for the last Year’s Account that has been examined by them, suggesting that they have completed that Examination. — It has been always customary for the Bank to advance to the Auditors, equally between them, a Sum for their Fees, at the Rate of One hundred Pounds a Year for every Million of Capital Stock in the Year's Account, and for every Million produced by the Long and Short Annuities, taken at the Rate of Twenty-five Years Purchase: which Calculation makes the Rate of the Allowance to the Auditors, for examining the Account of the Long Annuities, equal to the Rate of the Allowance to them for examining the Four per Cents. The Short Annuities are estimated at the same Rate with the Long Annuities; because the annual Trouble to the Auditor is in Proportion to the Number of the Proprietors, and to the Quantity of the Annuity, and not to the Duration of the Annuity j and when there has been a Loan, the Bank advances to them at the Rate of Fifty Pounds for every Million of Money raised, as the Fee for examining the Contribution Account. This Rate of One hundred Pounds a Year per Million on the Annuities appears, from an Entry in a Book at the Bank, to have been the Rate at

9 O which

5° Decetnbris. . 1783.

Elercnth Report on Public Aeewnt*.

which the Auditor's Fees were eftitnated and paid for examining an Account of Bank Annuities for Four Years, ending at Michaelmas 1720; and this Rate appears to have been adhered to ever since. It has been customary for the Bank to advance these Fees to the Auditors, upon their Application; after which the Bank present to the Treasury a Memorial, stating particularly all the Fees thus paid by them to the Auditor, together with the Fees and Charges paid at the several Offices, and praying to be reimbursed those Fees and Charges. The Sum thus received from the Exchequer, is an Article in the Charge upon the Chief Cashier in the succeeding Account: the Balance on the preceding Account, and the Sums imprested from the Exchequer, complete the Charge upon the Chief Cashier in every Account. Every Year, as soon after the 31st of December as the Accounts can conveniently be made up, the Lifts and Dividend Warrants paid within the Time of the Account, and ranged in numerical Order, and the Certificates for Prizes, are sent from the Bank to the Office of the Auditor, together with an Abstract of that Year’s Account. Before the Account is completed, the Chief Cashier procures from the Exchequer, Imprest Rolls for the several Sums that have been issued to him during the Two Years of the Account, and fends them to the Auditor’s Office: the Charges of Management allowed to the Bank, are expressed separately from the Sum for Interest in the Exchequer Order, countersigned by the Lords of the Treasury, and directing the Payment of those Sums to the Chief Cashier or Cashiers: This Order is brought to and endorsed by him, or one of them, as a Receipt in full upon that Order. The Bank are allowed the following Charges of Management: For the Annuities of the Year 1726, confuting of One Million, Three hundred Sixty Pounds a Year; and this has been the Allowance for those Annuities ever since the Year 1726: For all ttie 3 per Cent, and per Cent. Annuities, at the Rate of Five hundred Sixty-two Pounds Ten Shillings a Year per Million; except for near the Sum of Eight hundred thousand Pounds, raised in the Year 1731, now consolidated with the Three per Cents; for which Three hundred Sixty Pounds is allowed for that Loan to the Chief Cashier and Accountant, and no other Allowance is made to the Bank for the Management of those Annuities: For the Long and Short Annuities at the same Rate for every Million, estimating them at Twenty-five Years Purchase. This Rate of Five hundred Sixty-two Pounds Ten Shillings per Million, has been allowed to the Bank for Charges of Management, as he believes, ever since the Year 1742. The Ground of this Allowance is the Expence and Trouble arising to the Bark for Buildings, Officers, Clerks, Losses, Stationary, and various other contingent Charges.

The Allowance to the Bank for the Management of the Receipt to the Contributions to a Loan and to a Lottery, where the Prizes or Tickets are to be converted into Annuities, is at the Rate of Eight hundred and Five Pounds Fifteen Stallings and Ten Pence per Mil-

lion. This has been the Rate of Allowance, as he believes, ever since the Year 1719; except in the Year 1742, when Five hundred Pounds only, for receiving Eight hundred thousand Pounds, was allowed by the Act. The Allowance for the Lottery is in proportion to the Number of Tickets and Subscribers thereto, from One thousand Pounds to Two thousand Pounds.

After the Chief Cashier has paid all the Fees for the Account to the several Offices, he makes up his Account Current, and fends it to the Auditor; and if it is right, he signs it, and swears to it before a Baron of the Exchequer. The Balance remaining upon the Account confilts of unclaimed Dividends, Capital Stock paid off, and Lottery Certificates.

From the Year 1726 to the Year 1731, there does not appear to have been any other Annuities transacted at the Bank except those of the Year 1726. In the Year 1731, Eight hundred thousand Pounds Annuities were created, of which Seven hundred Sixty-nine thousand Two hundred Thirty-five Pounds Nine Shillings and Three Pence Three Farthings, 'are now a Part of the consolidated 3 per Cent. Annuities, the Remainder being paid off. — In the Year 1742, Eight hundred thousand Pounds Annuities more were created, and the Chief Cashier and the Accountant were directed by the Act to be paid, together, Four hundred Fifty Pounds a Year; which is at the Rate of Five hundred Sixty-two Pounds Ten Shillings per Million. In some Years, where the Lotteries have been blended with the Redemption of Annuities, or by any other Circumstances have created more Trouble and Expence to the Bank, they have in their Memorials craved a larger Allowance in Proportion. In the Years 1772, 1774, and 1775, the Bank were allowed Two thousand Pounds for each Lottery. In ffie Years 1743, 1747, and 1748, the Receipt of the Contributions to the Loans was attended with more Trouble and Expence than usual; in consequence of which, the Bank craved, and were allowed, a larger Sum than at the usual Rate of Eight hundred and five Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Ten Pence per Million. In the Years 1747 and 1748, they were allowed One thousand Pounds per Million on the Annuities. As feme of the Subscribers to Loans frequently pay in the Whole of their Subscriptions at the First Payment, and others are constantly completing their Payments, which immediately become transferable Stock, and, as the Annuities commence at the same Times with the Annuities of the like Kind, the Bank crave, and are allowed, the Charges of Management for the same Year in which they receive the Contributions.

A. Newland.

Eleventh Report on Public Accounts.

May it pleufe your Lordships,

In Obedience to your Lordships Order of Reference on the annexed Memorial of Abraham Newland, Chief Cashier to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, praying Repayment of Fees to the Treasury and Exchequer, and puffing the Accounts of the several Bank Annuities, and the Accounts of the Contributions to the Annuities and Lotteries therein mentioned; and to the Auditors of His Majesty’s Imprefts for their Fees, for Auditing the said Accounts, according to the Particulars thereto annexed:

We humbly report to your Lordships, That the Fees paid at the Exchequer, for the Imprest Rolls, to the Account of the Annuities for Two Years, to the 5th July 1779: The Fees paid at the several Offices of the Treasury and Exchequer, on passing the Account of the said Annuities for Two Years, to the 5th July 1777: And the Fees paid on passing the Account of the Contributions to the Annuities and Lotteries 1778, 1779, and 1780, are the uiiial Payments.

The Fees paid the Auditors of His Majesty’s Imprefts, for examining, auditing, and ingrossing the Account of the several Species of Annuities therein mentioned, are computed at the Rate of too/, per Annum, for each Million Principal; and the Fees for auditing the Account of the Contributions to the Annuities and Lottery 1779, are computed at the Rate of 50/. per Annum, for each Million Principal; being the same Rates as have from Time to Time been allowed the Auditors, by virtue of Warrants of the Lords Commissioners of Ills Majesty’s Treasury.

The Account of tire foregoing Fees and Charges, annexed to the said Memorial, amounts to the Sum of Twelve thousand Three hundred and Ninety-three Pounds Thirteen Shillings.

Which is most humbly submitted to your Lordships.

Auditor’s Office, 22d May 1782.

John Lloyd,

That in pursuance of an Act of Parliament, passed in the Twenty-first Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for raising the Sum of Twelve Million Four hundred and Eighty thousand Pounds by Annuities and Lottery, for the Service of the Year 1781, there hath been received at the Bank of England, from the Contributors -on the Terms of the said Act, the full Sum of Twelve Million Four hundred and Eighty thousand Pounds.

That your Memorialists have paid Twelve Million Three hundred and Eighty-seven thousand Six hundred and Twenty-four Pounds Five Shillings and Eight Pence, Part thereof, into the Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer; and Eighty-one thousand Seven hundred and Six Pounds Four Shillings and Four Pence, other Part thereof, for Interest, after the Rate of Three Pounds per Cent, per Annum, allowed by the said Act to such of the Contributors as advanced their Money previous to the Times appointed for paying the fame.

The Residue of the said Twelve Million Four hundred and Eighty Thousand Pounds, being Ten thousand and Six hundred Sixty-nine Pounds Ten Shillings, your

Memorialists pray your Lordships will allow them to retain for the Use and Benefit of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, for the Service, Pains, and Labour of their Officers employed in receiving, paying, and accounting for the said Twelve Million Four hundred and Eighty thousand Pounds, and the Charges thereof; viz'. Nine thousand Six hundred and Sixty-nine Pounds Ten Shillings, in respect of Twelve Millions, being at the rate of Eight hundred and Five Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Ten Pence per Million; and One thousand Pounds in respect of the Lottery; which Sums are in Proportion to former Allowances for the like Services.

Your Memorialists also pray, your Lordships will be pleated to allow the Annual Sum of Ten thousand One hundred and Twenty-five Pounds, for the Services respecting the 3 per Cent. Annuities, to commence from the Fifth Day of January 1781; and for the Services respecting the 41, per Cent. Annuities, the Annual Sum of One thousand Six hundred and Eighty-seven Pounds Ten Shillings; these Sums being agreeable to former Allowances for the like Services: and that your Lord-ships will be pleated to order the same to be paid to their Chief Cashier, for the Use and Benefit of the said Governor and Company of the Bank of England.

Signed by Order of the Court of Directors,

Francis Martin,

Assistunt Secretary.

Afterour hearty Commendations; Whereas the Yearly Sum of 54,600 /. is imprested to you at the Receipt of His Majesty s Exchequer, upon and by virtue of lundry Acts of Parliament, passed in the First Year of His Majesty’s Reign, to be issued, paid over, and applied in Manner following: That is to say, 45,500l. Annum, Part thereof, to pay Annuities, after the Rate of 5 /. per Cent, per Ann. for and upon the Sum of 910,000l. contributed for the Purchase thereof; 8,450/. per Ann. other Part thereof, to pay like Annuities for and upon the Sum of 169,000l., which was further contributed for the Purclmle thereof; and a Sum not exceeding 650 /. per Ann. Residue of the said Yearly Sum of 54,600l., as well for your own Salary and Allowance for receiving the Money to pay the said several Annuities, and applying the same to that Use, and for your Pains and Charges in keeping and rendering your Accounts thereof, as for the Salary and Allowance to the Accountant General of the Bank for the Time being, for his Service and Charge in performing the Duty and Trust incumbent upon him, by means of the said Acts. All which said Yearly Sums were made, by the said Acts, to commence from Michaelmas 1715; and the said Yearly Sum of 650/. for Salaries and Allowances, in Manner aforesaid, are thereby apportioned as followeth: That is to say, 250/. per Ann. for your own Salary; and 200l. per Ann. for the Salary of the Accountant General, with respect to the receiving, paying, and accounting for the said Yearly Sum of 45,500l. for Annuities, for and upon the Sum of 910,000l. contributed as aforesaid: and 100l. per Ann. for your own Salary, and 100l. per Atm. for the Salary of the Accountant General, with respect to the receiving, paying, and accounting for the said Yearly Sum of 8,450/. for Annuities, for and upon the further Sum of 169,000l. contributed as aforesaid, as in and by the said several Acts, Relation being the reunto had, may more fully appear. Now these arc, by virtue of the aforesaid Acts, to authorize and impower you, out of the Monies that have been, or shall from Time to Time be imprested and paid to you at the said Receipt, for the Purposes aforesaid, not only to retain and keep the several and respective Salaries and Allowances, so made payable to you as aforesaid, and which amount in the Whole to 350 /. per Ann. but also to pay over unto the Accountant General of the Bank, for the Time being, the several and respective Salaries and Allowances so made payable to him as aforesaid, and which amount in the Whole to 200l.* per Ann.: all which Salaries and Allowances are to commence from Michaelmas 1715, and to be paid Quarterly, in Manner as by the said respective Acts is directed and appointed. And for so doing, this, with the proper Acquittances in that Behalf, shall be as well to you for Payment, as to the Auditors, and all others concerned, for allowing such Payment from Time to Time upon your Account, a sufficient Warrant.

J. Aislabie,

To Tho' Maddox, Esquire, first or principal Cashier of the Bank of England, and to the first or prin- , cipal Cathicr of the Bank of England for the Time being.

Cashier and Accountant General of the Bank dormant Warrant on Account of Annuities.

After our hearty Commendations; Whereas by the Act passed Duodecimo Georgii Reg. for granting to His Majesty the Sum of One Million, to be raised by way of a Lottery, it is araongst other Things Enacted, That the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, and their Successors, shall from Time to Time, until the Annuities, after the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum per Ann. shall be redeemed according to the said Act, appoint and employ One sufficient Person within their Office in the City of London, to be their Chief or First Cashier, and One other sufficient Person, within the same Office, to be their Accountant General; and that the said Cashier, to whom the said Money shall from Time to Time be issued for Payment of the said Annuities, after the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum per Ann. shall from Time to Time, without Delay, apply and pay the same accordingly, and render his Account thereof according to the due Course of the Exchequer; and the said Accountant General, for the Time being, shall, from Time to Time, inspect and examine all Receipts and Payments of the said Cashier, and the Vouchers relating thereto, in order to prevent any Fraud, Negligence, or Delay; as in and by the said Act, Relation being the reunto had, may more fully appear: And whereas the Court of Directors of the Bank of England have, by their Memorial to us, humbly prayed, That such Allowance may be made to the Bank, for their Charges of Management of the said Annuities, as we should think reasonable: Now we, having taken the Premises into our Consideration, do think reasonable and fitting to grant and allow unto the Bank, to defray such their Charges of Management, the Sum of Three hundred and Sixty Pounds per Ann. to commence from Michaelmas last past, One thousand Seven hundred and Twenty-six: these are therefore to authorize and direct you, the First or Chief Cashier, out of the Monies of the Fund for the said Annuities, that shall from Time to Time be imprested to you at the Receipt of Exchequer, to retain in your Hands, for the use of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, so much Quarterly as in the Whole shall make up the Yearly Sum of Three hundred and Sixty Pounds: For doing thereof, this shall be to you, the said Cashier, for retaining the fame, and to the Auditors of His Majesty’s Imprefts, and all others concerned in passing and allowing such Payments, from Time to Time, a sufficient Warrant and Discharge.

R.

Whitehall, Treasury Chambers, Cha. Turner, the 20th Day of December 1726. Yonge,

Geo.

At General Court of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, the 26th April 1695.

The Governor acquainted the Court, That it was called (amongst other Things) to hear the Report of the Committee appointed the 20th of the preceding March, to consider of Gratuities for the Governor, Deputy, and Directors of the Bank of; who were of Opinion, that Three thousand Pounds be presented to the present Governor, Deputy, and Directors, as a Gratuity for their great Pains and constant Attendance of the Affairs of the said Bank, to the 25th of the said March, to be divided by them, as they shall think fit.

And were further of Opinion, that from the said 2r,tli of March, to the 25th of March 1696, Four thousand Pounds be presented, as a Recompence to the Governor, Deputy, and Directors, for that Year; and that the same be divided as follows:

To the Governor - - - 200

To the Deputy - - - 200

To each Director - 150

All which the Committee humbly submitted to the Judgment of the Court.

And upon putting the Question, If this Court do approve of the said Report ? the same passed in the Affirmative.

N° 15.

The Examination of Charles Harris, Esquire; taken upon Oath, 12th and 15th August 1783.

This Examinant faith. That the only Annuities transferable at the South Sea House, which are audited by the Auditors of the Imprest, are the Annuities of the Year 1731. The Account is made up every Three Years; and One Account only is passed of those Three Years. The Vouchers for this Account are examined, Part in one Office, and Part in the other; but the Account is drawn up in one Office only, and that alternately. Every Year, the Cashier of the South Sea Company fends to the Auditor’s Office, Dividend Books, containing the Names of all the Proprietors, with the Share of each in the Capital Stock; and the Annuity attending it; the Number of each Warrant; a List of the W arrants paid upon that Dividend Book; and the Arrears of former Dividends, with the Warrants thcin-selves ranged in a numerical Order; These. Books and Lifts are lignod by the Accountant of the South Sea Ilonfe: The Warrants are compared with the Entries Vo l. 99-

799

in the Dividend Book, and marked off. This Book, Eleventh and the Warrants for the Arrears, are then examined Report with the paid Lift, and the Cashier has Credit for °n Pub1^ the Amount of that Lift. After the last of the Three CC°Un Years is expired, the Cashier presents a Memorial to the Treasury, praying them to authorize the Auditors of the Imprest to allow him the Fees and Charges he has paid in passing the Account: This Memorial is referred to the Auditors, who examine and make their Report upon it. The Cashier fends the Auditor the Imprest Certificates, to verify the Articles in the Charge of Issues from the Exchequer: He fends, likewise, an Account Current, similar to that sent from the Bank.

The issues from the Exchequer, inserted in the Charge, include the Charges of Management, as well as the Half Year’9 Annuity. These Articles are the same both in ^he Account Current and in the Official Account, and follow the Imprest Certificates.

In the Dj(charge, the Total of the Charges of Management is the same in both. The Allowance is at the same Rate with the Allowance to the Bank, and the Auditor allows it by virtue of a dormant Warrant of the Treasury, dated the 29th November 1752. The Total Sum paid for Dividends, during the Three Years, is the same in both Accounts; but the particular Articles composing that Total, are formed in a different Manner. The Auditor states the Total Sum paid upon each Dividend during the Time of the Account; the Cashier states the Total Sum paid upon all the Dividends during each Half Year. The Total paid for Fees and Chorges is the same in both Accounts:

This is allowed pursuant to the Treasury Warrant annexed to the Memorial of the Cashier, and the Report of the Auditors. The Fee to the Auditors, upon this Account, is at the same Rate with that upon the Bank Account The Account Current is signed by the Cashier, and sworn to by him before a Baron of the Exchequer.

Harris,.

T. Anguish,

Rich4 Neave,

Sami Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

Will" Roe.

N* 16.

The Examination of Peter Burrell, Esquire,

Cashier of the South Sea Company; taken upon Oath, August 15th and 20th 1783.

This Examinant faith. That he is Cashier of the South Sea Company, and has been lb for about Eighteen Years. The only Account that he passes in the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest, is of the Annuities of the Year 1751: No Account is passed either of the South Sea Stock, or of the Old or New Annuities. In the Year 1720, they composed One Fund only, which was South Sea Stock. About the Year 1723, Fifty per Cent, of the Stock was separated from it by Act of Parliament, and converted into Annuities, called the South Sea Annuities. About the Year 1733, Seventy-five per Cent, of the remaining Stock was separated from it, and converted into Annuities, called the New South Sea Annuities. The Interest upon all these Funds is received from the Exchequer, at different Times of the Year, upon the Application of the Cashier. In the Beginning of every Year, a Treasury Warrant, and Exchequer Order, are made out for the Payment of the total Sum due for the succeeding Year’s Interest; together with the Charges of Management upon Twenty-four Millions Sixty-five thousand Eighty-four Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Eleven Pence, called the Old Capital; which comprehends the total Capital of the above-mentioned Three Funds; and this Sum is diiefted

to be issued without Account. Upon Application for any Part of this Sum, the Deputy Auditor of the Exchequer enters the Sum to be paid upon the Order; and the Cashier gives each Teller a Receipt for the Sum he receives of him. No Fee whatever is paid for any Part of this Business, either at the Treasury or the Exchequer. The Dividend Warrants, after they are paid, are examined in the Offices both of the Cashier and the Accountant; and are preserved in the Office of the Cashier. The Annual Sum allowed for the Charges of Management on the Old Capital, now constituting the Three Funds, is Fourteen thousand Twenty-two Pounds Three Shillings and Two Pence. As the Old Capital confided of a Variety of Funds, and as the Charges of Management of these Funds were computed at a different Rate, the Allowance for the Management of the whole Capital is not estimated at any One. given Rate. The Amount of the unpaid Principal and Dividends, as it flood the 5th

lad, was, on the Annihilations, Twenty-two thousand Three hundred Sixty-two Pounds Ten Shillings; and of the Stock Dividends, and Interest oa the Annuities, One hundred Seventy-three thousand Four hundred Thirty-two Pounds Two Shillings and Eleven Pence. The Sum for the Charges of Management has always been the fame, except that it has been diininished in Proportion as the Principal of the Old Capital has been paid off.

Burrell.

After our hearty Commendations: Whereas, by an Act of Parliament passed in the Twenty-fourth Year of His Majesty’s Reign, for granting to His Majesty the Sum of 2,100,000l. to be raised by Annuities and a lottery, and charged on the Sinking Fund, transferable at the South Sea House, we are authorized to settle and appoint, among other Things, such Allowances out of the said Fund, as we should think reasonable, unto the Chief Cashier of the South Sea Company, for receiving, paying, and accounting for the Annuities thereby established; and all'o to their Accountant General for his Service, Pains, and Trouble, in performing the Duty and Trust incumbent upon him by the said Act; which Allowances are to be for the Use and Benefit of the said Company, and at their Disposal only. And whereas, upon Consideration of a Memorial which hath been laid before us from the Court of Directors of the South Sea Company, we think reasonable to allow unto the said Company the Sum of One thousand One hundred Eighty-one Pounds Five Shillings per , for and

in respect of their receiving, paying, and accounting for the said Annuities, amounting to Two Millions One hundred thousand Pounds Principal Money, to commence from Christmas 1751; being computed in Proportion to former Allowances of the like Nature. These are, therefore, to authorize and direct you, the said Cashier, out of the Monies of the Fund for the said Annuities, created by virtue of the said Act of Parliament above mentioned, that shall from Time to Time be imprested to you at the Receipt of Exchequer, to retain in your Hands, for the Use of the South Sea Company as aforesaid, the said Sum of One thousand One hundred Eighty-one Pounds Five Shillings, Yearly, and every Year, computed from Christmas 1751, until the said Annuities shall be redeemed, or we shall think fit to signify our Pleasure to the contrary. And this, with proper Acquittances for the said Payments, shall be, as well to you the said Cashier, for retaining the fame, as to the Auditors of His Majesty’s Imprefts, and all others concerned in parting and allowing thereof, from Time to Time, upon your Accounts, a sufficient Warrant and Discharge.

II.

Whitehall, Treasury Chambers, G.

the 29th Day of November 1752. J. Campbell.

To our very loving Friends, the First and Chief Cashier of the South Sea Company, for the Payment of the Annuities for Two Millions One hundred thousand Pounds Principal Money, on an Act of Parliament passed in the Twenty-fourth Year of His Majesty’s Reign; and the Accountant

General of the South Sea Company, Auditors of His Majesty’s Imprefts, and all others who shall or may be concerned herein.

A true Copy,

Phil.Deare, Dcp. Audr.

To the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury.

The MEMORIAL of Peter Burrell, Cashier to the South Sea Company.

Humbly Sheweth,

That your Memorialist hath advanced and paid fevc-ral Sums of Money, for Fees and Charges, in parting the Account of Interest on 1,919,600l. 3 Cent. Annuities 1751, transferable at the Sea House; and

also of Receipts and Payments of Money imprest to him at the Exchequer, for paying the said Annuities, according to the Account hereunto annexed; together with the Allowance humbly craved by your Memorialist for his Trouble and Charges in the Premises, and obtaining his Quietus, amounting to 984/. 95. 4

Your Memorialist therefore most humbly prays, your Lordships will be pleased to grant your Warrant to the Auditors of His Majesty’s Imprest, authorizing them to allow the said Payment and Charges, in the Account of the said Annuities for Three Years, to the 5 th January 1781, now depending in their Offices, and preparing for Declaration, in order that he may be reimbursed the fame.

Burrell.

South Sea House,

25th October 1781.

Whitehall, Treasury Chambers, the 8th November 1781.

The Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury are pleased to refer the aforegoing Memorial to the Auditors of the Imprefts, who are to consider the fame, and to report to their Lordships their Opinion, whether the Sum prayed for therein ought to be allowed.

Grey Cooper.

After our hearty Commendations; Having considered your Report aforegoing, on the Memorial of Peter Burrell, Esquire, Cashier of the South Sea Company, praying Allowance of certain Sums of Money expended by him, for Fees and Charges in passing the Accounts therein mentioned, and for his Trouble and other his Charges in the Premises: We think the several Sums specified in your said Report, amounting together to the Suit. of Nine hundred Eighty-four Pounds Nine Shillings and Four Pence, just and reasonable to be allowed unto him for the Services aforesaid. These are therefore to authorize and direct you, to whom it

may appertain, in making up and passing the Accounts of the said Cashier, to give Allowances thereupon of the said several Sums specified in your said Report, amounting to the said Sum of Nine hundred Eighty-four Pounds Nine Shillings and Four Pence.

And this shall be, as well to you as to all other His Majesty’s Officers and Ministers herein concerned, a sufficient Warrant

N° 26.

The Examination of Mr. William Edwards, Deputy Accountant to the Bank of England; taken upon Oath, 14th, 19th, and 21st November 1783.

This Examinant faith, When the ’’Transfer Books of any Capital Stock are shut for the Payment of the Dividend, the Share of each Proprietor in that Capital is taken out from his Account in the Ledger, and entered upon a Slip opposite his Name. When all the Shares are thus extracted, they are call up, to see that the Total of them agrees with the Total of the Capital: These Shares are then infected in Blank Warrants; so that the Total in the Warrants is the Amount of the Capital. The Warrants are then examined with the Slips; the Number of Accounts upon the Slips having been call up, the Warrants arte told over, to see that the Number of them corresponds with the Number of the Accounts. The Warrants being lotted, and ranged in alphabetical Order, according to the Quantity of the Stock, are inserted in the same Order in Dividend Books, with the Folio of the Account in the Ledger, and the Name of the Proprietor: Thfefe Books are cast up, to see that the Total of them agrees with the Total of the Capital. The Entries in the Dividend Books are then numbered, beginning wkh the First Name in Letter A, N* 1, and ending in the last Name in Letter Z; which Number is the Number Of the 'Proprietors of that Fund. The Share of the Interdft is then entered in the Dividend Book, opposite the Share of the Capital; the Amount of both the Capital and Interest, in each Side of the Dividend Book, is cast up; and the Total of the Interest calculated upon the Total of the Capital. The Number in the Dividend Book is then entered upon the correspondent Warrant

The Interest is inserted from the Dividend Book, in the Margin of the Warrant, in Figures, and in the Body in Words at Length; the Agreement between the Figures and the Words is examined by a Clerk, who signs his Initials: a Duplicate of the Dividend Book is then made, and the Entries cast up. The Dividend

Book, the Duplicate, and the Warrants, are then examined and compared together, by Three Clerks, to see that they correspond; and the Articles in the Duplicate are marked off as they are examined: after which the Duplicate is deposited in a Place of Security, and the Warrants are signed by Clerks appointed by the Bank for that Purpose, and returned back to the Office where the Capital is transa&ed, where they are told over, and there deposited until applied for by the Proprietors. The Person who receives the Dividend, writes his Name in the Dividend Book, opposite the Name of the Proprietor; and signs the Receipt at the Bottom of the Warrant, which is witnessed by the Clerk who delivers it: the Teller who pays it draws his Pen across it, and enters it in a Book: after which it is sent to the Dividend Warrant Office, in the Department of the Cashier, where it is defaced by a Hole punched through it, and entered in a Cash Book: from thence it goes to the Check Office, in the Department of the Accountant where it is posted in the Check Ledger as paid. These paid Warrants are ranged in a numerical Order in this Office, and transmitted to the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest. A Lift of the unpaid Warrants is made out in the Annuity Office; the Amount of which, being added to the Amount of the Payments Collected from ffie Entries in the Books in the Check Office, makes the Amount of the Half Year’s Interest: and these Sums are afterwards agreed with the Accountant and Cashier. . The Warrants for the Payment of the Dividends upon the Bank Stock are in the like Form, and undergo the like Examination and Check: they are not sent to the Auditor, but remain in the Bank.

W. Edwards.

T. Anguish,

Richd Neaoe,

Sam1 Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

W" Roe.

N* 29.

The Examination of John Esquire, Clerk of the Debentures, in the Office of the Auditor of the'Receipt of His Majesty’s Exchequer; taken upon Oath, the 31st of October, and 18th and 21st of November, 1783.

This Examinant faith, That in the Account of the Public Debts at the Receipt of the Exchequer, transmitted to this Board from the Auditor, the First Article stated in the Column of Principal Debts, being One Million Eight hundred Thirty-six thousand Two hundred Seventy-five Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Ten Pence Three Farthings, does, as lie believes, consist of the Money subscribed into the Exchequer by the Purchasers of Annuities for Years, which were not subscribed into the South Sea Company: lTpon the Expiration of the

Annuities, this Principal Debt expires with them. The Second Article, which is on Annuity with Survivorship, is expired since the 5th of July last, by the Death of the last Nominee. The Annuities for Two and Three Lives stated in the Third Article, were first granted in the Year* 11>94; the last Additions made to them were by an Act of Parliament in the Year 1702: To entitle the Nominee, or his Assignee, to the Payment of One of these Annuities, a Certificate must be produced at the Exchequer, that the Nominee is living; his Name is continued in the Posting Book, which contains the Names of all who are supposed to be alive, until a Certificate is produced of the Death; when the Day of the Death is entered opposite to his Name, and the Certificate filed. The last Death that was certified, was a Death upon the 14th October 1781; the last Life that was certified, was upon the 5U1 January 1781.

It appears from the Polling Book, that the Number of Orders therein remaining, as of Lives at present existing, is Four hundred Forty; the original Number was One thousand Seven hundred and One: The Sums inserted, as the Principal Debts, in these Two last Articles, and in the Fifth Article, of Eighteen thousand Pounds, are also, as he believes, the Purchase Money of the several Annuities let opposite to them in the next Column, and expire with those Annuities. The Fourth Article, being Exchequer Bills made out for Two thousand Two hundred Pounds, has been inserted as a Public Debt ever since the Year 1727; but it does not appear that any such Bills were ever made out, or any Demand made for them upon the Exchequer: The Bills, upon which this Interest is supposed to be due, appear to have been cancelled in the Year 1727; and the Interest became due in the Year 1719. The Sum of Five thousand Two hundred and Fifty Pounds, for the Charges of Management of the First Article, is paid, pursuant to Treasury Warrants, to the Auditor, the Clerk of the Pells, and the Tellers.

The One Million of the Year 1726 has never been inserted amongst the Public Debts at the Exchequer, because the Public received no Money for it; it was given to the King to defray the Debts upon the Civil List. A Fund was created for the Payment of the Interest; and the Surplus of that Fund was reserved for the Disposition of Parliament, and is now appropriated as a collateral Fund to pay certain Salaries.

The Three hundred and Sixty Pounds a Year, allowed the Bank for the Charges of Management of these Annuities, is not inserted in the Column under the Title of Management and other Charges; it is paid out of the same Fund with the Annuities.

John Hughson,

T. Anguish,

Rich* Neave,

Samf Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond,

Will Roe.

A Petition of Henry Phillips, of Knightsbridge, in the Phillips’* County of Middlesex, being offered to be presented to Mf thod of the House; Provisow

Lord John Cavendish, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth. That in March 1781, the Petitioner presented a Petition to the House, stating, That, having been informed of the Ravages and Devafta-tions made during Sea Voyages on the Dry Provisions in His Majesty’s Navy, by Weevils, and other In-fefts, he had, after many Years incessant Study and Assiduity, discovered a cheap Composition, easy in its Application, and the Expence not exceeding Five Guineas, in eradicating Weevils, Spiders, Maggots, and Cock-roaches, out of a First Rate Man of War; and that the House is in Possession of numerous and incontrovertible Testimonies of the great Utility of the Petitioner’s Discovery; and that the Petitioner, having been the Author of an Invention of the utmost Consequence to the Health and Lives of Seamen

men in His Majesty’s Service, as the Commissioners for Victualling the Navy, and several respectable Naval Officers, testified in a Committee of the House in 1781, a Bill was, in consequence thereof, submitted to Parliament, for providing a Reward of 3,600 /. to the Petitioner, on his making a proper Discovery, for the Use of the Public, of the Competition of his Powder for the Destruction of lnfefts, but which Reward the House of Lords postponed until further Proofs of the Success of the Petitioner’s Invention, and ordered a particular Account of the Result of such Experiments, as were then making, or should be made, on Board any of His Majesty’s Ships of War, of the Efficacy of the Petitioner’s Pow der, to be laid before them at the Opening of the next Session of Parliament; in Obedience to which, the Commissioners of the Admiralty have presented to their Lordships such further Certificates as are come to Hand; and that the Petitioner, conscious from the Addition of the numerous and incontrovertible Teltiinonics in support of his Invention, that the Utility of his Discovery gives him a Claim to public Prottftion, is induced, notwithstanding the Invention has been acquired by Eighteen Years unremitted Application, at the Expence of 4,000l., and at the Hazard of his Life (he being now almost blind) to make known to Parliament, to the Commissioners of the Victualling, and to lay open to the Public, the Nature and Manner of preparing his Composition, that all His Majesty’s Subjects may reap the Benefit of it, upon receiving such Compensation for his Trouble and Expence, as by the House shall be thought reasonable and just.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Number of Land Forces, including Two thousand and Thirty Invalids, amounting to Seventeen thousand Four hundred and Eighty-three effective Men, Commission and Non-commissioned Officers included, be employed for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-four.
