PETITION of the Corn Distillers in and Smuggling, about the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have embarked very considerable Capitals in erecting Buildings and providing Utensils and Materials for car-

Zing on the Corn Distillery, under the Sanction of the iws; and that the Petitioners, though few in Number, comprise, in Importance and Extent of their Manufactories, upwards of 44ths of the whole Distillery of England, the Proportion paid by the London Distillery the last Year, ending 5th July, to the Public Revenue, being nearly as 310,000l. to 35,000l.; that, alarmed at the surprising Decrease of, and impending Ruin to, a Trade of lb much Importance to the Landed Interest as well as to the Revenue of this Country, the Petitioners have endeavoured to investigate the Causes of its late rapid Declension, and, the deeper their Researches, the more they are induced to impute it to the fraudulent Practices of the Smuggler and illicit Trader; and that the Com Distillery, which, upwards of Twenty Years ago, was a Market for, and took 500,000 Quarters of Com annually, has not, of later Years, made a Demand for more than 150,000 Quarters; and the great Encouragement to the Increase of Agriculture, and the refulring Benefit to the Landed Property, under the former State, are too obvious to suffer the late de-struftive Change to pals unnoticed; and that, with respect to the Revenue, the Petitioners conceive it will be found, on Inquiry, that, about the Year 1750, when the Impost or Duties upon Com Spirits were only about 12/. />er Ton, the Com Distillery yielded a Revenue to Government of about 500,000l. annually, and, to come nearer the present Time, that, in 1778, the Duties amounted to 540,000l. and upwards; in 1779, 1780,

1781, and 1782, additional Imposts were laid on, with a View to aid and increase the Revenue, and such Increase was estimated at upwards of 135,000l. additional

Yearly

836 i 2° Decembr^.1783.

Yearly Revenue; yet, in the Year 1783, it will be found that the whole Produce of the Distillery was about 335,000l. only; and thus, instead of the promised Increase of Revenue, by the additional Imposts, this one Article of British Manufactory, which, in 1750, at an Impost of about 12 I. per Ton, produced 500,000l.;

in 1778, at an Impost of 49/. per Ton, produced 540,000l.; in 1783, at an Impost of 62/. per Ton, produces only 335,000l.; which is 165,000l. short of what it was in 1750, and 340,000l. a Year short of the promiied Increase; and that the Petitioners, in the Course of this Inquiry, have every Reason to believe that it is not from any Decrease in the Consumption of Spirits in England that this Change arises, but, on the contrary, that the Demand and Consumption have greatly increased; and that this material Deficiency of the Public Revenue is owing to the Introdu6tion of Foreign Spirits by the Smuggler, and by the illicit Trade of secret Manufactories in Great Britain and other Evasion of Duties; and that the Petitioners have submitted this short Sketch, or comparative View of the past and present State of the Com Distillery, in order to lbew that, in proportion to the Increase of the Imposts, such has been the Increase of the Bounty or Profit to the illicit Trader, that the Temptation exceeds the Force of all our restriCHve Laws, and what was intended as an additional Aid to Government, has operated in Diminution of the Revenue, by encouraging fraudulent Practices, and; in Effect, prohibiting the fair Trader; and that, although the Petitioners conceive themselves entitled to the Protection and Encouragement of the Legislature, it is not their Interelis alone that are at Stake, the Corn Distillery is evidently of great National Importance, and the Defalcation of the Revenue calls not more forcibly for the Interposition of the Minister, than the Revival of a failing Market for our Staple the Com Trade, and averting the Injury to the Landed Property, call for the Attention of the Country Gentlemen; the Protection of the fair Trader, the Increase of his Manufacture, the Ends of Government, with respect to Revenue, and the maintaining or increating the Value of the Landed Property, being, as the Petitioners conceive, inseparable from their Interests: And therefore praying. That this important Matter may be taken into Consideration, and that Relief may be afforded, whether by such a Reduction of the late unproductive Impolts as may remove the Temptations to the fraudulent and illicit Trader, and consequently render further restrictive Laws unnecessary, or, by more effectual Restrictions, and better enforced Regulations, suppressing the Frauds, and making these additional Imposts answer the*Ends for which they were laid on, or. otherwise, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, who are appointed to

enquire into the illicit Practices now used in defrauding the Revenue of this Kingdom, and the moil effectual Methods of preventing the fame.

In order to authenticate the latter Part of the Disbursements stated in the above Account, I beg Leave to subjoin a Copy of Mr. Paine'* Report to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, upon his Examination of the Works at Somerset House, and the Bills for the last Year,

James Paine, Esquire, his Report, and the Account for the Year 1782.

Sir, f Somerset House, November 17th, 1783.

I beg Leave to acquaint you, for the Information of the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, that in Obedience to their Lordships Commands, signified to me in a Letter of the 31st August 1782, 1 immediately began to examine the Accounts of Sir William Chambers, as Superin tend ant of the Works carrying on at Somerset House: Which Examination having been compleated np to the end of the Year 1781, by the 19th of November in the same Year, I delivered in ray Report on that Day, with the Account' up to Christmas 1781; to which Report and Account 1 beg Leave to refer their Lordships. The remaining Bills then under Examination, up to the End of the Year 1782, have now also been compleatly examined, and every other Inspeflion made which the above-mentioned Treasury Letter required: And having now compleatly examined all the Tradesmen’s Bills for the Year 1782, and compared them with the Works done, and Materials furnished by each; having made a very attentive Survey of the Works up to the present Time; and having also compared the Bills with the several Abstracts made of the Mea-furements, and verified the Abstracts by the measuring Books, and the measuring Books by actual Rcadmeasurements of the principal Dimensions; I aiu enabled to certify to their Lordships (which I now beg Leave to do, by a Repetition of my former Report) that the Money has been very properly expended; that the Materials used, and the Worknrianftiip, are uncommonly good in their different Kinds; that the Measurments and Accounts have been taken and kept with the greatest Accuracy; and that in all other Points (as far as I am able to judge) the great Works at Somerset House, intruded to the Management of Sir William Chambers, have been very carefully and skilfully conducted, and with every due Attention to the Interest and Advantage of the Public.

The inch fed is the Account of the Disbursements up to the present Time, and the Bills up to the 31st December 1782. I have the Honour lo be, with great Respect,

To Richard Burke, Esquire, Treasury Chamber*. Sir> your most obedient humbIe StM’Jamet

THE House being met, the Clerk at the Table acquainted the House, That Mr, Speaker had lent for him that Morning, to desire him to inform the House, that having Yesterday received the melancholy Account of the Death of a very near Relation, he hoped the House would dispense with his Attendance upon his Duty for a Day or Two; and, if it would be attended with no Inconvenience to the public Business, that the House would adjourn for a short Time.

Whereupon it was moved. That the House would adjourn till Wedntsday Morning next, Ten of the Clock.

A Petition of Sir Robert Barker, Baronet, and John Call, Agents in Behalf of the Creditors of the Nabob of Arcott (Subjects of this Realm) resident at Saint George and elsewhere, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,. That, by an Instrument duly executed at Fort Saint George, in The East Indies, the 10th Day of August 1782, the Petitioners were appointed to be the Agents of the said Creditors, with foil Powers to do and execute for them, and in their Names, every Thing lawful to be done relative to the Claims of their absent Conltituents on the said Nabob; and that, by virtue of such Appointment, on or about the 28th Day of April' 1777. the President and Council, or Select Committee of Fort Saint George, did, by a Public Letter under their Hands, hold out and offer to Three of the said Creditors the Public Sanction and Security of the Fast India Company, for the Repayment of the Principal and Interest of Four Lacks of

Vo l. 3*1.

Pagodas, or such other Sum as they should advance for paying off the Arrears of the said Nabob’s Cavalry; and in Consequence of such Sanction and unquestionable Security I'o offered and pledged (without which the said Loan would not have been made) the said Three Creditors did advance and lend to the said Nabob, on or before the 14th Day of June following, the full Sum of Four Lacks of Pagodas on Four several Bonds, for One Lack of Pagodas each, at the Rate of 12 per Cent, per Annum, which said Sum, and Part of the Current Interest, still remains unpaid; and that, moreover, on the 26th Day of November 1777, as will appear by several Propolklsand Instruments made and signed by the said Nabob, to be communicated to the Governor General and Supreme Council, and to the President and Council of Fort Saint George, and to be carried into Execution under the Auspices of the Company, the said Nabob acknowledged himself to be indebted, and issued Bonds to sundry British Subjects, at the Rate of 12 per Cent, per Annum, to the Amount of about 35 Lacks of Pagodas (w’hich was termed the New Consolidated Loan) for the Repayment of which, with the Current Interest, he, the said Nabob, did then assign the Revenues of certain Districts; and that, soon after, by the Recommendation of the Court of Directors, and the Governor General and Supreme Council of Bengal, the said Nabob withdrew all Alignments of Revenues, and made other Regulations in lieu thereof, for discharging the said Debt, which, through the Necefli-ties of the State, have not produced the intended Effect; and that, in the Beginning of the Year 1781, the Committee of Correspondence of the Court of Directors took up the Consideration of this, as well as the Cavalry Loan, and formed the Outline of an Arj rangement for the Liquidation thereof, but Advices being received, the next Day, of the Invasion of The Carnatic by Hyder Ally, the Proceedings thereon were left in-

complete; and that the Governor General and Supreme Council, and the President and Select Committee of Fort Saint George, fenlible of the great Sufferings and Distress of the said Creditors, and that no Prohibition to the contrary was issued when the Loan was made, have lately transmitted to the Court of Directors certain Propositions for liquidating the said Debt, which, for Want of Time, have not yet been thoroughly difeufled or adopted; and that the Petitioners, conceiving from the State of the Premises, and by the Propofols made and Steps taked by the Nabob, the Court of Directors, and the Company’s Representatives Abroad, that the Authenticity and Validity of the said Creditors several Claims are fully established, and perceiving, by the Votes of the House, that a Bill is depending for the better Government of the Territorial Possessions and Dependencies in India, which, as they apprehend, will, by certain Clauses, essentially affect the just Claims and Property of the said Creditors, unless the Clauses relative thereto are altered and amended, do therefore pray the House to give Leave that they may be heard, at the Bar, by Counfet in their Behalf, and to grant such Relief in the Premises as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Hussey accordingly reported from the said Committee, That he was directed by the Committee to move the House, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, humbly to represent to His Majesty, That His Majesty s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, think themselves bound in Duty humbly to represent to His Majesty, that alarming Reports of an intended DilTolution of Parliament have gone forth:

That His Majesty’s Faithful Commons, dutifully acknowledging the Wisdom of the Constitution, in trolling to the Crown that just and legal Prerogative, and fully confiding in His Majesty's Royal Wisdom and Paternal Care of His People, for the most beneficial Exercise of it, desire, with great Humility, to represent to His Majesty the Inconveniences and Dangers which appear to them, from a Consideration of the State of the Nation, likely to follow from a Prorogation or DilTolution of the Parliament in the present arduous and critical Conjuncture of Affairs: The Maintenance of the Public Credit, and the Support of the Revenue, demand the moll immediate Attention: The Disorders prevailing in the Government of The East Indies, at Home and Abroad, call aloud for instant Reformation; and the State of the East India Company’s Finances, from the prelfing Demands upon them, require a no less immediate Support and Assistance from Parliament:

That His Majesty’s Faithful Commons are at present proceeding with the utmost Diligence upon these great Objects of Government, as recommended to their Attention by His Majesty’s Gracious Speech from the Throne, but which mult necessarily be fniitrated and disappointed by the Delay attending a DilTolution, and most especially the Affairs of The East Indies, by the afiem-bling of a new Parliament, not prepared by previous Enquiry, to enter, with equal Effect, upon an Object involving long and intricate Details, which His Majesty’s Faithful Commons have investigated, for Two Years pad, with the most laborious, earned, and unremitting Attention.

That His Majesty’s Faithful Commons, deeply aff fled by these important Considerations, impressed with the highest Reverence and Affection for His Majesty s Person, and anxious to pveferve the Lul’tre and Safety of His Government, do humbly beseech His Mujefiv, to suffer His faithful Commons to proceed on the ihifiness of the Section, the Furtherance of which is l'o essentially necessary to the Prosperity of the Public; and that His Majesty will be graciously pleased to hearken to the Advice of His Faithful Commons, and not to the l'ecret Advices of particular Persons, who may have private Interests of their own, separate from the true luterel'ts of His Majesty and His People.

And Mr. Hussey moved the House accordingly.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, humbly to represent to His Majesty, That His Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament afi’embled, think themselves bound in Duty humbly to represent to His Majesty, that alarming Reports of an intended DilTolution of Parliament have gone forth.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, think ourftjves bound in Duty humbly to represent to Your Majesty, that alarming Reports of an intended Dilsolution of Parliament have gone forth.

Your Majesty's Faithful Commons, dutifully acknowledging the Wisdom of the Constitution in trailing to the Crown that just and legal Prerogative, and fully confiding in Your Majestys Royal Wisdom and Paternal Care of Your People, for the most beneficial I'.xt reife of it, desire, with great Humility, to represent to Your Majesty, the Inconveniences and Dangers which appear to them, from a Consideration of the State of the Nation, likely to follow from a Prorogation or Dilsolution of the Parliament in the present arduous and critical Conjuncture of Affairs: The Maintenance of the Public Credit, and the Support of the Revenue, demand the most immediate Attention: The Disorders prevailing in the Government of the East at Home and Abroad, call aloud for instant Reformation; and the State of the East India Company's Finances, from the pressing Demands upon them, require a no less immediate Support and Assistance from Parliament.

Your Majesty’s Faithful Commons are at present proceeding, with the utmost Diligence, upon these great Objects of Government, as recommended to their Attention by Your Majesty’s Gracious Speech from the Throne, but which mult necessarily be fraf-, trated and difap|K>inted. by the Delay attending a Diff’olution, and most especially the Affairs of The East Indies, by the assembling of a new Parliament, not prepared, by previous Enquiry, to enter, with equal Erica, upon an Object ' involving long and intricate Details, which Your Majestys Faithful Commons have investigated, for Two Years past, with the most laborious, earned, and unremitting Attention.

Your Majesty’s Faithful. Commons, deeply affected by these important Consulcmtions, impressed with the highest Reverence and Affection for Your Majesty’s Person, and anxious to preserve the Lustre and Safety of Your Government, do humbly beseech Your Majesty to fuller Your faithful Commons to proceed on Vol. 39.

the Business of the - SefBon, the Furtherance of which is <b essentially necessary to the Prosperity of the Public; and that Your Majesty will be graciously pleased to hearken to the Advice of Your Faithful Commons, and not to the secret Advices of particular Persons, who may have private Interests of their own, separate from the true Interests of Your Majesty and Your People.

The said Address being read a Second Time;

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Address, to be presented to His Majesty.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House, as are of His Majesty’s Most Honourable Privy Council, do humbly know His Majesty’s Pleasure, when He will be attended by this House.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to St. Alban’* the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ for ' " ‘ the electing of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Saint Albans, in the County of Hertford, in the room of John Radcliffe, Esquire,

deceased.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Government Morning next, resolve itself into a Committtee of the of East India whole House, upon the Bill for the better Govern- emtones* ment of the Territorial Possessions and Dependencies

in India.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this Hoitfe will, upon Wednesday Reeeipt Duty. Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill to explain and amend so much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for repealing an Act, made in the " Twenty-second Year of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act for charging a Stamp Duty upon " Inland Bills of Exchange, Promissory Notes, or other " Notes, payable otherwise than upon Demand j" and " for granting new Stamp Duties on Bills of Exchange,

THE Lord Sheffield reported from the Committee, who were appointed to consider of the Expediency of purchasing the late Sir Gregory Page's House and Offices on Black with the Garden,

and Fifty-six Acres of Land, for the Purpose of a Royal Military Academy, and to report the same to the House; That the Committee had considered the Matter to them referred, and had directed him to make a Report thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee having examined several Witnesses, in relation to the Matter to them referred, submit the Whole of their Examinations to the Consideration of the House.

Colonel Stchelin, Lieutenant Governor of the Royal Military Academy at Woolwich, informed your Committee, That the Situation of the Barracks in the Warren is very unhealthy, and, facing the Marshes of , is consequently exposed to very bad Air — That the lower Apartments stand upon the Ground, without any Kitchen or Cellar under them, and they are about Four Feet below the Level of Plunutead Road; and when a South or South-West Wind prevails, the Walls and Staircases on that Side are very damfiahd wet — That the Number of Cadets is Sixty-four, and from the Number that are sick hi the Course of the Year, occasions a great Interruption in their Attendance upon their Studies — That Twenty-two have been ill with Agues within a Twelvemonth, or little ibore; and several of them, though cured, have relapsed, and are so subject to it, as to be every Day convalescent; which he imputes to the Situation of the Place — That none of the Cadets have died at Woolwich during the Si* Years of his Employment — That he ha* been Thirty-seven Years in and about Woolwich — That there are Seventeen Rooms appropriated to the Sixty-four Cadets — That when they are extremely ill, and no Hopes of their getting the better of the Disorder, they are lent to their Friends — That Two have been sent away very lately on Account of bad Health. — Being asked. If any had died in their Absence, Whether a Return would not have been made thereof? he said, He apprehends there would; but does not remember any such Return being ever made — That there are Five Beds in each of the Cadets Rooms. — Being asked, Whether there were other Students betides Cadets? he said, There are about Seven, and loine-times Ten; extra Students — That there are Two Sets of Barracks; the Rooms in the old Barracks measure 17$ Feet by 15I Feet, and the Height is 8f Feet; and the Rooms in the new. Barracks are 9 Feet high — That the Rooms are some upon the Ground, and some above Stairs — That the Barracks of the Cadets are not so healthy as those of the Officers, os being more exposed to the bad Air — That the Barracks are above the Level of the River at High Water — That the Cadets are not permitted to go out of the Warren without Leave or Pafles — That they dine in a Common Hall — That the Establishment has been increased, about a Twelvemonth, from 48 to 64 — That the Officers are not increased, except One additional Master — That there are no additional Buildings for the additional Number — That the Academy is roomy enough, but the Hall is not, there being scarcely Room to Itir — Tjiat thore are Two Academies, an upper one and a lower one — That there is a Lecture Room, that will hardly hold Eight

Persons and the Lc6lurer. — Being asked. Whether he really thought the whole Buildings insufficient for the Purpose of the Institution? he said, He thinks they are. — Being asked, Whether he thought so before the increased Establishment ? he said, He thought it was necessary there should be another Room for the Lefitures and Models — That the Academy was first built under the Direction of the Duke of Montagu, in the Year 1741, when he was Master of the Ordnance, and that it was then approved; and from that Academy the Regiment of Artillery and Engineers were formed, with few Exceptions. — Being asked, Whether he remembers any Time, that the Artillery could not be supplied with Officers? he said, Yes, about Two Years ago there were Twenty or Thirty Vacancies, which could not be supplied. — Being asked. Whether he experienced any Inconvenience from the Rooms being appropriated to other Purposes? he said, Yes, they could not read the Lectures in the Academy, for they must have brought in Models, which there is no Room for — That the present Model, on that Account, is obliged to be drawn uj) to the Cieling, and let down when Lectures are to be read. — Being asked, If there is not a Library there, and Mathematical Instruments, and other Machines necessary for the Institution? and how they were disposed of? he laid. There is not a proper Provision of Rooms for them. — Being asked, Whether, at the Time he mentions the Twenty Vacancies to have been in the Regiment of Artillery, it did not arise from some particular Form in the Establishment, by adding additional Officers ? he laid, It was before that Time. — And being asked, What occasioned those Vacancies ? he said, By an Augmentation during the War in the Companies, they being increased from Sixty to One hundred — That there were Ten Companies, and Four Battalions, and One Officer to each Company.

That People of all Descriptions go into the Warren, and it is not in the Power of the Officers to prevent the Cadets talking to those People — That they wish to prevent that Communication very much, as they think their Conduct and Morals would be better — Being asked. Whether, in Spite of all the Orders to the contrary, the Cadets do not get out sometimes without Leave? he said, Frequently. Being asked, Whether he thought any Discipline would prevent any Irregularity of the young Men, situated as they are in the Town of Woolwich ? he said, He thinks not. — Being asked, Whether there are not Circumstances in the State of the Town of Woolwich, that might lead him to think that* their

Morals may suffer by their getting out into the Town improperly ? he said, He does think so. — Being asked, Whether those Inconveniences, applied in the Three last Questions, would not equally apply to the new House on Black Heath ? he said, He believes the Distance of the new House is about a Mile from and he thinks that Distance is sufficiently great to prevent much an Evil of that Kind. — Being asked. Whether he did dot apprehend that, at Sir Gregory Page's House, it will be more easy to prevent the Access of improper Persons, and more in the Power of the Governor of the Academy to enforce good Order and Discipline, according to the present Regulations ? he said, He thinks it will, from the Circumstance of the whole Institution being in one House, and entirely by itself. — Being desired to inform the Committee, Whether, from his Observations, the Liberty the Cadets have had of mixing with the common People at JVootwich, has in the least Degree prevented the Academy from fending forth Men, that have been in their Profession a Credit to their Country and the Establishment? and whether Complaints have been frequent, that their Manners and Morals have been vitiated hv such Communication? he said, lie does not know it has,

Your Committee then called Doctor James Irwin; who informed them, That he had attended the Gentlemen of the Academy at Woolwich Forty Years — That Twenty Years ago the Cadets were in Lodgings in the Town, before the Barracks were built; at which Time they were more healthy than they have been since the Barracks have been built — That there were very few Cadets then; about Forty, and afterwards increased to Forty-eight — That he had made a Memorandum of the State of their Health for the last Three Years; viz.

In 1781, there were 68 Sick.

In 1782, — — 66

In 1783, — — 50

That many of them, though cured, have frequently

relap fed, Six or Seven Times in the Year — That the Number the Academy confided of in 1781, when 68 are stated to be sick, was only 48. — Being asked. Why he thought the Air worfc in the Warren than in the Town of Woolwich? he said, Because nearer the Marshes; and the North-East Wind blows upon them, which brings on Agues. — Being asked, Whether he thought their Sickuels arose in any Degree from the small Dimensions of their Rooms, and the Number of Gentlemen lying in such Rooms respectively? he said. Certainly, there are too many in a Room, Being asked, How many upon an Average lie in a Room ? he said, From Four to Five; and that they spend their lime in those Rooms, when not at their Study. — Being asked the Question, he said, There are more Houses in Woolwich now than formerly, but cannot say the Gentlemen can be lodged in it — That there are Seventeen Rooms in the Barracks, and Sixty-four Cadets — That he believes there are other Students besides Cadets. — Being asked, What Accommodation the Cadets have when they are ill ? he laid, There is an Hospital, consisting of Two Rooms; and when the Beds are down there is scarce Room to move — That he has not had any die; when they are very ill, they are sent to their Friends; and if any die, a Return would be made of their Deaths; but he does not remember any Instance of it — Being

asked, If he had any Instances of Gentlemen returning well? he said, Yes; and of their relapsing again, Six or Seven Times in the Year. — Being asked, If Agues were ever fatal, or cured by Change of Air ? he said.

Not fatal; often cured by Change of Air. — That the Expence of Medicine is considerable, and would be avoided by removing to Black Heath. — Being asked,

If the Cadets were brought up hardy ? he said, They are. — Being asked, Whether he has known many Soldiers, whole Constitutions have been shakened by Agues, and rendered unfit, for ever, for Service ? he said, He has, great Numbers. — Being asked. If he believed and was well allured, that there are such Inconveniences in the present Circumstances and Situation of the Academy at Woolwich, as to make it a desirable Object to be removed? he said, He thinks so certainly. — Being asked, Whether he had viewed and seen the late Sir Gregory Page's House on Black Heath; and whether he thought it a more desirable Situation, and much better adapted for the Conduct of the Cadets, and all the Purposes of the Academy, than the present Situation? he laid. He had not viewed it, but the Air is much better — That he has had 15 or 16 sick at a Time at W;put now he has only Four, this not being the sickly Sealbn. — Being asked, If he could tell the Nature of the Disease ? he said, They are intermittent — That feme have been ill Three Months — That he does not put their Names upon the Sick Lift, until they come into the Hospital — That sometimes Barracks are converted into Hof-pitals.

Mr; Eden, frotn the Select Committee, appointed Smuggling, id enquire into the illicit Practices now used in defrauding the Revenue of this Kingdom, and the most effectual Methods of preventing the fame, and to report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House, acquainted the House, That the Committee had made feme Progrefe in the Matters to them referred; and had directed him to make a Report thereof, together with a Resolution of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the fame, together with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report was read; and the Resolution of the Committee is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, that the illicit Practices used in defrauding the Revenue have increased in a most alarming Degree; that those Practices are carried on upon the Coasts, and in other Parts of this Kingdom, with a Violence and with Outrages which not only threaten the Destruction of the Revenue, but are highly injurious to regular Commerce and fair Trade, very pernicious to the Manners and Morals of the People, and an Interruption of all good Government; that the more secret illicit Practices in the internal Excise of this Kingdom, have also greatly increased; that the Public Revenue is defrauded to an Extent of not leis than Two Millions per Annum; and that these Enormities, and great National Lodes, well deserve the earliest and most serious Attention of Parliament.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Report, with the Appendix, be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Tuesday the 20th Day of January next.

The said Report is preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session.

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That he had received from Vice Admiral Sir Edward Hughes, Knight of the Most Honourable Order of the Bath, and Commodore Richard King, the following Letters, in Return to the Thanks of this House, signified to them by Mr. Speaker, in Obedience to their Commands of the 17th Day of December, in the last Session of Parliament:

Superb, in Madras Road, lft September 1783.

Sir,

I hud the Honour to receive, Two Days ago, by His Majesty’s Ship Crocodile, your very obliging letter of the lSth December, inclosing the Vote of Thanks of the Honourable House of Commons to me, for the im|)ortant Services performed by the Squadron under my Command in The East Indies, on the 17th of February, and 12th of April, of the last Year; and also the Vote of Thanks of the same Honourable House to Commodore Richard King, the Captains, Officers, and Seamen of the Ships under my Command at that Time.

I tfteem myself greatly obliged to you. Sir, by the very polite and friendly Manner in which you have been pleased to communicate the Vote of Thanks of the Honourable House to me and the brave Men who served with me on those Days; and, as I really want Words to express the strong Scnic 1 entertain of the great Honour conltrrcd on me by that Honourable House, I earnestly reqtuTt you will, Sir, be pleased to express in the belt Manner, my sincereft Gratitude to tire Vo l. 30.

Honourable House of Commons, for the very great Honour they have been pleased to do me, and their favourable Acceptation of my Services.

I remain, with great Regard and Respect, Sir,

Your most obedient.

Humble Servant,

Edward Hughes.

The Right honourable Charles I Vols ran Cornwall, Speaker of the House of Commons.

Hero, it Madras, September lft, 1783.

Sir,

The Approbation of my Country, signified to me Commodore in your Letter of the 12th of December 1782, hath imprefied me with the deepest Sense of Gratitude and Thank*. Respect; and I shall ever regard it as the most fortunate Period of my Life, that my Endeavours to do my Duty in the Service of my King and Country in The East Indies, on the 17th of , and 12th

of April, 1782, have been deemed worthy of such public and recorded Testimony as the Thanks of the Honourable House of Commons.

Permit me. Sir, to make my Acknowledgment to you, for the very obliging Manner . in which you have been pleased to communicate the Sense of the House to me.

I have the Honour to be, with the greatest Respect,

Sir,

Your most obedient, and

Most hundble Servant,

R. King.

And the Order of the Day being accordingly read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the State of the Nation;

The House resolvfed itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Hussey took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker refuined the Chair.

Mr. Hussey reported from the Committee, That they had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report, and had also directed him to make a Motion to the House, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be now received.

Mr. Hussey accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered iu at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followed!; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion «f this Committee, Tlat, for any Person or Persons in His Majesty’s Treasury, or in the Exchequer, or in the Bank of England, or for any Person or Persons whatsoever employed in the Payment of Public Money, to pay or direct or cause to be paid, any Sum or Sums of Money, for or towards the Support of Services voted n the present Session of Parliament, after the Parliament shall have been prorogued or dissolved, if it shall be prorogued or dissolved before any Act of Parliament shall have passed appropriating the Supplies to such Services, will be a high Crime and Misdeameanour, a daring Breach of a Public Trust, derogatory to the fundamental Privileges of Parliament, and subversive of the Constitution of this Country.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be laid before the House, Accounts of the several Sums of Money issued, or ordered to be issued, from the 19th Day of December 1783, to the 12th Day of January 1784, inclusive, to any Person or Persons, towards Naval Services, or for the Charges of the Office of Ordnance, or to the Secretaries of His Majesty’s Treasury, or to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, on Account of the Paymaster General of His Majesty’s Forces, or in any other Manner whatever, for and towards Services voted in the present Session of Parliament, but not yet appropriated, by any Act of Parliament, to such Services.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in the present Situation of His Majesty’s Dominions, it is peculiarly necessary that there should be an Administration which has the Confidence of this House and the Public.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the late Changes in His Majesty’s Councils were immediately preceded by dangerous and univerlal Reports, that His Majesty’s Sacred Name had been unconftitutionally abused, to afifeft the Deliberations of Parliament; and that the Appointments made were accompanied by Circumstances new and extraordinary, and such as do not conciliate or engage the Confidence of this House.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House. ob

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the Message from House, That he had a Message from His Majesty to the King — this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented Deffian the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. roopi’ Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered): and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty thinks it proper to acquaint the House of Commons, that the Two last Divisions of Hessian Troops, which were employed in America in the Service of Great Britain, not having arrived in The Downs, the Place of their Rendezvous, until the setting in of the Frost in the River Weser had made it impracticable for them to proceed immediately to the Place of their final Dcftination; His Majesty has found it unavoidably necessary to order the said Troops to be disembarked, and to be stationed in the Barracks at Hilsea, Dover, and Chatham; and at the same Time has given Directions, that they shall be re-embarked and sent Home as soon as the IVeser is navigable, every necessary Preparation for that Purpose having, by His Majesty’s Orders, been already made. , „

A PETITION of the several Trustees for putting in Execution an Act of Parliament, made in the Fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty King George the Third, intituled, "An Act for repairing and widening the Road from Odd

" House, in the County of Nottingham, to the Crols " Poll upon Smalley Common, in the County of Derby, and from Ilkeston to the Towns of Heanor and Shipley, in the said County of Derby, and from Trcar ell, " in the County of Nottingham, to the Town of Nottingham,"whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was

presented to the House and read; Setting forth. That the Trustees have proceeded to put the said Act in Execution, and have made great Progress in repairing and widening the Road therein described, but find that several of the Powers granted by the said Act are defective, hnd require Amendment; and that several Sums of Money have been borrowed upon the Credit of the Tolls arising by virtue of the said Act, which still remain due, and the Term of the said Act is near expiring; and that the said Roads cannot be effectually amended and kept in Repair, nor can the Money now due on the Credit of the Tolls be discharged, unless the Term and Powers granted by the said Act be further enlarged: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers of the said Act, in such Manner as to the House shall fectn meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Lord Eduard Bentinck, Mr. Vox.. i!9.

Frederick Montagu, &c.: And they are to meet upon Friday Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

In Support of the Allegations of the said Petition, your Committee find. That by an Act made in the Second and Third Years of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, intituled, "An Act for incorporating " the Proprietors of the Water Works in York Buildtags, and for encouraging their carrying on and " settling the said Water Works," the said Governor and Company were incorporated, and enabled to purchase, enjoy, and alien, Lands, Tenements, Hereditaments,

Goods, and Chattels, to them and their Successors, and give, grant, demise, alien, and dispose of their Lands, Tenements, Hereditaments, Goods, and Chattels, and do and execute all other Things, by Name of Incorporation, that to them should appertain, and to use a Common Seal to serve for all their Business; and the said Act appointed a Governor, and Six of the said Company, to be called Assistants, to have the Direction of all the Affairs of the said Company.

thereby directed and im powered, without waiting the Conclusion of the ranking of all or any of the said Governor and Company’s Creditors, to proceed (at the Suit or upon the Application of any Person or Persons having Interest) to the Sale of the Estates of the Company lying in Scotland, by public Auction, to the highest Bidder or Bidders, and that either in separate Baronies, or in Smaller Lots, as to them should appear most for the Interest of the Governor and Company and dieir Creditors; and for that Purpose the said Judges were thereby im powered and directed to proceed to the Consideration of the Proof then taken, and to take what further Proofs to them should seem necessary, of the Rent or Value of the said Lands and Estates, and of the Deductions from the said Rent, and thereupon to ascertain and determine the Yearly Free Rental of the said Lands and Estates, and of the different Lots in which the same ought to be exposed to Sale, and also the Value or Number of Years Purchase at which the said Lands might and ought to be exposed to public Auction or Sale: And it was further enacted, That in pursuance of such Sale or Sales, or upon the Purchaser or Purchasers finding Security, as is thereinbefore directed, the Judges of the Court of Session should pronounce and give out their Decree or Decrees of Sale in Favour of such Purchaser or Purchasers, in the same Form and Manner, and to the same Effect, as such Decrees are given by the said Court in the Sale of other Bankrupt Estates; and that the said Purchasers should have good and undoubted Title to the Lands and Estates purchased by them respectively, free of all Defects of Title, Incumbrances, and Debts of any Sort, excepting always such of the Debts of the Company as might be allocated on the said respective Purchasers for exhausting the Price offered by them, which should remain a Debt upon the said Purchasers on whom the same should be allocated, and a Charge upon the Lands so purchased by them respectively, until the same should be fully paid up and discharged.

And it was further enacted, That in case the ranking of the Creditors should not be settled and ascertained by Decree of the Court of Session, before the Time of Payment of the Purchase Money of the Lands and Estates io to be sold as aforesaid, the Purchaser or Purchasers should continue to hold the Purchase Money under the Security first taken for the fame, at such Rate of Interest, not being more than One and an Half per Centum per Annum under the legal Interest, as the Judges should determine, until they should issue their Warrants upon the Purchaser or Purchasers for Payment to the Creditors, according as they should be ranked and preferred by the said Judges, or for consigning the said Purchase Money in the Royal Bank in Scotland, or in the Bank of Scotland, for the Use and Behoof of, and to be forthcoming to the Creditors as aforesaid, or for re-employing the Purchase Money in such other Manner as should appear to the Judges to be most beneficial for the Interest of the said Governor and Company, and their Creditors: And after taking Notice, that it would be prejudicial to such Creditors as by their Rights or Diligences were entitled to early Payment out of the Estates of the said Company, to wait the Conclusion of the ranking of the other Creditors before they could draw their Money, it was enacted, That the Judges of the Court of Session should, and they were thereby directed, without waiting the claffing or ranking of the other Creditors, to issue their Acts and Warrants upon the Purchaser or Purchasers for Payment to such Creditors as had been or should be found preferable on the Estates of the Company, of such Sums of Money as should be found due to such Creditors: And it was further enacted, That all and every Sum and Sums of Money which should appear to the Judges of the Court of Session to be due to

A Petition of the Governor and Company of the Bank of Scotland, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act of the Parliament of Scotland, made in the Year 1C95, intituled, "An Act for erecting a Bank in Scotland,'' a Joint Stock, amounting to the Sum of Twelve hundred thousand Pounds Scots Money, or One hundred thousand Pounds Sterling, was allowed to be raised and paid Vol. 39.

in the Manner by the said Act directed; and it was thereby declared, that the Persons subscribing and paying to the said Stock in Manner therein directed, should be One Body Politic and Corporate, by the.

Name of The Governor and Company of the Bank of Scotland, under which Name they , should have perpetual Succession, and should have a Common Seal, and certain Rules were thereby prescribed, for the better ordering and managing the Affairs of the said Bank; and* under the said Act, and the Rules and Orders therein mentioned, the said Bank was soon after established, and has ever firice continued; and that, by an Act, passed in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to enable " the Governor and Company of the Bank of " land to encrease the Capital Stock of the said Company," it was enacted, that, within One Month after the passing of the said Act, or as soon after as might be, the Court of ordinary Directors of the said Bank should appoint a Book to be opened, and kept at the Office of the said Bank of Scotland, for receiving Subscriptions for an additional Capital or Joint Stock, to the Extent of Twelve hundred thousand Pounds Scots, or One hundred thousand Pounds Sterling Money, and no more, in which Book every Person or Persons, possessed of a Share or Shares of the then Capital Stock of the said Bank of Scotland, should be entitled to subscribe for as much of the said new or additional Stock as he, she, or they should possess of the old or original Stock at the Time of his, her, or their subscribing, and no more, or for a lesser Number of Shares, if such Person or Persons should so think proper; and that a Subscription was accordingly opened, and the said new or additional Capital or Joint Stock of Twelve hundred thousand Pounds Scots, or One hundred thousand Pounds Sterling Money, hath been subscribed for and paid into the said Bank, pursuant to the last in part recited Act; and that the said Bank, being a National Advantage, a further Increase of its Capital Stock would hill tend greatly to the Advancement of Commerce and Agriculture, and be otherwise highly beneficial to the Public: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Governor and Company of the Bank of Scotland further to encrease the Capital Stock of the said Company, under such Restrictions, Rules, and Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

and that the Commissioners, in pursuance of the Powers vested in them by the said Acts, have expended very large Sums of Money in erecting a large Pier and Key at or near the Mouth of the said River, in deepening the Channel of the said Port, in making several necessary Alterations and Additions in the said Pier, and in making divers other Works for the Improvement and Security of the said Port, Haven, and River, whereby great Advantages have arisen to the Navigation of the said River; and that the East End of the said Pier, from the Force and Violence of the Sea and Land Floods, and the Badneis of its Foundation, is at present in a ruinous State, and likely to fall down, and, in case the same should fall into the River, the Petitioners apprehend it will be injurious to the Trade and Navigation of the said Port, elpccially as the Mouth of the River may by that Means be choaked up, and the Passage of Ships and VesscU in and out of the said Harbour thereby totally prevented, to the great Prejudice and Obstruction of the Trade and Navigation of the said River, Port, and Haven; and that the Commissioners, for the avoiding thereof, have been advised by an able and experienced Engineer, and intended to have taken down a considerable Part of the said Pier, and to have rebuilt the same in a different Direction, so as that the Sea and Land Floods might not aft with such Violence thereon; and also be more beneficial to the Navigation of the said River, Port, and Haven; and they had actually begun that Work, but the Money to arise from the Duties granted by the said Two last mentioned Acts being infidiicnt for the Purpose of carrying on the said Work, they were thereby prevented from succeeding in the lame; and that the Expences of taking down and rebuilding that Part of the said Pier, and of such other Works, will, upon a moderate Computation, amount to 60,000l. and upwards; and that the Commissioners have borrowed Money on the Credit of the Duties payable by the said Acts, and are also indebted several Sums of Money on Account of the Works that have been carried on in pursuance of the said Acts; and the Petitioners are advised that the Navigation of the said River, Port, and Haven, might be further improved and extended, and that it would be of great Advantage to the Trade of the said Port of Sunderland, if the Wages of Persons, employed in casting Coals and Ballast from and out of Keels in the said River, Port, and Haven, into and from Ships and Keels there, were regulated and fixed: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to repeal the said several Acts of Parliament relative to improving and preserving of the said River, Port, and Haven, and to appoint Commissioners with full Powers to improve and extend the Navigation of the said River, Port, and Haven, and to raise sufficient Duties to be applied towards defraying the Expence of improving and extending the lame; and that the said Commissioners may have Power to regulate and fix the Wages of Persons employed in casting Coals and Ballast in the said River, Port, and Haven, as to the House shall seem meet.

The foregoing Anfuers contain every Information that the Office affords, in Obedience to the Orders of the House; but they do not include the Whole of the Works intended for the Three principal Dock Yards of Portsmouth, Plymouth, and Chatham.

in the Report laid before this Honourable House, on the Estimate of the Ordnance for the Year 1783, it was observed, " The Fortifications at Home depend upon the System that may be adopted. At the Cloie of " the lait War, the few Field Works that had been thrown up were totally neglected, and suffered to go to Ruin; " the (.'onfcquence of which was, an immense sudden Expence at the breaking out of this War. An opposite " Extreme of Fortifying every where has been since pursued. It is at present proposed to confine future Works to the principal Dock Yards. It is computed that to render and Plymouth complete, will- require

" 4 or .',00,000l. which, at 30,000l. per Annum, will be done in Eight or Ten Years. The other Sums for Fortifications are only for Repairs and Improvements of old Works, and to finish such Works in various Places " as are nearly done, or may be in lbme Degree completed at a small additional Expence, without which that " already laid out would be entirely thrown away."

The particular Plans will require much Time to digest and estimate. Improvements may be suggested, and Variations uppear adviseable, as the Ground is cleared, and the Works go on; but it is believed the whole Amount for Portsmouth and Plymouth need not exceed the Sums above mentioned. — The System for Chatham is now under Consideration; until it is determined, no Guess can be made as to the whole Expence that may attend it

No new Works of any great Importance are intended in any other Part of the Kingdom.

Richmond, &c.

Master General.

Then it was moved to resolve, That an Attempt in any One Branch of the Legislature to suspend the Execution of Law, by separately assuming to itself the Direction of a discretionary Power, which, by Act of Parliament, is vested in any Body of Men, to be exercised as they shall judge expedient, is unconstitutional.

Moved to resolve, That, according to the known Principles of this excellent Constitution, the undoubted Authority of appointing to the great Offices of executive Government is solely vested in His Majesty, and that this House has every Reason to place the firmest Reliance on His Majesty’s Wisdom, in the Exercise of this Prerogative.

The Question was put thereupon.

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Resolved by the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, in Parliament assembled, That, according to the known Principles of this excellent Constitution, the undoubted Authority of appointing to the great Offices of executive Government, is solely vested in His Majesty, and that this House has every Reason to place the firmest Reliance on His Majesty’s Wisdom in the Exercise of this Prerogative.

Moved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to acknowledge, with great Satisfaction, the Wisdom of our happy Constitution, which places in His Majesty’s Hand the undoubted Authority of appointing to all the great Offices of executive Government; we have the firmest Reliance on His Majesty’s known Wisdom and paternal Goodness, that He will always be anxious to call into and continue in His Service, Men the most deserving of the Confidence of His Parliament and the Public in general.

In this Confidence, we beg Leave to approach His Majesty with our moll earnest Assurances, that we will, on all Occasions, support His Majesty in the just Exercise of those Prerogatives which the Wisdom of the Law has entrusted to His Majesty, for the Preservation of our Lives and Properties: and upon the due and uninterrupted Exercise of which must depend the Blessings which His People derive from the belt of all Forms of Government.

The Question was put thereupon.

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

A Petition of the Governor, Deputy Governor, Af- Exeter Poor, fistants, and Guardians of the Poor, of the City and County of Exon, under their Common Seal, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act passed in the 9th and 10th Years of King William the Third, the Petitioners were incorporated for the better maintaining of the Poor of the City and County of Exon, with Power to raise a certain Annual Sum for that Purpose; and, by another Act, passed in the 31st Year of King George the Second, they were impowered to raise a certain Sum, to discharge a then incurred Debt; and that the Petitioners were, by another Act, passed in the 14th Year of His present Majesty, impowered to raise a certain Sum, for Discharge of a Debt then due, and also to raise an additional Annual Income for the several Purposes therein mentioned; and that, by the great Increase of the Poor of the said City and County, by the increased Price of Provisions, and the Expences incurred in embodying the Militia, the Petitioners have been obliged to contra6t a Debt of 3,500l. and upwards, which they are unable to discharge, and are therefore rendered quite incapable of anfuering the Purposes of the above-mentioned Acts: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enabling them to raise Money for Payment and Discharge of their Debt, and also to raise such further Sum, for the more effectual Support of the Poor of the said City, as the House shall think proper.

A Petition and Representation of Sir Ashton , Lem’* Knight, was presented to the House, and read; Setting Muftum, forth. That the Petitioner, in the early Part of his Life, having a Turn for Natural History, began to collect Specimens and Articles of every Kind, and, being flattered by his great Succcfs, resolved to remove his Museum to the Metropolis, not doubting but he could make it, by its Pre-eminence over all other Collections, of public Benefit, and a National Honour; and that, notwithstanding the Difficulty and Expence of this Undertaking, he entered upon it with determined Spirit, and pursued it in such a Manner as to have secured every capital Article that has offered itself, and, by selecting out of some Hundred Thousand Specimens, has actually formed a Collection superior to any Thing of the Kind in , or perhaps

to them all united, as it comprehends Subjects so rare and valuable as are not to be found in any other Cabinet; and that the Petitioner has perl'evered in this Pursuit at a very great Expence, encouraged by a firm Belief that it might be rendered worthy the Attention of the Public, in which he has been confirmed by the Opinion of Persons of the first Consequence; but it is now grown too great a Concern for any Individual, and that, notwithstanding this Collection has been thuB made, in Hopes that it would have been purchased for the Use and Benefit of the Public, yet, from the critical Situation of the Times, it has been thought improper to apply for the Indulgence of Parliament in the Mode he intended otherwise to have done, and it cannot easily be disposed of in the common Way of Sale: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to authorize and empower the Petitioner, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, to sell and dispose of the said Museum and Colle6iion, and the several Pieces composing the fame, in such Manner as the Petitioner, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, shall think proper, without being liable or subject to any Penalty or Forfeiture, imposed by any Act or Acts of Parliament against any Sale or Sales by Way of Lottery or Lots, Tickets, Numbers, or Figures; and that such Sale or Sales lo to be made of the said Museum, and of the several Pieces composing the fame, by the Petitioner, his Executors, Administrators, or Assigns, (before a Day in the Act to be specified) may be good and valid, any Law or Statute to the contrary thereof notwithstanding; or otherwise as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Right honourable James Earl of Derby, Lord of- the Manor of Meriden, in the County of Warwick, the Right honourable Earl of

Aylesford, Patron of the Vicarage Owner, of the Impropriate Tythes, and of about One Third Part of the Open Field Lands and Meadows, and of the old inclosed Lands, within the Parish of Meriden aforesaid, and the humble Petition of the Reverend Anthony Blijs, Vicar of the said Parish, and of the several other Owners of Open Field Lands and Meadows, and of old iuclofed Lands within the same, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That there are, within the said Parish of Meriden, about 100 Acres of Open Field Lands and Meadows, the Property of several Persons, lying intermixed in small Parcels, and in a very inconvenient Manner, in Parts of the Parish remote from each other, and subject, at particular Sea-fons, to a Right of Common over the fame, which it would be greatly to the Advantage of the Proprietors to enjoy in Severalty, freed and exonerated from all Manner of Rights of Tythes and Common, and for that Purpose to hnve specilic Shares allotted to them; and that there are also, within the said Parish, several old inclosed Lands, the Proprietors whereof are very desirous that the same should be exonerated from Tythes, and to make Compensation to the Impropriator and Vicar for their Right of Tythes over the fame; and that there is moreover, within the said Parish, a Tract of Heath, or Waite, confuting of upwards of 300 Acres of Land, and also some small Parcels of Land, lying dispersedly about the Parish, subject to the Right of Soil of the said Lord of the Manor, and to a Right of Pasturage of the several Owners of Estates in Meriden over the fame, but which, in their present barren and uncultivated state, yield very little Advantage to the Persons interested therein; and that the Petitioners are desirous that the said Heath and Commonable Pastures may be applied (after making Compensation to the said Lord of the Manor for his Right of Soil over the fame) as to the Remainder of them, to go in Aid of the Satisfaction to be made to the said Impropriator and Vicar for their Right of Tythes over the said Open Fields and Meadows, and over the old inclosed Lands, Heath, and Commonable Places, and, if the Shares of the Proprietors of Open Field Lands and Meadows are not of sufficient Value to exonerate them, then that the Residue of the Satisfaction be made out of their Open Field Lands and Meadows for such Tythes, but, if the Shares of the Proprietors of old Inclosures shall not be of sufficient Value to exonerate them, then that the Residue of the Satisfaction be made by Annual Payments ilfuing out of such inclosed Lands, or by Sums in Gross, so far as relates to the Impropriate Tythes, as shall be agreed between the Parties and the Impropriator; and that the said Proprietors, at a numerous Meeting held at the Bull's Head in Meriden, on Saturday the 8th of November last (pursuant to Advertisements inserted in the Birmingham and Coventry Newspapers for that Purpose) entered into Articles of Agreement for carrying the said Matters into Execution, for which Purpose they appointed Commissioners to make Compensation to the Lord of the Manor for his Right of Soil over the said Heath and Wastes, and to the Impropriator and Vicar for their respeCiive Rights of Tythes over the said Heath and Wastes, and also over the Open Field Lands, and Meadows, and over the old inclosed Lands within the said Parish, to settle and determine the several Claims of Common Rights, both over the Open Fields and Meadows, and over the said Wastes and Commonable Places, and to let out specilic Shares for

02

the Proprietors of Open Field Lands and Meadows, and to do all other Things necessary for completing the said Inclosure and Exoneration; and that the said Commissioners have made a considerable Progress in the said Business, and will shortly complete the same; but the Proceedings under the said Agreement cannot be rendered effectual without the Sanction and Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for establishing and confirming the Provisions made under the said Articles of Agreement, and the Proceedings of the Commissioners for carrying the same into Execution, in such Manner as to the House shall leem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Calvert and the Lord Hinchingbrook do prepare, and

bring in, the lame.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names Pawn-are thereunto lubscribed, on Behalf of themselves and broker*, others, Pawnbrokers within the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Bills of Mortality, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Thirtieth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for the more effectual Punishment of Persons who shall attain, or attempt to attain, Possession of Goods or Money by false or untrue Pretences, for preventing the unlawful pawning of Goods, for the easy Redemption of Goods pawned, and for other Purposes, certain Regulations were established for conducting the Business of a Pawnbroker; and that the said Act does not limit or ascertain the Amount of Charges for Warehouse Room, to be paid to the Pawnbroker, and therefore the Petitioners have, almost ever since the making of the said Act, taken such Sums of Money for the Warehouse Room of the Goods pledged, as have, in their Apprehension, been reasonable, and were necessary for the decent Maintenance of themselves and Families; and that the Petitioners and others, in the conducting of the said Business, have oftentimes refused to take Money tendered to them for the Redemption of Goods pledged, because such Money was inadequate to their necessary Expences, and, in Consequence of some of such Refusals, Actions at Law have been brought against several Pawnbrokers, in which such Tenders have been considered to be luflicient, and Verdicts have been given thereon against such Pawnbrokers; and the Petitioners and others, in endeavouring to obtain a reasonable Profit in their said Business, are liable, notwithstanding the said Act, to be feed at Law for supposed Offences against the Laws relating to Usury; and that, in case the Petitioners were to receive such inadequate Tenders, and the Trade is to be conducted on such low Terms, the Petitioners will not be able to carry on the fame, but it must be totally annihilated, whereby the Petitioners and their Families, and all others carrying on that Business,' must be driven to seek their Livelihoods by other Employments; and the said Act is in other respects

defective,

John Spottincoode, Esquire, being examined, said, That the most beneficial Consequepces to Individuals, and the Community at large, have arisen from the Establishment of public Schools, under the Authority and Directionalof the said Act — That although, at the Time when the same was passed, the Salaries thereby provided for the Schoolmasters might afford them a competent Support, the same are now, by Reaion of the Decrease of the Value of Money, and the very great Advance on the Price of every Ne-cessary of life, become very inadequate to their decent Maintenance — That, in order to promote the great and important Obieft, the proper Education of Youth in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, it is expedient that a public School be established in every Parish, and that the Masters of such Schools should be more comfortably provided for, and put on a more decent and respectable Footing, than they have hitherto been where such public Schools have been established by virtue of the said Act of Parliament

The House, according to Order, proceeded to take Smuggling, into further Consideration the Report, which, upon Wednesday the 24tl%Day of December last, was made from the Select Committee, appointed to enquire into the illicit Practices now used in defrauding the Revenue of this Kingdom, and the moll effectual Methods of preventing the fame; and to report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

And the Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

Resolved, Netmne contradicente. That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution,

That it appears, that the illicit Practices used in defrauding the Revenue have increased in a moll alarming Degree; that those Practices are carried on upon the Coalts, and in other Parts of this Kingdom, with a Violence and with Outrages which not only threaten the Deltruction of the Revenue, but are highly injurious to regular Commerce and fair Trade, very pernicious to the Manners and Morals of the People, and an Interruption of all good Government; that the more secret illicit Practices in the internal Excise of this Kingdom have also greatly increased; that the Public Revenue is defrauded to an Extent of not less than Two Millions per Annum-, and that these Enormities and great National Losses well deserve the earliell and most serious Attention of Parliament

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into Supply, a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That an Expedition having been concerted against the Spanish Settlements in The Philippine Islands, the same was undertaken by Troops composed of His Majesty’s 79th Regiment of Foot, and Europeans and Sepoys in the Service of the East India Company, who were transported to the Island of Luconia, in His Majesty’s Squadron commanded by Vice Admiral Cornish, assisted by fotne Ships belonging to the India Company, and, on the 6th of October 1762, the City of Manila was taken by Storm, and the City of Caviti surrendered without an Attack; and that the City of Manila, on the 2d of November following, was delivered up to certain Agents authorized by the East India Company to receive the same,

in Conformity to the Directions given by His Majesty to General Draper, who commanded the Land Forces employed upon the Expedition; and that His Majesty, anxious to preserve the said Conquest, gave Directions to His Admirals and Generals to be assisting to the Officers of the East India Company in holding Possession thereof, until His Royal Will and Pleasure should be further signified with regard to the future Disposition of the said Conquest, which was to depend entirely and absolutely upon His Majesty; and the India Company not having lent more Officers and Servants upon the Expedition than were necessary to take Charge of the City of Manila, and it being judged of great Importance that a Sea Officer should command at Caviti, where the Naval Arsenals and Storehouses were situate, Captain was appointed Governor of the City and District of;

and that Admiral Cornish, thinking it proper to (end Captain Kempenfelt to England with his Dispatches, ap|iointed the Petitioner to succeed him in the Government of Caviti, and, the Petitioner’s Commission, under the Admiral’s Hand and Seal, bears Date the 14th of November 1762, and he actually entered upon the Charge of Lieutenant Governor accordingly by virtue of the said Commission; and that Admiral Cornish having nearly repaired his Squadron by the Beginning of February 176,}, and being about to depart from Manila, the India Company’s Deputy Governor, on the 3d of that Month, represented to Admiral Cornish, that be had not the faintest Hope of prefer?-Vo 1. 39.

And also Lieutenant Governor Copley was heard: Who acquainted the House, That he did not set up the Chain, but only kept it up, as a Thing of great Use and Service to tl»e Place; and that he was desired by the Custom House Officers so to do; and produced a Certificate of those Officers for that Purpose: And also informed the House, That the former Lieutenants had received the like Duty, particularly in Colonel Gilbye's and Lord Time.

And then the Petitioners, and Witnesses, and Colonel Copley, withdrew.

The laid Certificate was read.

Resolved, That the levying a Farthing per Ton, or any other Sum of Money, upon Ships that come into the Port of Hull, upon Pretence of maintaining a Chain there, is an illegal Exaction upon the People.

And afterwards Colonel Copley was called in, and acquainted with the said Resolution, that he might not levy the pretended Duty any more.

And then withdrew.

Ordered, That the Informations delivered m to the House Yesterday, by Colonel Copley, be delivered back to him.

A Petition of a considerable Body of His Majesty s Protestant Subjects of the ancient Kirk of Scotland, resident in Lomlon and II cst mand other Parts of

South Britain, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Manner of taking an Oath in Sivt/and, as by Law eltabiished, is by holding up the Right Hand when the Oath is administered, and not by laying the Hand on, and afterwards killing, the Book; and that many of the Petitioners, being educated in the Principles of the Church of Scotland, adhere most firictly thereto, and others, of them, who entertain the like Scruples in the Mode of taking an Oath, cannot, in their Conferences, and consistently with those Principles, comply with the Mode practised in this Part of the United Kingdom; and that Men, void of Coni'cience and Honesty, knowing tire Principles of the Petitioners ou this Head, often take Advantage thereof by rcfuling to pay them their just Demands, whereby the Petitioners are frequently defrauded of their Projrcrtv, without having the Means to come at Justice; und that it is not from any Dif-affcfrtion or any Contempt of the Rules established by Government, that they do not comply with the common Ufugo of this Country in this Particular, but lucause the foiemu Mode in which their Form of Oath is administered is most agreeable to the Dictates of their Continences; and the Petitioners are heartily grieved, that, on this Account, they cannot be of the same Ser\ ice, nor perforin the same Offices to the Society in which they live, as the rest of their Fellow Citizens, very many of the Magistrates of this Country refusing to accept their Oaths in the Way they can only admit to be fworu; and that the Petitioners conceive the Mode of taking an Oath, by calling immediately on the Sacred Name, as adopted by them, is perfectly foiemu, and calculated to impress the Conscience with an Awe of the Supreme Being; and, as the Mode of Swearing, by killing the Book, is founded alone in Custom, the Petitioners hope that their Application for this Alteration in the Mode of administering the Oath to those of their Persuasion, will be deemed but just and equitable, especially when it is considered that they are entitled to take an Oath in this Manner in the other Part of the United King-doiu: And, that as this Request has been heretofore complied with by the Legislaturc in Favour of certain Dillenters called Quakers, and as, by Custom and Uiiige, Jews and others are permitted to make Oath in the Manner most agreeable to the Dictates of their own Conscience, therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, whereby the Mode of taking an Oath, in the Manner practised in North Britain, may, in all Cases where required by the Party, be admitted, instead of an Oath, in the usual Form.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that the Lord MuiLmd and Mr. Dempster do prepare, and bring in, the fame.
