A Petition of the respective Companies of Proprietors of the Birmingham Canal Navigation, and the Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigation, was presented to the

House, and read; Setting forth, That an Act was passed in the Eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining a Navigable Cut or Canal from Birmingham to Bilston, and from thence to Authority, there to communicate with the Canal then making between the Rivers Severn and Trent, and for making Collateral Cuts up to several Coal Mines; and and that another Act was passed in the Ninth Year of His said Majesty, to rectify a Mistake in the said first-mentioned Act, and to explain and amend the fame; and that another Act was passed in the Twenty-third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from a Place near Rider's Green, in the County of Staff, to Broadwater Fire Engine, and Six Collateral Cuts from the same to several Coal Mines, and also, a Navigable Canal from or near the Town of Birmingham, to join the Coventry Canal at or near Fazeley, in the Parish of in the said

County of Stafford, with a Collateral Cut to the lower Part of the said Town of Birmingham; and that the Canal and Collateral Cuts, authorized to be made by virtue of the said last mentioned Act, will communicate with the Canal and Collateral Cuts, made and completed by virtue of the Powers granted by the said first-recited Act, and nearly the whole of the Proprietors of the said Birmingham Canal Navigation, and the Proprietors of the said Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigation, are the feme Persons; and that, as the said respective Navigations will communicate with each other, and great Expences and Inconveniencies would be avoided by incorporating the fame, and making them one common Concern, it hath been agreed, that the feme should be consolidated, and the respective Companies of Proprietors of the said Two Undertakings have entered into Agreements for that Purpose; and that, by a Clause in the said last mentioned Act, it is recited, that at a Meeting held at Coleshill, in the County of Warwick, upon the 20th Day of June 1782, by certain Delegates from the re-foeftive Companies of Proprietors of the Oxford, Coventry, and GrandTrunk Canal Navigations, and from certain Subscribers to a new-proposed Navigation from the Collieries in the Neighbourhood of Wednesbury to Birmingham, and from thence to job the Coventry Canal in the Neighbourhood of Fazeley, it was proposed and agreed by such Delegates, on the Part of their respective Companies or Constituents, that, in order to effect a general Communication between the Oxford, Coventry, and Grand Trunk Canals, the Collieries in the Neighbourhood of Wednesbury, and Town of Birmingham, it would be necessary that the Coventry Canal should be completed between Atherstone and Heath, that

the Oxford Canal should be completed from Oxford to Banbury, and that the new Subscribers should execute a Canal from such Coal Mines to Birmingham and to Fazeley; and, the more easily to effect the Communication between Fazeley and Fradley Heath, it was agreed, that the Proprietors of the Coventry Canal should, by Authority of Parliament, or otherwise, relinquish to the

Proprietors of the Grand Trunk Canal, and to the Subscribers to such proposed Canal, that Branch of the said Coventry Canal lying between Fazeley wad Fradley Heath, and that the same should be executed by them at their joint Expence, the Subscribers to such new Canal allowing to the Proprietors of the Grand Trunk Canal 500l., as a Consideration for superintending and di-resting the Execution of such Branch of Canal; and it was further agreed, that the Profits arising upon that Part of the said Canal should be divided in Manner following;'that is to say, the Profits arising upon the Half Part thereof, from Fazeley towards Fradley Heath, by the Subscribers to the new-intended Canal; and the Profits arising from the other Half Part thereof, from Fradley Heath towards Fazeley, by the Proprietors of the Grand Trunk Canal; and that, when the feme should be completed, it should be equally divided between them, and each Part considered as the several and difrinft Property of the said Parties, and be supported accordingly; and it was therein expressed to be further understood and agreed, that the Tonnage to be taken for all Coals navigated from Birmingham throughout the intended Canal to Fazeley, and upon all or any Part or Parts of the Coventry and Oxford Canals, should not exceed One Penny per Ton per Mile; but it was thereby also understood, that the Subscribers to the said intended Canal were not to be restrained from taking any additional Tonnage for all Coals patting from the Collieries and discharged at Birmingham, or any Distanceupon the intended Canal short of Fazeley; and it is further recited, that the Canals and Collateral Cuts authorized to be made by the Company of Proprietors incorporated by that Act, and under the Authority of the same, had been substituted in the Place and Stead of the said proposed Canal from the Collieries at Wednesbury to Birmingham, and from thence to Fazeley aforesaid, and that the said Company had, in Consideration of the fame, agreed to ratify and confirm the aforesaid Agreement so entered into by the said former Subscribers, with respect to the Execution of that Part of the said Coventry Canal from Fazeley to Fradley Heath aforesaid; it is therein enacted, that the said Agreement so entered into by the said former Subscribers, and the several. Matters and Things therein specified and contained, to be done by and on their Parts, shall be binding and conclusive on the Company of Proprietors incorporated by the said Act, as fully and effectually as if they had been Parties thereto; and that, although by the said last mentioned Act it is enacted, that the Agreement so entered into by the said former Subscribers at Coleshill, and the several Matters and Things therein specified and contained to be done, by and on their Parts, should be binding and conclusive upon the Company of Proprietors incorporated by the said last mentioned Act, yet it is conceived, that the Authority of Parliament is necessary to enable such Proprietors to carry the said Agreement into Execution; and that, for the more speedily and effectually completing the said Birmingham and Fazeley Canal, it will be necessary to borrow a large Sum of Money, by Way of Loan, upon the Credit of the Tolls of the said respective Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigations, and it will be likewise necessary that feme of the Clauses in the said last mentioned Act should be explained, altered, and amended, and some further Powers given for the better carrying on, completing, and improving the said Navigations! And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to consolidate the said Two respective Undertakings of the Birmingham and Birmingham and Fazeley Canal Navigations, and for incorporating the said Two respective Companies of Proprietors, and the several Powers, Privileges, and Authorities by the said respective Acts of Parliament granted; and that such further Powers may be grunted to the Petitioners, as may be necessary to enable them tq borrow Money for

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Commissioners appointed, duly qualified, and acting, for putting in Execution an Act of Parliament, made in the Eleventh Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for improving and completing the Navigation of the Rivers Thames and Isis, and another Act, made in the Fifteenth Year of His said Majesty’s Reign, for amending the aforesaid Act; and also, of the several Subscribers and Contributors to the several Loans on the said Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by virtue of the said Acts, the Petitioners, and others of the said Commissioners for putting the same into Execution, have borrowed the Sum of 28,900l. (Part of 50,000l. which they were authorized by the said Acts to borrow) and have expended

the same in improving the said Navigation for an Extent of near Fifty Miles; and that, by Means of the said Improvements, the Price of Water Carriage on the said Navigation has beeu lefl'ened, and the Navigation of the said Rivers rendered more safe, certain, and expeditious, as far as the said Improvements extend; and that the said Commissioners, in order to continue, extend, and complete the said Improvements, according to the Tenor of the said Acts, have frequently made Application, by public Advertisement, for the borrowing of a farther Sum of Money, but have not been able to obtain any further Loan under the present Powers and the Securities they are enabled to give; and that, if they were impowered to ascertain, regulate, and determine, the Receipt of all the Tolls, Freight, and other Charges now paid, or to be paid, on the said Navigation, and if the present and future Subscribers were formed into a Body Politic and Corporate, for the Management of the said Navigation, subject nevertheless, in all Cales where the Public are concerned, to the Controul of Commissioners at large, the Petitioners conceive that a sufficient Sum of Money might be raised to continue, extend, and complete the said Improvements, according to the Tenor of the said Acts, and thereby they should be enabled to make a further Reduction in the Price of the Carriage of Goods on the said Navigation, as well as to render it progressively upwards more safe, certain, and expeditious: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to explain, amend, and enlarge the Powers and Authorities of the said recited Acts, and for effecting and obtaining the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Winchco Hartley, Mr. Elwes, See.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to lend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Improvement of tire great Road leading through the Counties of Anglesey and towards Ireland, is an Object of much public Import* ance, as it tends to facilitate the Intercourse between both Kingdoms, and for several Years past great Sums of Money have been Annually expended in amending the said Road, and making Bridges, Dams, and other Works, for the Improvement thereof; and that the Passage of Porthactkwy Ferry, over an Arm of the Sea, between the Counties of Anglesey and Carnarvon, called The Streights of Menai, is frequently attended with very great Delay, Inconvenience, and Danger, to Persons travelling with Mails and ExprelTes between England and Ireland, and to all other Persons having Occasion to pals the said Fern; and representing to the House, that it appears from the concurrent Opinions of several very eminent Engineers, that a safe and convenient Passage may be made across the said Arm of the Sea, by a Bridge from the County of Anglesey, to the opposite Shore, in the County of Carnarvon, at a Place near the said Ferry, called Ynysgeint; and, in case the same shall be made, it will be necessary to make a new Hoad through certain Lands on each Side of the said Bridge, in order to open a Communication with the said great Road; and that the making such safe and convenient Passage will be of great Benefit, Safety, and Convenience to all Persons having Occasion to travel the said Road, and of public Utility: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making such safe and convenient Passage, and opening proper Communications with the said great Road as aforesaid, by such Ways and Means, and in such Manner, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Mutter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of the several Persons resident in the Cities of London and Westminster, in the Borough of Southwark, and Parts adjacent, employed in the making and vending Beaver Hats, and Hats mixed with Beaver, Hare Wool, Coney Wool, Goat’s Wool, and other Materials, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others concerned in the said Manufacture in Great Britain, was

04

presented to the House, and read; Setting forth*

That the Hat Manufactory of this Kingdom is a very considerable Branch of Trade, in which several Thousand British Subjects are employed; and that Hare Wool and Coney Wool, the Growth of this Kingdom, are better in Quality than any other, and as those are the Staple Articles of this Manufactory,

English Hats have acquired such Reputation, that great Quantities of them are exported to Foreign Parts; and that, in Addition to the Produce of this Country, great Quantities of Hare Wool and Coney Wool have been usually imported from Flanders, Russia, and Germany, but for feme Time past very little of the said Articles have been imported from any of those Parts, owing, as the Petitioners apprehend, to their being detained for the Supply of Foreign Manufactures; and that Goat's Hair, or Turkey Goat’s Wool, is an Article much used in the said Manufactory, and pays a Duty of about Six Pence per Pound on Importation, though Foreigners, as also the Irish, who buy at the same Market as the English, do receive it, as the Petitioners believe, free of Duty, and as there is a Drawback on its being exported of Four Pence per Pound, our Rivals can have it cheaper even from this Kingdom than the British Manufacturer; and that, owing to the superior Excellence of British Hare Wool and Coney Wool, considerable Quantities have lately been exported to France, Flanders, and even America, notwithstanding the trifling Duties payable on their Exportation, which has oceafioned so great a Scarcity in those necessary Articles, that the Petitioners believe there is uot at this Time a sufficient Quantity in the Kingdom, even at the present -high Price, for the Supply of their own Manufactory; and that if the Practice of exporting to Foreign Countries Hare Wool and Coney Wool, the Produce of this Kingdom, is not by feme Means prevented, the British Hat Manufactory will be rendered of little Consequence, and many Families thereby left unprovided for; and that the Petitioners conceive, the only Methods of remedying those Mischiefs, and preserving the said Manufactory, would be, by laying an additional Duty on the Exportation of Hare Skins and Hare Wool, and Coney Skins and Coney Hare or Wool, from this Kingdom, or by prohibiting the Exportation thereof, and by allowing the Importation of Goafs Hair, or Goat’s Wool, Duty free: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House Audi teem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to tire Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. JVatson, Mr. Alderman Newnham, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of William Poy, Esquire, Inspector of Prosecutions in His Majesty’s Court of Exchequer, being offered to be presented to the House:

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition, was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That his late Majesty King George the Second, by his Royal Patent, dated 20th, 1741, granted to the Right honourable Stephen Poyntz, in consideration of his long and approved Services in high and confidential Employments, the Office of Inspector of the Prosecutions in his Court of Exchequer, and continued the same to the Petitioner, which Patent His present Majesty renewed and confirmed on His Accession to the Crown; and that, by the Terms of the said Patent, the Petitioner is entitled to hold the said Office, by himself or sufficient Deputy or Deputies, with the Fees, Allowances, Profits, and Advantages thereunto belonging, in as full and ample a Manner as the same were held and received by the said Stephen Poyntz, or any former Inspector of Profc-cutions; and that the Emoluments derived to the Possessors of the said Office, from its first Establitfi-inent, have been an Allowance of One Shilling in the Pound on His Majesty’s Share of the Money paid into the Exchequer for prohibited and uncustomed Goods; and that, by an Act passed in the Third Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, it is directed, that One Moiety of the Net Produce arising by the Sale of all Seizures (after deducting the Charges of Condemnation and Sale from the Whole) should be paid into the Exchequer, in lieu of His Majesty’s Share thereof, but, by a Clause in an Act made in the Twenty-first Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, it is directed, that instead of One Moiety of the Net Produce arising by the Sale of all such Seizures (after deducting the Charges of Condemnation and Sale from the Whole) being paid into the Exchequer, in lieu of llis Majesty’s Share thereof, the Commissioners of the Customs arc authorized, where they shall judge necessary, to order the Charges arising by the Condemnation and Sale, and all Manner of Law Bills, and other Charges of Management, to be paid out of His Majesty’s Share of the Produce arising by the Sale of all Goods which have been, or may be, seized and condemned, in like Manner as may be done out of any other Branch of the Revenue of the Customs which is by I,aw applicable to the Payment of Incidents; and that the said Clause, which so materially assists the Petitioners Interest, was inserted in the Act without uny Notice thereof having been given either to him or his Deputy; and, from the Title of the said Act, the Petitioner had no Rcalbn to apprehend that any such Clause was contained therein, and consequently had not then an Opportunity of submitting hb same oj.

to the Consideration of Parliament; and that the Commissioners of the Customs, by virtue of the difere-tionary Power given to them by the said Act, having judged it necessary to order all Manner of Law Bills, Purchase, Hire, and Equipment of Cruisers in the Service of the Revenue, and various other Charges of Management, to a very considerable Amount (which were formerly paid by Incidents) to be paid out of the Produce of Seizures, there has already been a great Decrrease of the Money paid into the Exchequer on this Account, and His Majesty’s Share of the Produce of the Seizures may in Time be l’till further reduced by being charged with a still larger Proportion of the Expences of such Management; and that the Petitioner has already suffered a very great Diminution of his Income, in consequence of Regulations made by the Commissioners of the Customs, and he has great Reason to apprehend, that his Income will continue to decrease, and that he may in the End be entirely deprived of his just Rights granted to him by the said Letters Patent; and that the Petitioner having faithfully discharged the Duties of his Office, and conceiving his Title to the Profits of it to be faered, and having made all his Arrangements in the certain

O o

Hope and Expectation that he should have been permitted to enjoy those Profits, in their full Extent, for the Remainder of his Life, he cannot, at this Period of it, and with a numerous Family, but severely feci lb considerable and unexpected a Diminution of his Income; but, if the House should be of Opinion that the abolishing the said Office of Inspector of Prosecutions would be for the Benefit of the Public, the Petitioner is willing, w'ith His Majesty’s Permission, to surrender up his Patent, trusting to the Justice and Equity of Parliament that an adequate Compensation will be made to him for the fame: And therefore praying the House to take his same into Consideration, and to grant him such Relief as to the House flia.ll appear just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That this House, impressed with the most dutiful Sense of His Majesty’s Paternal Regard for the Welfare of His People, relies on His Majesty’s Royal Wisdom, that He will take such Measures as may tend to give Effect to the Willies of His Faithful Commons, which have already been most humbly represented to His Majesty;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by inferring, after the Word " as," tho Words " by removing any Obstacle to the Formation " of such an Administration as this House has declared " to be requisite in the present critical and arduous " Situation of Public Affairs."

And the Question being put, That those Words be there inserted;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

and that the Petitioner John Goddard, from Motives of Friend-ship to, and Confidence in, the said Francis Dixon, did enter into the said several Bonds as one of his Sureties; and the Petitioner John Mayer, having been Cleric to, and afterwards taken into Partnership by, the said Robert Wcnsley (since deceased) in his Business of an Attorney, who was, for several Years, merely from Motives of Friendship, one of the Sureties for the said Francis Dixon, for the Purposes aforesaid, was afterwards prevailed upon to become one of the said Francis Duron’s Sureties to His Majesty in the aforesaid Two last mentioned Bonds; and that the Petitioners did not entertain any Suspicion but that the said Francis Dixon was perfectly regular in his Accounts and Payments to the Crown, till the Month of July 1781, when they were informed that the Commissioners of Taxes had put forne Stop to the said Francis Dixon's further Receipts in virtue of his Offices aforesaid; whereupon the Petitioners immediately applied to the said Francis Duron to know the State of his Accounts with the Crown, and having got an Account of the said Francis Dixons Debt to the Crown, immediately came to London, and gave Information thereof to the said Commissioners of Taxes, and then found that the said Commissioners had repeatedly applied to the said Francis Dixon to pay in his Balance, and that be had gone so far in deceiving the Commissioners, as well as the Petitioners, as to make an Affidavit, that a considerable Part of the Debt appearing on such Accounts to be due from him was uncollected and owing from the Country;' and that the Petitioners immediately procured Extents against the Estate and Effects of the said Francis Dixon, who suddenly destroyed himself on the 19th Day of July 1781; and that the said Francis was, at his

Death, indebted to His Majesty in 28,763 /. 16$. 3<L a Sum much more than both the Petitioners are worth; and the aforeihid Johnson Duron, the other Surety for the Land Tax, one of the Sons of the said Francis Dixon, was only a nominal Partner in Trade with his Father as a Merchant, and not possessed of any considerable Property; and that the Management of the ' Business, late of the said Francis Dixon, was, upon his Death, intrusted to the Petitioners, and they immediately afterwards got Possession of his Real and Personal Estates, thereby saving great Waste, as well as the heavy Expence of proceeding further with Legal Process; and that the Petitioners loon after prevailed with Three of the Sons of the said Francis Dixon, the eldest of whom was his Heir at Law, to release their Claim to their said FatKr’s Real Estate, and have had a Conveyance of such Real Estate made to themselves, the better to enable them to dispose of the fame, for securing the Debt due to the Crown, and for indemnifying the said Francis Dixons Sureties as far as his

Part thereof, and the Residue, being 304/. 7s. 10 id.remains in their Hands; and that the scattered Property of the said Francis Dixon was so Circumstanced as to require immediate and very extraordinary Attention as well as Skill in riif-poling thereof; and that the Petitioners have, both with unwearied Diligence and constant Attention, applied themselves to the Management and Disposition of such Property, having allotted a great Part of their Time to those Concerns for the lait Two Years, and upwards, and, by such Means, they have not only laved the Expence of Agents in the Country, but, as they conceive, have increased the Value of the Property of the said Francis Dixon, and rendered the same very considerably more productive than it otherwise would have been, and have done every Thing in their Power to forward the Sale thereof; and that the Petitioners did lately apply to the Lords of the Treasury, stating the several Matters aforesaid, and also, that Difficulties had arisen respecting the Title to the Real Estates of the said Francis Dixon, and that the said Petitioners were advised it would be necessary, in order to obviate such Difficulties, that an Act of Parliament should be obtained, to authorize the respective Purchasers to pay their Purchase Monies to such Persons as in such Act should be named, and to declare that, after such Payment, the Purchasers should hold the purchased Premises discharged of all Claims of the Crown, with such other Provisions as might be found proper, and, that the Petitioners were very desirous of paying the ftnall Balance in their Hands, and of rendering up all the Real and Personal Property of the said Francis Dixon, and after doing Juliice to the World in regard to the linall Sums they were themselves indebted, were ready and willing to give up such Part of their own Property, as their Lordships might think reasonable, towards Satisfaction of the Debt due to the Crown, and that, notwithstanding the y had been lo unfortunate as to enter into such Security, they hoped they might be permitted to retain some Part of their Fortune, so as to enable them, with their own Industry, to live with some Degree of Comfort, and therefore prayed their Lordships to give Leave that a Bill might be brought into Parliament for the above Purposes, and also, to authorize their Lordships to compound with the Petitioners, and to discharge them from the said Debt; and that the Petitioners, from the great Difficulty attending the disposing of Real Property in that Part of the Country where the Estates of the late Francis Dixon, and also of the Petitioners, are situate, are unable to ascertain how much the Property of the said Francis Dixon, and also of the Petitioners and the other Sureties of the said Francis Dixon, are able to satisfy of the said Debt due to the Crow n, yet the Petitioners hope, from the Funds albrefuid, they will be able to raile the further Sum of 10,000l.: And therefore praying, That Dave may be given to bring in a Bill for effectuating the several Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner as to the House limit seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

and that another Petition was therefore prepared, and intended to have been presented to this House on Thursday, the 19th Day of this Instant February, for Leave to bring in a Bill for taking down the said Church, and erecting a new one; and raising Money for that Purpose, which Petition was tigned by the Petitioner, and left with Lord Viscount mouth, the other Petitioner therein named, and his Lordship appointed Mr. Sleigh, who prepared the said Petition, to wait upon his Lordship in the Afternoon of Thursday, the 19th Instant, for his Lordship to sign the fame; and, that Mr. Sleigh being that Afternoon informed by one of the Clerks of this House, that there was a great Probability that the House might rife before the Time appointed by Lord Weyuouthfor signing the said Petition, waited upon his Lordship before the Time appointed, and his Lordship being then particularly engaged, Mr. Sleigh took the Petition from his Lordship’s, intending to get the same presented without his Signature thereto, but on his Return he found this House risen; and representing to the House, that no Service can be performed in the old Church, and, if the erecting a new one is deferred . for another Year, the Inhabitants of the said Parish during all that Time, and until such new Church is erected, will have no Place of public Worship, and for their Instruction in the Christian Religion: And therefore praying, That, for the Realbns aforesaid, the House will be pleased to admit the said Petition, in the like Manner as if the same had been presented on or before the 19th Day of this Instant, February, pursuant to the Order of the House.

which Inina a large Manufacturing Town for line Clotli, the Poor therein are exceeding numerous, and, although it is divided into Six Hamlets or Tythings, in each of which there is a Church or Chapel, yet, with respefi to the Relief and Maintenance of the Poor, is confnlered as One Parish, and governed by Four Overseers only — That there are now 1,244 Persons in the Parish, who receive Relief from the Poor Rates — That the Rates now raised upon the Parish, for the Relief and Support of the Poor, amount to near Five Shillings in the Pound, according to the Rack Rent of the Lands and Tenements within the Parish; and that the Stock in Trade is highly rated in Aid of the Land, without which the Land would he 1110ft grievotillv burthened — That, from Easter 1783 to the lotli of February last, the Money collected for the Lie of the Poor, and which it is apprehended will not he I'uiHcient to complete the Payments for the Year, amounted 103,143/. and upwards — That in the Year 1770 the Poor's Rates amounted to 1,931/. 14$. since which Time they have been gradually and con-lidcrahly inerealing every Year — That the principal Land Owueis do not live in the Parish, therefore the Office of Overseer generally fulls to Clothiers and Persons in a great Way of Trade, whose other Avocations render the executing of such an Office highly inconvenient to them, and prejudicial to their Affairs and Concerns; for which Realbn they generally appoint Deputies, who. arc Bakers, Shopkeepers, or others in interior Situations in Lh’c, who, from interested Motives, are induced to take the Trouble of executing the Office, and misapply or waste the Public Money, or take undue Advantage of their Situations, in supplying the Poor with Articles from their respective Shops, instead of paying them in Money, as they ought to do — That they pay them only Monthly, by which Means the Poor are driven to the Necessity of running in Debt wherever they can get Credit — They also take no Pains to visit the Poor, in order to dH-cover those who are proper Objctts of Charity, and deferring of Relief, from those who, by Means of Profligacy or Iillcncfs, are less entitled to public Support, ut the same Time that the Aged and Infirm, who may be incapable of attending the Overseer to urge their Situation, may languid* in extreme Misery mid Distress. — And the Witness further said, That it is apprehended a very considerable Saving might be made in the Parish Rates, and the Poor be more regularly and rtfeftually relieved and supported, if Power was given by Parliament to appoint an Extra Overseer of the Poor within the said Parish, with an adequate Salary, for the Idle Purpose of looking after the Poor, and distrihiiting the Parish Payments Weekly to the proper Objects.

Mr. Speaker reported to the House, That the House attended His Majesty on ffednesdat/ last with their Address; to which 11 is Majesty was pleased to give the following Answer; viz.

Gentlemen,

I ain deeply finfible how highly it concerns the Honour of My (.rown, and the Welfare of My

Vo l. 39. J

People, which is the Object always neatest My Heart, that the Public Affairs should be conduced by’ a firm, efficient, united, and extended Administration, entitled to the Confidence of My People, and such as ntay have a Tendency to put an End to the unhappy Divisions and Distractions in this Country. — Very recent Endeavours have already been employed, on My Part, to unite in the Public Service, on a fair and equal Footing, those whose joint Efforts appear to Me most capable of producing that happy Effect: These Endeavours have not had the Success

I wished.

966 S']0 Februariu — i A. 1784.

I wi£hed. I shall be always desirous of taking every Step most conducive to such an Object; but 1 cannot fee that it would, in any Degree, be advanced, by the Dismission of those at mefent in My Service.

I observe, at the same Time, that there is no Charge, or Complaint, suggested against My present M milters, nor is any One or more of them specifically objected to; and Numbers of My Subjects have expressed to Me, in the warmed Manner, their Satisfaction in the late Changes I have made in My Councils. Under these Circumstances, I trust, My Faithful Commons will not wish that the essential Offices of executive Government should be vacated, until I fee a Prospect that such a Plan of Union as I have called for, and they have pointed out, may be carried into Eft'eft.

Mr. Francis Child being examined, said, That at the Time of passing the said Act, there was no House or Building fit for the Pur|>ofe within the said Parish; and therefore the Trustees and Vestrymen hired a Workhouse at Mile End New Town, in the Parish of Stepney, which they have been obliged, from the great Increase of the Number of Poor, to make considerable additional Buildings thereto, and in lb doing have incurred a very heavy Expence upon the said Parish.

Air. Janies Dalton confirmed the above Evidence; and added, That notwithstanding the several additional Buildings a I >ove-mentioned, the said Workhouse is too final], und the Lodging Rooms very inconvenient, the People being obliged to deep Four or Five in a Bed; that the Kent, Taxes, and Common Repairs of the said Work-house, amount to lull 120/. per Annum: Then

and said, That the Poor arc daily increasing, inso much that since lie has been Master, there has been an Increase of above One hundred in a Year, and that more than One hundred and Fifty have been relieved out, there not having been sufficient Room in the House.

Mr. Richard Hooding, Surveyor, being next examined, produced a Plan and Estimate Ibr building a New Workhouse, which is calculated to accommodate Five hundred Persons upon the most frugal Plan: the Amount of the Estimate being between 3,300 /. and 4,000 /.

And it appeared by the Evidence of Mr. John Grunt, that the above Plan has been seen and approved of by the Committee appointed in full Vestry, for the Purpose of making this Application; and he added. That it is proposed to build the said Workhouse iu Brick Lane.

Mr. Dalton being further examined, find, That, by the said Act of the Eighteenth Year of the present Reign, the usual Mode of making the Rates for the Relief of the Poor of the said Parish w as altered to a Pound Rate in different Classes, according to the Yearly Rent or Value of the Houses, which has been found very inconvenient, and productive of much Collusion between Landlords and Tenants, whereby the Rates have repeatedly proved deficient to defray the necessary Charges of maintaining the said Poor; and a considerable Debt hath been unavoidably contracted thereby, which cannot be discharged, unless Power be given to alter the present Method of affelling the Monies, and for raising a further Sum of Money to discharge the said Debt.

This Evidence was corroborated by Mr. Thomas Buxton, and Mr. John Scott: And

Mr. Robert Phillips added, that the Poor’s Rate, at the Commencement of the last mentioned Act, produced about 3,000l. a Year, from which Time it has been gradually decrealing; and that although in the Year 1782 an additional Sixth was laid on, which was estimated to raise 600 /. a Year, the Hates have nevertheless so much decreased, as to produce now not more than the original Sum of 3,000 /.: Then

To prove the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition,

And a Motion being made, and the Question being proposed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, most humbly to represent to His Majesty, the Satisfaction His Faithful Commons derive from the late Most Gracious Assurances we have received, that His Majesty concurs with us in Opinion, that it concerns the Honour of His Crown, and the Welfare of His People, that the Public Affairs should be conducted by a firm, efficient, extended, united Administration, entitled to the Confidence of His People, and such as may have a Tendency to put an End to the unhappy Divi-lions and Diffractions of this Country:

To acknowledge His Majesty’s Paternal Goodness, in His late Most Gracious Endeavours to give Eftect to the Object of our late dutiful Representation to His Majesty:

To lament that the Failure of these His Majesty’s Most Gracious Endeavours should be considered as a final Par to the Accomplishment of l'o ialutary and desirable a Purpose; and to express our Concern and Disappointment that his Majesty has not been advised to take any farther Step towards uniting in the Public Service, those whole joint Efforts have recently appeared to 11 is Majesty most capable of producing so happy an Effect.

That this House, with all Humility, claims it as their Right, and on every proper Occasion feels it to be their bounden Duty, to advise His Majesty touching the Exercise of any Branch of His Royal Prerogative.

That we submit it to His Majesty’s Royal Consideration, that (lie Continuance of an Administration which does not poflels the Confidence of the Reprc-fentatives of the People, must be injurious to the Public Service.

A PETIT ION of the several Persons whose Newhaven Names are thereunto subscribed, Commissioners Urit)8e* and Trustees for repairing the Piers and Harbour of Neirhaven, in the County of Sussex, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for building a Bridge over the River Ouse, at Newhaven, in the County of Sussex-, and Setting forth, That the Petitioners, by virtue of an Act, passed in the fourth Year of his late Majesty King George the Second, for repairing, and keeping in Repair, the Pier, or Piers, and Harbour of Newhaven, in the County of Sussex, are impowered to provide Sluices for cleansing and scouring the said Haven, and to borrow Money upon Security of the Duties granted by the said Act; and that the Petitioners have been obliged to borrow considerable Sums of Money upon the Credit of that Trust, and have, of late Years, greatly improved the said Harbour, and, through that, the Navigation and Trade of the Town and Port of Lewes-, and, the Drainage of the Levels and Low Grounds hath been, by the Means aforesaid, greatly improved and benefited; and that the Petitioners apprehend, if a Bill should pass without proper Restrictions and Limitations, by which the Bed of the said River, and the Current of Water, may be preserved in their prefeu State, not the Drainage of the Levels only, and the scouring, cleansing, and preserving the said Harbour and Navigation, would be much endangered, but also the Security of such Persons who have lent Money upon the Credit of the above-mentioned Act would be diminished: And therefore praying, That the several Matters contained in their Petition may be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the Bill for building the said Bridge is committed; and that the Petitioners may be heard respecting the Matters of their Petition before the said Committee, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Proprietors of Lands, Merchants,

Traders, and others interested in the Navigation of the River Ouse, and Harbour of in the County of Sussex, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That, if the same should pass into a Law, without proper Clauses for restricting and limiting the Construction of such Bridge, it will greatly prejudice the Petitioners, by obstructing the Navigation of the said River and Harbour, and by lessening and impeding the Tides in their free Course, so as to cause Demurrage to the Craft navigated thereon; and that the Petitioners apprehend that there will be a strong Current at such Bridge, to the endangering of the Craft passing through the fame, and they have Reafnn to believe that an additional Freight for Goods carried in such Craft will be charged thereon, on Account of such Demurrage and Risque: And therefore praying, That the several Matters aforesaid may be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the 11 N Petitioners

Freuds Sir Charles Banbury reported from the Committee,

smon^ Wool- to w hom the Petition of the Manufacturers of Comb-combers. ing Wool, Worsted Yarn, and Goods made from Woifted, in the County of was referred; That

the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; tic.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. James Oakes being examined, informed your Committee, That the Yarns lpun in the County of Suffolk have, of late Years, greatly dccreased in their Value, occasioned principally, as the Witncls apprehends, by the Frauds and Abuses which are practised in the Keeling thereof — That many of the Spinners, being frequently so poor as not to be able to wait for Payment until they have executed the Whole of the Work they are employed in at one Time, Vo l. 39.

require to be paid for it in small Quantities as they proceed with it; the Manufacturers are therefore under the Necessity, as well for the Conveniency of themselves as of the Spinners, to appoint certain Shops or Places for the Spinners to deliver in their Yarn, from Time to Time, as they linish small Quantities of it, and to receive Payment for the fame; by Means whereof great Abuses are frequently practised by many of the Spinners in delivering Yarn badly spun, without the Possibility of being detested by the Manufacturers.

That, by several Laws now in being, certain Penalties and Punishments are inflicted upon Persons who shall reel false or short Yarn, or embezzle the Materials thereof; but that the good Effects of those Laws are in a great Measure frustrated within the said County, by the Unwiilingnels of Individuals to prosecute the Offenders, and thereby subject themselves to the Damage they might fuitain by the Resentment of the Persons who should be prosecuted; and that unless feme further Provisions and Regulations are made and established by Parliament, for preventing the said Frauds and Abuses, the said Manufacture mult greatly decline, to the great Prejudice of the Manufacturers, and the throwing out of Employ maoy Thousands of poor People.

Then an Act of the Seventeenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the more effectual preventing Frauds and Abuses committed by Persons employed in the Manufacture of Combing Wool, Worsted Yarn, and Goods made from Worsted, in the Counties of York, Lancaster, and Chester, was read; by which it appeared, that Power was given for the Appointment of Inspectors, the better to detest the said Frauds and Abuses, and for prosecuting of Offenders.

And the Witness added, That he had Reason to believe, that in consequence of the Provisions and Regulations contained in the said Act, the Yarns spun in the Counties of York, Lancaster, and Chester, have greatly improved, and other good Effects have been produced thereby; and he also added, That if the like Provisions and Regulations were made and established in the County of Suffolk, he conceived the like good Consequences would be produced.

Mr. William Buck was examined, who confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Oakes; and added, That the Yarns of the County of Suffolk have declined in Value, compared with other Counties, particularly the Counties of York, Lancaster, and Chester; which is principally owing to the fraudulent Reeling of the Yarn.

The Witness then informed your Committee, That, in consequence of an Application to the Clerk of the Committee, appointed by the said Act of the Seventeenth of His present Majesty, enquiring touching the Effect and Operation of that Act, he had received a Letter from the said Clerk, Ly which it appeared, that the Manufacturers had derived very great Benefit from the Regulations established by that Act.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for more effectually preventing Frauds and Abuses committed by Persons employed in the Manufiaftures of Combing Wool, Worsted Yarn, and Goods made from Worsted, in the County of Suffolk: And that Sir Charles Bunbury and Sir John Rous do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Post Meridiem.

MR. Speaker reported to the House, That the House attended His Majesty, this Day, with their Address; to which His Majesty was pleased to give the following Answer; viz.

Gentlemen,

I have already expressed to you how sensible I am of the Advantages to be derived from such an Administration as was pointed out in your unanimous Resolution; and 1 aiTured you that I was desirous of taking every Step most conducive to such an Objefit.

I remain in the same Sentiments; but I continue equally convinced, that it is an Objefit not likely to be obtained by the Dismission of My present Ministers.

1 mult repeat, that no Charge, or Complaint, nor any specific Objection, is yet made against any of them.

If there were any such Ground for their Removal

at present, it ought to be equally a Reason for not admitting them as a Part of that extended and united Administration which you (late to be requisite.

I did not consider the Failure of My recent Endeavours as a final Bar to the Accomplishment of the Purpose which I bad in View, if it could have been attained on those Principles of Fuirness and Equality, without which it can neither be honourable to those who are concerned, nor lay the Foundation of such a strong and liable Government as may be of lading Advantage to the Country; but I know of no farther Steps w l.icli I can take, that are likely to remove the Difficulties which obstrufit that desirable End.

I have never called in Question the Right of My Faithful Commons to odor Me their Advice, on every proper Occasion, touching the Exercise of any Branch of My Prerogative — I shall be ready, at all Times, to receive it, and give it the most attentive Consideration:

They will ever find Me disposed to shew My Regard to the true Principles of the Constitution, and to take such Measures as may bed conduce to the Satisfaction and Prosperity of My People.

Ordered, That His Majesty’s said Answer be taken into Consideration upon Monday Morning next.

A Petition of Messieurs James Stein, John Stein, and Smu^sing. James Haig, and Company, Corn Distillers in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have embarked considerable Capitals in erecting Buildings, and providing Utensils and Materials, for carrying on the Corn Distillery under the Sanction of the Laws, and relying with Confidence that they would be protested by Government, and encouraged by Parliament, in carrying on a Business which it is so much the Interest of the Public to promote; and that the Petitioners find, from Experience, that the Trade in which they are engaged is materially injured, by the Quantity of Spirits smuggled from Foreign Countries, and by the illicit Practices of secret Distillers in Great Britain; and that a Diminution of the Duties would, in the Apprehension of the Petitioners, prevent such illicit Practices, increase the Revenue considerably above its present Amount, and be of great Advantage both to the Landed Interest and fair Trader: And therefore praying, That this important Matter may be taken into Consideration, and that Relief may be afforded by such a Reduction of the Duties presently exacted, as may remove the Temptation to defraud the Revenue, and by such just and equal Restrictions and Regulations as may elieftually suppress the Frauds presently practised to the Prejudice both of the Revenue and of the fair Trader, or to do otherw ife, as to the House shall fcem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee who are appointed to enquire into the illicit Prafties now used in defrauding the Revenue of this Kingdom, and the most effectual Methods of preventing the fame.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That an humble Representation be presented to His Majesty, must humbly to testify the Surprize and Affliction of this House, on receiving the Answer, which His Majesty’s Ministers have advised, to the dutiful and seasonable Address of this House, concerning one of the most important Acts of His Majesty’s Government:

To express our Concern, that when His Majesty’s Paternal Goodness has graciously inclined His Majesty to be sensible of the Advantage to be derived from such an Administration as was pointed out in our Resolution, His Majesty should still be induced to prefer the Opinions of Individuals to the repeated Advice of the Representatives of His People, in Parliament af-iembled, with respect to the Means of obtaining lo de-Arable an End:

To represent to His Majesty, that a Preference of this Nature is as injurious to the true Interests of the Crown, as it is wholly repugnant to the Spirit of our free Constitution: That Syltems founded on such a Preference are not in Truth entirely new in this Country: That they have been the characteristic Features of those unfortunate Reigns, the Maxims of which are now justly and univerlally exploded; while His Majesty and His Royal Progenitors have been fixed in the Hearts of their People, and have commanded the Respect and Admiration of all the Nations of the Earth, by a constant and uniform Attention to the Advice of their Commons, however adverse such Advice may have been to the Opinions of the Executive Servants of the Crown:

To assure His Majesty, that we neither have dif-puted, nor mean in any Instance to dispute, much less to deny. His Majesty’s undoubted Prerogative of ap|iointing to the executive Offices of State such Persons, as to His Majesty’s Wisdom shall feera meet; but, at the same Time, that we must, with all Humility, again fubntit to His Majesty’s Royal Wisdom, that no Administration, however legally appointed, can serve His Majesty and the Public with Effect, which does not enjoy the Confidence of this House: That in His Majesty’s. present Administration we cannot confide; the Circumstances under which it was constituted, and the Grounds: upon which it continues, have created -just Suspicionsin the Breasts of His Faithful Commons, that Principles are adopted, and Views entertained, unfriendly to the Privileges of this House, and to the Freedom of our excellent.

Confutation: That we have made no Charge against ony of them, because it is their Removal, ami not their Pimiflunent, which we have desired; and that we humbly conceive, we arc warranted by the ancient Usage of this lloufe, to desire Inch Removal without making any Charge whatever: That Confidence maybe very prudently withheld, where no criminal Process can be properly instituted: That although we have made no criminal Charge against any Individual of His Majesty’s Ministers, yet with all Humility we do conceive, that we have stated to His Majesty very distinct Objections, and very forcible Reasons, against their Continuance: That with regard to the Propriety of admitting either the present Ministers, or any other Persons, as a Part of that extended and united Administration which His Majesty, in Concurrence with the Sentiments of this House, con-liders as requisite, it is a Point upon which we are too well acquainted with the Rounds of our Duty to presume to oiler any Advice to His Majesty, well knowing it to be the undoubted Prerogative of His Majesty to appoint His Ministers, without any previous Advice from either House of Parliament, and our Duty, humbly to offer to His Majesty our Advice, when such Appointments shall appear to us to be prejudicial to the Public Service:

To acknowledge with Gratitude His Majesty’s Goodness, in not considering the Failure of his recent Endeavours as a final liar to the Accomplishment of the gracious Purpose which His Majesty has in View; und to express the great Concern and Mortification, with which we find ourl'elves obliged to declare, that the Conlbla-tion, which we (liould naturally have derived from His Majesty's Most Gracious Disposition, is considerably abated, by understanding that His Majesty’s Advisers have not thought fit to suggest to His Majesty any farther Steps to remove the Difficulties which obstruct so definable an End:

To recall to His Majesty’s Recollection, that His Faithful Commons have already submitted to His Majesty most humbly, but most distinctly, their Opinion upon this Subject: That they can have no Interests but those of His Majesty, and of their Conltituents; whereas it is needless to suggest to His Majesty’s Wisdom and Dil’ccrnment, that individual Advisers may be actuated by very different Motives:

To express our most unfeigned Gratitude for His Majesty's Royal Assurances, that He does not call in Question the Right of this House to offer their Advice to His Majesty, on every proper Occasion, touching the Exercise of any Branch of His Royal Prerogative, and of His Majesty’s Rcadinels, at all Times, to receive such Advice, and to give it the most attentive Consideration: To declare, that we recognize in these Gracious Expressions those excellent and constitutional Sentiments, which we have ever been accustomed to Itear from the Throne, since the glorious jEra of the Resolution, and which have peculiarly characterized His Majesty and the Princes of His Illustrious House: But, to lament that these Most Gracious Expressions, while they inspire us with additional Affection and Gratitude towards His Majesty’s Royal Person, do not a little contribute to increase our Sulpicions of those Men who have advised His Majesty, in direct Contradiction to these Assurances, to neglect the Advice of His Commons, and to retain in His Service an Administration, whole continuance in Ollice we have so repeatedly and so dif-tinftly condemned:

To represent to His Majesty, that it has anciently been the Practice of this House, to withhold Supplies until Grievances were redrefied; and that, if we were to follow this Courl’e in the present Conjuncture, we lhouhl be warranted in onr Proceeding, as well by the most approved Precedents, as by the Spirit of the oj

Constitution itself: Rut if, in Consideration of the very peculiar Exigencies of the Times, we flionid he induced to wave, for the present, the Exercise, in this Instance of our undoubted legal and constitutional Mode of obtaining Redress, that we humbly implore His Majesty not to impute our Forbearance to any Want of Sincerity in our Complaints, or Distrust in the Justice of our Cause:

That we know', and are fore, that the Prosperity of His Majesty’s Dominions, in former Times has been, under Divine Providence, owing to the Harmony which has, for near a Century, prevailed uninterruptedly, between the Crown and this House: That we arc convinced, that there is no Way to extricate this Country from its present Difficulties, but by pursuing the same System to which we have been indebted, at various Periods of our History, for our Suceelles Abroad, and which is at all Times so necessary for our Tranquillity at Home: That we feel the Continuance of the present Administration to be an Innovation upon that happy System: That we cannot but expect, from their Existence under the Displeasure of this House, every Misfortune naturally incident to a weak and distracted Government: That, if we hud concealed from His Majesty our honest Sentiments upon this important Crisis, we should have been, in some Degree, responsible for the Mischiefs which are but too certain to ensue.

That we have done our Duty to His Majesty, and our Constituents, in pointing out the Evil, and in humbly imploring Redress: That the Blame and Re-fponlibility must now lie wholly upon those who have presumed to advise His Majesty to act in Contradiction to the uniform Maxims which have hitherto governed the Conduct of His Majesty, as well as every other Prince of His Illustrious House; upon those who have disregarded the Opinions and neglected the Admonitions of the Representatives of His People, and who have thereby attempted to set up a new System of Executive Administration, which, wanting the Confidence of this House, and acting in Defiance to our Resolutions, must prove at once inadequate, by its Inefficiency, to the necessary Objects of Government, and dangerous, by its Example, to the Liberties of the People;

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

Mr. 11 at son reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons resident in the Cities of Ism don and ll tslmin.sUr,in the Borough of South-

nark, and Parts adjacent, employed in the making and vending Beaver Hats, and Hats mixed with Beaver, Hare W ool, Coney Wool, Goat’s Wool, and other Vot. 39.

Materials, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others concerned in the said Manufacture in Great Britain, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. John Collinson, being examined, said. That the

Hat Manufactory of this Kingdom is a very considerable Branch of Trade, in which several Thousand British Subjects are employed — That Hare Wool and Coney Wool, the Growth of this Country, are better in Quality than any other, whereby the English Hats have acquired such Reputation, that great Quantities of them are exported to Foreign Parts — That he has worked Hare Wool and Coney Wool imported from different Foreign Countries, and has found by Experience that the same is greatly inferior to that of Great Britain, and cannot he worked up so well without a Mixture of the English — That ot late Years very little of the said Articles have been imported, owing, as the Witness apprehends, to their being detained for the Supply ot Foreign Manufactures.

The Witness further laid, That Turkey Goat’s Hair, or Wool, is a very material Ingredient in the Hat Manufactory. Then,

Mr. John Harris confirmed the above Evidence; and added, That the said Turkey Goat’s Hair, or Wool, pays a Duty of about Six Pence per Pound on Importation, rather more than Four Pence of which is drawn back by Foreigners when exported.

This Evidence respecting the above Duty was confirmed by Mr. Philip (owe;who said he was of Opinion that the taking oft the Duty on Importation of this Article would he a great Encouragement to the Hat Manufactory, the said Duty being Ten per Cent, upon its average Value at thi> Market

Mr. If’illiam li a!deck being then examined, said, That ow ing to the superior Excellence of British Hare and Coney Wool, considerable Quantities have lately been exported to France, Flanders, and America; that the Orders for Exportation have been so great that they could not be executed.

The Witness further informed your Committee, That an Agent for a House in Flanders had given him Orders for Ten, Twenty, or more Thousands of Skins, and that the Witness had fold him Two hundred Pounds Weight of Hare’s Wool, which was exported — That he had fold several Parcels to other Agents, which he had Realbn to believe were for the Purpose of Exportation to Foreign Markets — That if he had had the Skins he could have fold them for Nine Shillings per Dozen, which was an exorbitant Price, the medium Price being from Six to Seven Shillings per Dozen.

Mr. Collinson being again examined, said, That if the present Exportation of Hare Wool and Coney Wool is not prevented, he is of Opinion, there will not be n sufficient Quantity left in the Kingdom to supply the Demands of the Manufactory — And be it further of Opinion, that if the Exportation was prohibited, the Manufactory of tins Country would consume the whole Quantity grown; as great Numbers of British Hats, from their superior Excellence, are exported to Foreign Markets — That there are at present many Manufacturers out of Employ, ow ing to the Scarcity of Materials, which the Witness believes is occufioned by the Quantity exported. And

Mr. Thomas IVontneradded, That he had discharged Eight Men, out of Twenty-four, upon the above Account, having at the same Time Orders for Hats which he could not complete.

Mr. Gascoyne Junior, reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition and Representation of Sir Ashton Vol. 39.

Lever, Knight, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition and Repre-fentation; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in )ms Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition and Representation, Mr. Thomas Waring being examined, laid, That he had been Manager and Superintendent of the Collection of Natural and Artificial Curiosities, belonging to Sir Ashton Lexer, ever since it was brought to London in the Year 1775 — That Sir Ashton Lexer had been diligently employed, for Twelve Years before that Time, in forming his Collection — That it consists of Natural Curiosities, and Productions of Art; and that the various Specimens and Articles are in Number upwards of 26,000, which have been selected from more than 150,000 that have been in Sir Ashton Lever's own Possession, exclusive of a great Number procured from Foreign Cabinets — 'That his Collection is the most extensive and valuable of any in England, and contains many Articles not to be found in any other — That, according to his judgment, Sir Ashton Lever mult have expended at lead 40,0001, in making his Collection, and that it may probably have cost him near 50,000 — That Sir Ashton has, from Time to Time, received considerable Presents of curious Things, bat that the preparing those Articles for Public InspeCbion has put him to a considerable Expence — That if the Collection shall be kept in a Place proper for its Reception, and due Care and Attention be given to it, the Articles may be preservd for Ages in their present beautiful and perfect State; and that the Expence of keeping it at Leicester House, where it now is, amounts Annually to about 1,200 of which 660 Z. is paid for House Rent and Taxes. — And being asked, How the Public are' admitted to the Sight of the Collection ? be said, On paying a certain Sum for each Person’s Admission; and that the Money collected by those Means has amounted, from the Opening of it in February 1775 to the present Time, to about the grofe Sum of 13,5001. — And the Witness added. That, in his Opinion, it would be a great Loss to Sir Ashton Lexer, to dispose of his Collection by the common Way of Sale. Then, 4

Mr. Thomas Tenant, being examined, laid. That he had been upwards*of Twenty Years a Collector of Subjects of Natural History, and had seen all the Cabinets of Curiosities, both public and private ones, of any Note, in Holland, France, and Portugal, and those of Brussels, Dresden, Brunswick, and Vienna; and had also seen the Spanish Cabinet while collecting in Holland — That he had never seen any Collection mere rare, more curious, or more instructive, than Sir Ashton Levers, nor any that can be compared with it — That it exceeds all others in the Beauty and Preservation of the numerous Articles it contains, which are better selected than any he had seen elsewhere. — And being asked, Whether he had heard of any Commissions to purchase any of the Articles in Sir Ashton Lever's Collection ? he said, That an Idea being entertained abroad that the Collection is to be sold, he had Corn-millions to buy a great Number of the Articles for private Cabinets — And being further examined, he said, That, in his Opinion, this Collection is of such Value and Rarity as to be an Object of National Attention, and worth being purchased by the Public — And he concluded with saying, That if a Sovereign-Prince was to endeavour at forming such a Collection, it could not be done in less than Twenty Years, nor ever he made so extensive and complete, there being many Specimens in this that could not be procured at any Expence; and he thinks it would be attended with:

Mr. John Church being then called, informed your Committee, That he had amuled himself many Years in collecting Natural Curiolities; that he had lbcn all the Collections of any Note in England, and that the Whole of them put together would not form one lo rare and valuable as that at Leicester House — That the Articles there are in complete Beauty and Preservu-tion — That he had taken great Pains to form an Estimate of their Value, ufeertained by the Prices he had knowm similar Articles fell for at Public Sales or other-wile; and that, according to his Calculation, the Value of the Whole to be Ibid.is upwards of 53,000 /., in which Valuation he includes the Cafes and other Matters connected with the Articles as now exhibited — That he does not believe such another Collection could be made in a Man’s Life, and many of the Articles are lb rare, they could not be procured at all; and that, if the same proper Care be continued to be taken of the Collection as is now, he thought the Articles in it would preserve their Beauty for Ages — And the Witness added, That in his Opinon, Sir Ashton Lever's Collection is well worthy the Attention of the Public, to save it from being dispersed again by the present Possessor’s being obliged, or being induced, to part with it to Individuals, which would be a Dilbredit to this Count) y; and that it would be a great Lois to Sir Ashton Ltver to separate the Articles, in disposing of them by the common Way of Sale.

Your Committee also examined Sir William Hamilton, Knight of the most honourable Order of the Bath, who said, That he had seen Sir Ashton Levers Collection of Curiosities very often; and having a particular Love for Natural History, he has had an Opportunity, in different Joumies to and from Naples, of seeing every Mufeuin, both public and private, in Holland, France, Germany, Italy, and Sicily, and that he thinks Sir Ashton Levers Collection is in every Respect, taking it all together, the first Collection he has seen — That Sir Ashton Lever mult have been at a very great Expence in collecting it, and he thinks it is a National Object to preserve it and keep it together; and that Sir Ashton will rilk a great Lois if he should dil'pose of it by the common Way of Sale.

Sir John Thorold reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Merchants, Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants, residing at Sleaford and Boston, and the Country adjacent thereto, in the Parts of Kesteven and Holland, in the County of Lincoln, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found, that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Navigation Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had dire3ed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as folio weth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the luid Petition, Mr. John Varley being examined, said, That be made the Plan annexed to the Petition, and surveyed the Lands therein described; and that it is pra3icable to make Navigable, for Boats, Barges, and other Vessels, a certain Stream or River, and the Branches thereof, from Sleaford Castle Causeway, through the several Parishes mentioned in the Petition, to its Jun3ion with the River Witham, near Chappell Hill, in the County of Lincoln, which extends about Twelve Miles, in which there is a Fall of Water of above 43 Feet; by. Meaus whereof a Communication will be opened with the Port of Boston, the City of Lincoln, and the River Trent, to the Benefit and Advantage of the Land Owners, Traders, and Inhabitants of the several Parishes adjacent, by facilitating the Carriage of Coals, Wool, Corn, and other Commodities, at less Expence than is now paid for Land Carriage; and will also tend to the Increase of Trade and Commerce, and be of public Utility.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition' Mr. ..... I Fright, from the Admiralty Office, attending according to Order, produced various Certificates and Letters, bearing Testimony of the Efficacy of a certain Powder invented and prepared by the Petitioner, Mr. Phillips, for the Destruction of Weevils, Maggots, Spiders, and Cockroaches, and which Powder lied been used on Board many of His Majesty’s Ships of War, by Order of the Admiralty Board, at the Recommendation of the Commissioners for victualling His Majesty’s Navy. — And

Mr. John Watts, from the Victualling Office, also attending according to Order, produced to your Committee sundry other Letters and Certificates relating to the Efficacy of the said Powder, in destroying the above-mentioned Infefts. — And

Both the said Witnesses being examined, said, That the Letters and Certificates by them produced were the Whole of what their respective Departments had received ou the Subject — That there had not been any Letter or Account, stating that Mr. Phillips's Powder had been found to fail effecting the Purposes for which it had been recommended and used.

From the Perusal of the Letters and Certificates so produced to your Committee, k appeared to them that the Powder invented and prepared by the said Mr. Phillips, the Petitioner, had been used for the Preservation of Grain, Biscuit, and dry Stores, on board His Majesty’s Ships, Union, Fox, Daedalus, Diligent, Brune, Ambuscade, Princess Carolina, Leocadia, Brit annul, Iphigenia, Ocean, Eurydice, Agamemnon, Alarm, Jason, Marlborough, and Diligente; and that it had fully answered the Ends proposed of destroying tha above-mentioned Infefts, and preventing their Return; whereby the Ships Provisions had been preserved from being wasted or spoiled during Voyages of considerable Length.

First, Your Committee read an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for an Union of the Two Kingdoms of England, and Scotland: And also.

An Act, made in the Sixth Year of her said late Majesty, for settling and establishing a Court of Exchequer in the North Part of Great Britain, called Scotland: And,

In order to ascertain the Limits of the Frith of Forth, Your Committee also read an Act, made in the Ninth Year of her said late Majesty, for reviving, continuing, and appropriating certain Duties upon Coals to be Water-borne and carried Coastwise; and for granting further Duties upon Candles for Thirty-two Years; to rail'e Fifteen hundred thousand Pounds by Way of a Lottery, for the Service of the Year 1711; and for suppressing such unlawful Lotteries, and such Infuranoc Others, as are therein mentioned; — by which it appeared, that the Limits of the said Frith of Forth were from the Town of Dunbar to the Promontory of Redhead.

Your Committee next proceeded to enquire into the rrfj>eftive Boundaries of the Friths of Murray, Clyde, and Sohcay; and for that Purpose carefully inf|H*sted levend Maps produced to them, and also examined several Ship Masters conversant in the Navigation of the several Friths of Scotland: And first culled.

Captain Thomas Aikin, who being examined, said. He has been Fourteen Years Commander of a Ship in the Scotch Trade — That he is perfectly well acquainted with The Murray Frith; and that he always nndcrstood the Limits thereof to be from Kinnaird’s Head to Dunsby Head.

Captain Janies Crcavie, Commander of a Ship in

the S« ntch Trade, and has navigated on the East Coast of Scotland for about Ten Years, being then examined, confirmed the above Evidence, with respect to the Boundaries of The Murray Frith.

Captain William Dudingstone w as next examined, as to the Limits of the Friths of Clyde and Sohcay, who informed Your Committee, That he commanded His Majesty’s Frigate The Boxton, for Four Years, in the North Channel on the Friths of Clyde and Sohcay — That he has always understood the Frith of Clyde to be bounded by the Head Lands of the Mull of Can-tire, and the Point of Corseh; and the Boundaries of The Sohcay Frith to be from Saint Bees Head to Borough Head.

Captain William Fergmson being then examined refining The Solway Frith, informed Your Committee, That he was well acquainted with the same — That he has frequently navigated on the said Frith, and was a Masterof a Vefl'cl for Seven Years — That there is not a Port in the said Frith which he has not navigated to and from; and that he understands the Boundaries thereof to be Saint Bees Head on the South, and Borough Head on the North — 1That the said Frith of Sohcay lies to the Eastward of the said Head Lands. — The Witness also informed Your Committee, That he has frequently walked across from Bol-riexs to Dorneck; and that he understands the said Frith to !>e navigable to Rocklijfe when the Tide is in, but at Low Water may be forded as low down as Bolness. — And the Witness further said. That there is not a Port in the said Frith, within the said Boundaries, into which a Vessel can (ail, except when the Tide is in.

Robert Wells, Esquire, being examined, also informed Your Committee, That he is well acquainted with the Situation of The Sohcay , and that he considers the Limits of the same to be from Saint Bees Head, in the County of Cumberland, to Borough Head, in the County of Wigton.

And Your Committee was also informed by the Witness, That he has forded the said Frith of Solway,

Vul. 3<J.

from Bolness to Dorneck; which, when the Tide is in, is about Two Miles in Breadth.

Upon the Whole Your Committee have thought proper to come to the following llclblutions;

viz.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, that the Limits of the different Friths or Estuary Rivers in Scotland should be ascertained, to distinguish them from Sea, or Open Sea.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, that the Limits of the Frith of Forth, to distinguish it from Sea, or Open Sea, ought to be fixed from the Town of Dunbar to the Promontory of Redhead, as they are ascertained by an Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, "An Act for reviving, continuing, and " appropriating certain Duties upon several Commodities to be exported, and certain Duties upon " Coals to be Water-borne and carried Coastwise;

" and for granting further Duties upon Candles for " Thirty-Two Years; to raise Fifteen hundred thousand Pounds by Way of a Lottery, for the Service " of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and " Eleven; and for suppressing such unlawful Lotterics, and such Insurance Offices, as are therein " mentioned."

Resolved, That it appeal's to this Committee, that the Limits of Die Murray Frith, to distinguish it from Sea, or Open Sea, ought to extend from Kin-naird's Head to Dunsby Head.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, that the Limits of the Frith of Clyde, to distinguish it from Sea, or Open Sea, ought to extend from the Mull of Cantire to the Point of Corsehill.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, that the Limits of the Frith of Solway, to distinguish it from Sea, or Open Sea, ought to be bounded by Saint Bees Head on the South, and Borough Head on the North.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Leave should be given to bring in a Bill for ascertaining the Limits of the Estuary Rivers or Friilis in Scotland, and of the Frith of Solway.

Mr. Winchcombe Hartley reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Oxford Canal Navigation was referred, That the Committee had examined, and found that the said Petition is not within the-Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Navigation Bills, it not being proposed to extend the Navigation beyond the Limits already authorized by an Act of the Ninth Year of His present Majesty, nor to raise any further Sum of Money by Tolls or Duties for that Purpose; and that the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act, of the Ninth Year of His present Majesty, for making a Navigable Cut or Canal from the Coventry Canal Navigation to the City of Oaf ord, was read, 'whereby certain Persons therein named were enabled to raise and contribute among themselves the Sum of 150,000 /. for the Purpose of making and completing the said Cut or Canal: And

Thomas Walker, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Sum of 141,000l. only has been able to be borrowed upon the Credit of the said Act, which has been expended in the Execution of the Works directed to be performed; but the same not being sufficient to complete the said Cut or Canal, another Act was obtained, in the fifteenth Year of His present Majesty, to amend the before-mentioned Act, whereby the Company were authorized to borrow, by Way of Loan, on the Credit of the Tolls of the said Cut or Canal, the Sum of 70,000 /., at legal or left Interest.

Then the said Act was read: And

Mr. Walker being further examined, said, That the Sum of 70,000 /. has been borrowed, in pursuance Of the said Act,’ and that the Company have made and completed lb much of the said intended Canal as extends from the Coventry Canal, at Longford, to Banbury, in the County of Oaf ord, which is in Length about Sixty-three Miles, and have therein expended the Sum of 210,300l. and upwards — That the said

Company are desirous of completing the said Canal to the City of Oxford, but find that they cannot be able to finish the same unless further Powers are granted to them.

— And the Witness added, That he apprehends the further Sum of 60,000 /. will be necessary to be raised, upon the Credit of the Tolls of the said Navigation, for that Pumofe.
