A Petition of the Governor and Company of Merchants of England trading into The Levant Seas, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Trade between this Kingdom and Turkey has, for a long Series of Years, been carried on by a Society of Merchants incorporated by Charters, and regulated by A fts of Parliament; and that, in order to carry on the said Trade with Safety and to protest His Majesty’s Subjects in the Turkish Dominions, it has been found necessary that an Am-baffador should be sent from England to reside at Constantinople, and that Consuls, Vice Consuls, and other Officers and Servants, should be established in the other Parts of Turkey where British Subjects reside, and where the English Merchants carry on Trade, the whole Expence w hereof has been borne by the Turkey Company, which, together with many other Expences incident to the carrying on this Trade, has, of late Years, amounted to about 9,000l. per Annum-, and that the Trade to and from Turkey, once so flourishing, is now', from many unavoidable Events and concuning Circumstances, much reduced; and that the Assistance granted to the Petitioners, in the last Session of Parliament, enabled them to support their Expences for the last Year, but the Petitioners are sensible they should not discharge the Duty incumbent on them by their Charter, nor the Justice they owe to the Public (for whom they consider themselves as Trustees) if they did not, in the present Situation of the Trade, declare their Inability to support their necessary Expences, unless relieved by Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief as may be thought necessary and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Sir Charles Bunlmry reported from the Committee, who were appointed to inquire what Proceedings have been had in the Execution of an Act, passed in the Nineteenth Year of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to explain and amend the Laws relating to " the Transportation, Imprisonment, and other Pu- nishment of certain Offenders," and to report the same to the House; That the Committee had enquired into the Matter to them referred, and had directed him to make a Report thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the fame, together with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report was read; and is as followctli; viz.

Your Committee having proceeded to the Examination of the Matter to them referred, find, That in pursuance of the said Act, His Majesty did appoint John Howard, Esquire, John FothM. D. and George Whately, Esquire, Supervisors of the Buildings to be erected; who, after feme Time spent in Enquiries, reported to the Lord Chancellor, the Speaker of the House of Commons, the Justices of the Courts of King’s Bench and Common Pleas, the Barons of the Coif of the Court of Exchequer, and the Lord Mayor of the City of London, feme Spots of Ground whereon to erect such Penitentiary Houses as are by the said Act directed: — which were not approved of by them.

And your Committee further find, That Doctor Fothergill dying about this Time, Mr. Howard religned; and His Majesty, in compliance with the said Act, did, on the 2d Day of \March 1781, appoint Sir Gilbert Elliot, Baronet, Sir Thomas Charles Bunbury, Baronet, and 'Thomas Bawdier, M. D. Supervisors, in the room of the said John Harvard, Esquire, John Fothergill, M. D.-and George Whately, Esquire.

That the Supervisors having attentively considered the Objftions which had been made with respect to the Spots of Ground above mentioned, thought it necessary to make strict Examination of the most eligible Spots in the Neighbourhood of Lo/ulon, and particularly on the Banks of the River Thames, whereon to erect such Penitentiary Houses; and after having spent feme Time in that Enquiry, reported to the Lord Chancellor, and the other Persons, according to the Directions of the Act, Two Spots in the Neighbourhood of each other, — namely, Field

for the Penitentiary House for Males, and Battersea Rise for the Penitentiary House for Females; who, by their Opinions on the 28th of June 1781, thought proper to reject tire Spot in JVandsrvorth Field, and to approve the Spot at Battersea Rise, as proper for the erecting of Penitentiary Houses for both Males and Females.

Your Committee find, That the Spot so approved of is about Four Miles from Westminster Bridge; and is'situated at a Distance from any Town — That it consists of Eighty-two Acres of Ground, and reaches to the River Thames — That the Part of the said Spot, intended for the Site of the Buildings, is a riling Ground, which declines gradually towards the River, and is separated therefrom by a Plain, through which it will be easy, and according to the Plans it is proposed, to cut a narrow Canal from the River to the Foot of the Hill, so as to be received within the Boundary Wall of the said Penitentiary Houses; the Advantage of which, both in point of Convenience, Cleanliness and Health, by the abundant Supply of Water, and by the Flux and Reflux of the Tide, are manifest — That the Supervisors recommended the Whole of this Ground, partly in order to obtain a Communication with the River, and partly to prevent the erecting of other Buildings adjoining to the said Penitentiary Houses; but that a considerable Part of the said Ground may be fold again, with a Prohibition to build thereon; or may be let out at pretty considerable Rents, which may be applied towards defraying the Expences of executing the said Act.

Your Committee further find. That the Supervisors entered into a Treaty with the Proprietors of the said Grounds, and made an Offer of a Sum of Money for the Purchase thereof; which being refuted, a Special Jury was summoned and impannelled, according to the Directions of the Act; who, on the 10th of September 178a, assessed the Value of the said Lands at the Sum of 6,600l.

THE Supervisors are requeued to observe, that these Reductions from the original Estimate arise partly from the Omission or Alteration of such Parts of the Buildings which were considered as greatly contributing to the Perfection of the Design, but which might be omitted without essentially affecting the Purpose of the Act; and also from the reduced Price of some of the Materials since the first Estimate was made.

After which. His Majesty was pleased to make a Most Tha King’s Gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Spe*ch' Parliament, as fdlloweth; viz.

My Lords arid Gentlemen,

On a full Conficferation of the present Situation of Affairs, and of the extraordinary Circunlstances which have produced it, lam induced to put an End to this Session of Parliariient: I feel it a Duty which I owe to the Constitution and to the Country, in such a Situation, to recur as speedily as possible to the Sense of My People, by calling a new parliament

I trust that this Measure will tend to obviate the Mischiefs arising from the unhappy Divisions and Distractions which have lately subsisted; and that the various important 'Objects which will require Corisideration may lbe afterwards proceeded upon with less Interruption and with happier Effect.

I can have no other Object, but to preserve the true Principles of our free and happy jConstitution, and to employ the Powers, intrusted to Me by Law, for the only End for which they were given, the Good of My People.

My 'Lords, and’ Gentfcthen,
